News.title: I spent 28 YEARS walking around the world – I faced polar bears & fell down a cliff but toughest part was closer to home
News.content:
Next

SINCE leaving Britain 28 years ago to walk around the world, Karl Bushby has been held by Russian secret agents, faced polar bears and fallen down a cliff in remote Alaska.

But he feared the biggest threat to completing his epic journey would be the French bureaucrats who refused him permission to swim across the English Channel to home.



Former paratrooper Karl, 57, has not used any boats or any form of motorised transport during his 36,000-mile journey across Planet Earth.

So to get home to Hull, which he left in 1998 when he was just 29, he needed either to walk through the Channel Tunnel service tunnel, or swim.



Both methods were initially blocked by the French authorities.

Karl told The Sun, which joined him on part of his walk back through London: “I was thinking when I got to Calais that I could be here for the next year.”

The adventurer, who has a support team, continued: “Everything was a hard no — we’d just run into a bureaucratic wall.

“We were expecting, ‘The tunnel will be all right, they’ll let us through’ — absolutely wouldn’t budge an inch.

“We were like, ‘What, you can’t swim from France?’ It was a hard rule. No one had swum from France in 38 years, or something stupid.

“It was a borderline miracle that we got this to happen.”



But all of a sudden two weeks ago, Karl was given the green light to get in the water, and he spent nearly three days part-floating and part-swimming across the 21-mile waterway.

His dad Keith, 79, an SAS veteran, and brother Adrian, 54, were there to greet him in Dover.

Now Karl is on the final stretch back to East Yorkshire, where his mum Angela, 76, will be waiting for him at the garden gate.



Originally the trip was only supposed to take 12 years, but Covid, visa bans, red tape and other crises meant crossing through foreign nations was not simply just a case of putting one foot in front of the other.

Now he aims to be home on November 1, the same date as when he started his epic adventure from Punta Arenas, near the southern-most tip of Chile.

Karl, who served in Northern Ireland, dreamed up the extreme challenge as a way of proving himself after scraping through the military’s tough fitness tests.

He said: “My fitness was always just good enough, bottom of the barrel, so I was just passing my tests. When the guys were saying, ‘No, you’re not the kind of guy to do this’, I was saying, ‘No, I am the kind of guy’.

“And once that banter has started going, you show the young crowd you can do something stupid. So that kind of motivates the young man, when your muckers are giving you such a hard time.



“On top of that, there’s a young kid who’s got a wanderlust. Those things together mean that you’re going to go off.”

Karl arrived in South America with about £400 and found himself scavenging for food.

He said: “It was a physical challenge — walking through South America at first was tough. We didn’t have much money. In south Central America, we lived off what we found along the side of the road. You’d be amazed how much food people discard from cars. There’d be chips and sandwiches, which we’d eat.”



When he suffered a serious stomach infection in Chile in 2000 he was lucky that the kindly local who picked him up in their car was married to a doctor.

Karl recalled: “I was very sick. It was a moment of good fortune.”

The medic didn’t charge Karl anything for the blood tests or the antibiotics which rescued him.

It was a kindness that has been echoed in every country he has visited, with people offering food and hospitality, even when they had little for themselves.

Karl said: “The journey has changed my worldview. The amount of kindness you’ll get out there over these 28 years is just staggering. I’ve stayed with some of the poorest people in the world.”



Not that everyone has had good intentions.

Passing from South to Central America meant crossing the treacherous 60-mile Darien Gap that separates Colombia from Panama, a stretch of rainforests and mountains without a proper highway, where paramilitary groups and drug gangs hold sway.

Then later, just before he crossed the US border with Canada in 2003, most of his kit was stolen, including his tent.



Karl said: “There are also some people who aren’t so good.”

The wilderness presented even more dangers.

Trekking alone without a satellite phone in harsh conditions meant one wrong move could have ended his life, which it almost did more than once.

He recalled: “In Alaska there was a point where I actually walked off a cliff in a whiteout and fell an unknown distance in freefall.

“Luckily I hit a snowdrift and walked away from that one. You mess up out there in winter and you’ve got 20 minutes.”



Matter-of-factly he showed me a scar on his arm, saying: “I’d stabbed my wrist and ended up shooting blood into the desert in Patagonia a couple of days from anywhere. I was on my own. On that road there were only cars every 40 minutes.”

Karl’s biggest challenge was undoubtedly crossing the Bering Strait, just south of the Arctic Circle, a 56-mile stretch of treacherous ice which separates Alaska from Russia.

The ice can easily fall away, which it did once, sending his sled into the ocean.



Fortunately, Karl, who was making this part of the journey with French-American explorer Dimitri Kieffer, was able to pull it out of the water.

He said: “The Bering Strait was more a case of, ‘Let’s just have a go and see how far we get the first time’, not quite expecting to make it. Getting across the strait was a bit of a miracle.”

Humans don’t pass that way very often, which was probably a good thing, because their unfamiliarity meant that a polar bear was cautious about these strange beings on odd contraptions — with flares to scare it off.

Karl said: “Polar bears are the only large land mammals that will actually hunt humans.

“We came across them a couple of times. But me and Dimitri, we’re crossing the Bering Strait, two guys, a sled.



“The polar bear’s going to be like, ‘Yeah, I don’t know. That’s not food’.”

The men’s arrival also came as a surprise to the authorities in Russia, who thought they could be spies.

Karl said: “They got upset and we ended up being put on trial and became a bit of an international incident.



“The FSB [security service] and the border guards wanted to put us in jail for five years.”

Karl and Dimitri were moved from village to village in Siberia as they awaited their trial. After 57 days, an agreement was made to deport them rather than send them to prison.

Karl said: “Getting out of the jaws of Russia was another miracle, but you certainly wouldn’t get away with that today.”

The expulsion threw a major spanner into the works of his trip and it took years of negotiations to find a route across Asia.

That included becoming the first person to swim across the Caspian Sea from Kazakhstan — a remarkable feat achieved with his 44-year-old American friend Angela Maxwell in 2024.



It took them 31 days to cover the 186-mile stretch to Azerbaijan, whose coastguard provided support in their treacherous endeavour.

While Karl has done most of the mammoth trek solo, he has also been joined “a couple of times” by his 36-year-old son Adam.

He said: “It was important, because it was really the first time that he got to start to see what I was doing.

“That was a good experience. He’s like one of my best backers.”



As Karl’s global fame has grown, so has the financial backing available to him.

The German actor and film director Werner Herzog is making a documentary about Karl, who is also writing a book about his travels.

His epic journey has seen so many bureaucratic brick walls that only 15 of the 28 years were spent actually walking.

During the Covid lockdown, he lived in Mexico because it was cheap.



But whenever he managed to get his paperwork sorted out, he always made sure he restarted the trip from his last stop, so that the right distance would be covered.

Nothing, though, ever made Karl want to give up.

He said: “It was never, ‘Let’s give it a go and see how far we get’. I decided I was going to complete this, no matter what.”

Reaching the finish line will no doubt be disorientating.

He said: “Home, the UK, for so long was just a myth. It was a land so distant, so far away.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“‘It’s done’ are two words I’m going to have to get used to, and that’s going to be tough.”

News.title: Entitled youth only care about ‘Insta-worthy’ jobs – Burnham has to reenergise Britain’s Neets
News.content:
Next

IN the olden days, around 1990-something, “entitled” meant having a “legitimate, legal, or official claim to receive or do something according to rules, law, or membership”.

Today, to many of the TikTok generation, it means “believing you deserve more than others without responsibility or reciprocity”.





And therein lies the major problem with youth unemployment.

Writing in The Times yesterday, the Prime Minister has pledged his support to 18 to 24-year-olds, stating he will “invest in the success of our young people” rather than “pay for failure through the benefits system”.

To be fair, everything he says makes sense, and is admirable.

It is also hugely overdue following 14 years of mission-creep Tory complacency, and Keir Starmer.

Because, if only Keir “son of a toolmaker” Starmer had actually advocated for the picking-up of tools and apprenticeships, we might not be entirely in this fine mess.

Apprenticeships, then, are a key part of Andy Burnham’s Neet manifesto with 400 apprenticeships a year made available by accountancy, legal services and consultancy firms for under-25s.

As we have seen from The Sun’s brilliant Jobs Army campaign, young people ARE willing (and able) to work — they just don’t know where to start.

Until now, the incentive hasn’t been there. Rather, it’s been an endless vicious cycle, which has not been aided by AI rapidly replacing blue and white collar jobs.





Encouragingly, the Government is expected to announce plans aimed at giving young people thousands of job opportunities: the idea being to invest in upskilling youngsters, rather than simply handing them a blank benefits chequebook.

According to the latest data from the Office for National Statistics, there are almost a million Neets — 16 to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training — which makes for grim reading.

Even worse, around 39 per cent are unemployed while the remaining 61 per cent are economically inactive, meaning they are not seeking work.

In his op-ed, Burnham was quick to show compassion to the “yoof”.

He suggested two years of Covid lockdowns had thrown this generation off-kilter and that social media had eroded “confidence and sense of belonging”.

I’d go one further.

In a world that values likes and collagen brand deals over real-life connections and community, many teens today think all their problems can be solved by the swoosh of a smartphone.

Life of sofa-dwelling and PlayStation

“Influencing” has become the career choice du jour, with the belief that immeasurable wealth and happiness can be found with one viral post.



But for every millionaire influencer out there, there are a million more wannabes.

Ones struggling to get dressed of a morning, staring miserably at their phones 24/7, and depressingly feeding a mental health epidemic.

Arguably, even worse than this career fallacy, is the overriding sense of entitlement social media had created.

Some young people, especially the privileged percentile ably funded by The Bank of Mum and Dad, believe it is their DIVINE RIGHT to have a lovely life.

They firmly believe that working in a factory, or selling shoes (as my grandad did after World War Two) is beneath them. That they were, somehow, “meant for more”.

Because putting in a ten-hour shift that doesn’t know the difference between Instagram’s Paris filter and a carousel isn’t glamorous.

And it certainly isn’t worthy of a post. And there we have it.

Why work yourself to the bone when there’s a government hand-out just around the corner, and a life of sofa-dwelling and PlayStation ahead?

This sub-section of Neets do a grave disservice to the legions of talented, driven youngsters who could reenergise our stuttering nation if only they were given a chance.

If Burnham’s Labour is serious about slashing the mickey-taking welfare bill, then he must help employers, not cripple them.



Just as workers must be incentivised, so must both Big and Small Business.

Corr blimey, newbie Julie was only 27

SKIP over to the next item if you don’t wish to feel older than Methuselah.

But Celebrity Traitors star Julie Hesmondhalgh was TWENTY-SEVEN when she joined ITV’s Corrie in 1998 as its first trans character, Hayley Cropper, pictured above with onscreen husband Roy.

Feel it in M.I.A bones

NOW, of course, I’d hate to judge a book by its cover, but if this man ain’t guilty, I will eat not only my hat, but my winter coat and anything else that’s going begging.

Bones linked to seven missing women in America have been unearthed from a Philadelphia house of horrors – which was owned by this man Raymond Horsch until his death last year.

For anyone in any doubt – a very large underground safe was also found – here’s a previous mugshot of the grim weirdo.



QUOTE of the week from Jarvis Cocker’s late mother.

Asked about prospective alternative Christian names, she says in a new documentary about the rocker: “When you’ve got a surname like ‘Cocker’, you really couldn’t name him ‘Everard’.”

Indeed.

Pup’s Deir to heart

ON a similar Coronation Street theme, last week on a nice, autumnal walk I met another sausage dog owner. The miniature dachshund’s name? Deirdre Barlow.

Which, obviously, is absolutely brilliant. Except, it gets better.

The owner added: “She’s ‘Deirdre Barlow-Rachid’, though, when she misbehaves.”

Which, for anyone who remembers the “Free Deirdre” campaign, after the character was sent to prison, is v v funny.

Don’s fairer Secs

DONALD TRUMP’s version of DEI is blonde, blue-eyed, deeply tanned and attractive.



And look how that’s gone for him.

Katie Zacharia’s excruciating five-day tenure as White House press secretary came to an abrupt end on Friday after Trump, politely for him, suggested she “reconsider” the job.

If you haven’t already, Google her truly embarrassing debut briefing, which lasted 14 painful minutes, took in just three questions, and looked and sounded like a toddler speaking its first words.

And while I feel a bit sorry for this woman, ridiculed on a global level, she also pretended to have passed the bar exam, which turned out not to be true.

Going forwards, perhaps Donald – whose idea of “vetting” means taking dogs to get flea’d – should try some diversity.

FINALLY a government money-making scheme I am fully behind.

Andy “Man of the People” Burnham might actually be proving himself to be, well, a man of the people with his latest pledge: fining bus and rail passengers £100 for playing music out loud.

In a new scheme, Share The Journey, Not The Noise, headphone-swerving little runts could be issued with fines under new powers for local authorities.

10/10, no notes AB.

Taken aback



WHILE, sadly, the law prohibits me from saying what I really think about the ongoing Russell Brand trial, I can say one thing.

All those hours of Kundalini yoga have done the world of good for his posture.

And I’ll leave it there.

News.title: Ex-glamour model married to super-rich banker in furious neighbour row over plans to turn pub into boutique hotel
News.content:
Next

A FORMER glamour model who is married to one of Britain’s richest bankers has annoyed locals with plans to expand a country pub into a boutique hotel and yoga space.

Former Page 3 star Lady Loretta Rothschild took over ownership of the Seven Stars Inn in the tiny Wiltshire hamlet of Bottlesford earlier this year.



The 36-year-old, married to mega-rich banking dynasty heir Nat Rothschild, wants to add 10 bedrooms, a huge 70-seat restaurant and a yoga barn to the 16th Century boozer.

But locals fear the extensive plans could turn their peaceful village into tourist hell with extra traffic, noise, disruption, and say it is not in keeping with the Wessex Downs Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty.

Next door neighbour Chas Cronin, 67, is concerned the pub will be turned into a “Soho Farmhouse” scenario with constant traffic and noise.



The retired IT project manager for Shell and his wife Sally, 66, share a border with the former ‘biker friendly’ boozer in the rural backwater nestled in the heart of the Vale of Pewsey.

He said: “It is a bone of contention.

“Everyone wants the pub to reopen but not on that scale.

“It’s just so huge. It will take a lot away from our enjoyment of our garden

“The lane is very narrow and can’t be widened. It’s bad enough with delivery vans.



“With construction vehicles here for two years it’s going to cause an awful lot of congestion.

“That and the noise.”

Chas added he would have liked the Rothschilds to talk to him about the development.



He says the building of extra outhouses for posh hotel rooms will cause an “intrusion of privacy”.

Chas added: “The Rothschilds own a lot of the land around here and they have a lot of shooting parties.

“They are probably building this so they have somewhere for their friends to stay.”

The pub closed last August because the previous landlord could not make it profitable.

It was bought by Lady Rothschild for around £800k a couple of months later but has not since reopened.



Another objector to the scheme, Alison Tilling, said she recognised the importance of a successful village pub but feared the development would damage the hamlet’s rural character.

She concluded: “In short, great idea, wrong locality.”

Patrick Wilson also raised concerns about traffic, citing a forecast of 172 vehicle movements a day on the narrow country lane.



He described the proposals as “too intensive for a small rural site on a single-width lane in the North Wessex Downs National Landscape”.

Others in the village are supporting Lady Rothschild’s plans.

Jo Wood said: “At a time when Britain is losing pubs at an alarming rate, reportedly more than one a day, it is particularly encouraging to see substantial private investment being made in securing the future of such an important community asset.

“The financial strength and long-term commitment of the owners should not be underestimated.”

Local resident Simon Naylor welcomed the additional guest accommodation, saying it was difficult to find somewhere for visiting family and friends to stay.



He said: “The scale of the design is entirely in keeping with the character of Bottlesford and will breathe new life into the area and community.”

Former Sun Page 3 model Loretta is said to be on a mission to save the run-down pub from extinction.

She and Nat own the sprawling 3,500 acre Stowell Park estate nearby but spend much of their time living in the tax-haven Swiss Alps.

Loretta, who previously dated Alan Partridge comedian Steve Coogan, married the scion of the famous financier family in Klosters in 2016.

Originally from Essex, she pivoted from her modelling days to becoming a successful published author with her debut book Finding Grace receiving critical acclaim.



Loretta is said to have taken it on as a passion project.

Her hubby Nat – a member of the notorious Bullingdon Club at Oxford University with George Osborne – has been a tee totaller for 27 years.

Loretta told The Sun: “When I realised the Seven Stars was at risk of closing its doors for good, I simply couldn’t stand by and let that happen.

“Village pubs are the beating heart of a rural community like ours and restoring this wonderful pub isn’t just about saving a historic building, it’s about preserving a welcoming haven for everyone in the area and giving our local community a place they can be truly proud of for years to come.

“I’ve been overwhelmed with support for our plans from former regulars, neighbours and locals and I can’t wait to bring them to life.”

News.title: At least 15 gold miners killed after landslide strikes pit as desperate search now underway for buried workers
News.content:
MUD TRAGEDY At least 15 gold miners killed after landslide strikes pit as desperate search now underway for buried workers







Next

AT LEAST 15 people have died after a massive landslide pummelled a gold mine in Colombia.

More than 30 people were believed to be panning for the precious metal at the time of the disaster and it is feared that the death toll will rise.



Air support, cops and paramedics have been called to the scene as a major rescue operation gets underway for buried miners.

The torrent of mud and rock consumed the small-scale mine in Santa Bárbara de Iscuandé – a region in the country’s south, around 80 miles north of Ecuador – at around 8.30am local time.



At least nine of the victims reportedly belonged to the same family.

Residents have rushed to the aid of rescuers, using shovels and rudimentary digging tools to assist in the search.

Local minister Álex González said that the landslide took the workers by surprise.

Officials urged the government to deploy the hospital ship, Benkos Biojó , currently anchored in the neighbouring municipality of Guapi, to bolster medical efforts.

Emergency services have faced difficulty accessing the region due to the challenging terrain of the surrounding jungle.

Cartels operating in the area have been urged to respect humanitarian corridors and allow free passage for relief personnel.



Deadly accidents at unlicensed mines are not rare in Colombia, where locals dig for precious metals without much oversight.

Poor conditions and mounting criminal turf wars have exacerbated the problem in recent years.

Nine workers were killed in May after a blast at a coal mine in Sutatausa, about 45 miles north of the capital, Bogota.

It came just weeks after inspectors raised safety concerns due to a “potentially dangerous gas build-up”.

Colombia‘s National Mining Agency (ANM) said that “accumulations of gases ​such as methane” were believed to be responsible for the tragedy.



In 2023, 21 workers were killed in an explosion that ripped through coal mine tunnels in the same town.

Criminal actors have also created major issues for the local mining communities.

Last May, 13 security guards were kidnapped from a major gold mine and killed after being kept hostage for a week.

The security staff disappeared in the mountains near Pataz, northern Peru, as bloody mining turf war grips the region.

The group had been sent out to confront a group of illegal miners in the area, but were attacked and snatched.

Throughout the week, the gang sent threatening messages to the victims’ families.

The mining company that employed the workers, La Poderosa, said search-and-rescue teams recovered their remains.

News.title: Medieval-style trenches dug around parks in desperate bid to stop ‘whack-a-mole’ travellers invading city
News.content:
Next

A COUNCIL has dug medieval-style trenches around some of its parks in an attempt to prevent “whack-a-mole” travellers from illegally occupying them.

Defensive ditches – reminiscent of moats around the Midlands’ historic castles – have been dug around at least three Birmingham parks in the last few months.



It followed a summer of “whack-a-mole”-style problems where officials would invoke legal routes to clear caravans from public land, only for them to quickly pop up somewhere else.

Daisy Farm Park, off Maypole Lane, Highter’s Heath, had trenches dug out around its perimeter in recent weeks.



The same tactic has been employed at Manningford Road in Druids Heath.

Brandwood Police said a “trench was currently being dug out in Manningford Park to prevent any unlawful encampment”.



And trenches were also deployed at the entrance of Chinn Brook Recreation Ground, in Yardley Wood in August.

Birmingham has encountered scores of incidents where travellers have arrived in caravans, motorhomes and vehicles to set up camp across the city throughout the summer.



The city council said it was “committed to safeguarding public open spaces for the benefit of all users”.

It said it would continue to “review and monitor measures at individual locations”.

A council spokeswoman told said: “The council adopts a range of proportionate site-management measures to deter unauthorised vehicle access and unauthorised encampments on parks and open spaces where there is an evidenced history of recurring incidents.

“Increased encampment pressures, together with repeated damage to existing boundary infrastructure and access controls, have required the council to consider a wider range of preventative measures.

“The use of ditches, bunds and other landscape interventions forms part of a broader toolkit of options and is implemented only where considered necessary, appropriate and site-specific.



“The council remains committed to safeguarding public open spaces for the benefit of all users and will continue to review and monitor measures at individual locations.”

One commentator on Facebook said: “What if they shovel the soil on just the part they need to get entry?

“It will take them 5 minutes, job done. They dont have to refill the whole trench.”

While another added: “Why don’t councils just put a blanket ban on illegal traveller camps instead of one at a time.. would save loads of money.”

A third person wrote: “They will soon fill it in, to gain entry to the parks.”



It’s not the first time travellers have settled on Daisy Farm Park.

In March 2017, at least 10 caravans and other vehicles were spotted setting up camp.

Trenches have also been dug in the past around the country in an attempt to prevent travellers getting onto the land.

In September 2019, the parish council dug deep ditches around the sports fields and children’s playground in Swaffham Bulbeck, near Cambridge.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

While villagers in West Bergholt, Essex, took similar measures when a group of travellers tipped up on a farmer’s field.



Locals near Oakwood Park in Derby did the same after it became a magnet for travellers who would return again and again.

News.title: Autistic teen found dead in school toilet after discovering support worker he had ‘crush’ on was being replaced
News.content:
SCHOOL TRAGEDY Autistic teen found dead in school toilet after discovering support worker he had ‘crush’ on was being replaced







Next

AN autistic teen was found dead in a school toilet after finding out the support worker he had a “crush” on was being replaced.

The body of Sam Coutts, 18, was discovered at Queen Elizabeth Sixth Form College, Darlington, in January, following a meeting with the vice principal about social media posts where he revealed he had a crush on his support worker.



At an inquest in Crook, County Durham, his mother Kirsten said Sam would have felt ashamed after the meeting, which he was allowed to leave alone.

CCTV showed he went straight from the meeting to the toilets where his body was found three hours later by the college principal.



In a statement summarised by the coroner, Ms Coutts said: “The college did not care appropriately and acceptably for my son.

“They failed completely in their duty of care.”

Sam had previously suffered from bullying at secondary school and tried hard to mask his autism and did not want to be treated differently, the inquest heard.

He was studying A-levels in psychology, applied science and biology – which he hoped to read at St John York University.

His mother said in a pen portrait how change made him anxious and how he would go straight to bed after coming home from college if he was stressed.

His college was aware that he had autism and he was assigned a support worker, Lauren Crosby.



Ms Coutts said she was contacted by the college after the support worker apparently found Reddit posts he made talking about a crush he had on her.

Ms Coutts, a nurse, was sceptical about how the support worker found the Reddit posts, given that Sam’s account was not under his real name.

On January 13, the college called a meeting in which Sam was told he would have a different support worker.

The day before, his mother spoke to the safeguarding lead and said she urged staff to treat Sam gently.

Before the meeting, Sam told his mother he felt embarrassed and ashamed, she said.



He asked her if the Reddit posts made him seem “creepy and weird” and she reassured him that they did not, saying they had been respectful.

After meeting Sam, the college vice principal Theresa Amarawansa rang Ms Coutts to say that the teenager was “positive and fine”.

Ms Coutts said in her statement: “I said I find that hard to believe and the call ended.”

She missed a subsequent call from the college as she was on shift at a hospital, telling her that Sam was missing from his psychology lesson.

How to get help EVERY 90 minutes in the UK a life is lost to suicide It doesn’t discriminate, touching the lives of people in every corner of society – from the homeless and unemployed to builders and doctors, reality stars and footballers. It’s the biggest killer of people under the age of 35, more deadly than cancer and car crashes. And men are three times more likely to take their own life than women. Yet it’s rarely spoken of, a taboo that threatens to continue its deadly rampage unless we all stop and take notice, now.
