Heads Together,www.headstogether.org.uk

HUMEN www.wearehumen.org

Mind, www.mind.org.uk, 0300 123 3393

Samaritans,www.samaritans.org, 116 123

She tried to call back but was told staff were dealing with an emergency but she was told it did not involve her son.



After she left work that lunchtime, Ms Coutts said she saw police and paramedics activity at the college but reminded herself that she had been told on the phone that it did not involve her son.

Police were to then arrive at her home to say that Sam had died, the inquest was told.

Ms Coutts said her “vulnerable” autistic son would have felt that “a rug had been pulled” when he was told about the change in support worker.

She also stated how he was not found for three hours after the meeting, despite him being marked as absent from his lessons.

The inquest also heard how Sam had intervened when a family member had a mental health crisis three months before and he managed to save their life by talking to them.



His mother also described him as loving, gentle, quiet, engaging, adventurous and erudite, with a wicked sense of humour.

Later, the inquest heard a statement from Ms Crosby in which she said Sam emailed her on Christmas Day with a link to the Mariah Carey hit All I Want For Christmas Is You.

She said on her return to college after the holiday break, it was agreed that Sam may not have understood the implied meaning of the song, but that there would be a gradual move to get him to work with another, male, support worker with whom he had already formed a positive relationship.

Ms Crosby said she subsequently found Sam’s Reddit posts while she was browsing on the platform, but she did not know why they appeared on her feed.

She acted immediately and shared her concerns with members of the support team.



Vicky Wilkinson, head of additional learning support, said the Reddit posts had caused concern.

Asked about the potential harm to Sam in changing his support worker, she told the inquest: “The only alternative was to keep Lauren in place and that was not an option.

“The wording on the Reddit posts left us with significant concerns.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The inquest, which is expected to last three days, was adjourned until Tuesday.

If you are affected by any of the issues raised in this article, please call the Samaritans for free on 116123.

News.title: Dramatic moment Ukraine carries out first ever aerial drone evacuation of wounded soldier from frontline
News.content:
Next

THIS is the dramatic moment Ukraine carried out the first battlefield evacuation of a wounded soldier by aerial drone in the world.

Footage shared by the 92nd Assault Brigade showed a Gurzuf Defence six-rotor heavy unmanned hexacopter transporting the fighter after he had reportedly spent almost 500 days alone on the frontline.



Fellow soldiers used drones to deliver essential supplies and he continued to carry out combat missions – that is until he suffered severe leg injuries.

Evacuating him by ground was impossible because the ground is littered by landmines, while Russian drones continued to hover above.



Left without a choice, Ukrainian troops adapted a heavy hexacopter that was originally configured as a bomber.

The team first delivered special equipment with carabiners to the soldier, then sent the drone equipped with a winch.

It took one hour and 14 minutes to transport him across 38 miles.

In the video, the man is seen strapped into the drone and flying above a forested area to safety.

Applause erupted in the control room when the remote pilot successfully evacuated the fighter.

“This is a historic event, at least for our unit,” said Napalm, a commander with the 92nd Brigade’s unmanned ground systems company.



“This is the next stage that we will all eventually reach. We are already ready.

“An extremely complicated operation, but a successful one… It will go down in history…”

Meanwhile, the evacuated fighter was hailed as “a hero of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.”



Gurzuf Defence co-founder Pavlo Feldblium warned that aerial evacuation should not be treated as a routine practice – and that the risks to anyone who is wounded in the air are “simply too high”.

He added: “Our goal was never to create a platform exclusively for medical evacuation; rather, we developed a heavy-lift, modular, multi-mission platform.

“Naturally, we always understood that a drone with this level of payload capacity should also be capable of performing rescue missions.

“At the same time, we do not envision aerial evacuation becoming a routine, large-scale practice.

“When I hear talk of thousands of such missions, or claims that drones will allow us to consistently meet the ‘golden hour’ window, it sounds more like something out of the works of Ray Bradbury or Stanisław Lem.”



RECOMMENDED STORIES

The rescue came days after Ukraine began frontline testing of StarGate, a purpose-built aerial evacuation drone developed by SkyFall.

Ukraine has increasingly been relying on ground robotic systems to rescue wounded soldiers from high-risk frontline “kill zones” where Russian drone surveillance, artillery, and landmines make traditional medical evacuations lethal.

News.title: Pride of Britain Awards live: 'Remarkable' boy, 5, told he would never walk who raised £80k steals hearts
News.content:
The Daily Mirror Pride of Britain Awards with P&O Cruises is celebrating the achievements of the UK's incredible unsung heroes - follow our exclusive live coverage

Five-year-old Gregor Corse has been stealing hearts at this year's Pride of Britain Awards as he's celebrated for his determination and positivity that has helped him raise £80,000.

Gregor, who has an undiagnosed neurological condition that impacts his balance and motor skills, was described by his mum Iona as "the most remarkable little boy in the world". She was told he would never walk, but Gregor took his first steps at three-years-old, learning to move around the family's snooker table like his sporting hero, Stephen Hendry.

There wasn’t a dry eye in the house as pint-sized snooker fanatic Gregor brought the star-studded Pride of Britain audience to their feet, after being crowned Good Morning Britain Young Fundraiser of the Year. The five-year-old sensation from Orkney looked adorable in a traditional kilt and flat cap - hailed by judge Kate Garraway as the 'best dressed gentleman' in the room - as he collected the third award of the night to a thunderous standing ovation.

Gregor’s face lit up with pure joy as his ultimate hero, seven-time world snooker champion Stephen Hendry, took to the stage alongside reality star Pete Wicks and Sam Thompson, who dressed in a matching kilt to present him with his coveted award. " You’re going to beat me?" Stephen joked to the little lad, who beamed and happily accepted the challenge.

Paying tribute to the fearless youngster, Stephen said: "Gregor’s achievement is incredible. People do what they do, but you have no idea how it affects other people." Handing over the award, Pete added: "You are an absolute inspiration. We are so pleased to give you your Pride of Britain."

Determined to help others facing their own battles, Gregor set himself a challenge to walk '30 loops o’ the hoose' every day for 30 days without his walker around his Kirkwall home. In a heart-melting video played to the Grosvenor House crowd, Gregor explained his simple motivation: "I just wanted to give it a try, to help people! It makes me feel strong."

While his initial goal was to raise a modest £500 for Inclusive Orkney, the little boy’s grit captured hearts across the globe, quickly bringing in more than £75,000. Refusing to stop there, Gregor then took on a second challenge raising a further £7,000 for Clan Cancer Support and local youth mental health charity Soma’s Light. In total, the determined schoolboy has raised an incredible £80,000 for good causes.

As the whole room roared with applause, host Carol Vorderman echoed the sentiment of the entire nation, telling him: "Gregor, we cannot wait to see what you do next!"

News.title: Iran threatens 'world's internet' in terrifying 'reminder to the enemy'
News.content:
Iran threatens 'world's internet' in terrifying 'reminder to the enemy'

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has hinted at further disruption to global business involving crucial internet cables lying under the Strait of Hormuz

View 4 Images Iran has made a further threat over the Strait of Hormuz (Image: AP Photo/Razieh Poudat)

Iran has issued a chilling warning to the world over crucial internet cables lying under the Strait of Hormuz.

‌



‌



The vital shipping lane has been at the centre of the Middle East crisis with an Iranian blockade causing major disruption to the global supply of oil. Tehran has increased its attacks on ships in an effort to assert greater control of the Strait in the face of US attempts to shepherd tankers through.

‌



Now the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps have made an alarming reference to vital cables that run across the bottom of the Strait carrying internet and commercial data.

‌



IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mohebi said: "Seven major cables have passed under the Strait of Hormuz, all of which the world's internet and commercial data depend on; we are reminding them of this so that the enemy knows."

View 4 Images Hossein Mohebi has made threats over cables lying under the Strait of Hormuz (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

Oil tanker carrying 2 million barrels hit in Strait of Hormuz as IRGC issues warning READ MORE :

It is true that there are at least seven cables which lie beneath the sea in the Strait and that cutting them would cause major disruption for the region's connectivity.

‌



But, while more than 90% of data capacity between Europe and Asia passes through cables under the Red Sea, research firm TeleGeography, says the Strait of Hormuz cables mainly serves Gulf countries.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

The company states: "The Strait of Hormuz is a crucial artery, not only for the transit of oil and cargo but also for the data flowing through submarine cables on the seafloor."

‌



It added: "Beyond the Gulf countries, there is not much risk to Europe-Asia data traffic from hostilities in the Strait of Hormuz. Europe-Asia cables traverse the Red Sea, no closer than about 900 miles from the Strait."

In a separate threat Mohebi also posted on X what appeared to be an AI-generated image of a missile, captioned "The world will see what will happen."

View 4 Images Iran has warned that it can opt to use other ways to attack the US (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

‌



Iran has previously threatened that it was ready to look at different ways to target the United States and its allies.

Semi-official state media channels Tasnim and Fars had previously said that Iran could charge countries to use the internet cables that are under the Strait of Hormuz which could bring in hundreds of millions of pounds each year. They are similar threats to previous Iranian statements saying that they want to charge shipping.

The Iran-US conflict has spread to other parts of the Middle East with notable attacks in Yemen from Iran-backed Houthi rebels. Last week, at least 53 soldiers in a military camp were killed by ballistic missiles in one of the deadliest attacks since a resurgence in fighting this summer, Yemeni military officials said.

‌



View 4 Images Houthi rebels have been launching attacks on the Yemeni government (Image: HOUTHI MILITARY MEDIA CENTER HANDOUT/EPA/Shutterstock)

The Houthis have put their growing military capabilities on display on multiple fronts in recent weeks, repeatedly striking Saudi Arabia’s main international airport hundreds of miles away and seizing territory inside Yemen near a key shipping chokepoint.

And Iran is trying to hit military sites in Britain with the suspected plot to attack a US-run military air base in September “not unique,” the head of the MI5 spy agency said. He warned that both Tehran and Moscow are expanding their attacks against the UK.

Article continues below

Ken McCallum, who leads the UK’s domestic security service, said Tehran is seeking to intensify its attacks in Britain beyond the traditional targets of Iranians opposed to the country’s Islamic authorities.

That has included arson and sabotage attacks on Jewish sites that Britain says were carried out by Iranian proxies. McCallum said another “major shift this year has been Iranian ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites.”

News.title: Christa Pike botched execution chaos exposed as killer's lawyer had to call 911 herself
News.content:
Christa Pike botched execution chaos exposed as killer's lawyer had to call 911 herself

The botched execution of death row inmate Christa Pike led to chaotic scenes with a 911 call-handler believing an initial call about what had happened was a hoax

View 4 Images Christa Pike survived a lethal injection (Image: WVLT 8)

A lawyer for death row inmate Christa Pike had to call for an ambulance herself in chaotic scenes following her botched execution.

‌



‌



Medical help for Pike was delayed by confusion among first responders who, at first, did not believe she was still alive, according to 911 dispatch recordings.

‌



Pike who was sentenced to death for killing 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer in 1995 became the first person to survive a lethal injection after being given two doses of pentobarbital.

‌



And 911 dispatch records, from the day of the execution attempt on September 30, show that precious minutes elapsed as officials and responders tried to figure out whether a request for emergency help in the execution chamber was genuine.

View 4 Images Emergency vehicles arriving at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution (Image: AP Photo/George Walker IV)

Murderer who strangled his cellmate in bid to executed on death row is killed — nearly 18 years on READ MORE :

Pike's lawyer Kelly Gleason, had to personally call emergency services after initial reports from the prison were dismissed as a false alarm.

‌



She said on the call: "My client, Christa Gail Pike, is undergoing a state execution. She has completed the stages of the protocol and last we knew from the attorney who is present, she is still alive and breathing and needs immediate life-saving care."

The first call came from the scene came in at 8.40pm just over an hour after the attempted lethal injection got underway but the caller was unable to provide a code that would help verify the legitimacy of the request.

"Per supervisors here at the DEC (Department of Emergency Communications) we have been informed it is a false call," a dispatcher said at 9.03pm. "There is no medical assistance needed at Riverbend Prison."

‌



View 4 Images Pike was sentenced to death for killing 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer (Image: AP)

It wasn't until about half an hour after the initial call — close to 9.11pm — that prison officials affirmed it was real and began letting responders through the gates.

The initial call came from a person whose name and title were redacted. The caller told a dispatcher that they were at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution where they had tried to execute someone, but she was still alive.

‌



As emergency responders worked to verify the call, they were in touch with representatives of the prison’s Central Control, who said they "would have been the ones to call in" and they "did not make that call," according to a recording time-stamped at 9.07pm.

Around the same time, a first responder could be heard over the radio saying: "Somebody is outside the gate at the prison telling us that it's real and demanding us to go in. They say they are some sort of state official. I need somebody to get out to the gate and talk to those people."

View 4 Images Colleen Slemmer was brutally murdered in 1995 (Image: WVLT 8)

‌



The Nashville Department of Emergency Communications released, with some redactions, the batch of audio recordings from dispatchers. Police said the audio from the first 911 call was exempt from public disclosure under state law.

Two subsequent emergency calls were made, including one at 9.08pm by Ms Gleason. An ambulance entered through the gates at about 9.11pm and Pike was taken to hospital.

She was put on a ventilator her lawyers said they did not expect her to survive before she woke up and was discharged from hospital on October 10 before being returned to prison.

Article continues below

The Tennessee Department of Correction has not said what went wrong in the attempted execution. Governor Bill Lee paused further execution attempts pending a review and it’s unclear whether the state will try executing Pike again.

Medical experts have raised a few possibilities that could explain how Pike was able to survive, including potential drug quality issues and the placement of IV lines causing the drug to pool in her tissue. Before the execution attempt, Pike’s attorneys told courts and prison officials that she had a blood disorder that could cause clotting at injection sites.

Pike was 18 when she and her boyfriend at the time tortured and murdered Ms Slemmer, who they met at a job camp for troubled teenagers. She became the youngest woman sentenced to death the following year.

News.title: Close Nigel Farage ally appears to admit £5million Brexit comment slip up in undercover footage
News.content:
Close Nigel Farage ally appears to admit £5million Brexit comment slip up in undercover footage

One of Nigel Farage's closest allies admitted the Reform leader was not following the party line when he said a £5million gift was a reward for his Brexit campaigning, undercover footage shows

View 2 Images Nigel Farage is under investigation by the Standards Commissioner over his alleged failure to declare a £5million gift he received (Image: CREDIT LINE:BBC/Zinc Television)

One of Nigel Farage's closest allies admitted the Reform leader was not following the party line when he said a £5million gift was a reward for his Brexit campaigning, new undercover footage shows.

‌



‌



Dan Jukes appeared to suggest Mr Farage slipped up, saying the comment was not the "line to take from the press office". The Reform leader had initially insisted the £5m was to pay for his personal security but in May suggested it was a thank you for Brexit.

‌



Mr Farage is under investigation by the Standards Commissioner over his alleged failure to declare £5m he received from crypto-billionaire Christopher Harborne shortly before the 2024 general election. Separately, Mr Jukes last month stepped down as Mr Farage's aide after he appeared to discuss getting around foreign donations laws in a sting by undercover reporters.

‌



View 2 Images Dan Jukes to the right of Nigel Farage at their 2025 annual conference (Image: Jonathan Buckmasterr)

In new footage released by the Guardian, Mr Jukes quipped that the undercover reporter posing as a donor could give him a £5m gift when they were discussing how to benefit from money from abroad. He said: “I’m happy to take a £5m personal, unconditional gift, of course. I know a guy."

After the reporter said “that seems like it’s been quite tough", Mr Jukes added: “I’m a realist and I bat straight and it’s a little bit awkward." The reporter then asked whether Mr Farage had "changed the line" on the £5m gift on purpose, to which Mr Jukes said: "No... it was not deliberate."

‌



He added: “That was not the line to take from the press office. So I think now the line is it was a thank you for Brexit to pay for security so he is safe for the rest of his life.”

Labour chair Bridget Phillipson said: “Nigel Farage’s excuses for the £5million ‘gift’ from an overseas crypto-billionaire have never stacked up. Now his own senior aides have been caught saying it privately. It’s time for Farage to finally fess up with the public about what the money is for."

In May, Mr Farage told the Sun: "It's very unusual for someone to give up 27 years of their life to campaign for something. And this was given to me on an unconditional basis, completely unconditional basis. But frankly, it was given as a reward for campaigning for Brexit for 27 years."

‌



In interviews in June, the tetchy Reform leader said it's not the public's business how he spends the money, and that can splash it on Ferraris or betting on horseracing if he wants. He previously said the sum was to pay for his security. A spokesman for Mr Farage said: “The transcript you’re referring to accurately describes that the gift was for his security for the rest of his life.”

Last month, Mr Jukes was forced to step down after a sting by Channel 4 and undercover group Verbatim appeared to show him discussing how to disguise donations from foreign donors. Scotland Yard is investigating the claims. He denies wrongdoing.

Footage appeared to show Mr Jukes and former policy chief James Orr seeking to orchestrate funds from journalists posing as a wealthy American and his UK-based son. This included £32,500 for polls that made the front pages news, which Reform had allegedly commissioned.

Article continues below

It emerged earlier this month that Mr Farage has been interviewed by the parliamentary watchdog over the £5m probe, with the result of the investigation soon expected. Commons rules state new MPs must declare relevant gifts and donations in the previous 12 months.

Reform UK is also facing pressure after a documentary by ITV Exposure and Hardcash Productions, which aired on Sunday night, appeared to show Reform figures making sexist, racist and other concerning comments.

News.title: Major UK retailer loved by stars closes after 50 years as it plunges into administration
News.content:
Major UK retailer loved by stars closes after 50 years as it plunges into administration

Designers Guild, the luxury British homeware brand, has announced it will close after more than 50 years in business, shutting its King's Road store in London and its website.

View 3 Images Designers Guild is closing its store (stock image) (Image: Getty Images)

A renowned luxury British homeware retailer has announced it will shut its doors after more than half a century of trading. Designers Guild has fallen into administration following a spell of financial difficulties, meaning both its website and flagship store on King's Road in London will close.

‌



‌



Its designs were favoured by celebrities including Mick Jagger and Joan Collins, and were reportedly also loved by the Royal Family. The shop was founded in 1970 by Tricia Guild and was celebrated for its luxury products, including fabrics and wall coverings.

‌



Tricia and her brother and CEO Simon Jeffries said: "Designers Guild Ltd has been so much more than a business to me. It is my passion and my life's work.

‌



View 3 Images Mick Jagger was a customer of Designers Guild (Image: Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for Global Citizen)

"The brand was built over decades with an unswerving belief in the power of creative design and a constant striving to achieve only the very best.

‌



"Together we created and developed the idea of lifestyle, year after year seeking to bring into existence the most beautiful designs possible."

"While we are closing the business, we hope the many positive and happy memories will be the ones that stay with us.

View 3 Images Designers Guild had a location on the King's Road. (Image: Wikimedia Commons)

Article continues below

"The gorgeous fabrics, wonderful interiors, photo shoots in the most inspiring places around the world, daring and successful product launches, the opening of showrooms in Paris, Munich and Stockholm, the gradual growth and development of the King's Road store.

"But most importantly, the many lovely times spent with colleagues, suppliers, clients and friends over the years, and the thought that, in some small way, I have brought colour into people's lives.

"Above all, I am proud of the lasting legacy that Designers Guild Ltd leaves in homes around the world."

News.title: Woman found dead in Manchester home as police flood street and make 'murder' arrest
News.content:
Woman found dead in Manchester home as police flood street and make 'murder' arrest

Greater Manchester Police say the body of a woman has been found after officers were called to a disturbance at an address on Moss Side in the city - a 26-year-old woman was arrested

View Image Police have closed off the area in Moss Side (Image: Jason Roberts /Manchester Evening News)

A 26-year-old woman has been arrested on suspicion of murder after a woman’s body was found at a home in Manchester.

‌



‌



Greater Manchester Police said officers had been called to a disturbance at an address in Moss Side shortly before 1.30pm today (Monday).

‌



Emergency services found the body of a woman at the address on Crondall Street and a 26-year-old woman was then arrested and remains in custody, the force said.

‌



Crime scene investigators and tactical aid units have been pictured at the scene with around a dozen officers in hazmat suits seen behind a police cordon on the street. Police believe it is an "isolated incident," the Manchester Evening News reports.

Four people arrested after police officer shot in Nottingham city centre READ MORE :

A spokesperson for Greater Manchester Police said: “We were called to a disturbance at an address on Crondall Street, Manchester shortly before 1.30pm on Monday 19 October 2026.

‌



“Emergency services attended and sadly found the body of a woman. A 26-year-old woman has been arrested on suspicion of murder and currently remains in custody for questioning. A scene is in place as officers conduct their enquiries as part of this investigation."

Detective Chief Inspector Louise Edwards from GMP's Major Incident Team said: “We understand an incident of this nature will cause concern however we would like to reassure the public that we believe this is an isolated incident and there is no wider threat to the community.

“We would ask that people stay away from the scene and we’d like to thank the local community for their patience whilst officers undertake their work.

Article continues below

“If you have any information in relation to this incident, please get in touch via the reporting function on our website, Live Chat or by calling 101 quoting log 1631 of 19.10.26. Alternatively you can speak to Crimestoppers anonymously on 0800 555 111.”

News.title: Justin Bieber’s ex Sahara Ray dies aged 34 as family say 'she was so loved'
News.content:
Justin Bieber’s ex Sahara Ray dies aged 34 as family say 'she was so loved'

Australian model and swimwear designer Sahara, the daughter of surfer Tony Ray, had welcomed her first child earlier this year.

View 6 Images Model and swimwear designer Sahara Ray's death was announced today (Image: Sahara Ray / Instagram )

Sahara Ray, the model and swimwear designer who once dated singer Justin Bieber, has died aged 34.

‌



‌



Her family confirmed the sad news in a statement to TMZ saying: “She passed away last night surrounded by family at the hospital. She was so loved." No cause of death was given.

‌



Aussie Sahara, the daughter of surfer Tony Ray, had welcomed her first child, a daughter, earlier this year. In April, she shared a video of her playing with baby Snow Ray, three months, while Bieber’s 2025 hit Everything Hallelujah played.

‌



The model, who had just shy of 900,000 followers on Instagram, where she shared pictures from her life and of her swimwear line, wrote simply: "Baby snow hallelujah."

View 6 Images Model Sahara Ray had nearly 900,000 followers on Instagram (Image: Sahara Ray / Instagram )

View 6 Images Sahara Ray with Justin Bieber on a trip when they were both in their 20s (Image: Instagram)

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

The model was photographed on holiday in Hawaii with Justin in 2016 during a brief relationship that catapulted her into the public eye when she was just 23.

Sahara and the singer - known for songs including the No1s Sorry and Love Yourself - stayed at a villa on a luxury trip that was documented on her Snapchat.

‌



She also posted a picture of her posing topless beside a waterfall and shared a video of them skinny-dipping on Instagram. It came after she was linked to actor Cody Simpson in 2015 following his split from fashion model Gigi Hadid, 31.

View 6 Images The pair pictured together in a swimming pool in Hawaii (Image: Instagram)

In 2024, Saraha opened up about her health struggles, explaining that she had Guillain-Barré syndrome, where the immune system attacks the nervous system.

‌



She said the condition was brought on when a drunk driver hit her, explaining: "It basically sent my body into shock, which sent my body into this crazy sickness.

"I got really, really sick for like a week and a half to two weeks. During that time, I barely ate any food because I couldn’t keep it down, and my body got really weak."

She told her followers: "This has been really hard to deal with and I've been trying keep a good attitude and be hopeful that my feeling comes back." Strength did return to her legs and recent videos showed she longer required assistance to walk.

‌



View 6 Images Sahara at a music and golf event in California in 2023 (Image: Broadimage/Shutterstock)

View 6 Images Justin Bieber seen during this summer's World Cup final half-time show (Image: Getty Images)

Sahara is from Australia was brought up in Santa Cruz, California, and studied at the Fashion Institute of Design and Merchandising in Los Angeles.

Article continues below

After dating Sahara, Justin returned to his on-off relationship with Selena Gomez, which ended for good in 2018. He kindled his romance with Hailey Baldwin the same year and they married that September. They welcomed their first child together in 2024, Jack Blues Bieber.

News.title: France orders curfews amid violent riots across country as Emmanuel Macron begs for calm
News.content:
France orders curfews amid violent riots across country as Emmanuel Macron begs for calm

Ministers are set to introduce curfews across France after violent street clashes erupted in Paris, Lyon, Marseille and other cities over the weekend - with fears it could pave the way for the far-right to take control

View 6 Images Protesters in France have taken to the streets in masks and hoodies, setting fire to bins (Image: Poitout Florian/ABACA/Shutterstock)

France has ordered curfews as it tries to quell violent riots that have sparked days of ferocious street clashes across the country.

‌



‌



Protestors were told public gatherings would be banned from 8pm this evening in certain towns after blazes were ignited and businesses were looted in in Paris, Lyon and other cities over the weekend. Marseille has already hit protestors with a curfew, but they are expected to be rolled out to cover districts of Paris and other cities hit by violence.

‌



Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said he could not rule out the implementation of a state of emergency if the violence continued but added: “Curfews seem better adapted.”

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 6 Images Business leaders believe up to 3,000 shops were looted (Image: Urman Lionel/ABACA/Shutterstock)

France night of chaos sparked by rioters taking advantage of protests - buildings on fire and windows smashed READ MORE :

Lecornu said it was a “miracle” that no one had been killed. He said the government will offer “full transparency” as it probes the weekend’s violence. French police “lost control” in several cities during riots, interior minister Laurent Nuñez admitted.

‌



Protesters today blockaded the Louvre with demonstrators barricaded its iconic pyramid entrance, holding a banner saying: “French public services are falling apart.” The Paris museum announced: “Dear visitors, due to student strikes the museum is currently closed. We apologise for the inconvenience.”

View 6 Images Businesses were ransacked and buildings set on fire across France (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

‌



Macron has begged for calm after a mob smashed up luxury shops across the country and left hundreds of police officers injured. One French mayor claimed extremists were “organised to wage war”, “whipping the kids into a frenzy”.

Limoges Mayor Guillaume Guerin, whose town hall was reduced to ashes, said: “Those who organise everything, who bring the battering rams, who smash the windows and identify the basement entrances in this town hall so they can get in – they are not the kids. They are people who are organised to wage war.”

Experts fear the riots may pave the way for the far-fight's Marine Le Pen to take power in France. Le Pen, the leader of the populist right National Rally, is favourite to succeed President Emmanuel Macron in next year’s presidential election.

‌



She warned that the democratic system was in danger. She said: “We are experiencing a profound crisis of confidence [and] authority, which is a threat to democracy. Our country is trapped, even taken hostage, between violence and impotence.”

6 View 6 Images Some rioters set fire to the town hall in Limouges (Image: AFP via Getty Images) 6 View 6 Images Marine Le Pen is favourite to succeed President Emmanuel Macron in next year’s presidential election. (Image: Christian Hartmann/POOL/EPA/Shutterstock)

‌



Violence broke out in protest at rising living costs and poor conditions in schools. At least 2,400 people were arrested across the country. Authorities estimated that at least 3,000 businesses were damaged or looted in several cities in the weekend violence.

Nunez said on France Inter radio: "I submitted my resignation because I am responsible for everything that is happening. Now, the real issue is ensuring that this doesn't happen again. We obviously need to be better at anticipating the kind of mobilisation that is unfolding."

Nunez blamed violence on "hordes of troublemakers and looters" and "far-left activists," and said police strategy needs to be adapted "in the face of extremely mobile groups." Authorities said groups of hundreds of people sought confrontations with police and targeted public buildings, including city halls and other public offices.

‌



View 6 Images Police have been deployed across the country to stamp out violence (Image: Jerome Gilles/NurPhoto/Shutterstock)

Nunez acknowledged that authorities had "lost control" in some major cities on Saturday, when they targeted hundreds of businesses. "You can't look shopkeepers in the eye when hundreds of businesses have been looted and say we haven't lost control in some of these major cities," Nunez said.

Flames engulfed the 19th-century City Hall in Limoges, in central France, causing its roof to collapse and nearly destroying the building. In Paris, cleanup crews and firefighters cleared shattered glass and other debris from the streets.

Article continues below

Ouri Zagoury, owner of a video game shop near Paris' Place de la Republique, said he closed the store on Saturday afternoon but then saw looters forcing their way in on surveillance cameras. "There were so many people coming in and out. And even though I called the police, they said not to intervene, that they would come, but they never did, which is another problem," Zagoury said.

Riots have spread across Europe, with looters ransacking Milan this weekend and smashing up luxury shops in Paris. Streets were also set ablaze in Belgium, Portugal and Albania.

News.title: Watch: Are the French riots a warning of an intense election to come?
News.content:
Cities and towns across France have seen rioting, looting and vandalism over the weekend as protesters took to the streets.

It follows disorder last month when students began protesting over school conditions.

The protests became broader and represented other concerns some French people have about issues in the country.

French Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu announced on Monday that local authorities would be able to implement a partial curfew to protect people and businesses.

The BBC's Paris correspondent Hugh Schofield looks at how France is "reeling" from the violence and what it says about the upcoming election in the country.

News.title: Woman says she 'closed eyes and tried not to be there' during alleged Russell Brand rape
News.content:
Warning - this report contains graphic content

A woman who alleges she was raped by Russell Brand at a bar told the police "I just closed my eyes and tried not to be there" while the attack was taking place.

In a 2023 video interview with an officer shown to the jury at his trial, the woman said she had been speaking to Brand about him hosting the Channel 4 show Big Brother's Big Mouth when he allegedly sexually assaulted her.

Brand, 51, has pleaded not guilty to all seven charges in the trial - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.

The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009.

The woman told the Southwark Crown Court jury the "lad culture" of the 2000s stopped her from reporting the TV star.

She has accused Brand of grabbing her breasts at the bar in Soho in London in 2004 before dragging her into a toilet and allegedly raping her.

The pair had been attending a birthday party when the alleged incidents happened.

She said she waited two decades to come forward to the police because the thought of doing so "terrified" her.

She said his celebrity status meant "it would be his word against mine".

"I would be ostracised in my work environment or friends."

The complainant worked for MTV at the time and said she was often surrounded by famous people.

From behind a blue screen in the witness box she said times had changed.

In those days - she said - "you weren't believed as a woman and it was a lad culture of 'you wearing this, so you were asking for it' and all that rubbish you were told back then".

The complainant recalled Brand's "big weird grin" which she compared to the face of a clown as he allegedly launched forward and grabbed hold of her.

Brand's barrister, Ian Winter KC, suggested during cross examination that Brand and the woman went to the toilet consensually for a "kiss and a cuddle", but they abandoned the attempt to have a sexual encounter because of the filthy state of the flooded toilet.

The woman, who became tearful while giving evidence, has rejected this version of events.

She said she felt "dazed" after the alleged attack.

Pressed on her claim of being dragged into the toilets against her will, the defendant's barrister suggested it would have been "perfectly easy" for her to have struggled or asked for help.

She said she did not agree because he had been holding her quite strongly, saying "part of me was saying just get it over with so you can get out of here".

She described feeling numb and ashamed afterwards.

She told the jury she had later confided in a friend, telling them Brand had "tried to do it" - but held back from saying he had "succeeded" in raping her.

The woman told the prosecution barrister that she didn't even know at the time that the alleged oral attack would be legally considered as rape.

Earlier on Monday, the jury was shown a 2023 video interview with an officer in which the woman said she had been speaking to Brand about him hosting the Channel 4 show Big Brother's Big Mouth when he allegedly sexually assaulted her.

In her recorded interview with police, the woman said "he literally just grabbed my boobs out of nowhere in the middle of the conversation, just in the middle of a conversation and I just remember this weird maniacal grin, looming in front of me as he just grabbed my boobs".

A short while later, she said he "dragged me in the toilets" where the floor was flooded, before "he unzipped himself" and allegedly orally raped her.

She said the alleged rape was "swift", and left her "in disbelief and shock".

"The toilets were behind where he stood. It was literally just grab and pull. He was holding me quite strongly on the arm and pulled me in that direction," she said.

"Part of me was saying just get it over with so you can get out of here".

"I just closed my eyes and tried not to be there. I just remember it felt like a force. I definitely said I don't want to do this," she added.

After the alleged rape, the woman, who was in her 20s at the time, said Brand "turned to me and said 'oh I guess we should swap numbers now', like it was just all normal, like he hadn't just forced me to do that."

Brand denies all the charges he faces.

He has said that any sexual contact if it happened, would have been consensual.

The trial continues and is expected to last for six weeks.

News.title: Mission blasts off for Mars to grab a piece of its moon
News.content:
A spacecraft has launched from Japan headed for Mars' moon Phobos, where it will attempt to grab some moondust and bring it back to Earth.

If it is successful, this will become the first time a sample has been returned from Mars or its moons to be analysed in laboratories here on Earth.

The spacecraft is scheduled to arrive at Phobos in August 2027.

It is hoped that the Mars Moons Exploration (MMX) mission, which is led by the Japanese Space Agency, will solve the mystery of how Mars's moons formed.

Prof Sara Russell, from the Natural History Museum, who is the MMX mission's deputy for sample analysis, said: "There hasn't yet been a successful mission to go to Phobos and bring a bit back to Earth.

"I think this is an incredibly ambitious and fun mission," she said.

News.title: Born in jail to a mum with a heroin addiction - how US teenager Abby has been affected by drugs
News.content:
Generations of Americans have endured the drugs crisis.

In 2022, 110,000 people in the United States were dying from overdoses, mostly from opioids. The number has been dropping since, down to around 70,000 last year. But that doesn't mean the opioid crisis is over.

Former heroin user Karen knows how difficult it is to quit. She was still using heroin when she got pregnant with her daughter, Abby. She is now 17 years free from hard drugs.

Karen, now a recovery worker, says the drugs being used now are more dangerous.

Synthetic opioids are more powerful and in plentiful supply - and they have transformed the drugs landscape.

Read more on this story: A wave of homemade, synthetic drugs sweeps US and deepens crisis

If you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide, external.

A list of UK organisations that can help is available via the BBC Action Line.

News.title: Apu returns to The Simpsons with new voice after race row
News.content:
The Simpsons character Apu has returned to the show voiced by a new actor, after almost a decade away amid accusations of racial stereotypes.

Apu Nahasapeemapetilon - to give the much-loved shopkeeper his full name - re-appeared in Sunday's episode on US network Fox, titled The Revengening, but now voiced by India-born, US-raised actor Sunil Malhotra.

The character has been seen but not heard around Springfield since the October 2017 episode The Serfsons, and his big return to action had reportedly been a closely guarded secret.

Malhotra said in a statement posted on Instagram that it feels like a reclamation. "It truly is his homecoming," he said.

The character, who has been part of the long-running American animation series since 1990, was previously voiced by a white actor, Hank Azaria, putting on a heavy Indian accent.

Indian-American comic Hari Kondabolu made a documentary in 2017, titled the Problem With Apu, saying the character - a South Asian convenience store clerk - was founded on racial stereotypes.

The following year, an episode of The Simpsons addressed the controversy surrounding the Indian character for the first time, making a nod to the accusations but some viewers found it insufficient.

Others defended the show and said all its characters were stereotypes.

Azaria first announced he was stepping down from the role in 2020, and he later told Dax Shepherd's Armchair Expert podcast: "Part of me feels like I need to go around to every single Indian person in this country and personally apologise."

News.title: Inside the shadowy world of anti-Putin sabotage from within Russia
News.content:
"You will get a file... from me or a colleagueâ¦ with the proposed target. The file will contain [the target's] photo, his data, his details, date of birth, age, and a description of him. There'll be information on his car, if he has one. When you go to the target, don't take a phone," he told his volunteers.

Foma was once part of the Russian elite, so he claims to have a unique set of contacts and constant flow of insider information.

He showed Mamon on his laptop how he mapped military targets.

"This shows a database... the location of storage warehouses, and military units. Where generals liveâ¦ Where the pilots of strategic bombers who shell Ukraine live.

"In order to break the system, you need to understand how it works. Then you can aim for their weak points."

He said there were about "three dozen" people in his network split between Russia, Ukraine and elsewhere in Europe, with the contingent outside Russia providing logistical support, such as tracking targets' digital footprints.

Foma stressed that the GUR suggests the targets to be surveilled, but that he and his team check for themselves that these individuals should be considered military criminals.

"As a ruleâ¦ we also check the data [on that person]â¦ Only after that we say whether we work or not."

But he argued that his team's actions were justified.

"I want people who do terrible things on behalf of Putin and Russia in Ukraineâ¦ to understand that they'll have to pay for it. I want them to get scared."

Foma stressed that he only passed on intelligence to the Ukrainians, and his network did not carry out any assassinations themselves.

Of the assassination of Gen Sarvarov, killed in December 2025, he later texted Mamon to say: "Keeping track of him took quite an effort. He lived alternately with his mistress and his colleague. Covered his tracks and constantly changed his schedule."

But Foma did not share any plans with Mamon and the BBC in advance.

Ivan, however, was tight-lipped about the work he had been involved with, even after the event.

Foma did his own digging on Ivan.

After checking with his military intelligence contacts in both Ukraine and Russia, he thought it likely that Ivan had been involved in a plan to strike Russia's largest military drone factory at Yelabuga in June last year, external. One person was reported to have been killed in the incident.

Ivan stressed that the aim is always to try to avoid harming civilians.

Operations have clearly been risky for Ivan too.

"The most serious case was when my car was stopped for inspection and I had the handmade explosives on me. The risk was very high - however as you can see, I was not detected," he said.

To mitigate the risk of being compromised, "there is no clear structure" to the work, he said, adding he had never met and did not know the identity of others he had been working alongside.

Foma has the same rule for his operatives.

"As soon as you start gathering people in groups, in general chatsâ¦ leaving a mark on the internet, with a high probability this whole group will be quickly detained or destroyed," he said.

Ivan stressed there were few people left in Russia suitable for this kind of work.

"Most of the ideological people have either left the country or are already behind bars," he said.

Many Russians involved in sabotage work on their native soil are therefore either oblivious - for example lorry drivers unaware that their cargoes have been compromised - or are individuals who have been paid, the BBC understands.

Ivan, on the other hand, says he is doing this work for ideological reasons - he used to be a member of the political opposition. As such, his movements would be expected to be monitored closely by the Russian authorities.

So it was a surprise that he managed to frequently leave Russia and return.

News.title: Warning signs over threats to Australian politicians were rising before MP hit by car
News.content:
As increasingly frequent acts of violence against politicians have shocked the globe in recent years, Australia has watched on with a contradictory feeling: that attacks like that could not happen here, and that it was only a matter of time until they did.

Australians will tell you this is a largely peaceful society with a comparatively civil public discourse. Violence targeting politicians has been rare, the bungled assassination of Labor leader Arthur Calwell in 1966 now a distant and fleeting memory.

But MPs and public figures â backed by experts â have been warning of a volcano of threats against them as social cohesion cracks, polarisation intensifies and the tone of debate grows hotter.

And on Monday, their worst fears appear to have been realised.

Independent MP Helen Haines was struck by a car and severely injured outside her office in the regional Victorian town of Wangaratta.

Police say a 43-year-old man was arrested at the scene, and a knife seized, but they have not said Haines was hit deliberately.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, however, swiftly described the incident as an apparent attack.

He was briefed by federal police â whose counter terror squad is helping state officers investigate â and told the national broadcaster: "This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear."

Though he stressed no motive had been confirmed, Albanese earlier got emotional as he talked about the growing fear amongst MPs that they would end up targets.

News.title: The portraits that helped bring the lost Aberfan children home
News.content:
For almost 60 years, many of Aberfan's lost children have watched over living rooms, hallways and family gatherings across the village.

Some were painted from faded school photographs. Others were shaped by the memories of grieving parents, who wrote letters to an artist describing the children they had lost: the colour of their eyes, their favourite clothes, the flashes of personality that made them unique.

The portraits arrived in the years after one of Wales' darkest days. And for many families, they became far more than paintings.

In a new BBC programme, Unseen: The Aberfan Portraits, some have shared their paintings and spoken about how the art helped them grieve.

News.title: Four arrested after police officer injured in shooting
News.content:
Four people have been arrested - including a woman on suspicion of causing grievous bodily harm and possessing a firearm - after a police officer was shot in Nottingham city centre.

Nottinghamshire Police said the officer had approached two suspects at a bus stop in Angel Row shortly before 04:50 BST on Sunday.

The male officer remains in hospital and is in a stable condition, the force added.

Two women, 27 and 25, and a 24-year-old man were arrested after police stopped a vehicle in the Radford area of Nottingham on Sunday evening, while a 30-year-old man was arrested in Bedfordshire in the early hours of Monday.

The 27-year-old woman was arrested on suspicion of causing grievous bodily harm with intent, and possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life.

The 24-year-old man and 25-year-old woman were also arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender.

Separately, after stopping a vehicle in Bedfordshire, the 30-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender.

News.title: Companies exploiting welfare system by using residents as 'cash cows', BBC finds
News.content:
Some private companies are making huge profits and exploiting the welfare system by receiving housing benefits on behalf of residents but failing to give them the support they are required to, BBC Panorama has found.

Property agents are drawing people into the taxpayer-funded system using social media videos that offer free rooms, PlayStation consoles and even holidays.

The system - called supported exempt accommodation (SEA) - is designed for people in the UK with additional needs, including former prisoners, people recovering from addiction and women fleeing domestic abuse. It provides housing along with care, support and supervision.

For many residents it works well to help them get back on their feet, but charities, politicians and residents tell us parts of the system are being exploited.

There are often complicated, multi-layered financial and management arrangements in place.

Rather than going to residents, most welfare payments are made to non-profit registered providers. In many cases these providers then hire profit-making private companies to manage properties and deliver support.

Many vulnerable people are being used as "cash cows to generate income" that goes from the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) into "the back pocket of the landlords", said Patricia Coleman-Taylor, who runs Birmingham anti-poverty charity Narthex.

Panorama has learned the DWP paid out Â£410m for SEA in Birmingham alone in the last financial year.

The city is the epicentre of the sector, with more than 34,000 people living in SEA. For context, in London about 22,000 live in supported housing despite its population being more than seven times larger.

Labour MP Jess Phillips, whose Birmingham constituency contains large numbers of these properties, said companies spending taxpayers' money while providing a poor standard of support was "an absolute catastrophe" and bad landlords "can make loads of money".

But she added that there are some housing providers who "get this money who are absolutely providing supported accommodation".

The leader of the city council, Liberal Democrat Councillor Roger Harmer, told us that "taxpayers' money is being wasted. It's a scandal."

In Birmingham, BBC Panorama's investigation found:

Vulnerable people are being left with little to no support in often unsuitable accommodation

One big housing provider wrote off Â£1.8m because of payments to some former directors and companies they ran

Evidence that some are willing to make benefit claims for people who do not live in their properties

Supported accommodation was set up for people like Alysha.

When she escaped a violent relationship, she returned to Birmingham seeking shelter. But her family did not have room so she had to look elsewhere.

News.title: Man accused of mass train stabbing admits wounding
News.content:
A man accused of a mass stabbing on a train in Cambridgeshire last year has pleaded guilty to 12 counts of wounding with intent.

Passengers and staff were injured on the 18:25 Doncaster-London service on Saturday, 1 November after it left Peterborough, causing it to make an unscheduled stop at Huntingdon railway station.

Anthony Williams, 33, has denied 14 counts of attempted murder, relating to the train and to incidents in London and Peterborough, and is due to stand trial next week.

Appearing at a pre-trial review at Cambridge Crown Court, Williams, of Langford Road in Peterborough, pleaded guilty to the lesser wounding charges and several other offences.

He appeared via video link from Rampton Hospital in Nottinghamshire.

At an earlier hearing, Williams pleaded not guilty to attempting to murder Jonathan Gjoshe, Sachin Balakrishnan, David Presland, Scott Bletcher, Scott Green, Kevin Deely, Stephen Crean, Raza Aslam, Michael Paffett, and Samir Zitouni on the train near Huntingdon on 1 November.

In front of Mr Justice Calver this Monday, Williams pleaded guilty to 12 counts of wounding with intent and two of attempting to wound with intent in relation to incidents on the train, and earlier in Peterborough and London.

News.title: Trial hears Robinson 'intimidated' Daily Mail reporters
News.content:
Political activist Tommy Robinson used "bully-boy, intimidatory tactics" to frighten two Daily Mail journalists, forcing them to employ security or leave home, a court has heard.

The 43-year-old from Bedfordshire, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, is charged with two counts of harassment causing fear of violence towards reporters Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber.

Opening the trial, prosecutor Ben Holt said the case was about Yaxley-Lennon's reaction to what he perceived to be "an unnecessary intrusion into his holiday" in the aftermath of the 2024 Southport attacks.

Robinson, who founded the English Defence League, entered not guilty pleas to the charges in July last year.

Holt said Dirnhuber had to move house because of the alleged harassment, while Young was given a close protection officer by the Daily Mail after photographs of his wife and children were posted on Robinson's X account.

The judge at Southwark Crown Court, Mr Justice Cavanagh, told the jury: "This is not a trial about or an assessment of the defendant's political views."

Ben Holt, for the prosecution, described Yaxley-Lennon as a "well-known public figure" with a "large, vocal online following" that now included more than two million followers on social media website X.

Robinson posted on X before the trial began to thank the social media platform's owner Elon Musk for funding his case â and said his court fees to date had cost him Â£400,000.

News.title: PM says youth unemployment is a 'catastrophe and a moral failure'
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has warned the UK faces an "economic catastrophe and moral failure" due to the nearly one million young people not in education, employment or training.

Writing in the Times newspaper, external, Burnham has laid out his case for the government to "invest in the success of our young people" rather than "pay for failure through the benefits system".

"Benefits will become the backstop, not the starting point," Burnham wrote in his piece published in Monday's paper.

This week, the government is expected to announce plans aimed at giving young people thousands of job opportunities. The Conservative Party has labelled the government's youth employment strategy "a disaster".

According to the latest data from the Office for National Statistics, there are almost a million people aged 16 to 24 known as Neets - not in education, employment or training.

Around 39% are unemployed while the remaining 61% are economically inactive, meaning they are not seeking work.

The number of 18 to 24-year-olds claiming unemployment-related benefits stands at 331,000, almost double the number in 2016, but lower than the peaks of around 500,000 seen after the financial crisis in 2008 and Covid in 2020.

The UK government will spend Â£353bn on welfare next year, just under half of which will go on the state pension; while the remainder is spent on benefits such as health, disability and unemployment payments.

In his opinion column, the prime minister said this reflected a "generation being denied its chance to get on in life".

"This is an economic catastrophe and a moral failure. And it must change," he wrote.

Burnham said two years of Covid lockdowns, social media that erodes "confidence and sense of belonging", an education system focused on the "university route", job markets with "too few opportunities" and failures of previous governments have all contributed to the Neets crisis.

"Today, the welfare system provides an assessment, a payment and, after that, goodbye," Burnham wrote. "Too often there is no support, no offer of skills and no opportunity to get a job."

He flagged a shift in the approach to welfare, which he said "will no longer begin by establishing which benefits a young person is entitled to" but rather "begin with their ambitions and the help they need to achieve them".

"We either invest in the success of our young people or pay for failure through the benefits system. We cannot afford to do both," Burnham wrote.

Ministers are this week set to release plans for 22,400 apprenticeships a year in businesses such as accountants, legal services and consultants, in addition to 40,000 placements in the construction industry.

The Conservative shadow business and trade secretary Julia Lopez said: "Labour have been a disaster for youth jobs. Their tax hikes and red tape have made it harder for businesses to hire, invest and grow, destroying opportunities for young people looking to take their first step on the career ladder."

The party has said they would cut Â£36bn a year from the welfare budget including by reintroducing the two-child limit for Universal Credit and restricting who receives housing benefit.

Green Party deputy co-leader Mothin Ali accused Labour of planning a "welfare cuts charter that would take support away from young people who are already struggling and vulnerable".

News.title: Schools 'explosive device' email a hoax, say police
News.content:
An email threatening that "an explosive device" is located within hundreds of schools in Northern Ireland is being treated as a "hoax" by the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI).

Assistant Chief Constable Ryan Henderson said police take "incidents of this nature very seriously" however "at this stage we consider risk to the public as low".

Some schools have closed after receiving the email, however others have decided to stay open and are taking advice from the PSNI.

Police Scotland said they are investigating emails sent to schools and are also treating threats as a hoax.

One school in Lambeg emailed parents to say that they should "come immediately" and collect children adding: "Please don't panic the children are all safe."

The email originated from outside the UK police say and similar emails have been received by some schools across the UK.

The PSNI said up to 300 schools have reported receiving the same emailed message which contained a generalised threat.

"Checks have not, at this time, resulted in anything untoward," added the PSNI.

"Based on enquiries and information to date, police are treating this email, which originated from outside the UK, as a hoax."

Henderson said police "understand the concern in the community, not to mention the disruption it has caused in some school communities and for students and parents".

"We will continue to liaise with schools impacted and have been working closely with the Department of Education and the Education Authority this morning to provide reassurance."

Police enquires are continuing.

"We have made contact with police colleagues in other parts of the UK and Republic of Ireland as part of these enquiries and to establish if there is a potential link," a PSNI spokeswoman said.

News.title: Bikes 'not for jousting,' says Lime after duel video
News.content:
E-bike rental company Lime has said its bikes are "not for jousting" after footage of two riders dressed as knights charging at each other in an east London park circulated over the weekend.

Hundreds of people congregated in London Fields, Hackney, to watch artist Jack Carden and actor Camtholomew the First joust, while riding the bright green rentable e-bikes.

The videos on social media showed them dressed as knights in armour, complete with chainmail and lances, attempting to knock each other off the bikes.

A spokesperson for the company said: "While we appreciate the medieval spirit, safety must always come first."

News.title: Home sellers cut asking prices on 3,000 properties a day
News.content:
Home sellers cut asking prices on more than 3,000 properties a day on average in Britain during September, according to figures from Rightmove shared exclusively with the BBC.

The property website said the total was the highest of any month for 15 years and was driven, in part, by a glut of homes on the market and some sellers setting unrealistic expectations.

The proportion of listed homes that eventually had a price cut peaked in 2023 and has remained relatively high since.

One seller - Stewart, from Leicester - said some properties were being filtered out of buyers' search results.

He sold one property, and was now selling his late mother's, and both included an element of leasehold which more buyers have been avoiding. However, he said no one thing defined whether a property would sell at a certain price.

"Part of the issue is trying to work out the right selling price. Properties were on the market high and low but were not selling," he said.

He turned down an offer made on his home a day after it was listed. It was below the asking price and he held out for better offers that never came. In the end, he sold after 18 months for Â£30,000 less than the original asking price.

Colleen Babcock, of Rightmove, said: "Once a home has been on the market for a while and then has a price reduction, some buyers start asking questions, even when there is nothing wrong with the property.

"In a market with so much choice, first impressions matter."

Property portals say buyers are now having to be choosy, with many working to a tight budget as mortgage rates have risen to three-year highs.

News.title: From a ‘glass skin’ facial to an 18-step head spa, these are the beauty treatments I tried on a trip to Seoul
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The capital of South Korea is a beauty lover’s playground, where centuries-honed medicinal practices are utilised alongside the most cutting-edge tech. It’s the birthplace of snail mucin serums, sheet masks and skin boosters such as the Rejuran Healer, famous for being a shortcut to luminous “glass skin” – an aesthetic that has made K-beauty a global phenomenon.

Unlike in the UK, treatments are seen as essential maintenance rather than vanity, so the numerous spas and clinics are constantly innovating. Plus, there’s a neighbourhood to suit every tribe of beauty lover; Gangnam and Apgujeong are the places to know for high-end clinics, while Seongsu is packed with trendy flagship stores and pop-ups.

A major draw for the ever-growing number of medical tourists is the fact that most treatments cost around 30 to 50 per cent less than in the UK, Europe and the US – and many aren’t even available outside of South Korea yet.

The sheer volume of what’s on offer can be a minefield (I’ve been down the BeautyTok rabbit hole to prove it), but many beauty destinations offer assessments and diagnosis before treatments to make them hyper-personalised, and this is a large part of what makes them so effective.

open image in gallery Writer Hayley Spencer travelled to South Korea to test out viral K-Beauty treatments ( Hayley Spencer )

Dr Christine Hall, GP, aesthetic specialist and K-beauty expert based at the Taktouk Clinic in London, explains: “You can have your skin or scalp analysed; you can look at hydration, pigmentation, elasticity. So much technology is used to understand exactly what you need rather than just giving everyone the same solution.”

I visited Seoul this spring and after dedicating half my trip to exploring the beauty scene, here are five experiences I’d recommend for your first visit.



1. A seshin (traditional body scrub)

One of my favourite beauty experiences in South Korea was heading to a traditional bathhouse, or jjimjilbang. They’re a popular third space for groups of family and friends, and many are open 24/7; ideal when you’re adjusting to the eight-hour time difference.

They are often cavernous, with a network of steam rooms and pools for contrast therapy, as well as salt rooms and charcoal saunas, and some even have bars, games rooms or restaurants.

Be sure to book in for an authentic body scrub known as a seshin. It’s not for the faint-hearted, as every bit of dry skin will be sloughed from your body while you lie on a massage table – but you’ll leave with the silkiest skin of your life.

I recommend women-only Spa Lei in Gangnam (entry from around £8, and scrubs for £22.50); or Paradise City CIMER in Incheon, close to the airport, which has six floors, including one with a virtual spa room with changing LED scenery.

open image in gallery In Seoul, beauty pop-ups often stay open later ( Hayley Spencer )

2. Lymphatic drainage massage

Booking a spa appointment as close as possible to my plane’s touchdown time was one of the best decisions I made when organising my trip to Seoul. I’d correctly predicted that I’d be jet-lagged, achey, and look a tad puffy after a day spent travelling, so I had booked in for a facial and aroma body treatment, including full-body lymphatic massage (around £130 for 90 minutes) at Art de la Peau in Myeongdong.

Korean therapists are known for their skills in deep tissue lymphatic massage techniques, encouraging lymph flow with acupressure and TCM (Traditional Chinese Medicine) principles. It might not be super relaxing, but the results will speak for themselves.

After my treatment – which also included toning with a plasma device and a modelling vitamin mask – I left looking more sculpted, feeling lighter, and my skin had a mirror-like shine.



3. In-depth scalp treatment

In South Korea, hair and scalp care are taken as seriously as skincare. Head spas, broken down into 12, 18 or even 21 steps, are among the city’s most viral treatments, and I went to EcoJardin salon’s tourist-friendly flagship in northwest Seoul for the 18-step version (£190).

It starts with a trichology assessment under a digital microscope. Then once your scalp is diagnosed, your therapist will carry out everything from cupping on your upper back to a personalised oil regime on your scalp – and the most Instagrammed step: wearing a mushroom-like cap, inflated by steam to open the hair follicles. After your hair is blow-dried and perfectly coiffed, you’ll be shown your scalp up close again – now miraculously clean and shiny.

Hair cuts cost around 40 per cent less in Seoul than in major UK cities, so consider adding one to your appointment. Or you could try a digital perm – the treatment that gives K-pop stars their impossibly shiny, permanently bouncy hair.

open image in gallery Hayley had her scalp health analysed on a trip to South Korea ( Hayley Spencer )



4. Personal colour analysis

Another experience you’ve likely seen all over Instagram, and which feels quintessentially Korean, is a colour analysis. During a consultation, your skin tone, hair colour and eye colour are all analysed against “seasons” of colours, and an expert will deem which most suits you. It’s a fun dress-up experience that might reveal the beauty holy grail: your perfect shade of lipstick, or explain why a trending colour washes you out.

As Dr Hall explains: “For example, I’m a ‘winter deep’ – meaning navy, burgundy and black are my best colours.” She recommends cool-toned makeup, silver jewellery and ash tones for my hair.

In larger branches of the prolific chemist and beauty mecca Olive Young, makeup is often organised by colour categories or seasons – so it can be useful to have one before you shop. The N Seongsu flagship branch offers them for free – arrive early to secure a slot for the same day. Colorize Store in buzzy Myeondong is also a very popular option (£80).

5. The full glow-up experience

Seoul’s beauty scene is famously overwhelming in scale and scope, so outsourcing a schedule of appointments to the experts is not just a luxury, but a shrewd move in terms of making the most of the timeframe you have, and getting the cadence correct. You’ll also be provided with a translator on site to remove any language barrier.

As well as the best massages, facials, hair treatments and skin analysis, a beauty concierge can make bespoke recommendations for tweakments or medical procedures if desired, ensuring the clinics match your budget and goals.

Whether you’re interested in Rejuran (the super popular rejuvenating Polynucleotide derived from salmon DNA), or pioneering non-surgical skin-tightening treatments such as Xerf or Oligio, you can be sure you’re in safe hands, as experts such as Jennifer Seo, founder of Aneue Concierge, try all of the treatments themselves.

“I look for partners with a great artistic eye, creating natural and youthful outcomes with their procedures,” she explains. Itineraries with white glove service start from £1,122.

Hayley was a guest of Art de la Peau; her stay was hosted by Virgin Atlantic and Mondrian

How to get there

Virgin Atlantic operates direct daily flights from London Heathrow to Incheon International Airport, starting at £889 economy. Flight time is around 12-13 hours.

Where to stay

The Mondrian Seoul Itaewon is a colourful, design-led stay within easy reach of Gangnam and central neighbourhoods. B&B rates, which include an extensive continental breakfast spread, start at £200 for a Signature King Room.

News.title: Using a drone, AP's Jae C. Hong frames Long Beach's waves crashing into oceanfront homes
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Jae C. Hong is a staff photojournalist based in Los Angeles and has worked for The Associated Press since 2007.

Here’s what Hong had to say about how he captured this extraordinary photo:

Why I shot this photo

I had been following news reports for several days about powerful waves hitting beachfront homes in Long Beach, California, and the damage seemed to be getting worse. Monday was expected to be one of the last days of the strongest waves generated by the remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel, so I decided to go see this for myself.

The waves had been pounding these homes for days, washing away sand and threatening their foundations. I was struck by how little protection seemed to remain between the homes and the ocean.

How I made this photo

I used a drone because it was the only way to get the perspective I wanted. Rather than just shooting from high above and looking down at the ocean, I wanted to get as close to ground level as possible to show the height of the waves as they smashed into the homes.

At the same time, I had to keep a safe distance from the crashing waves and ocean spray to avoid losing the drone to the sea.

Why it works

I think this photo shows the power of nature and what happens when waves keep pounding the same place over time. These weren’t necessarily the biggest waves, but the damage they caused after days of relentless pounding was striking. Shooting from roughly the same level as the homes helped to convey the height of the waves and just how vulnerable the buildings had become.

___
