Sports.title: Tottenham v Coventry: Premier League – live
Sports.content:
10m ago 15.51 EDT HALF-TIME: Tottenham Hotspur 1-0 Coventry City James Maddison’s brilliant goal offers us an uplifting moment and gives Spurs the lead. They’ve been the better team, but Coventry have looked dangerousish at times, and will fancy themselves to get something from the game as long as it stays 1-0. Share

12m ago 15.49 EDT 45+3 min Spurs end the half with more controlled possession, then Kudus slides in behind for Gray, hitting the line, who tries to win a corner but the ball ricochets off Dasilva and back on to him, so it’s a goalkick, which should take us to the break. Share Updated at 15.55 EDT

14m ago 15.47 EDT 45 min Kudus teases Dadsilva, controlling on his thigh and lifting ball over head in what, I believe, the youtdem call a chapeau. So when he looks to move by on the outside, Dasilva hauls him back and is booked. Share

15m ago 15.46 EDT 44 min A warning for Coventry and again Thomas-Asante is in behind but Van de Ven, who played him onside, uncorks his famed recovery pace, sliding in to make a fine challenge. Share

16m ago 15.45 EDT 43 min I think we may have a correct answer: “That’s Parma Violet every day,” reckons Rob Watson. “Ask any kid from the 70s….” This 80s kid agrees. Without doubt the worst-tasting sweet ever, I’d rather eat pot pourri. View image in fullscreen Photograph: Cliff Day/Alamy Share Updated at 15.48 EDT

17m ago 15.43 EDT 42 min Spurs knock it about, probing, with Coventry sitting in shape, a back five with three in front looking to get around the ball. They force play backwards, and the home side start again. Share

19m ago 15.41 EDT 40 min I wonder if, at half-time Lampard will instruct a midfielder to sit on Maddison because, so far, he’s enjoying far too much freedom. Share

20m ago 15.40 EDT 39 min Coventry have been better these last few minutes but Spurs still look dangerous, Marmoush finding Tonali, who punches a pass in behind for Solanke; he spins, hits with his laces … and the ball flies over the top. Share

22m ago 15.38 EDT 37 min Kinsky comes for the corner and the ball passes between his hands, but Spurs get it away anyway. Share

23m ago 15.38 EDT 36 min Cheers as Kulusevski warms up, then Cherif barges away from Tonali, shooting from distance … and winning a corner when a decent effort is created. He then tussles with Maddison, who goes down and the ref speaks to both. Share

24m ago 15.36 EDT 36 min “Coventry’s club shop describes this kit as ‘a purple-toned base … with a contemporary dotted pattern in dark purple and shades of orange,’” advises Eric Bader. “All of which is completely impossible to distinguish on television. But really, it’s lilac.” Share

25m ago 15.35 EDT 35 min He swings out and Thomas heads away. Share

26m ago 15.35 EDT 32 min Coventry lose the ball down the left so Solanke carries it forward and Spurs move it about, intimating confidence. They’ll know, though, that they need a second goal, and they’re seeking one, Maddison dictating so much of their play and winning a free-kick with an adroit turn away from Grimes, who can’t help but tread on him. Marmoush will deliver, 30 yards out, right of centre. View image in fullscreen Dominic Solanke on the move. Photograph: Jonny Weeks/The Guardian Share Updated at 15.40 EDT

28m ago 15.32 EDT 31 min And, though Marmoush’s delivery is headed clear, the ball ends up with Maddison, just outside the box on its left corner, so he swerves in one of those nasty crosses the keeper can’t come for in case someone gets a touch, powerless to intervene as it drifts just wide. Share

29m ago 15.31 EDT 30 min After a frantic opening, things have quietened a little, but as i type, Solanke dashes in behind chasing a Maddison pass and Spurs win a corner. Share

30m ago 15.30 EDT 27 min “When I worked in fashion,” brags Gary Naylor, “we’d have called that colourway Magenta. And if it were in stretch corduroy, ‘Hot Magenta’. Hmmm, maybe I read too much Jennings as a kid, but Linbury Court’s magenta uniform was, in the cover illustrations, much redder than this kit. View image in fullscreen Photograph: Jennings Share

34m ago 15.27 EDT 25 min Coventry’s striker lands awkwardly on a shoulder – Cherif don’t like that, can’t believe I failed to make that pun last Monday night, apologies to all– so takes some medical attention. He should be fine. Share

35m ago 15.25 EDT 23 min The free-kick comes to nothing but Coventry have steadied a little. Still, Spurs go at them again, Robertson crossing, again into a decent area, forcing Thomas to head away though Rushworth would probably have collected. Share

37m ago 15.24 EDT 22 min “Puce or maybe mauve,” says Matthew Cobb of the Coventry kit, but I think it’s purpler than puce and pinker than mauve. Meantime, Thomas-Asante gets away inside the centre-circle – he’s been lively thus far – so Solanke pulls him down and is the second man to be booked. Share

39m ago 15.22 EDT 21 min …and his delivery is decent too, between keeper and defensive line, but Coventry get the ball away. Share

39m ago 15.21 EDT 20 min My SkyGo crashes, returning just in time for me to see Yirenkyi arrive late on Gray, introducing studs to heel at cost of a yellow card. Robertson will send in an outswinger…. Share

41m ago 15.20 EDT 17 min Coventry had started the game well, too, bursting with confidence after consecutive wins, but Spurs are all over them now; they need to consolidate and take care to stick in the game. Share

42m ago 15.19 EDT 15 min I can’t imagine how awful the last year-odd has been for Maddison, watching his career dwindle and his mates struggle, fighting through long, lonely sessions of pain and rehab. He is buzzing. Share

43m ago 15.17 EDT WHAT A GOAL! Tottenham Hotspur 1-0 Coventry City (Maddison 14) Five hundred and thirty-six days of pain and desperation, gone in a moment of glorious ecstasy! Kudus moves down the right and snaps back to Maddison, near the corner of it, and he sweeps a luxuriant dipper that loops over Rushworth and in! What a feeling that must be, and Spurs lead in a league game for the first time this season! View image in fullscreen Maddison curls in a beauty to give Spurs the lead! Photograph: Dylan Martinez/Action Images/Reuters View image in fullscreen A strange feeling befalls the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. Photograph: Alex Pantling/Getty Images Share Updated at 15.22 EDT

46m ago 15.15 EDT 13 min “With the benefit of hindsight,” says John Brennan, “it might look like Tottenham made a mistake selling Troy Parrott but if you go back to 2024 when they sold him, there was no way that you could argue they should keep him. He had four loan spells in the Championship and League 1 without pulling up any trees. He then had a loan spell in Holland with a team who got relegated. He had a decent record there but he hit a purple patch at end of 23-24 which included a couple of hat tricks that made it look better than it was. I don’t think there was any Tottenham fan saying he was the answer and perhaps more importantly, I don’t think he would have developed without the game time he got at AZ which he was not going to get at Tottenham.” Yeah, he was someone I knew about when he was really young, whose development stalled. I guess it’s the job of the club to persevere, so perhaps they might’ve done well to loan instead of sell him. Share

47m ago 15.13 EDT 12 min Maddison plays into Solanke and keeps running, but his mate turns and thunders a shot into the nearest defender. Share

48m ago 15.13 EDT 11 min The corner is decent too, picking out Thomas at the back post. He heads behind, then the whistle goes for infringement indeterminate. Share

49m ago 15.12 EDT 10 min Coventry have settled nicely, moving the ball through midfield before Sakamoto takes a pass from Thomas-Asante, moving it on to Van Ewijk outside him before collecting the return, shooting hard … and into Van Hecke’s swede, the ball falling behind without the defender knowing much about it. Share

51m ago 15.09 EDT 8 min Now Sakamoto loses Gray, moving outside then in before curling into the corridor, Kinsky doing just enough, coming for the all and missing but getting it away with a trailing leg. View image in fullscreen Jan Paul van Hecke bundles over Brandon Thomas-Asante. Photograph: Jonny Weeks/The Guardian Share Updated at 15.12 EDT

52m ago 15.08 EDT 7 min nice from Rudoni, diddling Tonali down the left with clever feet and wearing the inevitable foul. He’ll swing into the box, but doesn’t get enough elevation, so Spurs clear easily enough. Share

54m ago 15.07 EDT 5 min It looks like Spurs are indeed playing a back three, Robertson the left wing-back and Kudus nominally on the right, but not really. Share Updated at 15.07 EDT

55m ago 15.06 EDT 3 min What colour are we saying this Coventry away kit is? View image in fullscreen Photograph: Alex Pantling/Getty Images I guess they’ve got form. Share Updated at 15.06 EDT

1h ago 15.03 EDT 1 min From kick-off, Coventry go backwards then load up their right-hand side, a long punt flicked on by Rudoni and Thomas-Asante latches on, but he’s pretty wide in the box, lashing a cross-shot that Kinsky gathers on the dive. Or, in other words, the plan worked pretty well, but needed a man in the middle to profit from the ball in. Share

1h ago 15.01 EDT 1 min The players take the knee and off we go. Share

1h ago 14.59 EDT It’s strange that Spurs paid so much for Mateus Fernandes, but have used him so sparingly. My guess is that tactically, he’s not doing what De Zerbi wants, but he’s a class above their other options, so I’m surprised we’ve not seen him stuck into the no 8 position and allowed to settle. Share

1h ago 14.52 EDT I’m looking forward to seeing Rudoni and Cherif tonight. Rudoni is one of those personalities whose belief is so strong it’s almost a skill, and he’ll relish the chance to show what he can do tonight. He’ll be looking to run off Maddison, I imagine, while Cherif will fancy himself to win the physical battle with Van Hecke and shoot quickly with little backlift. Share

1h ago 14.46 EDT De Zerbi tells Sky that Spurs have injuries and he likes putting players in their best positions, so Gray and Maddison will both play midfield. Savio and Bergvall played well in Manchester but are injured, while Udogie felt his knee so they didn’t want to take a chance on him. Spurs had a training camp in Marbella last week, which was important for his vision to create relationships and mentality in the team. Share

1h ago 14.37 EDT Coventry, meanwhile, will know Van Hecke lacks pace, so I’d expect Cherif to play on him while, in behind, Rudoni takes chances, gambling with ambitious passes and shots. If Tosin is indeed at right-back but even if he isn’t, Dasilva and Sakamoto will look to double-up down the left, while Yirenkyi and Grimes restrict the central spaces Spurs will be hoping to control. If their wide players are brave enough to keep the width, they can make chances tonight. Share

1h ago 14.32 EDT Where is the game? Spurs will look to dominate possession, with Gray and Tonali dictating play, so Maddison, Kudus and Marmoush can buzz about behind Solanke. The absence of a proper winger means they’ll probably look to create centrally, Solanke attacking space for little balls in behind, before going wide to put crosses into a well-populated box. Share

2h ago 14.23 EDT “None of this is De Zerbi’s fault,” reckons Dave Estherby, “yet lose tonight and surely, he’s toast.” I’m not sure about that. I’m guessing, but I’d be shocked if, when he took the job, he didn’t insist on certain levels of spending and control. On top of which, he picks the team, so I’d say some of their failings can be attributed to him, but I’d be shocked if he gets the flick, even with a defeat tonight. My impression is the board have committed to him and, given the underlying data isn’t terrible, I expect them to stick with their man. Share

2h ago 14.18 EDT Spurs’ principal problem so far this season has been scoring goals. De Zerbi is famed as Mr Buildup and seems to have inculcated decent method in his charges. But he can’t stick their chances away for them and, in Dominic Solanke, they have a 29-year-old striker who, if we’re being honest, has put together one serious season in his career. I wonder if anyone regrets selling Troy Parrott. Share

2h ago 14.15 EDT Thinking a little bit more about the Spurs formation, I find it hard to believe De Zerbi sticks Maddison in a two-man midfield – in ant event, but all the more so after so long out. BBC reckon it’ll be 3-4-2-1, but my sense is Tosin plays right-back and has been included to guard against Coventry’s aerial threat. Share

2h ago 14.12 EDT Email! “Quick point of order about the preamble,” says Kieran McHugh. “Basically correct until the last sentence. As a Spurs fan I can attest that this will not be fun.” That’s exactly what makes it fun. Share

2h ago 14.11 EDT I guess it’s possible Spurs stick with four in defence, but it’d mean Tosin playing right-back, which seems unlikely; we shall see. Share

2h ago 14.09 EDT Just the one change for Coventry, meanwhile: Ephron Mason-Clark drops to the bench, with Tatsuhiro Sakamoto coming in for his first Premier League start. Share Updated at 14.43 EDT

2h ago 14.08 EDT Taking a closer look, the headline news for Spurs is that James Maddison makes his first start in 536 days, while Dejan Kulusevski is in the matchday squad for the first time in 526 days. And if we want another number, they’re the only team in the top six divisions yet to have won a game this season. Otherwise, by the looks of things, Roberto De Zerbi has to three at the back, with Tosin Adarabioyo coming in for his first Premier League start, while Micxky van de Ven, Andy Robertson and Omar Marmoush also come in; dropping out are Marcos Senesi, the injured Destiny Udogie, Conor Gallagher, Lucas Bergvall, and the also injured Savio. View image in fullscreen A fan holds a sign aloft in honour of Dejan Kulusevski. Photograph: Javier García/THFC/Shutterstock Share Updated at 15.01 EDT

2h ago 14.01 EDT Teams Tottenham Hotspur (3-4-2-1): Kinsky; Tosin, Van Hecke, Van de Ven; Gray, Tonali;, Maddison, Robertson’ Kudus, Marmoush; Solanke. Subs: Dubravka, Senesi, Gallagher, Tel, Fernandes, Kulusevski, Davies, Olusesi, Williams-Barnett. Coventry City (4-2-3-1): Rushworth, Van Ewijk, Thomas, Pinnock, Dasilva, Yirenkyi, Grimes, Rudoni, Sakamoto, Thomas-Asante, Cherif. Subs: Bentley, Simms, Mason-Clark, Mluni, Awoniyi, Onyeka, Kesler-Hayden, Torp, Hamer. Referee: Andy Madley (Huddersfield) View image in fullscreen The Four Kinsky’s. Photograph: Justin Setterfield/Getty Images Share Updated at 14.37 EDT

Sports.title: Will that do? Lamine Yamal conjures another magical spell as Barça pass first test | Sid Lowe
Sports.content:
When at last it was time for Lamine Yamal to leave, the 19-year-old’s number going up before the 90th minute for only the second time since the opening day, Real Betis fans whistled him all the way to the touchline where Barcelona’s coach was waiting. His work here done, Hansi Flick invited him to take the weight off his feet and his shoulders, not that he wanted to. First, though, he took Lamine Yamal’s head in his hands and, leaning in away from the amateur lip readers, tried to make himself heard over the noise. “I told him I was proud of him because he played a fantastic game,” he said.

At least he could think of something. When Lamine Yamal had opened the scoring just nine minutes into the match that was supposed to find out how good Barcelona really were, it hadn’t been easy. Nothing erudite, anyway. On the morning that Barcelona went to Betis – first versus third, a proper opponent at last – Jorge Valdano had lamented that sometimes he doesn’t have the words, and he always has the words. Valdano had just watched Lamine do that, whatever that was, in Istanbul – an “almost rabona,” the kid called it – and now he had a problem. “If he keeps doing strange things, we’re not going to be able to explain it,” he wrote.

To which Lamine Yamal responded by doing another strange thing that same afternoon, scoring another brilliant goal to set Barcelona on the way to a 5-2 win over Betis in a game that made history. And if Lamine Yamal had been a little lucky three days before, momentarily losing control only for the rebound to bounce back to him like the ball knew where it would rather be, this was all him and very him. The move started with Gerard Martín losing his boot and ended with pretty much everyone else losing their heads. In Martín’s momentary absence, Rodri dropped into defence and began it from there, the ball moved across the box and back until it was played up to Lamine Yamal. His superb pass with the outside of the boot unlocked everything and then, receiving again just inside Betis’s half, he set off.

There’s a moment, Lamine Yamal says, when you can sense the anticipation, feel people getting up one after the other all along the stand, a wave accompanying you, moving with you. At that moment, he says, there’s some inner power and you feel like Superman or Spiderman; the defenders are robots, he says, and however good a robot is, however well programmed to stop him, a human is better. Too fast, too agile, too inspired. Too much thought gone into this, too much psychology. Man against the machines, code this. He rolled the ball one way with his left foot, flicked it the other with the heel of his right, and from the edge of the box, sent it flying into the far top corner.

View image in fullscreen Lamine Yamal tries to get away from Dani Ceballos and Facundo Bernal. Photograph: Antonio Pozo/PRESSINPHOTO/Shutterstock

Somehow. Sometimes you have nothing new to say, you know? It’s not big and it’s not clever but sometimes only swearing will do: sometimes only holy shit! hits the spot. Sometimes you can be sitting alone on the sofa and still shout: ’Oh, my god!’, call them in to watch this. But it won’t be the same when they do, even if it’s sort of better: a chance to slow it down and break it down, see the detail, work out how he did it, like you’re ever going to do that. Because for all the expectation, it’s still a shock seen live, the purest reaction of all.

Words? Pah! This weekend, Gabriel Jesus put it best: as the ball passed him, he just held his head in his hands. Lamine Yamal ran to the corner. Fermín López chased, wiping his brow: woah, what was that? Adeyemi went wagging his fingers. On the touchline Flick almost took off his assistant’s hand with the hardest high five. Teammates ran towards him not so much celebrating as laughing, so good it’s funny and even funnier for being repeated, an outrageous goal his catchphrase. Lamine Yamal sat alongside Jules Koundé on the advertising board, arms crossed like it was easy, like ’what are you lot losing your heads about?’ Maybe it is. And there is something in the way he hit it that felt a little like he put it in the top corner because, well, why not? Might as well.

Lamine Yamal got up, stood holding the corner flag, looking about: will that do? If this was the first test Barcelona have faced, it hadn’t taken him 10 minutes to score again, and like that. And that’s the thing. Who knows, this might not even have been the best goal of the weekend: there were glorious moments from Arda Guler and Kylian Mbappé in Madrid’s win against Sevilla. Javi Rodríguez’s run was wonderful for Celta against Alavés. And Pablo Martínez’s shot in Málaga’s 2-5 loss to Real Sociedad was ridiculous. It might not have even been the best shot of this game had Gio Lo Celso’s “goal” not been ruled out. And it definitely might not even be the best Lamine Yamal has scored, but this keeps happening. Statement after statement.

He didn’t stop there either: there was an absurd pass from which Adeyemi should have scored. A run through three. Another assist. And the moment that got the Betis fans whistling him: when, with Fermín on the ground and Lamine Yamal going over, Facundo Bernal pushed him, he took a run up and pushed Bernal back, and the defender head-butted him, seeing red. The game hadn’t stopped with his first either; instead, Rodri said afterwards, it had “everything”. Always watch Betis, especially when they’re playing Barcelona: unbeaten in 15 home games, the last time anyone beat them here was Barca too. And it finished 5-3. This time they were only one short.

View image in fullscreen Barcelona's Gabriel Jesus celebrates scoring their third goal with Lamine Yamal. Photograph: Marcelo del Pozo/Reuters

Barcelona had dominated the first 25 minutes, the ball theirs alone but Valentín Gómez headed in to make it 1-1 before Rodri made it 2-1. Within two minutes, Lo Celso had smashed in an extraordinary 25-yard shot on the bounce and the turn to make it 2-2, only for it to be ruled out for a handball fourteen seconds earlier. All that before half-time. And yet it was summed up better by the 30 seconds that passed between Álvaro Valles making a superb save at one end and Joan García matching it at the other; by the 59 seconds that passed between that and Gabriel Jesus getting the third. Or the two minutes 59 seconds between that going in and Ez Abde making it 3-2. Then the fight that followed it, Lamine Yamal tumbling maybe a touch too hard and Bernal walking.

By the time Lamine Yamal did, at last encouraged to rest, Eric García had scored the fourth and it was done. “With this result, we had to make the change,” Flick said; with tensions rising too. Dani Olmo added a neat fifth and it finished. Betis were furious. Asked how it had left him feeling, the manager, Manuel Pellegrini, said: “impotent.” Lo Celso’s goal shouldn’t have been ruled out and Gabriel Jesus’s should, he said. Ask how he felt, Fran García said “frustrated, angry … and tired”. They had given everything, the ovation as generous as their effort had been. “This is one of the hardest games in La Liga,” Rodri said, but Barcelona had won again.

That’s nine from nine, a new record. Now, a word of advice from Mr Wolf. When it comes to historic starts, Barcelona’s previous record was under Tata Martino, who you may remember but probably don’t. “This is a nice thing but we want to win titles,” Flick said; Martino did not. Betis were the first team Barcelona have played in the top half of the table. The rest currently sit in 19th, 18th, 17th, 16th, 15th 14th, and 11th. Harder games are coming: PSG next, then Real Madrid. They also have an injury crisis at the back. But no one is playing like them, and certainly not scoring like them. They have scored 39 league goals, 48 in 11 matches in all competitions.

Quick Guide La Liga results Show Deportivo A Coruña 1-1 Levante, Espanyol 0-1 Atlético, Villarreal 0-0 Elche, Real Betis 2-5 Barcelona, Valencia 0-0 A Bilbao, Osasuna 2-0 Racing Santander, Celta Vigo 2-1 Alavés, Málaga 2-5 Real Sociedad, Real Madrid 4-1 Sevilla Monday: Getafe v Rayo Vallecano Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

When Robert Lewandowski, Ferran Torres and Marcus Rashford went in the summer, when they didn’t manage to sign Julián Alvarez, you couldn’t help asking where the goals were going to come from. The answer was everywhere. Thirteen different players have scored. It turns out that they have the best striker in Europe: Raphinha, the man who is just filling in there, has scored more than anyone else. They may also have the best player at 19, the kid who came back a World Cup winner and still wasn’t satisfied.

“After the game against Elche at the start of the season, people were saying: ‘He’s not right’,” Lamine Yamal said. “But I was calm at home, thinking: ‘I’ve just won the World Cup, I’ve not had a break, I know my body: bit by bit I’ll get to the point where I explode and start to score. And those same people will suddenly be saying I’m the best.” In the first two games, against Elche and Athletic, Lamine left little. Since then he has scored or assisted in every match. Nine goals, 10 assists, and most of them brilliant. He went to the international break and scored after 104 seconds at Wembley, 70 in Seville, and 320 in Oviedo. Here, on the day they said this time it’s for real, it took him 530, heads in hands, words stuck in throats, and another win on the way.

“It was amazing, a match for all the people who love football,” Flick said. “For me Lamine is the best in the world. I’m happy about his performance; this is what I love to see. And when you see the first goal, it’s unbelievable.”

Unbelievable. That’ll do.

Sports.title: Uefa demands Fifa releases documents relating to World Cup sell-off scheme
Sports.content:
Uefa has given Fifa a two-week ­deadline to release key ­documents relating to Gianni Infantino’s World Cup sell-off plan and other ­governance issues in its latest critique of football’s world ­governing body.

A letter sent to Fifa’s general secretary, Mattias Grafström, by his counterpart at Uefa, Theodore ­Theodoridis, is accompanied by an eight-page document that has more than 50 questions about Fifa’s ­handling of dozens of issues over the past 12 months. These include the proposed sale of 20% of its commercial rights, the Folarin Balogun affair, the peace prize and relations with Donald Trump and the arrangements for next year’s Fifa presidential election. Uefa’s document also makes a number of allegations about potential conflicts of interests at Fifa, as well as repeating calls for a “genuinely independent” governance review.

Uefa’s latest intervention ­follows last week’s meeting of the Fifa ­council in Zurich, the first time it had gathered since the emergence of the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) ­controversy in July. Infantino listened to questions on FFE and other ­matters, but declined to provide substantive answers, instead asking council members to submit them in writing before their next meeting in Doha on 16 December.

In a letter sent on Monday, ­Theodoridis wrote: “These explanations have not begun ­satisfactorily to address a number of ­fundamental questions raised by Council members.

“Others remain unanswered, and the information and documentation requested have not been provided.

“Following the invitation made during the meeting to submit our questions in writing, we therefore enclose a consolidated set of questions and requests for information.

“We formally request a substantive written response to each question, together with all ­supporting ­documentation by Monday 2nd November. Any refusal to disclose information or documents should be justified individually, with a clear explanation of the specific grounds relied upon.

“These questions require answers now. They cannot be deferred until the next meeting of the Fifa Council – nor can future governance reforms substitute for scrutiny of decisions already taken and accountability for them.”

View image in fullscreen Aleksander Ceferin (centre), the Uefa president, and Theodore Theodoridis, the organisation’s general secretary, pictured in 2023. Photograph: Massimo Pinca/Reuters

The accompanying document and list of supplementary questions constitutes a damning takedown of Fifa’s leadership under Infantino, who, as it stands, is on course to be re-elected unopposed as president next year, although Uefa is increasingly hopeful of identifying a candidate to take him on before nominations close on 18 November.

Uefa also wants answers on the processes behind other major decisions taken by Fifa over the past 12 months including moving the men’s World Cup draw to Washington DC from Las Vegas, the introduction of hydration breaks and the 27-minute half-time at the World Cup final.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“A series of decisions, transactions and interventions involving the Fifa President, the President of the United States and individuals associated with him raise serious questions concerning potential conflicts of interest, transparency and institutional accountability,” Uefa states.

The amount Fifa is paying to rent office space in Trump Tower is also queried, as is a report in the Times last week that Infantino in 2024 “received substantial additional remuneration which was not disclosed in Fifa’s annual report”. Fifa has said it “does not pay a second salary to the Fifa president and complies with all reporting requirements in relation to compensation”.

Uefa also raises concerns about March’s presidential election, specifically regarding the involvement of Bruno Chiomento, the chair of Fifa’s electoral committee. “We understand that Mr Chiomento has known the Fifa President for approximately 20 years and is regularly invited to Fifa events and competitions at Fifa’s expense,” Uefa’s document states. “We further understand that he attended the entire 2026 World Cup as an accredited individual, with his expenses covered by Fifa for more than five weeks.”

Uefa has also requested a complete list of Fifa guests in VIP and VVIP areas at the World Cup final, on the grounds that “numerous guests were apparently given priority over Presidents of Member Associations and Secretaries General of Confederations”.

Fifa has been contacted for lcomment.

Sports.title: Cristiano Ronaldo receives 30-day suspension and £215 fine over Portugal walkout
Sports.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo has been suspended for 30 days by the Portuguese ⁠FA after leaving the national team camp following a rift with the coach, ⁠Jorge Jesus, over ⁠his role in the side. The federation’s disciplinary council said it had upheld the charge against ⁠the 41-year-old forward in full and imposed a fine of €255 (£215).

Ronaldo left Portugal’s base in ⁠Copenhagen before their Nations League match against Denmark earlier this month, having accused ‌Jesus of twice ‌breaking his word about his role after he was an ‌unused substitute against Norway. Jesus denied making any agreement with Ronaldo but left the door open for his return after Portugal’s 2-1 win.

The disciplinary council’s non-professional section found Ronaldo had intentionally committed an offence under Article 160(1) ‌of the federation’s disciplinary regulations. Proceedings were opened on 9 October over facts reported two days earlier.

The statement did not specify which matches or activities the suspension would cover, or whether time already served under a provisional suspension would count towards the 30-day sanction.

Ronaldo later ⁠apologised for failing to acknowledge supporters after the Norway match and for leaving his teammates, saying he remained available for selection after serving any ‌punishment arising from the incident.

The Portuguese FA president, Pedro Proença, has said everyone within the federation wanted Ronaldo to return to the national team once the matter was resolved.

Sports.title: Crystal Palace to give Sage more time but manager under serious scrutiny
Sports.content:
Pierre Sage has been granted more time to fix Crystal Palace’s defensive issues but he has been warned that things must improve quickly after the 5-0 defeat at Brighton on Sunday.

The Frenchman’s future was in serious doubt after his side conceded three times inside the opening 10 minutes before equalling the 70‑year record for the club’s heaviest defeat against their arch-rivals. The thrashing means Palace have conceded the most goals in the Premier League: 17 from seven games.

The club chair, Steve Parish, is understood not to have been fully convinced by Sage since the 47‑year‑old was appointed to replace Oliver Glasner in the summer. Parish is believed to have considered parting company with Sage on Sunday after 10 matches but decided against a change given that Palace are 14th and not in immediate danger.

Sage is expected to remain in charge not only for the Europa League game at Besiktas on Thursday but also the Premier League match against Newcastle on Sunday. But it has been made clear to the former Lens manager that his position is under heavy scrutiny. Kieran McKenna, who Parish approached while the Northern Irishman was at Ipswich, and Thomas Frank will be among the contenders if Sage is sacked.

Tensions between Sage and Parish date to the summer transfer window when Palace failed to secure the manager’s main targets to replace Maxence Lacroix in central defence. Two loanees, Axel Disasi and the teenager Honest Ahanor –, were signed instead from Chelsea and Atalanta respectively. Palace also missed out on Malick Fofana to Sunderland on deadline day despite Sage making the Belgium forward, whom he coached in Lyon’s youth teams, a priority. Palace instead signed Darío Osorio on an initial loan and the Chile forward has played only a handful of minutes.

Parish was unhappy with Sage’s treatment of Jaydee Canvot after the France Under-21 international was dropped from the squad for the home defeat by Ipswich last month. He is also understood to have been angered by Adam Wharton being substituted in that match after Disasi was shown a red card in the first half.

Some behind the scenes at Palace have been pushing for Sage to be sacked, but Parish is thought to recognise the headache caused by Disasi’s three-match suspension and injuries to Chadi Riad and Takehiro Tomiyasu and would prefer to give him an opportunity to turn things around.

Chris Richards has apologised to Palace supporters after failing to acknowledge them after the Brighton game. “I want to apologise for walking off after the game,” the USA defender wrote on Instagram.

“I was emotional and embarrassed with the result – I know how much this club means to all of you. We have to take responsibility, do better and show that on the pitch.”

Sports.title: Semenyo’s eight-week injury absence leaves Manchester City short on cover for Haaland
Sports.content:
Antoine Semenyo has been ruled out for eight weeks with a knee injury, leaving Enzo Maresca short of alternatives to Erling Haaland, who is a doubt for Manchester City’s Champions League game at home against AEK Athens on Tuesday.

Semenyo limped off against Ipswich on Saturday and Haaland hobbled off at full time with a foot injury. City are eager to get their European campaign back on track after losing against Paris Saint-Germain last Wednesday. Maresca has said he will make changes and has admitted previously that Haaland will require resting at some point. Semenyo would have been the most obvious replacement but Phil Foden and Iliman Ndiaye could be utilised.

“To replace Erling it’s always difficult but we have some different options; we’ll see tomorrow,” Maresca said. “To lose Antoine or any player for us is not good. Then in terms of Erling, we said that we can use Antoine as a 9 but also we have different players that we are going to try and to find new solutions.”

Maresca witnessed a number of his players limp away from the win against Ipswich: Haaland, Semenyo, Mateo Kovacic, Matheus Nunes and Nico O’Reilly, who all featured at the World Cup. Maresca had made six changes, showing the need to rotate amid a hectic schedule of seven games in 21 days in October for City, many of whose players also had international commitments at the start of the month.

“We try to manage all the players in the best way, try to keep them fit,” Maresca said. “Even sometimes things happen that you cannot control, like Antoine’s injury. We try to save him, we try to keep him fresh.”

The fixtures mean it is difficult for Maresca to get training time as he tries to instil his style. “We try and do what we can on the pitch to go through a few things and tactics before the games,” the defender Marc Guéhi said. “It’s just a lot of recovery, sleep, to make sure the body is right for the next game,. It’s been enjoyable, to be honest; not to train, just playing games, which is fun.”

Guéhi was among the players who opted not to take a knee at the weekend as part of the Premier League’s “No Room For Racism” campaign. “I haven’t been taking the knee for a while now,” he said. “I’d always clap just because of what that actually signifies.” He wants greater action to combat racism in sport. “I hope we can do a bit more but we will just see. Hopefully the message is still getting out there, which is important.”

Sports.title: Brighton are the apex B club – their next target should be a Champions League place | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
For two or three years now, it’s been standard to nod approvingly at how well-run Brighton, Brentford and Bournemouth are, and to move on. What else is there to say? It’s true, of course – these are sides who have made the most of relatively limited resources. But there’s also an underlying assumption in the designation: that these are clubs who have no higher aspiration, that their limit is earning praise for upper mid-table finishes.

This season, perhaps, offers an opportunity to change that. Other than Arsenal, every major club is undergoing significant transition. Manchester City may have started the season with seven straight wins, but there’s every chance the punishment for their multiple breaches of Premier League regulations takes them out of the race for the top five. In that context, why shouldn’t one of those efficient smaller sides qualify for the Champions League?

Brentford began the weekend in third and with, perhaps, a slight sense of frustration that they had drawn four games. Again, they will feel they might have done rather better on Saturday; they were leading Liverpool 1-0 when Yehor Yarmolyuk foolishly flicked his head towards Jérémy Jacquet and was sent off just before half-time. The result was a 2-1 defeat and a sense of an opportunity missed. Bournemouth have not had the easiest start under Marco Rose, but Sunday’s 2-0 win over Sunderland perhaps hints at a brighter future.

Which left Brighton to carry the charge of the B clubs, which they did in emphatic style, ending a run of four derbies without success with a crushing 5-0 win. Crystal Palace had been extremely fortunate to survive a first-half battering from Nottingham Forest last week. They were thoroughly outplayed in the early stages again, and this time found themselves 3-0 down inside 10 minutes. Perhaps the opening goal, a cross headed into his own net by Jaydee Canvot, was fortunate, but it was an error induced by the intensity of Brighton’s start. The second goal, a perfectly weighted drive from just inside the Palace half from Diego Gómez, spoke of a side playing with immense confidence. Already this season, 11 different players have scored for Brighton in the league. They have become the image of a side without stars, the whole far greater than the individuals who comprise it.

The difference from February, when Brighton last played Palace, is stark. They lost that game 1-0, meaning they had won just one of their previous 12 Premier League games. Generalised grumbling had begun to curdle into calls for Fabian Hürzeler to be sacked. When they lost Carlos Baleba, Jan Paul van Hecke, Danny Welbeck and James Milner over the summer, there were reasons to wonder whether they could keep going with the process of continuous renewal.

There were the usual assorted signings, the usual mix of Premier League experience and exotic unknowns. The 19-year-old centre-back Luka Vušković, who spent last season on loan at Hamburg from Tottenham, already looks at home (and who really thought, when Spurs and Brighton effectively swapped centre-backs, with Van Hecke moving to London, that Brighton would not end up with the better of the deal?). The 21-year-old Spanish midfielder Chema Andrés, who arrived from Stuttgart, sparkled from the bench against Arsenal and has excelled in the two games since.

But the stand-out performer this season has been a far more familiar name: Pascal Gross, who returned in January after a season and a half at Borussia Dortmund. No player in the Premier League has registered more than his four assists this season. Nobody has run further. He has three goals. He averages a league-high 3.0 key passes a game. To bring back a player who is now 35 has been a masterstroke.

The victory over Arsenal before the international break suggested a team capable not merely of accumulating points against the league’s lesser lights, or even of challenging the elite, but of overwhelming them. Arsenal were suffocated by the Brighton press and, while a couple of low-xG long-range finishes in the first half helped, the fact is that Brighton dominated the match to a remarkable extent.

The question is whether they can keep it going. Just as their transfer policy is now an accepted feature of the Premier League, so too is Brighton’s mid-season slump. They haven’t won a game in December since 2023. Is this squad strong enough to sustain the challenge? Europe seems not to be unsettling Brighton as it did on their first foray, or as it appears to be draining Bournemouth, Crystal Palace and Sunderland – which may be a reflection on the relative quality of the Conference League.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

They are doing this without Kaoru Mitoma, Yankuba Minteh and Mats Wieffer, all of whom should be back at some point over the next month. That suggests the depth of this Brighton squad. It’s always a major step for a club unfamiliar with the Champions League to haul themselves into the top five. At times it often feels a mental barrier as much as anything.

But if any of those B clubs are ever going to break into the Champions League, they may never have a better opportunity than Brighton do this season.

Sports.title: Konsa bullish about Arsenal’s Champions League hopes as Bayern clash looms
Sports.content:
For Ezri Konsa, it was just a wonderfully satisfying challenge. The Nottingham Forest striker Liam Delap had stolen in behind him up the inside left channel on Sunday. There were 93 minutes gone, Arsenal were 1-0 up and it was now or never for Forest. Konsa decreed that it would be never, curving his covering run back, matching Delap for pace and stretching into the perfect block tackle.

So, another win for Arsenal: their 10th in 11 matches this season. Another clean sheet. And for Konsa, a continuation of what has been a dreamlike couple of months. Do points-saving last-minute challenges mean more when the defender is actually a fan of the club, too? Basically, yes.

“I’ve been asked this a lot,” Konsa says with a smile, when the subject of his boyhood allegiance is raised. “And, yes, I was [an Arsenal supporter]. I had a lot of Arsenal kits when I was younger. You dream of playing for big clubs like this. When you’re a kid, you see the likes of Arsenal, growing up, and the amount of quality players they’ve had throughout the years and to be here – and not only to be here but to be here with close friends – makes it even more special.”

Konsa is talking about Eberechi Eze, in particular; another boyhood Arsenal fan, with whom he is especially tight. Many supporters have seen the clip of Eze greeting Konsa at the training ground after the latter had completed his £51m move from Aston Villa and how they crack up with laughter before embracing. It is infectious. But Konsa knows a clutch of other Arsenal players from England duty – Declan Rice, Bukayo Saka, Noni Madueke, Myles Lewis-Skelly, Ben White – and he credits them with helping him to settle in.

The 28-year-old’s adaptation has been quick and it has needed to be with William Saliba injured. After making his Arsenal debut as a substitute at Villa – Konsa’s scriptwriters have been hard at work – he has played in every minute of the club’s Premier League and Champions League matches. The victory at Forest, where Arsenal had drawn 0-0 in each of the previous two seasons, was significant. It was not a performance of any attacking pace or spark. Perhaps it made the points feel more precious.

“We hadn’t won here in two seasons, the boss was going on about it,” Konsa says. “It’s something we wanted to change as players and these are the games you have to win. If you want to win titles, you have to come away to tough places like this and get three points.”

View image in fullscreen Ezri Konsa does battle with Liam Delap during Arsenal’s 1-0 win at Nottingham Forest. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

Things are about to get even more interesting for Konsa and Arsenal because on Wednesday they face Bayern Munich at the Allianz Arena in the Champions League. “It’s against my international teammate as well,” Konsa says, and he is straight into an appreciation of Harry Kane, the England captain, who has been on fire since joining Bayern from Tottenham in 2023. Kane’s scoring record for the club bears repeating: 155 goals in 157 appearances.

Konsa has a good record against Kane, having faced him seven times, six of them for Villa against Spurs. The seventh and most recent came in October 2024 when Konsa was in the Villa team that beat Kane’s Bayern 1-0 at Villa Park in the Champions League. It was Villa’s first home match in the competition for 41 years. The defender has four wins against Kane’s teams and three losses. Kane has only scored twice against him, both from penalties.

“The Villa-Bayern game … to beat them at home and keep a clean sheet … it was very special for the players and the fans,” Konsa says. “I don’t really look much at those kind of stats [against individual players] but I am relishing the challenge.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The dynamics against Bayern appear different for Konsa this time. It was a famous victory for Villa that night, in part because of the tie’s history; the club beat Bayern 1-0 in the 1982 European Cup final. Villa were underdogs as they felt their way back into Europe’s elite competition. Arsenal will kick off as Bayern’s equals and among the favourites to win the tournament, having lost on penalties to Paris Saint-Germain in last season’s final.

Konsa won the first trophy of his career a week before that when he was in the Villa team that defeated Freiburg in the Europa League final. He says he has felt the determination of the Arsenal squad to go one step further in Europe.

“One hundred per cent,” Konsa says. “As players, the standards we have, the goals we have … we want to win everything – the Champions League, the Prem. Whatever trophies are in front of us. When I came to Arsenal, I wanted to win. I was hungry to win. Last season I got my hands on the Europa League and this season I want more.”

Sports.title: The secrets of Christian Wade's success: On brink of PREM try-scoring record, he reveals his star-studded Wasps finishing school, all-you-can-eat pizza, why defenders are just 'obstacles'... and building 'the best team in the world' at Newcastle
Sports.content:
On Friday night, Christian Wade hopes to toast to a slice of rugby history with a shot of tequila. Newcastle’s winger is one score away from equalling Chris Ashton’s record of 101 PREM tries. An achievement worthy of a night out on the Toon. Wade scored his first top-flight try for Wasps in 2011 and his career has taken him to rugby league and American Football but now, more than 15 years later, he is on the brink of rewriting English rugby union’s history books. ‘Hopefully I’ll have my family and friends around when it happens – but we need to win first!’ Wade tells Daily Mail Sport. ‘We’ll probably go for dinner and commemorate the day. My missus is a big foodie, so we do go and try different spots. There's one pizza spot we go to called Sanco. It's all-you-can-eat pizza for £16 a head. Other than that, I’ll just crack on with my business!’ No matter how much pizza he eats, Wade will never be one of the big beasts of the rugby world. He is just 5ft 9in and 13st 5lb, relying on his speed, elusive skillset and a few other secrets to sit on the brink of history despite this only being his ninth full season in the PREM. He took four years out in his prime to pursue an NFL dream with the Buffalo Bills, spent eight months last year playing rugby league for Wigan Warriors and had a two-year spell in France with Racing 92. ‘I just admire guys who are able to get the job done year after year,’ explains Wade, 35. ‘Guys who look after their bodies – LeBron James, Cristiano Ronaldo. When you watch them, you know you’re not going to see much of a drop off. I think people underestimate how hard it is to stay consistent. On Friday night, Christian Wade hopes to toast to a slice of rugby history with a shot of tequila The Newcastle wing is one try away from equalling the PREM record - despite this only being his ninth full season in the league

Your browser does not support iframes.

‘I know my body very well and I've had my own team since 2013. I've had my own physio and multiple trainers across the world. I've got people here and in America, depending on where I'm at. I usually do a two-hour massage therapy session in one sitting per week – and I use the pool quite a lot. ‘Your body's your money. It’s the way you make money so it doesn't make sense to not invest in it. Guys go out to socialise, go drinking and stuff like that, but you could spend the same amount of money on your body and the return will be a lot bigger. You know what I mean?’ Despite his laidback demeanour, Wade is a dedicated student of the game. ‘It’s not just as simple as catch and run,’ he says. ‘There's a science behind it. I’m a student of how I can use my body to manipulate defenders. 'I was talking with (Newcastle back-rower) Sam Graham about one of the moves we did here at the Red Bulls. I was telling him that I don't see defenders, I just see bodies as obstacles. You react to what they do. Some of it comes down to instinct. ‘My awareness of my surroundings just came to me. I think I’ve just got a natural eye for the line. Evasion, using the space, using my footwork, ball placement, messing around with how I hold the ball in two hands. I used to watch videos of Jason Robinson, Joe Rokocoko and Sitiveni Sivivatu. I’m a bit of a visual learner. I would just be on YouTube for hours, watching loads of different clips. ‘If I've got the ball on the edge and I know I'm going to run, then I'm usually holding the ball with one hand. But before that, it's in two hands because I don't know if I’m going to kick or pass. Shane Williams used to do that quite a bit. You keep the ball in two hands to keep your options open.’ England centre Seb Atkinson tells Daily Mail Sport that he was astounded by Wade’s ability to use grubber kicks to create scoring opportunities when the pair were Gloucester team-mates for a season two years ago. ‘He’s always been known for beating people one-on-one but what really impressed me was his support play,’ Atkinson says. ‘There are a lot of things about him that people underappreciate. He’s got a really good kicking game. He can grubber the ball down the touch line while running at full speed and it will just roll and roll without going out, which is pretty handy for a winger.’ A hat-trick against Exeter in round three this season took Wade’s try tally to a round 100. His nifty finishing ability has dazzled crowds over the years, but his favourite try came against Leicester back in 2011. Wade burst onto the scene with Wasps in 2011 and quickly became one of the league's most feared wingers 'I don't see defenders, I just see bodies as obstacles,' he says. 'You react to what they do. Some of it comes down to instinct' Wade represented England at Under 20s, A and once at senior level - but never quite made his mark on the international stage ‘There have been a few but my favourite was probably when I scored a hat-trick in my first game against Leicester. It was a kick return and Hugo Southwell – blast from the past – caught it and threw a massive pass across the field. I was able to run and score in the corner. That was fun, being young, playing against our rivals at Adams Park. ‘I've been able to do a lot. I can’t complain. Playing for Wasps in the post-Lawrence Dallaglio era, we went through a lot back then. We nearly went into administration. They invested in a group of young guys like myself, Elliot Daly, Joe Launchbury and Joe Simpson. We built a team that eventually got to the PREM final. 'On that journey, I got to play with some of the world's greatest players. Guys like Kurtley Beale, Charles Piutau, George Smith, Piri Weepu, Juan de Jongh, Lima Sopoaga, Danny Cipriani, Kyle Eastmond, Dan Robson. My first director of rugby was Sir Ian McGeechan! Imagine that? That’s some legendary s*** right there! 'Shaun Edwards was my first head coach. He was on me pretty hard in the early days. I was just like, “Bro, he is always on me, man”. But if he’s on you then you know he cares about you. It was awesome. They set my expectations and the foundations.’ In the early years of his career, there was a clamour for Wade to become England’s starting winger. Yet his only cap came against Argentina in 2013, when many of the front-line players were on the British & Irish Lions tour of Australia, which he later joined as an injury replacement. International rugby is dominated by big beasts but Wade has no hard feelings about his lack of Test exposure. ‘I wouldn't say it was a frustration,’ he says. ‘When Stuart Lancaster got named as coach after the 2011 World Cup in New Zealand, I was brought onto that summer tour of South Africa. I was only 21 at the time. I’d played England Under 20s the year before that with guys like Owen Farrell. ‘Things were obviously on the right trajectory. There was a lot of competition with guys like Chris Ashton, Mike Brown and Ben Foden. Ultimately, my opportunity came and I pulled my hamstring two days before the autumn internationals. That obviously opened up the door for guys like Jonny May and Jack Nowell. At elite level, you get your opportunity and if you don't take it you may never get another one. That's pretty much what happened with me. ‘Of course I would have liked more opportunities to play for England, but I did everything I could. I was never really frustrated with that. That's just how it goes sometimes. I went on to do the NFL stuff, came back to France, did the England stuff, did the Lions stuff, and now I'm back here with the Red Bulls where we're looking to build the best rugby team in the world. We're at the beginning of our journey, paving the way.’ Wade was called up to the British & Irish Lions tour of Australia in 2013, playing a tour match against the ACT Brumbies Wade spent four years of his prime on the practice squads of the Buffalo Bills, but never made it into an NFL match Chris Ashton (left) has held onto the try record for four years, but now Wade (right) is ready to streak clear Newcastle host Sale on Friday night in the northern derby. They are edging closer to their first win of the season and it could be the perfect setting for Wade to hit his big scoring milestone. Having proudly held the record since 2022, Ashton claimed that he would ‘rather be at home on his own’ when it gets broken – although TNT Sports have ensured the retired winger will be commentating on Newcastle’s next two fixtures. ‘Is he winding me up?' asks Wade. 'I haven't seen it, but I see him around and we're on good terms. It's all banter, isn't it? We’ve got to give you something to talk about. Make it a bit more exciting. ‘I bump into him every now and again. Even when I was at Wigan, he'd come up to a game. We're cool, bro. But obviously for the purposes of TV and stuff, it’s something to talk about, which is cool. 'But you never know… his comments might be more on the serious side. Hopefully we’ll find out!’

Sports.title: Cristiano Ronaldo will miss NO games and is handed a measly £215 fine - which will take the £488,000-a-day superstar just 38 SECONDS to pay off - for walking out of Portugal camp
Sports.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo will miss NO games and is handed a measly £215 fine - which will take the £488,000-a-day superstar just 38 SECONDS to pay off - for walking out of Portugal camp

Cristiano Ronaldo has been fined £215 and is free to play for Portugal despite his explosive walk-out last month.

The superstar, 41, has technically been banned for a month by Portuguese football chiefs - but that punishment is backdated to his strop on September 30, reports in his homeland claim.

That means his ban will be served by the time Portugal's next fixture against Denmark rolls around on November 14, so Jorge Jesus will free to play him.

Meanwhile, his piddling fine of £215 will take the billionaire approximately 38 seconds to recoup on his £488,000-per-day salary at Saudi Arabian moneybags Al-Nassr.

It was a saga which threatened to end Ronaldo's international career, derail the national team, and undermine the authority of manager Jesus.

Ronaldo was livid after being left on the bench despite warming-up for Portugal's Nations League win over Norway on September 27 – the first time he has been an unused substitute during his 18-year international career.

Cristiano Ronaldo is free to play for Portugal despite his explosive walk-out - as his ban doesn't reach their next game

The five-time Ballon d'Or winner - a billionaire who earns £488,000 every day - has been fined £215

That led to him skipping three training sessions and abandoning the camp for Portugal's last two matches of the international break, fleeing to Spain via private jet.

He did not even watch their next match against Norway because he was soaring away on his plane with his family.

The former Manchester United star was vexed at how Jesus had handled his press conference after leaving him on the bench.

Ronaldo insisted that Jesus had broken a promise to apologise to the 'Portuguese people' and his team-mates for not bringing him on.

He claimed he had been guaranteed 30 minutes of football against Norway after the Portuguese FA persuaded him not to retire following the World Cup.

The five-time Ballon d'Or winner even offered to retire if that was what the coach and head of Portuguese FA wanted, only for them to reiterate their desire to have him.

Jesus was ultimately vindicated in his decision to exclude Ronaldo - he has won all four of his matches in charge of Portugal and they look a more balanced team for it.

The 72-year-old has handled himself with grace throughout the episode, maintaining that Ronaldo would be welcomed back with open arms - a stance his team-mates have publicly backed.

Even so, Ronaldo released a stinging 1,996-word statement accusing Jesus of 'broken promises'. He said the manager had agreed to deliver an eight-point mea cupla taking responsibility for leaving him on the bench after a supposed pact to play him.

Jesus did concede it was a mistake to make him warm up but gave a different narrative of events, saying: 'The match in Norway was not part of the plan I drew up for him. However, I felt that he had managed to recover physically from the first match and I warned him that I might have to use him. Cristiano agreed.'

Manager Jorge Jesus has insisted that Ronaldo is welcome back, and so have his team-mates

But Jesus deviated from eight-points that Ronaldo expected the Portugal boss to address

'The status doesn't give players preferential treatment. The status is about respect for their careers. Like I do with Cris. 'I always put the issue first, the plan, which is drawn up with the player, and I'm the one who decides. They know, even the presidents know. The president is in charge at the club, I'm in charge at the team.'

Another of Ronaldo's requests was for Jesus to say: 'I made a mistake by putting someone of the stature of Pelé or Maradona on to warm up and then not putting him in the game. If it were today I would not do it.'

The Portugal boss appeared to have followed some of the request, even referencing legends Pele and Maradona during his press conference as he acknowledged he had made a mistake with his handling of Ronaldo.

Jesus, however, had continued by again stressing that he can promise players 'whatever I want' but he would not change his mind on decisions regardless of the status of the player.

'I told Cris that he wasn't going to play these two games,' Jesus said.

'I thought during the game, maybe I'll need him and he'll warm up. And then I didn't put him in the game.

'Any player, when we're warming up for 20 or 30 minutes, and then they don't come on. No one is happy about that. Much less Cris. Much less Pele, Maradona, that's the status.

'When the game started, I told him to warm up at the 45th minute, I didn't know what I was going to do. That's what I did wrong, I should have had him warm up about 15 minutes later.'

Jesus, however, added: 'The game dictates what I'm going to do. I thought I had even discussed it with him, but maybe until I needed him in the final minutes.

Jesus' comments ultimately led to Ronaldo walking out of the Portugal national team camp

'But the game dictated other things and I didn't put him in.

'I can promise whatever I want. I'm a coach, I told the player he wasn't going to play, but I'll put you on the bench.

'Since I saw the game my way, he didn't come on. There will never be a player who will change my mind. Never, zero.'

Another of Ronaldo's requests was for Jesus to confirm his desire for him to be part of the Portugal squad by saying 'I want Cristiano in the National Team. In fact I do not want him a little, I want him a lot.'

The request was not touched upon by Jesus in his comments to the media, as well as highlighting Ronaldo's love of the national team.

Jesus, however, had previously referred to Ronaldo as being a 'symbol of Portugal' in a joint press conference at the start of the international break.

Throughout, the ex-Al Nassr boss has remained magnanimous.

He explained: 'It's up to Cris to decide his own life. In the next call-up, if Cris is playing and wants to be in the national team, why not?

'Resentment? Nothing, it was a misunderstanding. In my opinion, it's easy to resolve. When will I resolve it? I don't know. The game is over, and only afterwards will we know how things will turn out.

'It's not up to me. To reach an agreement with two people, both people need to talk and agree. That's not up to me.

'Just because it was him, and perhaps rightly so because he's a symbol, this whole problem of him coming on, warming up, not coming on. How many players warmed up today and didn't come on? Will there be a problem? No.

'With Cris it's different, he's a symbol. But is it a problem? For me it wasn't a problem. If Cris wants to and is playing for Al-Nassr, he'll be in the next squad. We talked before this squad and we can talk before the next one. It's Cris who will decide.'

Sports.title: Pierre Sage at risk of becoming first Premier League manager sacked: Crystal Palace chiefs concerned amid strained relationships
Sports.content:
Pierre Sage at risk of becoming first Premier League manager sacked: Crystal Palace chiefs concerned amid strained relationships

Pierre Sage is under growing pressure at Crystal Palace and could become the first Premier League manager sacked this season after an embarrassing 5-0 defeat against rivals Brighton.

Palace chiefs have raised concerns about Sage’s defensive approach for several weeks and considered sacking him in September but a goalless draw against Leeds bought him more time.

However, the backline continues to ring alarm bells at Selhurst Park, leaving Sage’s position at risk.

Palace have the worst defensive record in the league, conceding 17 goals in seven Premier League games.

The French coach is also understood to have a strained relationship with key decision-makers, who doubt his defensive methods.

The Daily Mail previously reported that his decision to bench Jaydee Canvot after a bad game irked chairman Steve Parish.

Pierre Sage said he didn't know how long he would be given to turn things round at Palace

Speaking after Palace’s 5-0 defeat at Brighton, Sage was unsure whether he would be given more time in the job.

‘I don’t know,’ Sage said when asked if he would keep his job. ‘I just want to apologise to the fans because it’s not normal to show this face for this club against this other club and we are not at the level we expected.

‘I am really sorry for that because I know how important it is for them. We didn’t show that today. It was really important for us too. We didn’t understand in which context this game was played.

‘I will always give my best. When we lose, I’m really frustrated, but I always take the lesson and try to change things. But it’s the same when I win because I know we can improve.

‘I don’t want to accept the level of the moment if we can do better. Today the work is really important to do and I will do it. It’s my job and I like to change this kind of thing.’

Sports.title: Now even RED CARDS go digital! Referee uses a 'smartphone' to dish out his punishments - but fans are not convinced
Sports.content:
A referee has gone viral for seemingly showing a player a red card on his phone - in an eerie experiment which could change football forever. Eduardo Varela has become the first referee in history to send a player off with a digital red card in a trial in a Copa Uruguay clash between Nacional and Rentistas. And the smartphone-like device - which also displays yellow cards - logs every booking, substitution, goal, and penalty for the wider Uruguayan football system. That allows the administration to keep better track of statistics and, in due course, hopefully relay them to fans and the media whatever the level of match. But the initiative has already come under scrutiny due to problems with visibility. In one test match between Defensor Sporting and Plaza Colonia, the sunlight rendered it almost impossible to interpret the device from a distance, meaning the experiment had to be abandoned. Uruguay have been trialling digital cards which track and upload data from matches Referee Eduardo Varela became the first man to send somebody off digitally The device is only in the trial stage but it has been an idea three years in the making. Developers REFe are exploring adding LED lighting around the device to make the colours clearer to spectators. Their ultimate ambition is for the technology to be adopted by South American ​governing body CONMEBOL and eventually FIFA. 'We have seen all kinds of comments, positive and negative. We ⁠have even ​laughed at the memes,' said Mauro Sacco, director of REFe. 'The important thing is that ​people are talking about it. Any innovation takes time.' Fellow director Diego de la Pena added: 'It's a project with room for improvement. It looked much better live than it did on TV. The challenge we face now is to improve ​it for the whole audience. 'The ⁠yellow card has to be yellow, the red card has to be red, and it has to be visible to people at the ground and on ​television.' For the most part, fans online have ridiculed the innovation. 'It doesn't generate any improvement to the game or to the spectator… not everything has to be digital,' one fan wrote on X. 'It'll be a problem if the battery runs out,' pointed out one supporter. Another wrote: 'This is completely unnecessary and probably heavier to carry than two cards, a solution to a problem that doesn't exist!' One predicted: 'The most unnecessary technological replacement in life, soon we'll see brands on the cards, that's for sure.'
