Reporting from Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh said Gantz’s election withdrawal announcement “was not really expected”, but added that many would see it as being “in line with how he’s conducted himself” after entering politics in 2018.

“This is a man who entered into unity governments with leaders – especially Netanyahu – that he expressly opposed,” said Odeh.



Gantz’s message for unity is narrow, Odeh added, as it referred to “a unity government of Zionist parties, so no Palestinian Israeli parties, no non-Zionist parties in the government, even if that means bringing in Netanyahu again”.

‘Irrelevant and inconsequential’

Netanyahu’s Likud party and the far-right coalition it leads is locked in a tight race with a self-styled Zionist opposition alliance heading into the election, according to recent polling, although neither side appears on track to win a parliamentary majority.

Two Arab-led electoral lists representing the Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up about 20 percent of the population, are projected to win 13 seats and could be critical to any post-election coalition – but both main blocs have ruled out forming a government with them.

Opposition leaders, including Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot, who is seen as a potential prime minister candidate, welcomed Gantz’s decision as “correct” and “responsible”.

Alon Pinkas, a former Israeli ambassador and consul general in New York, told Al Jazeera Gantz’s exit from the race does not change the playing field as he was not going to have a major impact on the election.

“Electorally, his departure from the political system is completely irrelevant and inconsequential,” he said. “In terms of the politics, it is also inconsequential,” adding that Gantz had lost “a lot of his aura” when he “overstayed his welcome in the Netanyahu government”.

World.title: Mauritius lifts curfew imposed amid wave of violent protests
World.content:
Unrest on the archipelago came after police shot a woman during a rally over rising costs and water shortages.

Mauritius has lifted a nighttime curfew that was imposed last week amid a rare wave of violent demonstrations.

The government announced on Monday that the “favourable evolution of the situation” had allowed the end of the curfew. The protests on the Indian Ocean archipelago began last week over water shortages and the rising cost of living, but violence exploded after a police officer shot and seriously wounded a woman on Saturday.

“The curfew currently in effect will not be extended, effective today,” the office of Prime Minister Navin Ramgoolam said in a statement.

“The last curfew ended at 4:30am on Monday 19 October, and it has not been extended. Roads are open, all schools have reopened with classes running as usual, and daily life is back on track,” the Mauritius Tours tourism operator confirmed on its website.

The unrest saw at least 188 people arrested on charges including looting, arson, damage to police stations, and possession of explosives in the following days.

The police officer who shot the woman in the neck has been arrested and brought to court, authorities said.

The island nation of Mauritius is usually viewed as a model of stability and prosperity in Africa. The last major unrest was in 1999, when a renowned singer died in police custody.

However, the unrest provoked a British government update of its travel advice, which urged people travelling to the popular holiday destination to take care.



“The Government of Mauritius introduced temporary curfews during the evenings and overnight, covering most areas of the main island, which lasted from 12 October to 18 October, ending at 4.30am on Monday 19 October,” the British government said in a statement.

“Stay away from demonstrations and large public gatherings and follow the advice of local authorities,” it warned tourists.

World.title: Ronaldo banned for 30 days, fined $285 by Portugal over spat with Jesus
World.content:
Share Ronaldo banned for 30 days, fined $285 over spat with coach Jesus on social media

Cristiano ‌Ronaldo has been suspended for 30 days by the ⁠Portuguese Football Association for leaving the national team camp following a rift with coach Jorge Jesus over ⁠his place in the side.

The federation’s disciplinary council said on Monday that it had upheld the charge against the 41-year-old ⁠forward in full and imposed a fine of 255 euros ($285).

Ronaldo left Portugal’s base in Copenhagen before their Nations League match against Denmark earlier this month, having accused Jesus of ‌twice breaking his word about his role after he was an unused substitute against Norway.

Jesus denied making any agreement with Ronaldo but left the door open for his return following Portugal’s 2-1 win.

The disciplinary council’s non-professional section found Ronaldo had intentionally committed an ⁠offence under Article 160(1) of the ⁠federation’s disciplinary regulations. Proceedings were opened on October 9 over facts reported two days earlier.

The statement did not specify which matches or activities ⁠the suspension would cover, or whether time already served under a provisional ⁠suspension would count towards the 30-day ⁠sanction.

Ronaldo later apologised for failing to acknowledge supporters after the Norway match and for leaving his teammates, saying he remained available for selection ‌after serving any punishment arising from the incident.

Portuguese FA President Pedro Proenca has said everyone within the federation ‌wanted ‌Ronaldo to return to the national team once the matter was resolved.

World.title: Chuck Schumer urges FCC to block AI robocalls before elections
World.content:
United States Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer of New York has urged the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) not to approve a petition by the conservative group Club for Growth to allow AI-generated robocalls ahead of the November midterm elections.

“Under this change, campaigns could use their opponents’ voice to send out a message that is, at best, disingenuous and, at worst, a blatant lie,” Schumer said on Monday.

The petition was originally filed on August 31, and the public comment period began on September 4 and expires on Monday.

Earlier this month, Anna Gomez, the Democratic member of the FCC, urged her colleagues not to allow consideration of the petition brought by the national conservative fiscal policy organisation.

Her concerns echoed Schumer’s. “[If] the FCC allows a dark money group to flood Americans’ phones with AI-generated robocalls they never agreed to receive, it would bring chaos so close to Election Day,” commissioner Gomez told the Reuters news agency at the time.

There is precedent for the concerns being raised. In the 2024 presidential election, ahead of the New Hampshire primary, voters received an AI-generated version in the voice of President Joe Biden, the then Democratic incumbent, telling them not to vote. The FCC said that a political consultant working with longshot primary challenger Dean Phillips was responsible.

At the state level, Louisiana, Tennessee and Vermont passed laws this year requiring disclosures for AI-generated campaign phone calls. While robocalls have been used in political campaigns for years, FCC rules prohibit such calls to cellphones without prior consent, but the restrictions do not apply to landlines.



Club for Growth’s president, David McIntosh, in a statement earlier this month, said that the group is asking for “the FCC to treat First Amendment-protected political speech the same way it already treats wireless calls about package deliveries, bank accounts, and doctor’s appointments”.

“There is no one at the FCC that has expressed any interest in moving to an order on this or any of the petitions, and there are zero plans to do so. The FCC seeks comment on petitions that come in as a matter of normal procedure,” a spokesperson for the FCC told Al Jazeera.

World.title: Australian MP critically injured after being hit by car in apparent attack
World.content:
Australian MP Helen Haines is critically ill in hospital in Melbourne after being hit by a car in what Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says may have been a deliberate attack.

The independent MP, 65, was struck outside her constituency office in Wangaratta, in the state of Victoria, on Monday afternoon.

A man, 43, from the nearby town of Tarrawingee was detained at the scene by a passerby and police say a knife was found in the car.

Police are investigating whether it was an "intentional act" but say they do not believe there is an "ongoing threat to the community".

Political leaders have expressed shock and dismay, with Albanese saying "there is no place for violence in a democracy".

While Albanese said it was too early to understand the motive behind what had happened, he did say the political temperature had been rising in Australia.

His Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke backed up that statement with figures showing that reports of threatening or harassing behaviour towards politicians had risen from 951 to 1,067 in the past year.

Haines was hit by a white Toyota Landcruiser at 15:35 (04:35 GMT) outside her office on Murphy Street in Wangaratta, police say.

The town, which has a population of around 30,000, is a few hours north-east of Melbourne.

A witness told Australian broadcaster ABC they had heard a bang and seen a woman pinned between two cars, external.

Haines was initially taken to a hospital in Wangaratta but later moved to Melbourne by helicopter.

After being subdued and detained by the passerby, the suspect was arrested by police.

Announcing that counter terror police were involved in the investigation, the prime minister said: "This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear."

In a statement, Victoria Police said: "At this stage, police are investigating as to whether this was an intentional act.

"It is not known yet if the parties are known to each other... The investigation remains ongoing."

World.title: Ukrainians dying because US restricting intelligence sharing, Zelensky adviser tells BBC
World.content:
Ukrainians have died because Kyiv is still not receiving reliable US warnings of incoming Russian attacks, according to a key adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky.

Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov told the BBC that lives had been lost because there had not been time to warn citizens about ballistic missile strikes, saying: "It's dangerous... I think it's really very bad... People [have] already died."

The adviser also said restrictions to Ukraine's use of the Starlink internet network were ongoing.

The White House said there had been no changes to intelligence sharing with Ukraine.

Ukraine first reported an interruption to US intelligence sharing last week, as a row with the Trump administrations over its controversial deal to import Russian oil sent relations to new lows.

Despite the denials from Washington, many in Kyiv suspect the issues are not a coincidence.

On Monday morning, Zelensky wrote on social media: "Overnight two ballistic missile attacks were reported on the capital, one without warning, the second with only minimal time to take shelter."

Hours earlier, an interview the president did with NBC was published, in which he said intelligence sharing had been restored after a three-day pause.

"We are very thankful for this," he said. "Only [the] United States has this unique intelligence to tell our side when Russia uses ballistic missiles."

But Beskrestnov told the BBC that American intelligence continued to be incomplete and inconsistent, and that the US had failed to provide a clear explanation for the issue.

"This looks very strange," he said. "Sometimes we receive this information before the attack, another time we [do] not."

He continued: "And for example, last night we received it, but... one minute before the attack."

However, he said other collaboration with US continues, adding: "Intelligence data keeps flowing, and the issue is solely with the air raid alert component."

Beskrestnov also said the US had given no clarity about who was responsible for the ongoing restrictions to the Starlink internet network and its military service Starshield, which Kyiv uses to provide connectivity for drones, helicopters and military communications.

Last week, Starshield restricted the speed at which mobile units could move while staying connected to the network to 100mph (160km/h).

This has limited Ukraine's ability to shoot down incoming drones or to launch mid-range drone attacks into Russian-occupied areas.

Starlink owner Elon Musk said last week that the US government ultimately controls access to Starshield, which was designed for the Pentagon, suggesting it may therefore be behind the restrictions. Trump has denied involvement.

Beskrestnov said he thought both issues occurring at the same time was "probably" a deliberate move to put pressure on Ukraine.

He told BBC News: "It's probably the United States trying to say [to] us, 'let's have the conversation, negotiation with Russia, you should find the compromise'."

Beskrestnov also said Ukraine had its own radar data to provide some limited warning of incoming attacks, but was urgently looking into using alternative communication systems.

He added: "Now we understand that something begins to happen with Starlink, and we're not sure what will be the next step.

"We understand that we should be prepared for some problems in future. And now we're thinking about an alternative for Starlink, not only for air defence, for communication between our forces, between our staff, for civilians also, because we don't know what we should expect in future regarding Starlink."

Earlier on Monday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there had not been a "pause" to intelligence sharing.

"I don't know where [Zelensky is] getting these things or why he's saying these things to the press," he told reporters on Monday.

Rubio said he could not comment on the incident, adding: "I know a few nights ago there was a software problem involving their early warning system."

The BBC has contacted Starlink for a response.

A White House official said there were no changes to intelligence sharing operations between the US and Ukraine.

The official spoke on background to discuss intelligence matters. Trump is focused on ending the war, the official said, and added that the US has provided more aid to Ukraine than any other country.

World.title: Kenya cult leader who told parents to starve children guilty of 191 murders
World.content:
The leader of a Kenyan doomsday cult, Paul Mackenzie, has been found guilty of murdering 191 people, all but one of them children.

Mackenzie ordered members of his cult to starve their children to death so they could "meet Jesus".

His doctrine said that education was forbidden and modern medicine was "evil".

Twenty-eight other leaders of his cult were also convicted of murder. They had all pleaded not guilty, repeatedly insisting that nobody was forced to die.

Warning: This article contains details which some people might find distressing.

Delivering her eight-hour judgement in the port city of Mombasa, Justice Diana Mochache said Mackenzie's followers believed he was "Jesus's mouthpiece".

One of his co-accused said Mackenzie had told his followers that anyone who "resisted the directive to fast must be forced to go to heaven through kicks and blows".

Burials inside the forest where the cult was based were called "weddings". Those who died "were celebrated as having wedded with Jesus", the judge said.

One witness stated that a pregnant woman had been barred from nursing her new-born baby, who died 12 days later. "She was instructed to fast to death and follow her children," the witness said.

Mackenzie's former head of security, Enos Amanya Ngala, was initially accused but then entered a plea deal and became a witness for the prosecution.

Mackenzie and other leaders of the cult also face a raft of other legal cases, including for terrorism, radicalisation and denying education to children.

But this is the first time the pastor has faced a verdict on the most serious charges of murder. He is due to be sentenced on 6 November.

He was arrested in 2023, after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast, where Mackenzie had led his followers from across the country.

Stephen Mwiti, 48, said he lost all six of his children to the cult. His former wife was one of those convicted of murder alongside Mackenzie.

"I'm a happy man, that all persons have been convicted," he told the BBC outside court.

"All six of my children died in Shakahola forest," Mwiti said ahead of the verdict, visibly emotional holding a photograph of his family. "I only found and buried the remains of my son Samuel."

World.title: Ex-OpenAI worker accused of planting device had Saudi support says court filing
World.content:
A Saudi national charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's meeting rooms has been accused of having "considerable support" from the Saudi government, according to a court filing, external in California.

US prosecutors claimed Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked for the AI firm, was in "frequent communication... with a member of the Saudi royal family", and say a member of the country's military paid for a one-way flight to Saudi Arabia for his wife and son after his arrest.

It was argued the 35-year-old engineer therefore posed a flight risk and should be detained, pending trial.

The Saudi government did not immediately respond to BBC requests for comment.

Alfozan had worked at OpenAI for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant an audio recorder.

The AI company discovered the device, which was plugged into the back of a TV in a conference meeting room and covered up with toilet paper, on 30 September.

A camera was placed in the room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering and appearing to look behind the television where the audio recorder had been inserted.

He was arrested by the FBI on 9 October and his contract with OpenAI was terminated.

The court filing claimed the suspect's alleged conduct could pose "a danger to the national security of the United States", because executives from the tech firm met with government officials in the room during the days the device was believed to have been installed.

It said Alfozan's arrest came three days before he was scheduled to fly from San Francisco to Riyadh on a one-way itinerary with his wife and son.

Following the arrest, the document claims the defendant's wife told FBI agents who interviewed her that "her US visa was expiring" and so she and her son were "permanently moving back to Saudi Arabia", and her husband intended to do the same.

On 10 October, the day after Alfozan was arrested, his wife and son flew from San Francisco to Doha, Qatar. They travelled on a one-way business class ticket booked and paid for by a Saudi military official.

"Ultimately, the defendant has little incentive to remain in the United States to see this case through," the prosecutors argued.

The FBI investigation is ongoing.

Alfozan is scheduled to âappear â in federal court in San Francisco later on Monday. If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (Â£188,000) fine.

World.title: Alberta heads to polls to decide whether to hold vote on separation from Canada
World.content:
People in the province of Alberta head to the polls on Monday to decide whether to hold a binding referendum at a later date on separating from Canada.

The vote was called earlier this year by the leader of the province, Danielle Smith, after a grassroots group gathered about 300,000 signatures on a petition that asked for a binding referendum on separation.

Many of those who support separation say the oil-rich province's economic growth has been stifled by the environmental policies of Canada's central government in Ottawa.

But those who want Alberta to remain part of Canada - who include Prime Minister Mark Carney - have called for the country to show unity in the face of external pressures.

Polls have suggested that the majority of Albertans would vote to remain in Canada, though the pre-vote debate alone has proven divisive.

Another group collected signatures for its own petition that opposed separation, which was signed by more than 400,000 people. The province's population is about five million people.

If Albertans do vote on Monday to move ahead with a binding referendum, that could happen as soon as 2027, Smith has said.

Smith's decision to allow Monday's vote came in spite of the fact that a court blocked the pro-separation petition, saying it failed to consult indigenous First Nations whose land would be affected if the province separated from Canada.

Following the judge's ruling, First Nations groups have branded Smith's decision to allow the voting process to play out as "undemocratic" and "authoritarian".

Smith, the leader of the United Conservative Party of Alberta (UCP), has defended her decision to put the issue to voters. She opposes separation herself, but says the process gives the province's residents a chance to have their say on the issue.

The key question on the voting paper will ask: "Should Alberta remain a province of Canada or should the Government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?"

World.title: Exiled critic of Rwandan president found beheaded
World.content:
A former Rwandan army sergeant major, who became an outspoken critic of President Paul Kagame, has been found beheaded in neighbouring Uganda.

Robert Kabera, 50, fled Rwanda after being accused of sexual assault, which he denied. He sought asylum in neighbouring Uganda, citing political persecution.

Ugandan police spokesperson Kituuma Rusoke on Monday said that Kabera's head had still not been recovered. His body was discovered by local residents on the outskirts of Kampala over the weekend.

The Rwandan government has not publicly commented on the killing. Several critics of Kagame have been killed, both in Rwanda and abroad.

His widow, Jeanne d'Arc Rwigema Uwizeye, told BBC Great Lakes in a written message that she now feared for her family's safety.

"It is scary. I feel crazy, the children and I don't have security," she said.

According to his family, Kabera had travelled to inspect a construction site about 45 km (30 miles) outside Kampala before his death.

Kabera built a public profile as a musician and YouTuber, attracting more than 144,000 subscribers to his channel, which featured over 800 videos, many criticising Kagame and his administration.

Reacting to news of his murder, exiled opposition group Rwanda National Congress (RNC) called for a thorough investigation and for those responsible to be brought to justice.

In a statement on X, the RNC said: "Today, his family is grieving, his voice is gone, and Rwandans in exile are confronting a terrifying question: where can we be safe?"

His death adds to concerns about the safety of Rwandan dissidents living in exile.

In 2014, Patrick Karegeya, a former Rwandan intelligence chief who helped set up the RNC, was found dead in his hotel room in Johannesburg, South Africa.

Karegeya fell out with President Paul Kagame and was arrested twice, serving an 18-month prison sentence for insubordination and desertion before fleeing to South Africa in 2007, where he became a vocal critic of the government.

Following his death, Kagame made remarks widely seen as a warning to other critics.

"Any person alive who may be plotting against Rwanda, whoever they are, will pay the price. Whoever it is, it is a matter of time," he said.

In 2019, South African authorities issued arrest warrants for two Rwandans accused of murdering Karegeya.

World.title: Houthi missile strike on Yemen camp kills 50 security recruits, local authorities say
World.content:
Monday's attack in Shabwa is one of the deadliest reported since the start of the escalation.

Shabwa province's media office said in a statement that ballistic missiles struck the Martyr Ahmed al-Sulaimani Training Centre, where recruits from several provinces were undergoing training to be members of the internal security forces. According to a preliminary assessment, 53 were killed and more than 200 injured, it added.

A video posted on social media appeared to show several bodies scattered across the ground.

Shabwa's deputy governor, Fahad al-Khalifi, told AFP news agency that hospitals in the province were overwhelmed and had been forced to transfer the most seriously wounded to neighbouring Hadramout and Aden, where the government is based. Some of them were in a critical condition, he said.

Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said the attack constituted a war crime because the internal security forces training centre was not a military target.

He also accused the Houthis of "attempting to fabricate a false media victory, boost the morale of its collapsing elements, and cover up the defeats and setbacks it is suffering across various combat axes".

The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, said in a statement that the missiles targeted a gathering of "Saudi enemy" forces at al-Alam camp, which he said was run by Saudi officers.

There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities.

In a separate development, Houthi-run media reported that a Saudi air strike on a home in the Sahar district of the Houthi-controlled northern province of Saada on Sunday killed at least 10 people and injured 23 others, many of them women and children.

According to the Houthi-run health ministry in north-western Yemen, a total of 141 people had been killed in Saudi strikes over the past seven weeks.

The government's health ministry, meanwhile, said last week that at least 1,282 people had been killed in the conflict across Yemen since 6 August.

In Saudi Arabia, at least 19 people have been killed in Houthi attacks targeting the kingdom's airports since the beginning of October.

Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.

A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.

The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

World.title: US airman dies as daredevil descent goes wrong before Texas college football game
World.content:
A member of the US Air Force died after he fell while abseiling from the ceiling of a Texas stadium ahead of a college football game.

Footage shows the serviceman plummet feet first to the turf midfield at San Antonio's 170ft (52 metre) high Alamodome on Saturday during a ceremony ahead of the game between the University of Texas at San Antonio and the Naval Academy.

The airman, identified, external by the military as Sgt Ian Patterson, a Tactical Air Control Party instructor at Joint Base San Antonio, died in hospital.

The incident is being investigated. The game between the UTSA Roadrunners and the Navy Midshipmen continued as planned following the tragic incident.

A collegiate athletic association said the decision to press ahead with the fixture was made before the airman's death had been confirmed.

"We extend our deepest condolences to his family, friends, teammates and members of the 57th Wing," the American Conference, external said in a statement.

US Air Force Brig Gen Scott Mills said in a statement issued by Nellis Air Force Base: "This tragedy is felt deeply across the 57th Wing.

"Tech Sgt Patterson and his service mattered immensely to our wing."

Patterson, from Fort Stewart, Georgia, had served in the US military for 15 years, according to Nellis Air Force Base.

He held multiple military decorations and was in 2022 named the Air Force Special Warfare Enlisted Instructor of the Year at the Headquarters Air Force level.

UTSA president Taylor Eighmy said: "I want to extend my deepest and most heartfelt sympathies to the service member's family, his fellow airmen, squadron and all those whose lives have been touched by this heartbreaking tragedy."

World.title: Nigerian Secondary School Flag Football League kicks off Season 5 with ₦3.7m prize pool
World.content:
The Nigerian Secondary School Flag Football League (NSSFFL) will begin its fifth season on Tuesday, with organisers promising cash rewards for top-performing schools and renewed efforts to expand opportunities for young athletes.

Nancy Damhindi, vice president of the Nigerian American Football Association (NAFA), said the competition has become a structured school-sports programme that connects students, schools, coaches, and communities through flag football.

Speaking at a press conference in Lagos on Monday, Ms Damhindi said the new season would build on the league’s progress while strengthening grassroots development and educational opportunities for student-athletes.

The preliminary competitions will lead to Aketi Bowl IV, the national championship scheduled for 17–20 November in Abuja.

League coordinator Oluwatobi Abe said the participating locations were selected following preseason assessments and development activities designed to determine which areas were ready to host competitive tournaments.

The locations announced for the preliminaries are Oyo, Akwa Ibom, Lagos, Ogun, Ondo, Benue, Cross River, Bayelsa, and Kwara states, along with the Federal Capital Territory (FCT).

Mr Abe, popularly known as Coach Tobi, said NAFA had conducted activation and reinforcement exercises in areas where the sport had previously been introduced.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“We were very intentional as to our developmental pathway,” he said, adding that the association used its assessments to select locations ready for the competitions.

National champions to receive ₦1 million

Mr Abe said the first-placed teams in the boys’ and girls’ divisions at the national championship would each receive ₦1 million.

The runners-up in both divisions will receive ₦500,000 each, while the third-placed teams will get ₦350,000 each, bringing the total prize money to ₦3.7 million.

He clarified that no prize money would be awarded at the state-level preliminaries, where the emphasis would remain on participation and identifying schools to represent their respective locations at the national tournament.

Mr Abe said the clarification followed questions about prize money during the previous season’s qualifiers.

The preliminary competitions are scheduled to run from 20 to 30 October, beginning in Oyo State at Bishop Phillips Academy, Iwo Road.

Other venues include Community Secondary Commercial School in Akwa Ibom; Government Secondary School, Garki, in the FCT; CMS Grammar School, Bariga, in Lagos; and St Peter’s Secondary School, Akure, in Ondo State.

Kwara will host its competition at Queen Elizabeth Secondary School, Ilorin, on 26 October, followed by Ogun on 27 October at St Peter’s Unity College, Abeokuta. Benue’s games are scheduled for 28 October at Goldman Secondary School, Gboko, while Bayelsa will conclude the preliminary schedule on 30 October at Bellary International Schools, Yenagoa. Cross River will also host its competition during the schedule.

Scholarships and international opportunities

Beyond the competition, NAFA seeks to create educational and international opportunities for participating students.

Mr Abe said Unique Open University has supported the league since its pilot season in Lagos in 2022, offering scholarships to outstanding teams.

Initially, scholarships were available to the first-, second- and third-placed teams in both divisions. From the second season, however, the awards were limited to the national champions in the boys’ and girls’ categories.

He said recipients could, with their parents, decide whether to study at the sponsoring institution or pursue other educational plans.

Mr Abe cited Divine Ayogu, a former Baptist Academy player who participated in the league’s pilot season and later represented Nigeria at the national team level, as an example of the opportunities the sport could provide.

He said a partnership with Nigerian American Football Outreach helped Ayogu secure a scholarship in the United States.

NAFA is also developing an under-13 programme to introduce younger children to the sport through the storybook Jojo and the Winning Play, alongside plans for a collegiate league.

Ms Damhindi said flag football’s scheduled debut at the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games could offer another pathway for Nigerian athletes, though qualification would depend on the applicable process.

Schools urged to sustain participation

Ms Damhindi acknowledged the Nigerian School Sport Federation (NSSF) as a key partner in organising the competition and connecting it to the country’s school-sports system.

She also highlighted support from Browns Nigeria and NFL FLAG through the One Ball, One Flag, One Future initiative, which provides about 2,000 American footballs and 5,000 flag football kits.

During the question-and-answer session, Segun Omodunni, representing the NSSF president, said school principals were required to confirm students’ enrolment before they could represent their schools, with state-level officials also involved in the verification process.

The organisers said their immediate priority was to deliver credible competitions and give students opportunities to develop their skills, pursue education, and progress toward national and international competition.

World.title: Dauda Lawal: When performance speaks louder than political noise, By Karen Ibrahim
World.content:
BPolitical criticism is essential to the smooth functioning of democracy, a fact that Governor Dauda Lawal, a political science graduate, undoubtedly understands. He also understands that the ultimate purpose of government is to serve the people, and not to satisfy the expectations of political stakeholders,who want the scarce public resources for themselves and cronies.

Against this background, the recent agitation by some politicians over his administration’s approach to governance should hardly have come as a surprise to close watchers of Zamfara State. For decades, political relationships in the state have been shaped by expectations of patronage. Lawal’s apparent determination to depart from that established pattern was therefore bound to generate resistance.

Governor Lawal’s measured response at the All Progressives Congress (APC) stakeholders’ engagement is very instructive. His proposed remedy—to publish contract beneficiaries, the projects awarded and the amounts involved—is significant. If implemented comprehensively, it would enable the people and other critical stakeholders to know who got what contract, at how much and whether the projects were executed according to specification. With this there would be no hiding place for those “chop and clean mouth” politicians who out of deliberate mischief attempted to pitch Governor Lawal against the people.

While Governor Lawal firmly rejected the claim that party members have been ignored and acknowledged a shortcoming in strategic communication, he has raised a fundamental question: should governance be driven by the personal expectations of political stakeholders or by what the government delivers to the wider population? Should party members not be more concerned about the performance of their elected officials than about what they have personally received? Should the question not be, “What has Zamfara State gained from our party?” rather than, “What have I personally gained?”

Political parties exist to win elections and implement policies that improve the lives of the people, not to serve as platforms for distributing contracts, appointments and other personal benefits among their members. No doubt, competent and committed party loyalists deserve recognition for their sacrifices and legitimate opportunities to participate in governance, but their contributions should reflect a sense of civic responsibility rather than an expectation of personal reward.

The true measure of a party’s success in government is its ability to translate its electoral mandate into tangible improvements in people’s lives. Roads built, schools rehabilitated, hospitals equipped, security strengthened and economic opportunities created are the dividends that justify the trust citizens place in a political party. When these benefits extend beyond party lines to the wider population, governance becomes an instrument of collective progress rather than an exercise in political patronage.

This is the fundamental distinction that political stakeholders must understand. Their loyalty should be measured not simply by what they have personally gained from the government, but by what the government has achieved under the mandate they helped secure. A party member who demands a contract but ignores the construction of roads in his community, or who complains about exclusion while public schools and healthcare facilities are being reconstructed, risks losing sight of the larger purpose of political participation.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

When Governor Dauda Lawal assumed office on May 29, 2023, Zamfara State faced real challenges that went far beyond what he had imagined. The administration inherited unpaid examination fees that prevented thousands of students from participating in the 2023 WAEC examination, billions of naira in outstanding WAEC and NECO exams liabilities, pension arrears accumulated over several years, salary backlogs and other issues that affected the smooth running of the state. His administration settled more than ₦3.2 billion in examination debts, and pension and gratuity liabilities that ran into billions of naira.

These were problems that adversely affected children whose educational futures were held hostage by the unpaid fees, pensioners who had waited in vain for their entitlements and workers who depended on their salaries to sustain their families. The government also inherited the challenge of insecurity, deteriorating infrastructure and weakened public service.It was against this background that Lawal declared a state of emergency in education and launched his Rescue Mission, with a promise to rebuild the state, and restore public confidence in governance.

Since taking office, Governor Dauda Lawal’s administration has undertaken concrete interventions to address Zamfara State’s inherited challenges. More than 500 schools have been renovated and equipped, while the declaration of a state of emergency in healthcare paved the way for the rehabilitation and equipping of general hospitals across all 14 Local Government Areas. A major milestone was reached in June 2025 with the commissioning of the remodelled Ahmad Sani Yariman Bakura Specialist Hospital, equipped with functional MRI and CT scan facilities.

Infrastructure and education provide further evidence of the administration’s priorities. In July 2024, the government approved the reconstruction of the 108-kilometre Magami–Dansadau road at approximately ₦81.19 billion to Dantata & Sawoe Construction Company as the lowest responsive bidder following due process. The road is vital to connecting farming communities to the markets. Meanwhile, an ₦11.7 billion initiative under the World Bank-supported AGILE programme seeks to improve access, retention and completion rates for adolescent girls in public schools.

These interventions, alongside investments in agriculture, workers’ welfare and revenue reforms, reflect an administration prioritising public investment. Its 2025 budget allocated approximately 72 per cent of expenditure to capital projects. Although insecurity and other inherited problems remain unresolved, these measures demonstrate a determined effort to address longstanding challenges through tangible projects and targeted interventions.

The challenges confronting Governor Dauda Lawal may well be one of the underlying reasons Zamfara State, like many other states in Nigeria, has struggled to achieve the level of development its people deserve. An entrenched feature of Nigeria’s political culture is the entitlement mentality of some party members, who regard political power as an investment from which they must recoup returns, rather than a public trust to be exercised in the collective interest.

This transactional approach to politics encourages patronage, distorts public spending priorities and places personal interests above the welfare of the people. In such an environment, some party members expect political loyalty to be rewarded with contracts and appointments, regardless of competence or the broader public interest.

What has made the difference in Zamfara State is Governor Dauda Lawal’s strength of character, resolve and commitment to delivering good governance. Leadership demands the courage to show the way, even when doing so comes at a political cost. Leaders must not allow the fear of electoral defeat to prevent them from taking difficult but necessary decisions in the public interest.

Evidence from Governor Lawal’s administration shows that he has not shut the door against party members or denied them opportunities to participate in governance.Rather, he has drawn a line between legitimate political inclusion and the entitlement to public contracts, regardless of competence or capacity. When it comes to major infrastructure projects, the public interest must take precedence, which explains the administration’s decision to entrust critical projects to reputable companies capable of delivering to the required standards.

How would Governor Lawal have delivered the world-class Gusau International Airport, undertaken major road projects and constructed the hospitals if he had allowed political pressure and the fear of offending influential party members to dictate his decisions? Sometimes, the difference between a leader who transforms a state and one who merely manages its problems lies in the courage to stand firm when the right decisions are politically inconvenient.

Across Nigeria, abandoned public projects running into trillions of naira illustrate the consequences of awarding contracts to politically connected companies that lack the capacity to execute them. The problem also extends beyond contract awards to public appointments, where political loyalty sometimes takes precedence over competence, leaving critical institutions in the hands of people ill-equipped to deliver results. When loyalty to political patrons becomes the principal qualification for public office or access to public contracts, the consequences are borne by ordinary people.

The scale of the problem is not merely a matter of public perception. BudgIT’s Tracka project-tracking report, published in February 2026, examined 2,760 federally funded projects across 28 states. It found that 471 projects were not executed, 99 had been abandoned, and 92 projects worth ₦15.07 billion were classified as fraudulently delivered.

Separately, the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC) has documented public assets diverted for personal use. Ultimately, patronage may reward a few politically connected individuals, but it is the public that pays the price.

The Rescue Mission represents a deliberate attempt to break with the practices of the past by placing public investment and service delivery at the centre of governance. The state’s budgetary priorities offer one measure of this commitment. In 2024, the government signed a ₦426.56 billion budget into law, with ₦308.2 billion, representing approximately 73 per cent, allocated to capital expenditure covering critical sectors such as security, education, agriculture, healthcare and infrastructure. The 2025 budget sustained this emphasis, allocating ₦393.33 billion, or approximately 72 per cent, to capital projects. Taken together, these figures indicate a consistent policy direction: prioritising investments intended to improve public infrastructure and the quality of life of citizens over the expansion of recurrent administrative spending.

The security challenges confronting Zamfara State must also be understood within Nigeria’s constitutional framework. Although governors are popularly regarded as the chief security officers of their states, they have no direct operational command over the armed forces, which remain under the control of the Federal Government. This often leaves governors in the position of glorified Chief Security Officers, held accountable for security outcomes without controlling the principal forces responsible for combating terrorism.

Governor Dauda Lawal has not used these limitations as an excuse. His administration established the Community Protection Guards, invested in operational vehicles and security equipment, and strengthened collaboration with federal security agencies. These interventions demonstrate a commitment to confronting the crisis within the limits of his authority.

The persistence of insecurity does not mean Governor Lawal has not given the fight his all. The people of Zamfara deserve security, and achieving it requires both sustained state-level initiatives and a more effective, coordinated response from the Federal Government.

The debate over Governor Dauda Lawal’s Rescue Mission should not be reduced to how many party members have secured contracts, appointments or other personal benefits. The most important question is whether Zamfara State is moving forward and whether public resources have translated into better schools, functional hospitals, improved roads and greater opportunities for its people.

The answer is a big yes. Governor Lawal has shown that his responsibility is to govern in the public interest, and not to surrender state resources to party members. The success of the Rescue Mission will ultimately be determined not by how many political interests it satisfies, but by the lasting improvements it delivers to the lives of the people of Zamfara State.

World.title: $6billion Mambilla Power Contract: Ex-governor Liyel Imoke testifies against former power minister Agunloye
World.content:
Former Minister of Power and Steel, Liyel Imoke, said Monday that the controversial Mambilla Hydropower station contract was awarded by his predecessor Olu Agunloye with the approval of the Federal Executive Council (FEC).

Mr Imoke said it was unnecessary to formally cancel the contract after he assumed office, because the contract never received the blessing of the FEC in the first place.

The former Cross River State governor was fielding questions at the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Abuja, where he appeared as the sixth prosecution witness in Mr Agunloye’s corruption trial.

Mr Imoke succeeded Mr Agunloye as the power minister in July 2003 and served until January 2007, during former President Olusegun Obasanjo’s administration.

Mr Imoke later became the Governor of Cross River State in May 2007 and served in that capacity until May 2015.

The Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) called Mr Imoke as its sixth prosecution witness against Mr Agunloye, who faces seven charges including disobedience to a presidential directive, conspiracy, forgery and receiving gratification.

The charges stemmed from his roles in the award of the $6 billion Mambilla Hydroelectric Power contract in May 2003 to Sunrise Power and Transmission Company Limited (SPTCL). An arbitration panel in Paris, France, recently cleared Nigeria of any liability regarding the contract while it accused PTCL of fraud in its …..

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The project was a proposed 3,050 MW hydroelectric facility located in Kakara village, Taraba State, which never saw the light of the day.

The prosecution said Mr Agunloye disobeyed a presidential directive issued in 2003 during a Federal Executive Council meeting regarding the contract.

It added that Mr Agunloye disobeyed the directive by signing a letter addressed to SPTCL, purportedly conveying “the approval of the Government of the Federal Republic of Nigeria for the construction of the 3,960 megawatts Mambilla Hydroelectric Power Station.”

The EFCC also accused Mr Agunloye of conspiring with Leno Adesanya, the major prompter of SPTCL who the agency indicated was at large, to falsify a document titled “Construction of 3,960MW Mambilla Hydroelectric Power Station on a Build, Operate and Transfer Basis” in 2003.

Other allegations include receiving gratifications of over N5 million from SPTCL and Mr Adesanya.

Mr Agunloye has denied all seven charges.

An arbitration tribunal recently exonerated Nigeria regarding the contract after finding that the award of the contract to SPTCL was tainted by bribery.

‘Null and void’

Trial Judge Jude Onwuegbuzie listened on Monday as Mr Imoke, under cross-examination by Mr Agunloye’s defence lawyer Adeola Adedipe, a Senior Advocate of Nigeria (SAN), maintained that the Mambilla power station contract was null and void in the first place, and required no formal pronouncement for its cancellation.

“A contract awarded in contravention of the FEC will not require cancellation,” the politician said.

“I did not cancel the contract because the FEC did not approve it, and so it was null and void. The minister does not have the power to award a contract.

“It is null and void as far as the FEC and the presidency did not give approval to the award of the contract.”

Similarly, the Mambilla Hydroelectric Power project became a subject of international concern.

Controversial contract

The project, first awarded in 2003 to SPTCL by the President Olusegun Obasanjo administration, is the subject of decades of a legal dispute. An arbitration tribunal in Paris recently resolved the matter in favour of Nigeria and against SPTCL, which had accused Nigeria of breach of contract.

Mr Obasanjo, in 2023, accused Mr Agunloye of fraudulently awarding the contract to the company without approval.

However, the former minister dismissed these claims, alleging that he was being used as a scapegoat to escape sanctions by the arbitration panel in Paris for abandoning contractual agreements on the project.

The project, intended to generate 3,960 megawatts of electricity, was designed to be executed on a build, operate, and transfer basis.

Imoke’s review of the contract

On Monday, Mr Imoke went down the memory lane about the controversial contract.

Mr Imoke, who took office as the power minister in July 2003, recalled writing a letter dated 3 September 2003 in response to SPCL’s payment inquiry about the Mambilla power contract.

“When I received the letter (from SPCL), I requested the file relating to the project. While reviewing the file, I saw the extract of the minutes of the FEC meeting and other documents.

“I read the deliberations and the directives from the FEC to the then Minister of Power and Steel, which stated that the memo of the defendant (Mr Agunloye) be withdrawn and directed the Minister to invite more proposals with a view to ensuring constructive deliberations and to explore various investment options,” Mr Imoke said, while being led in evidence by prosecution lawyer Abba Mohammed, a Senior Advocate of Nigeria (SAN).

Following his review, Mr Imoke said, he confirmed that the FEC did not approve the contract.

He said he then forwarded his findings to SPCL.

Fielding questions under cross-examination by Mr Adedipe, the former governor stated that he did not report Mr Agunloye.

Mr Adedipe asked, “As a good citizen of Nigeria, is it not in your place to report an unlawful act?”

But EFCC’s lawyer, Mr Mohammed, objected.

The judge sustained the objection and urged Mr Adedipe to rephrase the question.

He then asked the witness if he had a civic duty to report an unlawful act. Mr Imoke replied in the affirmative.

Mr Adedipe further asked if Mr Imoke’s record indicated that Mr Agunloye engaged in a criminal activity by awarding the contract.

Again, Mr Mohammed objected. He stressed that only the court could make such a finding.

The judge sustained the objection, asking Mr Adedipe to rephrase the question.

He then asked the witness if he notified the FEC after becoming aware of the circumstances surrounding the contract.

Mr Imoke answered, “No, I did not.”

Thereafter, Mr Mohammed requested an adjournment to attend to an urgent matter.

The judge granted the request and adjourned the case to 2 November.

Highlight of the case

In December 2023, EFCC declared Mr Agunloye wanted over the case.

The following day, Mr Agunloye surrendered to the EFCC for interrogation regarding the failed multi-billion-dollar Mambilla Hydropower project.

The anti-corruption agency later arraigned Mr Agunloye in January 2024 on charges regarding the Mambilla power project contract.

Following an amendment to the original charges less than a month later, the EFCC re-arraigned Mr Agunloye on 3 February 2024.

It again rearraigned him on 18 September 2025, after a further amendment of the charges.

The EFCC has already presented six prosecution witnesses in the trial.

Mr Agunloye faces seven counts of forgery, receiving gratification, and disobedience to presidential directives, all of which he pleaded not guilty to.

The trial has thrown up contention regarding the minutes of the 21 May 2003 Federal Executive Council (FEC) meeting during which the then-president was said to have issued the directive regarding the Mambilla power project that Mr Agunloye is accused of disobeying.

The prosecution earlier tendered the minutes, which originated from the Office of the Secretary to the Government of the Federation (SGF), as an exhibit in the trial.

Umar Babangida, an EFCC investigator who testified in the case as the third prosecution witness, told the court last year that Mr Obasanjo had been interviewed regarding the case.

He also cited a November 2023 letter Mr Obasanjo wrote to the incumbent Attorney-General of the Federation’s office, indicating his willingness to testify about the controversial Mambilla Hydroelectric Power project in any arbitration court or forum whenever the need arose or should his testimony be considered “necessary in the national interest”.

However, the prosecution has yet to confirm if Mr Obasanjo will be presented as a prosecution witness.

Mr Agunloye filed a suit against the EFCC, alleging abuse of his fundamental rights.

In March 2024, the Federal High Court in Abuja dismissed the suit.

However, earlier this month, Mr Agunloye won a libel case against the EFCC over the agency’s portrayal of the trial in a publication.

In the case, Judge Peter Kekemeke of the FCT High Court found the EFCC liable for defaming Mr Agunloye in its publication regarding the former minister’s trial.

The judge awarded N10 million against the EFCC for publishing the libellous article on its social media platforms against Mr Agunloye.

World.title: Soldiers rescue 11 passengers from kidnappers in Kogi
World.content:
Troops of the Nigerian Army have rescued 11 passengers after foiling a kidnapping attempt along the Kabba-Ayere Road in Kabba-Bunu Local Government Area of Kogi State.

The operation followed an encounter with suspected kidnappers on Sunday and a follow-up search on Monday, according to the army.

Hassan Abdullahi, an Acting Assistant Director of Army Public Relations at the 12 Composite Brigade, disclosed this in a statement issued on Monday.

Mr Abdullahi said troops deployed at the brigade’s patrol base in Kabba were on routine patrol when they received credible information about suspected terrorists attempting to abduct passengers travelling in a commercial vehicle.

“On arrival, the troops made contact with the terrorists and engaged them, forcing them to abandon the victims and flee into the surrounding bush,” he said.

The troops initially rescued nine passengers, including the vehicle’s driver. The driver and two other passengers who sustained injuries were evacuated for medical attention, while the commercial vehicle was handed over to the appropriate authority.

During a follow-up operation on Monday, troops searched the area and rescued two additional passengers who had fled into the bush during the encounter, bringing the total number of rescued passengers to 11.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Abdullahi said the operation demonstrated the army’s commitment to protecting lives and property and improving commuter safety in Kogi State.

Security concerns

The operation comes amid continuing security concerns in Kogi State, where kidnappings and attacks on travellers have raised fears about road safety.

In recent weeks, incidents involving abductions and killings have underscored the risks faced by residents and commuters travelling through parts of the state and neighbouring areas.

PREMIUM TIMES has reported on the abduction and death of Rosemary Adukwu, a councillor representing Ogugu Ward III in Olamaboro Local Government Area. She was reportedly abducted on 30 September while travelling to Onitsha, and her death was later announced by the local government chairman.

The army urged the public to provide timely, credible information to security agencies to support ongoing operations.

It said troops would sustain efforts to deny criminal groups freedom of action and protect residents and commuters across Kogi State.

World.title: Fake Drug Allegations: NAFDAC investigates death of NYSC member
World.content:
The National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC) has begun an investigation into the death of a member of the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC), Etimbuk Daniel, at the NYSC camp in Enugu State.

The Director-General of NAFDAC, Mojisola Adeyeye, disclosed this in a statement on Monday.

PREMIUM TIMES earlier reported that Mr Daniel died while undergoing his compulsory three-week orientation course at the NYSC camp in Enugu State.

The deceased corps member was the immediate past President of the Students’ Union Government (SUG) of Akwa Ibom State University. He hailed from Akwa Ibom State, South-south Nigeria.

Investigation

Earlier, the President of the National Association of Nigerian Students (NANS), Akinteye Afeez, in a statement posted on Facebook on 11 October, claimed an unnamed doctor had confirmed that the drug the NYSC member took in the orientation camp before his death was fake.

In the Monday statement, Mrs Adeyeye, a professor, said NAFDAC would investigate the claim and determine whether there was any “use of substandard or falsified medicines” in treating the NYSC member.

“The agency urges the public to avoid drawing conclusions about the cause of death pending the outcome of its investigations,” she said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The NAFDAC director-general said preliminary information indicated that the NYSC member was first taken to the camp clinic on Wednesday, 7 October, with symptoms suggestive of “severe malaria and a history of peptic ulcer disease.”

She explained that he was treated and stabilised before being discharged with oral medications the following morning.

Mrs Adeyeye said Mr David returned to the clinic on Saturday, 10 October, with right thigh pain, profuse sweating and recurrent episodes of low blood pressure.

“Due to his deteriorating condition and poor urine output despite fluid resuscitation, he was referred to the University of Nigeria Teaching Hospital, Ituku-Ozalla, where he became comatose.

“Resuscitation efforts were unsuccessful,” she said.

Preliminary findings on cause of death

Mrs Adeyeye said “preliminary clinical assessment” indicated that the suspected cause of death of the NYSC member was acute kidney injury secondary to severe dehydration and shock.

“The agency notes that these findings are preliminary and do not, in themselves, establish whether the medicines administered contributed to the death,” he said.

What we’ve done so far

The director-general said NAFDAC officers have now visited the camp clinic, interviewed the attending medical personnel and other staff, and collected samples of the medicines for laboratory analysis and further regulatory action as necessary.

“The agency will take appropriate action based on the outcome of its investigations,” she assured.

The official said NAFDAC has commiserated with the family of the deceased.

She urged Nigerians to remain calm as the investigation continues, assuring them that the agency is committed to ensuring medicines available in Nigeria meet the required standards of safety, quality, and efficacy.

“Members of the public may direct complaints and enquiries to the NAFDAC,” she said.

PREMIUM TIMES earlier reported that the Nigerian Senate, on Thursday, ordered an investigation into the death of the NYSC member.

The Senate also resolved to investigate the state of health infrastructure in NYSC camps across the country.

World.title: Activist urges Nigerians to reject candidates without environmental plans
World.content:
Environmental activist Nnimmo Bassey has urged Nigerians to deny electoral support to politicians without concrete plans to clean up polluted communities and restore damaged ecosystems, warning that the country’s emerging critical-minerals industry could repeat the environmental devastation caused by decades of oil extraction.

Mr Bassey, executive director of the Health of Mother Earth Foundation, said political candidates should be required to explain how they intend to address oil spills, gas flaring and environmental degradation before seeking votes.

“Any candidate that does not have concrete plans for the remediation and restoration of the deeply damaged environment should not be given a single vote by the electorate,” he said.

He spoke on 17 October at the eighth graduation ceremony and annual leadership lecture of the Kebetkache Women Development and Resource Centre/Centre for Leadership, Strategy and Development Leadership School in Port Harcourt, Rivers State.

Delivering a lecture titled Leadership for Environmental Justice in the Niger Delta, Mr Bassey challenged political leaders to account for the consequences of resource extraction on communities whose livelihoods depend on their land and waterways.

He cited the persistent fire at the Ororo-1 oil well off Awoye community in Ondo State, gas eruptions in Bille community in Rivers State, and an uncontrolled crude oil fire at Oil Well 9 in the Ofiomina-Ama Alakiri community in Okrika, also in Rivers, as examples of environmental crises that should inform voters’ decisions.

The Ororo-1 well fire has continued for years, while residents of Bille have faced threats from toxic gas emissions, according to previous media investigations.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

PREMIUM TIMES reported in June on the dangers posed by toxic gas leaks in Bille.

Mr Bassey’s remarks come on the heels of growing attention to Nigeria’s mineral resources following an agreement signed by Nigeria and the United States in September to attract American investment into the country’s estimated $700 billion mineral sector. The agreement is intended to encourage investment across the mining value chain.

The environmental activist warned that shifting from fossil fuels to minerals used in renewable energy technologies would not automatically produce a just energy transition if communities continued to lose their lands, livelihoods and access to natural resources.

“Changing the energy source without changing this underlying logic will not deliver justice,” he said, cautioning that mineral extraction could reproduce the same patterns of dispossession associated with the oil industry.

He explained that the proposed transition must be guided by environmental protection, community consent, public accountability and the equitable distribution of benefits.

Warning over mining

Mr Bassey said Nigeria’s pursuit of critical minerals raised concerns about community safety and the environmental consequences of mining, especially given the country’s history of pollution and weak accountability in resource extraction.

He recalled the lead-poisoning crisis connected to artisanal gold mining in Zamfara State, which killed hundreds of children in 2010, and referred to fatal mining-pit collapses in Plateau State.

He also cited the deaths of young mining suspects in custody in Niger State, arguing that the incidents reflected a leadership gap in the management of the country’s natural resources.

PREMIUM TIMES reported in September that at least 37 illegal mining suspects had died in detention in Niger State under controversial circumstances.

Mr Bassey warned that without responsible leadership, the pursuit of mineral wealth could expose more communities to environmental contamination, unsafe mining practices and the loss of livelihoods.

He said leaders must question whether communities had consented to extraction, whether legal requirements had been followed, what benefits residents would receive and how potential environmental damage would be prevented or remedied.

He also called for stronger checks on the Petroleum Industry Act, particularly its provisions for Host Communities Development Trusts.

Under the law, oil companies are required to contribute three per cent of their actual annual operating expenditure in the preceding financial year to the development of host communities.

However, Mr Bassey questioned the arrangement under which oil companies appoint members of the trusts’ governing boards and the provisions allowing funds to be used to repair petroleum infrastructure damaged by third parties.

He insisted that policies should be judged by their actual effects on communities rather than by the promises made when they were introduced.

Women, community leadership

Mr Bassey said environmental justice required leadership beyond elected officials and people in formal positions.

He identified women organising to protect their water sources, young people documenting oil spills, fishers demanding investigations and residents challenging pollution as examples of leadership in communities affected by environmental destruction.

He said women often bore the burden of environmental damage because of their roles in farming, fishing, collecting water, preparing food and caring for families, yet remained underrepresented in decisions about land, energy and natural resources.

He asked leadership institutions to equip women, young people and marginalised communities to participate meaningfully in decisions affecting their territories.

“True leadership listens before it speaks,” he said, adding that communities possessed knowledge and experience that should inform development decisions rather than being treated as passive recipients of government or corporate policies.

Mr Bassey also said development should be measured not by roads, buildings, public revenue, or economic growth, but by whether people can breathe clean air, drink safe water, feed themselves, and live without fear of environmental destruction.

“The Niger Delta does not need leaders who merely manage the consequences of injustice. It needs leaders who will work with communities to dismantle the conditions that produce it,” he said.

He asked the graduands to apply their training in public institutions and communities, stressing that leadership should be measured by the condition in which people, institutions and ecosystems are left.

He congratulated the graduating students and welcomed incoming students, urging them to prioritise accountability and public service over the pursuit of positions.

World.title: Nigeria’s Permanent Representative presents $14bn UN budget to Tinubu
World.content:
President Bola Tinubu has received the United Nations’ proposed 2027 budget from Nigeria’s Permanent Representative to the UN, Jimoh Ibrahim.

Mr Ibrahim, who chairs the UN General Assembly’s Fifth Committee on Administrative and Budgetary Matters, presented the seven-volume document to the president after its submission by the UN Secretary-General, Antonio Guterres.

He described the presentation as historic, saying it was the first time in 66 years that Nigeria would chair the committee responsible for the UN’s budget and administration.

“This is the first time in 66 years that Nigeria will chair the Budget and Administration Committee. It is the first time, and we do not know when it will happen again in history.

“So, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu is making history by being able to receive this budget. He is the first Nigerian president in 66 years to receive the UN budget from the United Nations,” he said.

According to the envoy, the proposed regular budget stands at about $3.4 billion, while the peacekeeping budget is about $8.5 billion.

He put the combined figure at about $ 14 billion, equivalent to between N36 trillion and N40 trillion.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“It is not a small matter for a country to receive the entire UN budget.

“I am happy that the president has received the seven volumes of the proposed budget.”

Mr Ibrahim said the document remained a proposal and would undergo detailed negotiations and approval by member states before implementation.

“It is the proposal submitted to member countries. Thereafter, the budget is discussed in detail, the figures are adjusted, and the final budget is approved before spending commences,” he explained.

He declined to disclose Nigeria’s expected benefits from the budget, saying negotiations with other committee members were ongoing.

“As for Nigeria, I do not want to discuss what Nigeria will get from the budget. That would be going too far, because my colleagues and I are still discussing it,” he said.

Mr Ibrahim also highlighted the scale of UN spending, citing the construction of a 260 million-dollar conference centre in Kenya.

“A lot is happening. As of today, the United Nations is building a $260 million conference centre in Kenya. You can see what that means,” he said.

Nigeria officially assumed the chairmanship of the United Nations General Assembly’s Fifth Committee, responsible for the organisation’s budget and administrative affairs on 3 September.

As Fifth Committee chair, Nigeria will oversee deliberations on the organisation’s budget, financial governance, human resources, institutional efficiency, oversight, and the resources needed to implement mandates approved by Member States.

NAN reports that the Fifth Committee holds a strategic position within the General Assembly, as decisions on peace and security, development, human rights, humanitarian operations, and other areas of the UN system ultimately require financial and administrative support.

Its recommendations therefore directly affect how the General Assembly finances and implements its mandates.

(NAN)

World.title: Abiodun swears in two new commissioners
World.content:
Ogun State Governor, Prince Dapo Abiodun, has sworn in Mr Olayemi Sanusi and Mrs Adenike Ademokun as commissioners, charging them to place the interest of the state above personal considerations, political differences and sectional loyalties.

Abiodun gave the charge on Monday during the swearing-in ceremony held at the Governor’s Office, Oke-Mosan, Abeokuta, where he urged the new commissioners to demonstrate integrity, humility, fairness and commitment to public service.

The governor charged them to remain accessible to the people, listen attentively to their concerns and exercise prudence in the management of public resources, stressing that their appointments must translate into tangible benefits for the people.

He also emphasised the importance of continuity in governance, urging the commissioners to preserve institutional knowledge, maintain proper records and ensure that ongoing projects and programmes were completed.

Abiodun advised them to familiarise themselves with the priorities of his administration, understand the status of existing projects and bring fresh energy, sound judgment and a strong sense of responsibility to their assignments.

“Public confidence grows when citizens can see that those they entrusted with leadership understand their needs and act to address them,” he said.

The governor further urged the new commissioners to embrace teamwork, respect the professionalism of the public service and collaborate effectively with the ministries, departments and agencies under their supervision.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Your ability to listen, inspire confidence, make informed decisions and translate policies into outcomes will determine the contribution you make to our collective mission.

“Bring your experience to bear, remain willing to learn and support your colleagues in the pursuit of common objectives,” he said.

Abiodun noted that the value of public office should be measured by the problems it helps to solve and the opportunities it creates, adding that the responsibility before members of the State Executive Council was to consolidate existing achievements, address unfinished priorities and leave behind a stronger and more prosperous Ogun State.

Describing the period as the final lap of his administration, the governor said the remaining months required urgency, discipline, political maturity and an unwavering commitment to excellence.

“We are now in the final lap of this administration. This period demands urgency, discipline, political maturity and a steadfast pursuit of excellence.

“Your appointments, therefore, come at a very significant moment. You are joining a government with substantial achievements and important responsibilities still to fulfil.

“History will assess our stewardship through the consequences of our decisions and the difference our service has made in the lives of the people.

“Let us, therefore, approach the months ahead with a clear sense of purpose and a determination to make every opportunity count,” he said.

Speaking on behalf of the newly sworn-in commissioners, Mrs Adenike Ademokun expressed appreciation for the confidence reposed in them, assuring the governor that they would not take the appointments for granted.

She pledged their commitment to giving their best in support of the administration’s efforts to sustain development and improve the welfare of residents across the state.

World.title: All I want to hear in Rivers is Tinubu – Wike says in meeting with Fubara supporters
World.content:
Nyesom Wike

By Davies Iheamnachor

Minister of the Federal Capital Territory and leader of the Rainbow Coalition, Nyesom Wike, has said that all he wants to hear in Rivers State is Bola Tinubu for a second term.

Wike also declared that supporting President Bola Tinubu’s second-term bid is the strategic key to unlocking unprecedented political appointments, infrastructure development, and lasting national relevance for the oil-rich state.

This came as the Minister had a strategic meeting with strong followers of the governor of the state, Sir Siminalayi Fubara, and Fubara-aligned Youth Leaders in Port Harcourt on Monday.

This came less than 24 hours after he (Wike) led members of the State Assembly, Local Government Area Chairmen and Top leaders of the coalition to a closed-door meeting of top supporters of the governor at the private residence of Fubara in Port Harcourt.

Addressing the meeting on Monday, Wike stressed that aligning with the federal government would secure the state’s position as a powerhouse in national politics.

The Minister urged party faithful, youth groups, and stakeholders to put past grievances behind them, forgive past missteps, and rally solidly behind President Tinubu.

Wike said: “All I want to hear in this state is Tinubu and nothing but Tinubu. If we play the role we are playing now, and we are one of the first three states that get the highest number of votes, we will get more of the appointments.”

Wike noted that the current administration has broken records in terms of high-profile federal appointments awarded to indigenes of the state.

He opined that a massive voter turnout for the President would guarantee even greater stakes and bumper opportunities for the state’s populace, particularly the youths.

Wike, while reflecting on his political journey and stewardship, noted that his primary motivation is ensuring that the state remains a central fixture in national decision-making, where no president can afford to sideline the state’s leadership.

He noted that local political structures across different platforms are collapsing into a unified front to back the President, adding that political transitions and alliances naturally come with friction, rumours, and minor disagreements

Wike, however, called for calm and reconciliation at the grassroots level, assuring those who may have felt sidelined that structured reconciliation committees are working to ensure no genuine member of the family is left behind.

He added: “We are talking for survival and growth. I am not going to be governor again; this is for your own interest. I want this state to grow. I want this state to play an important role in the politics of Nigeria.”

Earlier, Mr Ezebunwo Ichemati, former Mayor of Port Harcourt, who spoke on behalf of the governor’s supporters, declared the readiness of the group to work closely with Wike to deliver Rivers to Tinubu and other candidates under the Rainbow Coalition.

Ichemati said that the meeting marked a major turning point in the Rivers political landscape, signalling a consolidated front between the Wike and Fubara camps as strategic preparations intensify for the 2027 general elections.

The former Mayor declared that the group is fully committed to joining forces with the political coalition to deliver Tinubu, including Mr Kinsley Chinda, in the 2027 election.

Ichemati said: “Every family has its own peculiarity in problems. What matters most is that the family comes together, the children watch what has divided them, and decide to move forward.

“If today a marriage faces a problem, some children will go to their father, some will go to their mother. But when a truce is made, the family comes back together—and that is what has happened today.”

World.title: They thought I’d be sleepy – Tinubu thanks ADC for keeping him awake
World.content:
By Bayo Wahab

President Bola Tinubu has taken a swipe at the African Democratic Congress (ADC), thanking the opposition party for keeping him awake as he addressed supporters of the CityBoy Movement and the Relax Tinubu Is Fixing Nigeria (RTIFN) group.

“Some people thought by now I would be tired and sleepy since I arrived here on time, thank you ADC,” Tinubu said during a ceremonial meeting with the support groups in Abuja on Monday.

The remark comes as Tinubu prepares for the 2027 presidential election, in which former Vice President Atiku Abubakar is the ADC’s presidential candidate.

The President said the grassroots mobilisation efforts of the support groups would allow him to rest easy, expressing confidence in their reach and organisational structure.

According to him, the CityBoy Movement had introduced a new approach to political mobilisation by building a network beyond the gathering of crowds at political events.
