World.title: France vows to crack down after protests spiral out of control
World.content:
Paris — French officials were considering declaring a state of emergency and implementing local curfews Monday as the nation reeled from a weekend of violence. Widespread anti-government protests in many large cities descended into riots, with damage to historic properties and thousands of arrests.

In hard-hit Marseille, France's second-largest city, all large gatherings were banned Monday in the wake of the violence, which started weeks ago as protests by young people furious over the state of their schools, but quickly snowballed into national demonstrations over the rising cost of living and declining public services.

The 19th-century town hall in the city of Limoges was burned to the ground on Saturday by masked rioters who hijacked marches across France, looting stores, torching cars and buildings and clashing with police as the protests turned violent.

More than 2,500 people have been arrested, France's Justice Ministry said.

The U.S. State Department issued an advisory Monday urging Americans to "avoid the areas of the demonstrations."

A man walks past a row of burned vehicles on Rue Yves Toudic, destroyed amid nationwide protests against the cost of living, in central Paris, Oct. 19, 2026. Kiran RIDLEY/AFP/Getty

In an address Sunday evening, French President Emmanuel Macron, vowed that "those who sought to bring down the republic will be held accountable."

Speaking Monday, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu blamed at least some of the violence on "an ultra-left movement intent on orchestrating profound disorder in the country leading up to the presidential election" in April.

He said police "had lost control" during the unrest, and as the Yellow Vests protest movement, which organized the weekend rallies that turned violent, called for a new round of demonstrations on Saturday, he called for regional authorities to impose "partial" and "localized" curfews to protect businesses.

"I'm absolutely determined to restore public order," Lecornu said, adding that the government was ready to impose a national state of emergency, "if needed."

Speaking of the alleged agitators, Lecornu said there was "⁠an entire network that could be mobilized to challenge the presidential election schedule and the very holding of the presidential election," adding that the government was committed to protecting the country's democratic process.

⁠"There is no way we will allow violent minorities to impose an agenda of violence and, quite obviously, prevent us from holding this election," he said, acknowledging that the protests by high school students over classroom conditions were legitimate, but adding that "the freedom to demonstrate is being undermined."

While French officials have not suggested any link between the unrest and immigration, President Trump claimed one in a brief social media post on Monday, saying: "The migrants have taken over France. They must CLOSE THE BORDERS, FAST!"

Damage to landmarks

Capital city Paris has seen the worst of the unrest, and residents woke up Monday to streets littered with debris and burned vehicles. But severe damage was inflicted across the country, with centuries of heritage being damaged or destroyed by flames.

Fire guts the historic City Hall building in Limoges, central France, during protests Oct. 17, 2026. PASCAL LACHENAUD/AFP/Getty

Video captured the moment the clock tower of Limoges' historic town hall, in southwest France — a landmark that had stood for nearly 150 years, surviving both World Wars — was engulfed in flames and came toppling down.

The tourist office in the eastern city of Lyon stood for years in one of France's most famous, beautiful city squares. But vandals, many of them masked, rampaged around the building and set it on fire, too.

The city hall in Marseille, on the Mediterranean coast, which dates back to the 1600s, was also stormed and vandalized with graffiti.

Protesters block entrances to the Louvre Museum in Paris to express their support for a nationwide student protest movement, Oct. 19, 2026. Luc Auffret/Anadolu/Getty

On Monday, hundreds of protesters gathered outside Paris' iconic Louvre Museum in support of the school students who initiated the demonstrations more than a month ago.

What protesters say they want

The protests began as demonstrations by high school students about a month ago, with thousands taking to the streets peacefully to vent frustration over crumbling schools, overpacked classes and teacher shortages.

But it grew into a nationwide outpouring of anger over the soaring cost of living — salaries that aren't keeping up with inflation, and crumbling public services.

More than 500,000 people took to the streets on Saturday, when the unrest peaked. But as the government alludes to, there have also been opportunists — people and groups looting, vandalizing and attacking police as they try to control the crowds.

"There are so many reasons," Kamil Alahyan, 18, told French news agency AFP. "The politicians who lie, the ultra-rich who've been raking in more and more wealth over the last 10 years … everyone has a different reason."

Anae, a 24-year-old student in Grenoble, told AFP she had completed her studies but now has "no income. I've got no money. I don't necessarily have a secure future. Our planet is burning. And we've got a government that's making a joke out of us!"

World.title: The AI doom scenario you've never heard of may be hardest to stop
World.content:
It seems that almost daily, a big tech company releases a new AI-driven digital assistant. Muse by Meta, Gemini by Google, dots by OpenAI. By the time this article is published, a new one from [insert tech company here] will probably have a press release touting its ability to manage your work and life — to take things off your plate, automate your processes, speed up your tedious tasks. It sounds helpful and, to lower the bar, harmless.

But some researchers say this is the beginning of a treacherous path for humankind, one where bots take more and more off our plate until all that's left is an empty vessel, and we human users become nothing more than thoughtless "approvers."

It's not just a threat to jobs. They warn that allowing our skills and knowledge to deteriorate, and surrendering our critical thinking to AI, poses an existential danger to humanity.

One term for this path is "gradual disempowerment" — a scenario where AI displaces human labor in the economy, replaces human decision-making in all key societal concerns, erodes human creativity, and degrades human cognition along the way.

And though the word "gradual" is in the name, that does not mean the problem is something to worry about far in the future, according to experts.

"I put gradual disempowerment on the very top of my list," said Jay Chooi, the founder and CEO of Robocurve, a company that tracks and measures AI-driven robotics capabilities.

Chooi believes gradual disempowerment is just as worrisome as the threat of engineered pandemics and more destructive cyberattacks, which could be accelerated by capable AI.

"It's a civilization-scale problem," Chooi said of gradual disempowerment. "A lot of people feel very powerless, because it requires a lot of effort and a whole-of-society approach to solve it."

What is "gradual disempowerment" and how could AI cause it?

The term "gradual disempowerment" stems from a paper published in early 2025.

At the heart of the gradual disempowerment scenario is AI technology continuing to advance in capabilities, as it has rapidly since the launch of ChatGPT in 2022.

AI models may soon be better at nearly all cognitive tasks than humans — solving frontier math problems, doing hard science, coding, writing and creating art and music, to name a few of the areas where AI increasingly excels. At the same time, advances in robotics could lead to AI-powered robots performing better than humans at physical labor like packing boxes, constructing homes, building cars, painting murals, mining for rare minerals, and even building IKEA furniture.

We like to think that in an ideal world, the best applicant generally gets the job, and they are paid based on the level of demand for their skills. But imagine if a human is never the best person for the job. That's a world that some AI prognosticators and whistleblowers expect.

It's a world where an AI agent or AI-enabled robot is better at every task and sub-task that it takes to do my job and your job. They move faster than us, think deeper, have more patience and stamina. They more cordially answer phones, do more thorough research, and more dexterously wield a scalpel or a nail file. Plus, they never need to sleep or take sick days, they never show up hungover or moody, and they never threaten to leave for a better job.

To picture gradual disempowerment more clearly, here's a scenario: Let's say you run Hammer Co., a company that manufactures hammers. You have line workers who shape the steel heads and wooden handles and then fit them together, and managers who keep the factory running smoothly. You have people who maintain your supply chain and teams to handle marketing, sales, accounting, and all the other functions that help your business thrive.

But then a tech company comes out with AI-powered Hammer Bots. The robot workers can make hammers far faster than your human workers, while AI agents can run the business side with little oversight. They'll work all night, never make mistakes, and cost far less than your happy, well-paid staff. You don't want to fire your human workers. You see them around town and have known their families for years, after all.

But your competitor gets the Hammer Bots. Most customers just want the cheapest hammers — they don't care who or what makes them. As CEO of Hammer Co. you either compete or die. So you fire all your humans and get Hammer Bots to replace them.

Now, try to envision this is the case for every company, and every job. With normal free-market incentives, the company that stays loyal to its human employees will be outcompeted by the company that gets AI to do the work instead.

Here's where gradual disempowerment comes into play.

The fewer humans that participate in labor, and the more work that's outsourced to AI agents, the more humanity becomes dependent on AI for decision-making and the more human skills deteriorate. How long until the finer points of hammer-making will be forgotten?

With AI making all our complex decisions for us, humans become less capable of understanding and overseeing those decisions or of pushing back against them.

"If people aren't actually practicing the skills that the agents are doing for them, they lose the ability to have that skill, and so now you become reliant," said Margaret Mitchell, an AI research scientist at Hugging Face and co-author of another recent paper on the importance of keeping humans in the loop in an AI world.

"What happens when something goes wrong? There's no human you can point to who can fix it. So now you've become fully dependent on these systems to fix themselves, and what if that's not possible?"

A risk to democratic governance

It's not just economics and labor at risk. Take the military, for example. All or most decisions in war involve humans today, even if AI contributes to the process, but the balance is likely to shift as the technology becomes more capable.

If the United States uses AI to make decisions in battle, its enemies across the field will be pressured to do the same. The side that leans more heavily on humans will be slower and less efficient. Human soldiers need food and rest. Robot soldiers will not. Human decision-makers are limited in the scenarios they can conceive and plan for; AIs can take into account all of human knowledge.

"The states need citizens. They need us because we pay taxes and we fight for the states in the military," said Jan Kulveit, a co-author of the gradual disempowerment paper and co-founder of ACS Research Group.

States also use people to enforce laws. But what if law enforcement is all automated in the future?

"If, or when, existing states don't need their citizens, they're less likely to be democratic," said Kulveit.

Kulveit compares theoretical future countries that are mostly run by AI to oil states today. He said the oil states tend to be authoritarian because they don't rely on most of their citizens to pay taxes and don't need citizens' votes to rule. States that rely on AI to run the economy and military could have similar outcomes, said Kulveit.

If that is the case, and citizens no longer are the backbone of labor or warfare in a world of gradual disempowerment, then humans lose perhaps their greatest leverage against those in power.

"A lot of people are talking about rogue AI hacking into data centers and taking over the world, but it is not in the mainstream consciousness that like AI could literally take over the world just by continuing to do what it's supposed to do, which is automating everything," said Jay Chooi of Robocurve.

"Organizations are all going to have a very strong economic pressure, and political pressure, to phase out humans and move work more and more into robots or AI."

How does humanity avoid gradual disempowerment?

Humans ceding control to AI, say the gradual disempowerment authors, is almost a natural transition once very advanced AI is here.

Gradual disempowerment "does not need to emerge from a deliberate scheme or powergrab by AI systems," wrote Kulveit and his colleagues. "In the short-term, it is being incentivized by the perceived value that AI systems can bring to economic, cultural and state functions."

"We can't be in the situation where we are competing with the machines," said Kulveit. "Because if we are just competing with the machines, we will probably lose."

The gradual disempowerment authors believe stopping our disempowerment may be a heavy lift for humanity, since it involves complex systems that feed into each other — government, culture, and the economy.

"This may be a bigger challenge than merely preventing AI systems from pursuing overtly harmful goals," they write.

One first step in slowing disempowerment is keeping indicators of how much work is being ceded to AI, and of what kind of specific jobs AI systems are capable of handling. If thousands of workers are being displaced by AI in, say, call center jobs, it helps to know that in granular detail.

But measurement isn't enough without action, Mitchell said. She argues that removing humans from the loop in AI processes both worsens oversight and degrades the skills of the human overseer. Therefore, companies and leadership in all fields must take proactive steps to keep humans engaged.

"This general practice within tech is we want our systems to be frictionless," said Mitchell, referring to the idea that everything should move fast and without obstacles. "There's this sense that the less friction the better, but there's been a push within the more ethical AI community that strategic friction can be good because it can draw people's attention to critical issues that otherwise they might overlook."

Mitchell argues that strategic friction — keeping humans in the work loop at predetermined steps — can be done both by developers of AI, companies like OpenAI and Anthropic and Google, and by companies and organizations that deploy AI. Thoughtful and purposeful design of AI can benefit society as a whole, and the individuals who use it.

Kulveit agrees that AI should be thoughtfully designed to add value to humans, not necessarily replace our every task.

"You want to carve out places where we agree that we will not allow competitive pressures to remove humans from the loop," he said. "It would be nice if the companies train the AIs to be more complementary to humans. Currently, the AIs are implicitly trained to be a replacement for humans. But you can imagine training the AIs so they are better at explaining to us what's happening."

Kulveit is describing AI that doesn't just spew out the answers to whatever question you ask it, at the very least in sectors where it is critical to include human expertise and decision-making, like war. Quick and easy answers can be helpful, but they can also make you dependent and credulous, believing anything the chatbot tells you, whether right or wrong.

But AI can be more than that. It can help you not just by doing the work for you, but by educating you along the way. That way the human worker continues to learn while using AI as a partner, not a substitute.

"There has been such a singular focus on capability or functionality of these systems to the detriment of people, to the detriment of users," said Mitchell. "If your only goal is to get a high score on a benchmark, then you are not going to be taking into account cognitive support design. But if your goal is to make a system that works really well for people — like if the race is for a utility as opposed to benchmark score — then you end up designing fundamentally different systems."

If gradual disempowerment really is a large-scale risk, compared to more talked-about doom scenarios — like AI helping to design bioweapons or chemical weapons — it may suffer from a relative lack of vividness.

"We know what it means for a robot to take over the world. We know what it means for countries to nuke each other," said Chooi. "AI taking over the world is very legible in the human consciousness. But gradual disempowerment? No one has made a movie about gradual disempowerment."

But to Chooi, gradual disempowerment is very easy to picture.

"All the organizations have the incentives to adopt it and phase out humans," he said. "This is a very logical conclusion. It's not very hard to see it."

World.title: Elon Musk pledges to give a SpaceX share to every U.S. child
World.content:
Elon Musk said in a social media post on Monday that he plans to give one of his SpaceX shares to each child in the U.S., writing that the gift "will be the first of many."

Musk didn't specify how the shares would be distributed or other details of how the pledge might be fulfilled. The offer arrived a day after artificial intelligence company Anthropic announced that it will commit 5% of its shares to a new "public benefit" fund.

Anthropic said it will contribute an additional 2% of shares at its board's discretion for every 50% increase in the company's value, above a set threshold.

Shares of SpaceX, which will report quarterly earnings on Tuesday, rose $3.46, or 2.7%, to $149.49 in Monday morning trading.

The SpaceX CEO is the company's largest shareholder with a 10.5% stake, according to financial data firm FactSet. His stake included 4.8 billion shares of SpaceX when the company went public earlier this year, an event that briefly made Musk the world's first trillionaire.

There are about 73 million children in the U.S., according to Census Bureau data.

Musk, the world's richest person, is currently worth about $904 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

Anthropic made its pledge to commit a portion of its shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, which it described as "a new entity," at a time when AI researchers from leading labs are warning of doomsday scenarios with potentially catastrophic outcomes that extend far beyond job losses.

Anthropic said the company has a two-pronged mission, with its research providing both a public benefit component and for-profit value. The new fund will give it more flexibility to make large donations to nonprofits or gifts to specific populations, the company added.

Anthropic also called out AI's impact on workers, acknowledging that tech advances could "cause instability" for many employees, and noted that it has already committed $200 million to analyzing and addressing AI's effects on parts of the labor force.

"Because of the way the Fund is structured, the more Anthropic grows, the larger the share of the company that can be dedicated expressly to the public good," Anthropic said.

Musk could conceivably use the recently created Trump Accounts program to gift SpaceX shares to U.S. children. The accounts, under new rules laid out by the Treasury, allow donors to deliver stock to the accounts without paying capital-gains taxes.

Michael Piwowar, executive director of Georgetown McDonough's Psaros Center for Financial Markets and Policy, called Trump Accounts the "perfect vehicle" through which Musk could deliver SpaceX shares to recipients.

"One of their great features, in addition to $1,000 seed money, is the ability of philanthropists to make philanthropic donations to a class of individuals," he said.

The Treasury Department is automatically enrolling up to 60 million children in the Trump Accounts program.

Piwowar added that with Musk's donation, "American children will immediately be invested in the American dream."

The tax-deferred accounts, created under Mr. Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill tax and spending bill for U.S. citizens born between Jan. 1, 2025, and Dec. 31, 2028, are eligible for a $1,000 seed donation from the government.

World.title: Starvation cult leader found guilty of murder of 190 children
World.content:
A self-proclaimed Kenyan preacher and his associates were found guilty of murdering 191 people, all but one of them children, in an infamous starvation cult by a Mombasa court on Monday.

"I am satisfied that the prosecution has proved the case against all the 29 accused persons for the murder of 190 children and one adult," the judge said.

Hundreds of bodies have been discovered since 2023 at the cult base inland from the Kenyan beach resort of Malindi, in what became known as the "Shakahola Forest Massacre."

Paul Mackenzie is alleged to have incited his acolytes to starve to death in order to "meet Jesus."

Mackenzie and his associates pleaded not guilty to 191 counts of murder in 2024. He has also denied charges of manslaughter and terrorism in separate cases.

The Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions welcomed the "momentous" verdict, with director Renson Ingonga telling reporters: "Getting a conviction of such counts...is not something that comes that easily."

In the three years since the grisly discovery, more bodies of children, women and men have been unearthed, bringing the total to well over 400.

Self-proclaimed pastor Paul Mackenzie looks on during his court appearance at the Mombasa Law Court in Mombasa on Oct. 19, 2026. SIMON MAINA /AFP via Getty Images

Mackenzie looked impassive as he arrived at Mombasa Law Courts on Monday with 29 other accused, who descended from a barred-window bus handcuffed in pairs.

Relatives of the victims were also in court, many making their way to Mombasa from rural communities along the coast.

Francis Wanje, 62, lost eight family members, including his daughter and two grandchildren, in Shakahola.

"This day, to me, is a very, very important day," he told AFP before the session started.

"We are expecting a ruling that will be a lesson to the whole public, so that such kinds of things will not happen again," he said, expressing anger over the initial government inaction.

There have been calls in Kenya for tougher regulations on religious organizations after it emerged that Mackenzie had been arrested twice in the past but released.

The prosecution alleges that Mackenzie "initiated and directed" extreme fasting at his 800-acre ranch in Shakahola Forest, claiming there was a "structured hierarchy of death" which said children should die first, followed by teenagers, women and then men.

The children mostly died from starvation, but also from "asphyxia, neck compression and traumatic head injury," prosecutors said, based on postmortems and police reports.

Mackenzie's lawyers said the case was "largely founded on circumstantial evidence, hearsay accounts and inconclusive forensic findings."

Case exposed

Mackenzie was arrested in April 2023, after a rights group tipped off authorities and some followers were rescued.

The subsequent police operation exposed hundreds of shallow graves, with a soaring death toll that required a pause in excavations as local morgues ran out of space.

The Kenya National Commission on Human Rights said in 2024 that the death toll was 429. Some victims are still unidentified.

In January, Mackenzie was charged over another 52 bodies found at a nearby village.

The exhumed bodies of victims of a religious cult are laid out in the village of Shakahola, near the coastal city of Malindi, in southern Kenya Sunday, April 23, 2023. AP

The self-styled pastor has a history of extremism and evaded law enforcement for years.

He established the Good News International Church in 2003, and set up branches in Nairobi and along Kenya's coast that attracted thousands of devotees, though he claimed it closed in 2019.

Followers have told their families and officials they believed Mackenzie when he preached that starvation was the path to salvation. He allegedly split members into smaller groups assigned biblical names. It's believed these smaller groups died together and were buried together in mass graves.

State pathologists have said many of the exhumed victims died of starvation, but some showed signs of strangulation.

Mackenzie was arrested in 2017 over charges of "radicalization" but was acquitted. He was arrested again in 2019 in relation to two child deaths at Shakahola, but released on bail.

Investigators have said Mackenzie was a taxi driver in the early 2000s, before he created the Good News International Ministry. Locals have said he quickly drew followers with fiery sermons at his church on the coast in Malindi, then from across Kenya with his online presence.

Several surviving members of the group have told family members that what he preached would often come true, citing as an example his prediction that "a great virus" would come, just before COVID-19 hit the country. As people struggled during the pandemic, financially and medically, Mackenzie preached about leaving the difficulties of life behind and "turning to salvation."

World.title: Australian prime minister says lawmaker critically injured by car is 'no accident'
World.content:
Australian prime minister says lawmaker critically injured by car is 'no accident'

toggle caption i Mick Tsikas/AAP Image via AP

MELBOURNE, Australia — A car hit an Australian federal independent lawmaker on Monday, critically injuring her in an apparent deliberate attack, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said. The driver was arrested.

Helen Haines, 65, was struck by a Toyota Land Cruiser SUV outside her electoral district office mid afternoon in the city of Wangaratta in Victoria state, a police said.

Albanese said the national counterterrorism team, incorporating police and intelligence agencies, was investigating.

"This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear. We don't know what the motivation is," Albanese told Australian Broadcasting Corp.

toggle caption i Lukas Coch/AAPIMAGE via AP

The 43-year-old driver was arrested at the scene by a passerby. He will be interviewed in relation to the incident, police said.

Sponsor Message

"A knife was located by police and seized from inside the Toyota," police said.

"At this stage, police are investigating as to whether this was an intentional act," police added.

Haines, who was first elected to the Parliament in 2019, was taken to a hospital with critical injuries, police said.

The episode has renewed safety concerns for Australian lawmakers, in a country where politicians have historically been highly accessible to the public and usually go about their business without security officers present. But public incitement against officials is growing.

Australian Federal Police Commissioner Krissy Barrett said in 2025 that threats against parliamentarians had doubled over the past three years. Police data showed more than 1,000 such threats against politicians in the 2025-2026 financial year, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Monday.

Albanese told the ABC it was "unfortunate" that an increasingly polarized political climate had already led to security changes for Australia's lawmakers.

"I think there has been a rise in temperature and there has been too much shouting, not enough discourse, not enough polite conversation and disagreement," he said Monday. There was "no question" that social media played a part, Albanese added.

In Britain, murders of politicians have prompted bolstered security. Labour lawmaker Jo Cox was shot and stabbed in 2016 by a far-right extremist, and Conservative David Amess was stabbed in 2021 by an attacker inspired by the Islamic State group.

Sponsor Message

In July, the former politician and reality TV contestant Ann Widdecombe was found slain with a hammer at her home. A man has been charged with murder and terrorism-related offenses.

World.title: 2026 midterms could be the most expensive on record. And, Macron condemns protests
World.content:
2026 midterms could be the most expensive on record. And, Macron condemns protests

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

The 2026 midterm elections are set to become the most expensive on record. More than $15 billion has been raised to influence the outcome and control of Congress.

toggle caption i Justin Sullivan/Getty Images

🎧 Democratic nominees in House and Senate races are raking in incredible amounts of donations, even though the Democratic Party remains unpopular, NPR's Stephen Fowler says. Republicans are also unpopular, largely due to issues like the war in Iran, gas prices and the economy. A few megadonors, such as Elon Musk, are donating money to super PACs to try to push voters to elect Republicans. In the 13 competitive races highlighted in the Cook Political Report, Republicans are being outraised by a 5-to-1 margin. Both parties are spending heavily, indicating that Democrats might have a chance to win in several locations. Currently, 75% of planned ad buys are in toss-up races or those leaning Republican.

At least one person died and more than a dozen were injured in a major Ukrainian drone strike yesterday on Saint Petersburg, Russia's former imperial capital. The attack targeted strategic sites, including a key port oil terminal. Over the weekend, Russian missile strikes in Ukraine killed at least 11 people. This conflict continues as President Trump says that relieving pressure on Russia is the best way to end the war.



🎧 The recent attack on Saint Petersburg appears to mark the largest one on the city since Russia's 2022 invasion, NPR's Charles Maynes tells Up First. While it's unclear how many drones struck the city, Russia's Defense Ministry reported intercepting 1,000 drones across various regions that night. Trump seems to be working to protect Russian oil facilities after cutting a deal with President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel. The move was aimed at lowering gas prices for U.S. voters before the midterm elections. Trump has called previous Ukrainian strikes a "disgrace," even as Russia continues to strike Ukraine, Maynes says. He adds that the president blames President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for attacks that allegedly raise U.S. fuel prices, despite economists attributing the price increase mainly to Trump's war in Iran.

French President Emmanuel Macron denounced violence over the weekend that he says has overshadowed largely peaceful protests across the country. The unrest began as a student protest for better conditions and has expanded to include public-sector workers protesting high energy prices, the rising cost of living and social inequality. The Interior Ministry reported about 2,300 arrests and nearly 1,000 injured police officers.



Sponsor Message

🎧 NPR's Eleanor Beardsley, who was in the streets of Paris yesterday, witnessed burned bikes, shattered glass and graffiti on looted stores saying things like "tax the rich." She spoke with 23-year-old Sarah Berlia, who says she believes these actions come from a frustrated generation facing dwindling rights and opportunities. Beardsley says the protest culture in France often attracts "troublemakers," but the scale of current events is massive. The protests have had political implications, as France is six months away from a presidential election. Far-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon has joined the protesters, while far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who is leading in the polls, has condemned the violence and the government.

Living better

toggle caption i Siv Dolmen for NPR

Living Better is a special series about what it takes to stay healthy in America.

Saunas are gaining renewed attention in the wellness world for their potential to improve mental health. This trend reflects the growing interest in the broader wellness movement and social connection, especially post-pandemic. While scientists understand how saunas affect the cardiovascular system, they are just beginning to explore their impact on mental health. Here's what they know so far.

🥵 When our skin detects heat, it sends signals to a primitive brain area that prompts our body to cool down. This pathway also influences mood and pleasure, which is associated with depression.

🥵 Heat triggers an anti-inflammatory response similar to the effects of exercise, which is known to help with depression and other mental health issues.

🥵 Heating people up can act like a "thermoregulatory workout," helping their bodies cool down more efficiently over time.

Picture show

toggle caption i Jennifer Teresa Villanueva

Artist Jennifer Teresa Villanueva has captured her family's everyday life through her lens for eight years, revealing moments of love, care and sacrifice within their Chicago home. The personal project took root in 2018, sparked by her grandmother's hospitalization. It started as a way to better understand her grandmother's daily routines, and soon it blossomed into a heartfelt exploration of the immigrant experience. "I am interested in what happens when the camera enters a home where everyone already knows one another," Villanueva told NPR. "There is no distance between photographer and subject. I am photographing the people who raised me, and I am also photographing the home that raised me." See photos from the project and read more about Villanueva's work.

World.title: A Kelvin wave raised sea levels on the West Coast. More are coming
World.content:
A Kelvin wave raised sea levels on the West Coast. More are coming

toggle caption i Dillon J. Amaya/North Carolina State University

One of the first major signs of this year's "Super El Niño" has reached the U.S. It's called a Kelvin wave – a deep ocean wave that's currently raising sea levels along the West Coast.

Scientists have long known about Kelvin waves, but this year, the phenomena grabbed the public's attention with video explanations receiving thousands of views across TikTok and X .

"It does surprise me – I mean, here it's been around all this time," says Mark Cane, who created one of the first models to forecast and predict El Niño . "I'm sure Lord Kelvin is happy in his grave."

Sponsor Message

(Lord Kelvin, the British physicist who also developed the Kelvin temperature scale, first described the wave back in the late 1800s.)

Kelvin waves can develop along the equator during El Niño years, when a vast region of water in the Pacific Ocean becomes much warmer than usual.

Some of this warm water, in the form of a Kelvin wave that stretches thousands of miles, moves slowly east beneath the ocean's surface until it reaches South America. Then it splits, traveling north along the West Coast and as far south as Chile.

"It's like an enormous bathtub sloshing around," Cane says, professor emeritus of earth and climate sciences at Columbia University. "But the slosh is very peculiar, because it only goes west to east along the equator in a Kelvin wave."

These are not the massive, highly visible waves that crash into shorelines during major storms and hurricanes .

"It's not a wall of water, it's not a tsunami, it's not a wave you can surf," says Dillon Amaya, an assistant professor of atmospheric sciences at North Carolina State University. "It's a planetary-scale wave."

A Kelvin wave's impact is gradual, raising sea levels as it moves up the coast, and bringing with it an elevated risk of floods and warmer water temperatures.

Sponsor Message

What's the impact?

Kelvin waves can increase the risk of flooding and coastal erosion.

By themselves, Kelvin waves don't cause flooding, Amaya says. Instead, they load the dice, making flooding more likely by raising sea levels.

"It makes the background conditions more favorable towards coastal flooding, but what you need are triggering factors," Amaya said, such as a major storm or very high tides.

Josh Willis, a climate scientist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, says Kelvin waves raise the chances of a "triple whammy" along the California coast: "El Nino, the high tide and the storm surge all coming at once."

That's exactly what some Southern California communities experienced in early October. Sea levels were already higher than normal because of the Kelvin wave – about six to eight inches, Amaya says. Then, when Tropical Storm Rachel hit, a storm surge flooded neighborhoods and left oceanfront homes partially submerged .

"That storm surge was almost certainly made more devastating because of the Kelvin wave," Amaya says.

Warmer water temperatures

toggle caption i Dillon J. Amaya/North Carolina State University

Kelvin waves also bring warmer water up the coast, which can be disruptive and put stress on marine life .

"We've seen tropical fishes in places that we don't normally see them," Amaya says. "Like a whale shark was spotted off the coast of San Diego."

The Kelvin wave can push down nutrient-dense cold waters that support productive marine ecosystems. Amaya says researchers have already seen evidence of sea birds dying in response to warmer water temperatures along the coast.

When is the next Kelvin wave?

There are usually five to six Kelvin waves during a strong El Niño year, Amaya says.

Amaya predicts the next Kelvin wave will reach San Diego in late October or early November. Several more waves are expected through the fall and early winter, he says. Kelvin waves usually subside before the peak of El Niño.

Sponsor Message

World.title: The real reason it's going to take a while to know who won in some midterm races
World.content:
The real reason it's going to take a while to know who won in some midterm races

toggle caption i Justin Sullivan/Getty Images

Stephen Richer no longer runs elections in the fourth-largest county in the country.

But for the rest of his life, he'll remember the feeling when polls closed on an election night.

More than a million ballots staring at him and his staff. Every moment that passes without them fully counted means another conspiracy theory sprouting online.

"Those days, those were hell for me," said Richer, a Republican who served as the clerk and recorder for Arizona's Maricopa County. "You'd have a limited number of workers, and you'd have a limited amount of space, and you'd be doing everything that you possibly could. … And yet you have everyone blowing up your phone, everyone saying that you're incompetent or corrupt or worse."

Sponsor Message

This midterm year, election officials in competitive congressional districts will face that same pressure.

But they will also face a hard reality: that those races might not be called until days after Election Day.

Here's an FAQ on why that is, and what it could mean this year.

Why do we know the results immediately in some places, and in others it takes days or weeks?

It comes down to the margin of victory.

Which sounds strange, since who wins an election and by how much shouldn't impact how long it takes election officials to count ballots.

But the reality is what most Americans think of as "election results" — the winners announced on election nights across TV networks and social media — are not the result of all ballots being counted, but rather, races being called by news organizations that determine the winners based on a state or district's demographics and initial returns. (NPR relies on The Associated Press for its race calls.)

Those determinations come a lot faster when races aren't close.

"Margins matter," said Richer, who noted that in recent elections, there has been a lot less scrutiny on Utah than there has been on his home state of Arizona, or certain contests in California, despite the states counting votes at similar speeds.

Sponsor Message

"In Utah you can call all the races very quickly because the Republicans there have high margins," Richer said.

That gives the illusion of elections there being complete, but no state is done counting ballots on election night, even if it seems that way because notable races are called early.

Loading...

So you're saying the timing of results isn't at all tied to vote-counting speed?

Not exactly.

The closer the race, the more election analysts need to see before they can make a call. So the faster states count ballots, the faster those determinations can be made.

This is why the longest wait times every election usually come from places that have competitive races and which also count slowly.

Like, California?

Exactly. California has become the poster child for long results times because of both those factors: a bevy of competitive congressional districts, which help determine the balance of power in the U.S. House, and a vote count that's been among the slowest in the nation.

Add in that President Trump, the most prominent purveyor of election misinformation in the country, has long targeted the liberal California, and experts see a perfect storm for false voting narratives.

"It's progressive, it likes mail ballots, it gets [postmarked] mail ballots after Election Day," Richer said. "It just all adds up to a fairly incendiary situation."

Charles Stewart, an elections expert at MIT, put it more simply.

"California just has a big target on its back," said Stewart.

California's slow vote counting caused a lot of conspiracy theorizing during the state's June primary. Is this fall going to be a rerun?

Kim Alexander is cautiously optimistic that won't be the case.

She runs the California Voter Foundation, which has been advocating for ways to speed up California's vote tally without giving up the state's generous voting access policies, like mailing every active registered voter a ballot.

Sponsor Message

"We have all these amazing rights and opportunities that we give to our voters, and the price we're paying is a longer vote count," Alexander told NPR. "But that doesn't mean that it has to be this long."

toggle caption i Justin Sullivan/Getty Images

The single biggest cause for California's slow count comes from a phenomenon Alexander calls "the pig in the python" problem: a logjam of millions of vote-by-mail ballots getting returned on Election Day that need to be processed.

Those ballots take longer to count than in-person votes, as officials need to deal with envelopes and verify signatures to make sure mail ballots are cast by the people they're supposed to be cast by.

Some counties see up to 50% of their vote-by-mail ballots turned in on Election Day, Alexander said, which means processing work doesn't even begin until later in the week.

"I can't tell you how many people who are informed and engaged and … when I tell them that the cause for the long vote count is voters holding on to their ballots to Election Day and turning them in, they look at me and they're like, 'That's what I do,'" Alexander said. "And I'm like, 'I know! You're part of the problem!'"

The state allocated $40 million to speeding up its counting this year, and part of that money is going to voter education.

Alexander is optimistic that once voters learn they can play a role in speeding up the process by voting earlier, or by utilizing other voting methods that allow for quicker counting, they will respond.

"California has been beaten up by this president for over a decade over our election process, and it's gotten pretty worrisome," Alexander said. "I think that California voters, if they feel they can do something to respond to that, many will take action."

Sponsor Message

To that point, research conducted earlier this year found that when voters in California's San Joaquin County received postcards urging them to vote earlier, they were more likely to meet the recommended deadline that allowed for election-night counting.

Alexander noted one more change that could mean less spotlight on California this year: fewer competitive House districts.

Ahead of the 2022 elections, the state had nine districts that the Cook Political Report considered competitive. But this year, in part because voters approved a mid-cycle gerrymander to respond to gerrymanders in Republican-controlled states, the state has just three.

That makes it less likely the entire country will be waiting on California to know who controls the House.

OK, anywhere else we should be watching when it comes to results speed?

Using the formula discussed earlier (competitive races + slow vote counting), it's impossible not to look at Alaska.

According to data from the MIT Election Lab, Alaska was the last state in 2024 to reach 95% of its ballots counted.

Election Day was Nov. 5 that year, but the state's lone House race — which Republican Nicholas Begich won by fewer than 10,000 votes — wasn't called by the AP until Nov. 20.

This year, polling shows a tight Alaska Senate race. That means, if results fall a certain way in other states, the entire country could be waiting weeks to know which party will control the U.S. Senate next year.

World.title: Michigan's Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed campaigns in GOP stronghold
World.content:
Michigan's Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed campaigns in GOP stronghold

Michigan's Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is campaigning in the GOP stronghold of Michigan's Upper Peninsula, an area that hasn't voted for a Democrat in Congress in over a decade.

Transcript

MICHEL MARTIN, HOST:

Back in the U.S., let's go to Michigan, where both of the Senate candidates have been focusing on urban areas with lots of voters, like Detroit and its suburbs. With about two weeks to go until Election Day, the Democrat in the race is also carrying his message into a Republican stronghold. Michigan Public Radio's Russ McNamara reports.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

ABDUL EL-SAYED: How are we doing, Marquette?

RUSS MCNAMARA, BYLINE: Hundreds packed a rally on the campus of Northern Michigan University to hear Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed's stump speech last week. It capped a whirlwind three-stop tour, covering a couple hundred miles across the state's rural and rugged Upper Peninsula. The goal for El-Sayed is to reach out to Yoopers, a nickname for people who live in the Upper Peninsula, or UP, and draw in support from conservatives. It's a tall order. Approximately 60% of them voted for Donald Trump two years ago. El-Sayed told reporters that he learned a lot from this campaign trip to the UP and a prior one in June.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

EL-SAYED: Yoopers are commonsense, thoughtful people, and they don't like paying more in gas than they need to, don't like paying more in groceries. And they don't like being taken advantage of by a billionaire from New York.

MCNAMARA: Still, Yoopers have a healthy skepticism for outsiders, according to Republican state representative Karl Bohnak. He's well known here. Before entering politics, Karl Bohnak was a TV meteorologist for about 30 years. He's backing the Republican candidate in this toss-up race, former Congressman Mike Rogers.

KARL BOHNAK: To be honest with you, I don't pay much attention to Abdul. I don't even really know what his message is. I think he meant something like Medicare for All. But the only question I would have is, who's going to pay for that?

MCNAMARA: Healthcare is an issue in the Upper Peninsula, with many having to drive 100 miles or more to see a specialist. Data from Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services show that nearly 1 in 3 UP residents are enrolled in Medicare, with 7% without insurance altogether. Bart Stupak was the last Democrat to represent the UP in the U.S. House choosing not to run for reelection in 2010. He endorsed Representative Haley Stevens in the Democratic primary but believes El-Sayed's messaging can resonate with Yoopers.

BART STUPAK: Just showing up helps him tremendously to try to connect with not just Democrats, but all the voters, even those Republicans who are disenchanted with the party right now.

MCNAMARA: Trips across rural Michigan are one part of a broader strategy to reach Republicans for El-Sayed.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

EL-SAYED: We got to be willing to invite them to a decision they have yet to make.

MCNAMARA: Speaking to a crowd in Escanaba, El-Sayed called on his supporters to connect with conservative family and friends to explain his key messages of Medicare for All and getting money out of politics.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

EL-SAYED: Reach out to them, OK? We have an opportunity to build our country, not just watch it get torn down.

MCNAMARA: While El-Sayed attempts to bridge a partisan gap, there is some hesitancy among moderates within his own party. In an interview late last week with Michigan Public Radio, former Congressman Stupak says some of El-Sayed's positions give him pause.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED NPR CONTENT)

STUPAK: I would have voted by now, but I just want to see how this plays out a little bit more. Yeah, I'm a Democrat, but that doesn't mean I vote for every Democrat that shows up on a ticket.

MCNAMARA: With razor-thin margins in this U.S. Senate race, rural conservatives would be a nice get for El-Sayed but mean little if he can't shore up his own base.

For NPR News, I'm Russ McNamara in Marquette, Michigan.

(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

World.title: Solar power is changing agriculture in Pakistan, but some fear it could cause issues
World.content:
Solar power is changing agriculture in Pakistan, but some fear it could cause issues

Solar power is transforming agriculture in Pakistan. But in a country already facing water scarcity and extreme weather, some fear their widespread use could cause problems.

Transcript

MICHEL MARTIN, HOST:

Solar power is transforming agriculture in Pakistan. Farmers are using it to run water pumps that lower their electricity costs and boost production. But in a country already facing water scarcity and extreme weather, some fear this will create new problems. Betsy Joles has more.

BETSY JOLES, BYLINE: Muhammad Abdullah (ph) stands alongside a tub full of minnows. It's part of the fish farm he helps run in Sallhoke Chatha, in Pakistan's Punjab province.

MUHAMMAD ABDULLAH: Maripa (ph) silver, bighead grass.

JOLES: He lists off some of the species wriggling in the water below. Once these fish are mature enough, they'll be moved to man-made ponds outside. The water in them needs to be changed frequently. Otherwise, the fish will die. For that, Abdullah uses well water pumped from the ground by a solar-powered motor. The pumps run for around 11 hours a day in the summer, cutting the farm's energy bill by about half.

ABDULLAH: (Non-English language spoken).

JOLES: Only those who have a lot of money can work without solar, Abdullah says. Many in this area got into fish farming because staple crops like wheat and corn didn't grow well there. Thanks to solar, access to groundwater has become much cheaper. But Mudassar Kharal, another fish farmer from the area, says no one is really keeping an eye on how much of it is being used.

MUDASSAR KHARAL: There is no check and balance.

JOLES: Some Pakistani water experts warned that solar-powered pumps could worsen the country's over-extraction of groundwater. Bashir Ahmad, director of the Pakistan Agricultural Research Council, says their use is particularly concerning in areas that are otherwise unfit for farming.

BASHIR AHMAD: Adoption of this saltwater pumping in those areas is really scary.

JOLES: Since 2023, there's been a push to cultivate some unproductive lands under the army-backed Green Pakistan Initiative. It's mostly focused on large-scale corporate farming and promotes the use of solar-powered pumps in arid parts of the country like Balochistan. Proponents believe it will help bring farming up to date with high-efficiency irrigation. Critics say it only adds to water woes. Here's news about a thousand acres of barren land being developed under the project from Pakistani broadcaster ARY.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

UNIDENTIFIED REPORTER: Green Pakistan Initiative (non-English language spoken).

JOLES: Pakistan's agriculture industry is supported by a river-fed canal system. But the country's reliance on groundwater has steadily increased in the past few decades as pressure on farmers has grown. Researcher Khalid Jamil wanted to find out whether farmers using solar to power their pumps were extracting more groundwater than those using diesel. His Ph.D. findings, published in the Journal of Agriculture and Food Research last year, found that in 77% of cases surveyed, they were.

KHALID JAMIL: It's just human behavior. If you get something free, you do not feel the need to save it.

JOLES: That means extra stress on the already overburdened aquifer that Pakistan draws from.

(SOUNDBITE OF HORSE NEIGHING)

JOLES: The paradox is that for individual farmers using solar, water has become one less thing to worry about.

(SOUNDBITE OF ENGINE CHUGGING)

JOLES: In the Punjabi village of Kot Ratta Sakhi, farmer Ibrar Hussain (ph) still relies on diesel-powered pumps to irrigate his rice fields. Solar panels are top of his mind.

IBRAR HUSSAIN: (Non-English language spoken).

JOLES: "Everyone has put them up. We also want to put them up and benefit from them," he says. The question is whether Pakistan can afford any unintended consequences.

For NPR News, I'm Betsy Joles in Punjab Province, Pakistan.

Copyright © 2026 NPR. All rights reserved. Visit our website terms of use and permissions pages at www.npr.org for further information.

World.title: Alberta voters weigh future in Canada
World.content:
Alberta voters weigh future in Canada

toggle caption i John Diep/Bloomberg via Getty Images





EDMONTON, Alberta — For decades, Alberta separatism remained on the political margins. Now, voters in the oil-rich Canadian province are deciding whether to take the first step toward a future referendum on independence.

The nonbinding referendum vote on Monday is the first time the province has put the question of separation to a public vote, in what Elections Alberta has described as the largest electoral event in the province's history.

Polls indicate that Alberta voters will overwhelmingly reject the option of beginning the legal process toward a referendum on separation.

Pollsters generally estimate that about one in five Albertans support separation from Canada. But the vote has brought the question of Alberta's place in the Canadian federation to the forefront of public debate.

Sponsor Message

The questions on the ballot

Essentially, this is a referendum about whether to hold another referendum on separation.

There are 10 questions in total. The first nine address immigration, access to provincial services such as health care, education and other social services, and potential changes to the Canadian Constitution. Voters can answer yes or no to each of these questions.

Question 10 offers voters two options. Option 1 asks whether Alberta should remain part of Canada, while option 2 asks whether the province should begin the legal process toward holding a referendum on separation.

Western alienation and grievances against Ottawa date back decades, including to the administrations of Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau, Justin Trudeau's father, during the 1970s and 1980s.

"I feel the Canadian system is broken. I know we aren't living in hell on earth. But it's the trajectory we're worried about and where things are going," says Cory Morgan.

Morgan founded the Alberta Independence Party in 2000 and is also the founder of Pathway to Independence, a third-party advertising group that advocates for an independent Alberta.

toggle caption i Megan Albu/AFP via Getty Images

"Even if we don't get over the line on Monday, I would hope that some people understand that something large is brewing here and if we don't get some change, it's going to continue to grow," Morgan told NPR.

Sponsor Message

Support for separation intensified among some Albertans following COVID-19 lockdowns and vaccine mandates. Premier Danielle Smith said in May that it was "time to have a vote, understand the will of Albertans on this subject, and move on."

The referendum campaign brought Prime Minister Mark Carney back to his hometown of Edmonton on Friday, where he urged Albertans to keep their province in Canada ahead of the vote.

"A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities for Albertans and Canadians," Carney told the rally.

What's at stake?

Alberta is one of Canada's wealthiest provinces and is home to the world's fourth-largest known oil reserves. The province contributes to Canada's equalization system, which provides federal funding to provinces with lower fiscal capacity. Some Albertans argue that the province should retain more of its revenue rather than see funds redistributed elsewhere in the country.

"We want to make a new country where we can stop sending our money 1,000 kilometers away in Ottawa," says Jeremy Clive, a 23-year-old pilot and university student from rural Alberta.

Leaving the Canadian federation would not be as simple as holding a referendum.

"It requires negotiating your way out," says Jared Wesley, a political scientist at the University of Alberta. "The Supreme Court has stated clearly that in order to leave, a province must negotiate with nine other provinces and the federal government to secure an amendment to the Constitution to remove themselves."

In 1995, Quebec held a referendum on sovereignty that narrowly rejected independence. The vote helped set the stage for Canada's Clarity Act, which Parliament passed in 2000.

The act states that secession negotiations can begin only after a referendum question and its result meet standards of clarity. It does not specify a fixed percentage that constitutes a clear majority. Any separation would also require constitutional negotiations involving provincial and federal governments.

Sponsor Message

"It's a bit ironic that separatists are a bit frustrated with the inability to change the constitution and they are using that as a pretext to leave, but, in order to leave, they need to change the same constitution with a much higher threshold for agreement," says Wesley.

toggle caption i Megan Albu/

AFP via Getty Images





What happens if Albertans vote for a separation Referendum?

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith has said she will respect the result and begin the process of holding a legally binding referendum, subject to the applicable legal requirements. That would not happen immediately.

The province would also need to consult with First Nations. Treaties between First Nations and the Crown predate Canadian Confederation, and First Nations groups have objected to the idea of an independent Alberta.

In May, an Alberta court ruled that a separatist petition seeking to trigger the referendum violated Indigenous rights because the province had failed to consult First Nations. The province has appealed the decision.

The economic cost of Alberta independence

A government-commissioned report by the University of Calgary's School of Public Policy estimated that separating Alberta from Canada could cost as much as $170 billion Canadian dollars over five years. The report examined two scenarios involving a relatively smooth transition.

Under both scenarios, Alberta's debt would rise substantially as the province assumed a share of Canada's federal debt. The report projected that costs could range from $324 billion to $442.3 billion Canadian dollars.

An independent Alberta would also face billions of dollars in additional interest payments compared with what it currently pays as part of Canada.

Thomas Lukaszak, founder of Forever Canadian, a pro-unity movement, and a former deputy premier of Alberta, has spent 18 months campaigning across the province for Alberta to remain in Canada. He points to Quebec's 1995 referendum as a warning about the potential economic effects of separation.

"Several hundred thousand Canadians moved out of the province of Quebec and moved to other provinces," says Lukaszak. "And until today, the province of Quebec hasn't recovered economically from that because industry and investment has left Montreal and I'm fearing that the same thing would happen to the province of Alberta."

Sponsor Message

When will the referendum results be available?

According to Elections Alberta, unofficial results for referendums with this many questions will be posted 48 hours after polls close. Recruiting enough staff for the vote has been a challenge, and Elections Alberta staff are expected to work around the clock to tally the results.

"This story won't end once the ballots are counted," says Wesley.

The referendum has highlighted deep divisions among Albertans. The question of separation is likely to remain prominent in the lead-up to the provincial election next year.

World.title: Former journalist Pamela Wallin resigns from Senate
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Sen. Pamela Wallin has unexpectedly resigned from the upper chamber with a few remaining years before her slated retirement date.

The clerk of the Senate received a resignation letter from the longtime Saskatchewan lawmaker effective Sunday, according to the Senate of Canada.

Her biography on the Senate website lists her as a former senator.

The reason for her resignation, which was first reported by iPolitics, is not yet known. Wallin turns 75, the Senate's mandatory retirement age, in 2028. CBC News has reached out to her office for comment.

Wallin was appointed to the Senate on the advice of Prime Minister Stephen Harper in 2009.

She had a trail-blazing career as a broadcaster and became the first woman to be named bureau chief for CTV News in Ottawa in 1985.

After she became embroiled in the Senate expenses scandal that started in 2013, she was asked to leave the Conservative caucus in the upper chamber.

An audit determined that about $140,000 in expenses she charged to the Senate were improper as they covered travel related to her positions on corporate boards.

The RCMP investigated Wallin's expenses but didn't lay any charges. In 2013, she apologized for mistakes she may have made when filing travel claims and paid back just over $150,000, which included interest.

Wallin was suspended without pay by her Senate colleagues in 2013, but returned to the upper chamber in 2015.

She sat as an Independent until she joined the Independent Senators Group in 2017. She would switch to the Canadian Senators Group in 2019, who she had sat with since.

Prior to her appointment to the Senate, Wallin served as Canada's consul general in New York. She was named an officer of the Order of Canada in 2007.

World.title: It’s referendum day in Alberta. Here’s what you need to know
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Albertans will cast their ballots in a historic referendum Monday, weighing in on 10 questions about the future of the province.

Already, Elections Alberta says 1.3 million people across the province have voted either by special ballot or in advance polls.

The referendum features 10 questions. Questions one through nine centre around immigration and the Constitution.

Question 10 asks if voters support Alberta remaining a province of Canada, or if they support the provincial government beginning the process of holding a second, binding referendum on separation.

WATCH | Alberta voters head to the polls: Alberta heads to polls to vote on separation referendum | Duration closed caption 4:55 It's referendum day in Alberta, where voters will cast ballots on 10 questions covering immigration, constitutional changes and whether the province should hold a referendum on separating from Canada.

If you are voting on referendum day, here is what you need to know.

Where to vote and what to bring

Polls are open across the province from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m.

Unlike in advance voting, on referendum day voters are required to vote at their designated polling station. If you’re not sure where that is, you can enter your address on Elections Alberta’s website to find it.

Voters must be over 18, and a resident of Alberta.

To vote, bring a piece of government-issued photo ID with your address on it, like a driver’s licence, or two pieces of ID including at least one with an address. An attestation form from an authorized signatory will also be accepted.

What if lines are long?

While polling stations are set to close at 8 p.m., if voters are in line before 8 p.m., they will still be allowed to cast their ballots.

“The location will stay open until everyone in that line has had the opportunity to vote,” said Elections Alberta spokesperson Maia Hanrahan.

What if you’re not sure your special ballot’s been counted?

Elections Alberta received requests for more than 600,000 special ballots, and encouraged Albertans to post them in by Oct. 9 in order to meet the Oct. 16 deadline.

If your mail-in ballot was not received by the deadline, or if you applied for a special ballot but never mailed it in, you can still vote on referendum day.

After marking their ballots, voters place each of their 10 ballots in its corresponding box. (Janet French/CBC)

“I'd encourage [voters] to first have a look at that link that they received when they applied for that special ballot. They will be able to see there if it's marked as received and that they've cast their ballots,” said Hanrahan.

“If they're not marked as received, they can go and attend in person to vote.”

Do you have to vote on all 10 questions?

No, says Hanrahan. Voters can vote on all 10 questions, just one, or however many of the 10 questions they would like. She suggests voters familiarize themselves with the questions to speed up the process.

Each referendum question is on a separate, colour-coded ballot. After marking an X on their ballots, voters fold them and place each one in its corresponding box. The ballot will be counted no matter how it is folded, Hanrahan said.

Voters can also request a replacement ballot at the station if they mark an option they don’t want, or if they accidentally tear or rip a ballot.

Can you wear pro-Canada or pro-Alberta apparel?

“People can wear what they'd like to the voting locations. The only rule there is that they can't be wearing something that would be classified as referendum advertising,” said Hanrahan.

That means wearing an Alberta flag baseball cap or a T-shirt with the Maple Leaf is fine, but wearing a campaign slogan, or a message on how to vote on any of the questions, would not be.

When will we know results?

Election officers will count the ballots by hand and the count must be completed within 48 hours under provincial rules.

Question 10, the ballot related to separation, will be counted first. Then counters will deal with the other questions in order, starting with the first question.

Hanrahan says workers will not wait for all polling stations to finish their count of the 10th ballot before moving on, meaning results may start coming in for the other nine questions before the 10th question has been declared.

For live results and analysis on referendum night, watch Alberta Votes: Referendum Night starting at 7 p.m. MT on CBC TV in both Calgary and Edmonton, CBC Gem, CBC News YouTube, CBC News App, CBC News Network and listen live on CBC Radio One.

Referendum results will also be covered live on the CBC Edmonton and CBC Calgary websites.

Then, tune into Alberta Morning on Oct. 20 starting at 5:30 a.m. MT on CBC Radio One and CBC TV in both Calgary and Edmonton.
