World.title: 'You Can See Everything' sells out theatres, and people can't stop talking about it
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

You Can See Everything is the movie everyone wants to talk about but no one wants spoiled.

Maybe that's why so many people rushed to theatres on opening weekend to see the nearly three-hour documentary about Theranos founder and convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes.

Whatever the reason, the film made more than $15 million US in ticket sales during its debut weekend — the second-largest opening weekend for a non-musical documentary in domestic box office history, behind only 2004's Fahrenheit 9/11.

It's a considerable achievement, considering You Can See Everything had a limited release at just 855 theatres in Canada and the U.S.

The reviews following its debut were overwhelmingly positive: rated 99 per cent fresh on Rotten Tomatoes, and scoring a 4.8 on Letterboxd, making it the highest-rated movie in the site's history. (Both those ratings have come down since then, but only slightly.)

As the five-star reviews started pouring in online, so too did the comments: "My mouth was agape for basically the entire last two hours," from Letterboxd user James (Schaffrillas).

"Just an absolutely phenomenal crazy fever dream of a documentary," said user vgoodatkissing.

You can read everything — no spoilers here

The documentary's premise is straightforward. A film crew, including dual director-producers Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, briefly move in with Holmes, her partner Billy Evans and their children, and document their lives, 34 days before she is due to start serving an extended prison sentence for fraud.

Toronto film critic Teri Hart says watching You Can See Everything in theatres was a visceral experience.

"People were actually physically leaning into the screen," she told CBC News. "There were gasps at times; people applauded at the end of the movie, lots of laughter."

"You leave this movie and you don't know if you want to talk about Nathan Fielder, if you want to talk about Elizabeth Holmes, if you want to talk about Billy or if you want to talk 'where did they put the camera.'"

The trailer gives audiences a glimpse into Fielder and Holmes's unusual dynamic.

"Nathan Fielder is not afraid of awkward. Nathan Fielder is not afraid of asking questions in a way that is unlike anybody else," said Hart. "He has a level of provocateur, I think, that is so fascinating to watch.

Boundary-pushing directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim documented Elizabeth Holmes's life during the 34 days before she was sent to prison for defrauding investors. (A24)

"Place him with Elizabeth Holmes, who also has a unique way of communicating, and you have magic."

Indeed, the documentary delivers on the intense and deliberately uncomfortable interviews that Fielder, a Canadian who was born in Vancouver, became known for on shows like Nathan for You, as well as his paradigm-shifting approach to the truth.

Hart calls the documentary a theatrical experience few people will have ever had — one that may lead audiences to question what we think of as the truth.

Another win for A24

You Can See Everything was distributed and partly produced by A24, the same company behind some of this year's most talked-about films, including Olivia Wilde's The Invite, the Anthony Bourdain biopic Tony and the record-breaking horror Backrooms.

"A24 is a distributor that has a brand. And that brand is — to my mind — working with auteurs, working with writer-directors or even just directors that really have a specific vision and have a strong, strong artistry associated with them," said Hart.

WATCH | CBC's Jackson Weaver has more on the documentary: Nathan Fielder searches for truth in You Can See Everything | Duration 2:45 Nathan Fielder's You Can See Everything gazes into the abyss of Elizabeth Holmes. The documentary about the jailed Theranos founder examines the absurd nature of truth.

She said that's helped A24 make a splash, as the company pushes back against the general consensus that Hollywood has no new ideas.

As a movie lover, Hart said she is grateful for anything that gets people back in the theatres and talking about what they've seen. She says You Can See Everything is a great example of that.

"They're, like, shocked and surprised or walking out of the theater with all kinds of thoughts and ideas and questions. Because let's be clear, this movie does not tie anything up with a nice pretty bow. It does not. So people have questions.

"And I think that that is a really thrilling experience for people to share with strangers. "

World.title: McGill law school grapples with fallout after paroled murderer excluded from campus
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Some students and alumni in McGill University's law faculty have signed a petition calling for the school to allow Jeffrey George Ewert, a convicted murderer on day parole, to return to campus.

Ewert began attending law classes at McGill in August, but has not been on campus since early October.

In a story published Friday, students told CBC News they were upset the university had not disclosed their peer’s violent history and some expressed feeling unsafe.

But the petition, drafted by three law students and signed by more than 100 students and alumni, argues the exclusion undermines Ewert's access to education and rehabilitation as an Indigenous man and a survivor of the Sixties Scoop.

Addressed to senior university administrators, the petition acknowledges student safety concerns but says Ewert should not be excluded from campus.

"We are asking that Jeff be given the chance to do what the rest of us are doing, which is to attend class and learn," the petition says.

"A ban from the premises, with no conversation beforehand and no finding of misconduct, takes that chance away."

Annica Dickens, one of the authors of the petition and a third-year law student, said in an email that "public discomfort should not, on its own, be treated as proof that someone poses a threat."

She added: "His past is serious, and I don’t want to minimize the harm experienced by his victims or their families. But we also have to consider who he is today, his behaviour since then, and the safeguards that are in place."

Now in his 60s, Ewert was convicted of second-degree murder and attempted murder for two attacks in B.C. in 1984.

He sexually assaulted and killed one woman and, less than six weeks later, beat and choked a 15-year-old so severely that she was paralyzed and disabled for life, according to a summary of his case in his parole board file.

Jeffrey George Ewert began attending law classes at McGill University in August. Some students told CBC they were upset his violent criminal past was not disclosed. (Name withheld/Instagram)

Ewert is serving a life sentence and was granted day parole in 2025. While various clinical assessments ranked Ewert’s risk of reoffending as moderate to high, official parole documents say with close supervision at a halfway house and clinical follow-up, that risk “seems to fall more into the moderate risk category.”

Ewert is currently living in a halfway house. He declined an interview with CBC.

Debate among students

The CBC report has sparked heated debate among faculty, students and alumni.

An online discussion on Facebook features McGill law students on all sides of the controversy: some argue their peers should be more compassionate toward those convicted of a crime, while others say there should be more respect for students who feel unsafe.

"I can recognize the importance of reintegration, while also questioning how our university is handling the situation for students with such trauma," one person posted anonymously in the Facebook discussion.

"You never know what someone has been a victim to in their life and how that might impact their reaction, especially after having experienced such violence firsthand."

The administration, meanwhile, has tried to calm concerns among the student body.

Tina Piper, the law faculty's dean, said in a letter to students that the university took "prompt action as soon as we became aware of this situation earlier this month."

Piper said she has been working with the administration on next steps.

"I want you to know that my highest priority is to ensure the safety and well-being of all members of our faculty," Piper said in the note, obtained by CBC.

"This situation is not unlike one you may encounter in your future legal career and now is a good time to practise how you want to be in the world."

In a separate email, McGill provost Angela Campbell also tried to reassure the university community.

She wrote that when information came to their attention about a situation that could "compromise a safe learning environment," the university took measured, decisive action.

The provost added that a "fair process" is underway that "balances the rights and interests of everyone involved."

WATCH | Convicted murderer on campus generates debate at McGill law: Convicted killer attending McGill law school divides students over safety, 2nd chances | Duration closed caption 5:35 A convicted murderer’s presence at McGill University's law school while on day parole has sparked debate over public safety and rehabilitation. Several students say they feel vulnerable and frustrated by a lack of transparency regarding Jeffrey George Ewert's violent past against women, while his lawyer and student supporters argue he deserves a second chance.

Ewert 'an example of rehabilitation,' lawyer says

Ewert’s lawyer, Nora Demnati, said his admission to McGill’s law program was a continuation of two decades of legal advocacy while he was in prison.

Ewert heads the Canadian Prisoners’ Labour Confederation, a group that advocates for labour rights for inmates.

She said the situation has “put tremendous stress on someone who’s like, honestly, an example of rehabilitation,” said Demnati.

While Demnati said she understands the concerns of some students, she believes they come from an “uninformed” reading of the parole decisions.

“Parole is based on progress and work and it’s on merit," said Demnati in an interview with CBC last week.

When Ewert’s parole was extended in June, some of his conditions included not to enter a drinking establishment, to immediately report all sexual and non-sexual relationships with women and to allow his case management team access to all his telecommunication activity.

That latter condition was added by the parole board because Ewert had been viewing women’s profiles on social media, starting discussions with them and exploring a dating site without notifying his case management team.

He was reprimanded by the parole board in 2025 after he had contacted and collected the phone numbers of multiple women.

As parolees are adjusting to life outside prison, Demnati said it’s normal for there to be occasional breaches.

“People on parole have breaches a lot of the time,” she said. “It does not lead necessarily to an increase in the risk and it does not lead to a conclusion that the risk cannot be managed anymore.”

World.title: Anthropic sued by major Canadian news publishers for copyright claims in Ontario court
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A coalition of news publishers that includes Canada's largest newspapers is suing the AI company Anthropic in an Ontario court.

Postmedia, Torstar, The Globe and Mail and The Canadian Press say Anthropic infringed on their copyright by using their content to develop its large language AI model, Claude.

"Anthropic has capitalized on the commercial success of its AI models, building an expansive suite of services, and raised significant capital — all without obtaining a valid licence from any of the News Media Companies," says the statement of claim.

"In doing so, Anthropic has been substantially and unjustly enriched to the detriment of the News Media Companies."

The lawsuit, filed on Oct. 6, was first reported by the news site Cartt.ca. Anthropic has not responded to a request for comment. The allegations have not been proven in court.

The statement of claim says Anthropic breached the news media websites' terms of service and circumvented technological protection measures they put in place to restrict copying of their content.

The claim says the news outlets "are responsible for generating a significant portion of Canada's journalistic content — from daily print broadsheets to round-the-clock digital news coverage," and collectively have millions of readers.

"To obtain content for ingestion into its models and services, Anthropic deliberately 'scrapes' (i.e. accesses and copies) enormous amounts of text data from the internet and from the Plaintiffs' Websites," the claim says.

The news outlets say Anthropic then uses that content, without authorization or consent, to develop its AI models. It says Anthropic also scrapes content on an ongoing basis in response to user prompts.

WATCH | Canadian news organizations including CBC sue OpenAI: Canadian news organizations, including CBC, sue ChatGPT creator | Duration 2:02 CBC/Radio-Canada, Postmedia, Metroland, the Toronto Star, the Globe and Mail, and The Canadian Press have launched a joint lawsuit against ChatGPT creator OpenAI, for using news content to train its ChatGPT generative artificial intelligence system. The news organizations say OpenAI breaches copyright by 'scraping content' from their websites.

"Notwithstanding concerns raised by several content creators across various industries, including through numerous other lawsuits and public criticism, Anthropic has done nothing to curtail its unlawful behaviour," the statement of claim says.

The same companies also launched, alongside CBC/Radio-Canada, a lawsuit against OpenAI in 2024. That case has yet to be settled.

News publishers abroad have also sued tech companies for using their articles to train AI systems. The New York Times sued OpenAI for its use of the paper's copyrighted material, and the Justice Department sided with the tech company last month.

World.title: Quebec's reserves of maple syrup almost depleted, says new report
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The head of Quebec's maple syrup producers' association says the province's strategic syrup reserve has run dry amid high demand for the product.

Québec Maple Syrup Producers president Luc Goulet says government support will be needed to ensure the industry doesn't miss out on opportunities to grow the sector.

Maple syrup yields depend on weather conditions. As a result, the producers' association has established a strategic reserve to ensure prices and supply remain relatively stable.

Last year, U.S. commercial customers stocked up, fearing that U.S. President Donald Trump would carry out his threat to impose tariffs.

Goulet says the buffer has been exhausted as sales continue to rise.

"Our strategic reserve has been reduced to zero," Goulet said in an interview at the release of a report on the industry's economic benefits.

That means the industry could lose customers if weather conditions are less favourable for maple sap flow, he said.

Goulet cites the stock shortages in 2007 and 2008 as an example.

"We lost some markets because the product wasn’t available," Goulet said. "Then, consumers very quickly turn to another sweet product. And once that happens, those consumption habits are established."

Quebec maple syrup is gaining market share abroad, according to the president of the Maple Industry Council, which represents authorized buyers.

Louis Turenne notes that exports increased by 9.34 per cent in 2024 compared to the previous year. The pace accelerated in 2025 with a 15.8 per cent increase as the threat of new tariffs loomed over the industry.

In 2026, exports rose at a slower rate — 2.48 per cent from January through August compared to the same period the previous year.

"It's always hard to beat an exceptional year," Turenne said.

Currently, nearly 65 per cent of maple syrup exports go to the United States. (Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press)

Goulet acknowledges that satisfying the demand of eager consumers is a nice problem to have.

However, he believes the industry can still grow. "There is still a great deal of untapped potential in Quebec’s maple groves," he said.

Investments from Quebec City "are too low for our liking," says Goulet, who hopes to have the ear of the newly elected Parti Québécois government.

"When we’re told that we have an industry that's thriving, that we’re growing, and that we don’t need support — well, I no longer accept that line of reasoning at the government level," he said.

For his part, Turenne believes that Quebec could encourage increased production by providing financial support to producers, and helping processors in their search for new markets abroad.

Currently, nearly 65 per cent of maple syrup exports go to the United States.

"We’ve made significant progress in diversifying our markets in recent years. Twenty years ago, that figure was 80 per cent," Turenne said.

“But we need to accelerate the opening and development of European, Australian, and Asian markets to become less dependent on the U.S. market,” he said.

Industry concentrated in Quebec

While the maple leaf graces the Canadian flag, the syrup industry is heavily concentrated in Quebec.

More than 70 per cent of North American production is in the province, according to the industry group's report, released Thursday.

When production, processing, and specialized equipment manufacturers are included, the maple syrup industry contributed $1.21 billion to the gross domestic product in 2025, the report said.

In total, the sector employs more than 10,000 full-time equivalent workers and generated $285 million in tax revenue, excluding municipal taxes and fees for the lease of public lands.

This figure does not include the sugar shacks that many Quebecers visit in the spring.

"Sugar shack operations are more akin to the restaurant industry," Turenne said.

The maple syrup producers' group used the recent election campaign to highlight the industry's importance as an employer and economic driver, and Goulet says the candidates were often surprised by the important role it played.

In some municipalities, "if you take away maple syrup production, you might as well shut down the villages," Goulet said.

World.title: The Simpsons' Apu is back in Springfield after nearly a decade — with a new voice
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Apu Nahasapeemapetilon has spoken on The Simpsons for the first time since 2017, returning in Sunday's episode, "Treehouse of Horror Presents: The Revengening."

The character has appeared in the background in the years since, but remained silent amid criticism that he reinforced racial stereotypes.

Apu is now voiced by Sunil Malhotra, an Indian-American actor whose credits include The Legend of Korra. He succeeds Hank Azaria, a white actor who voiced the character for 27 years.

In 2021, Azaria, apologized for his role in creating and performing the character. "Part of me feels like I need to go around to every single Indian person in this country and personally apologize," he said on Dax Shepherd's Armchair Expert podcast.

Apu's last speaking appearance before his return was in "The Serfsons," which aired in 2017.

The debate over the character's portrayal gained momentum that same year after Indian-American comedian Hari Kondabolu released the documentary, The Problem with Apu, which examines the character's cultural impact and the racial stereotypes critics say he embodies.

"When you see Hank Azaria doing that voice in person ... without the guise of a cartoon, then all of a sudden it's like, that's a white guy making fun of me," Kondabolu says in the documentary.

"It's different all of a sudden, it no longer feels like a character."

On Instagram, Sunil Malhotra shared a photo of himself dressed as Apu beside Janina Gavankar, the voice of Apu's wife, Manjula. Their animated characters appear alongside them beneath a "Homecoming" banner as confetti falls.

"Bringing Apu back feels like a reclamation," Malhotra wrote on Sunday. "It truly IS his homecoming."

Apu's return brings another new voice

Gavankar is also new to The Simpsons, taking over as Manjula from white actor Tress MacNeille. The recasting is part of a broader shift, as the show announced in June 2020 that characters of colour would be voiced by actors of color.

Since then, Alex Désert has taken over as Carl Carlson and Kevin Michael Richardson as Dr. Julius Hibbert. With Malhotra now voicing Apu, the character joins that roster of recast roles.

The Kwik-E-Mart owner's comeback was kept a secret until the episode aired. In Sunday's episode, Apu is revealed as a mysterious figure, then makes his return unmistakable, proclaiming "I am Apu."

The Simpsons showrunner Matt Selman told Variety the character and his family will appear more regularly going forward. "We love this character, and wanted to bring him back in a smart, Simpsons-y way that allowed him to evolve," he said.

In an interview with Variety, Malhotra says he initially had reservations about taking on the role, and wanted to know whether the series could bring Apu back in a way that acknowledged past mistakes.

He said his conversations with Selman and co-executive produxcer Cesar Mazariegos helped reassure him and described recording Apu's emphatic return as a meaningful moment.

CBC News reached out to Selman and Malhotra for comment but has not yet received a response.

Apu's surprise return has received mixed reactions online. Some fans welcomed the character's return. One X user wrote, "Apu is back after almost a decade! Curious to hear Sunil Malhotra bring the character back to life."

Another called the return long overdue, writing that Apu was "one of America's great fictional immigrants," and closed with the character's catchphrase, "#ThankYouComeAgain."

X user @SarahTran68 reacts positively to Apu's return to The Simpsons, writing "Apu is back after almost a decade! Curious to hear Sunil Malhotra bring the character back to life." (SarahTran68/X)

Others questioned the choice.

One X user wrote, "As a brown man, man I miss Hank Azaria as Apu."

Another X user wondered if the show still mattered, writing, "Astounding that anyone still watches. Can't say I've seen an episode in over 20 years. Maybe it's time to just let it go?"

World.title: Scott Stinson: Ontario’s electricity-import deal with U.S. undercuts Doug Ford’s energy tough talk
World.content:
Article content

The new deal to import electricity to Ontario would seem to undermine any future sabre-rattling that Ford might do on the energy file, although there are several caveats to be noted here. The Independent Electricity System Operator (IESO) is, as the name suggests, not making decisions at Ford’s behest. And its contract with Alpha Generation is a short-term arrangement to provide electricity in case Ontario needs it during the cold winter months and while the Pickering nuclear plant is undergoing a refurbishment. In the days since the Alpha contract was announced, the IESO said that Ontario will still be a net exporter of electricity to the United States and that it exported seven times as much as it imported last year. The new contract is about increasing the flexibility of the provincial power grid during the high-peak demand of the winter months.
