World.title: TV host gets 30-day detention in Georgia over Facebook post: reactions
World.content:
Journalist jailed over Facebook post in Georgia

Popular Georgian TV host Vakho Sanaia was sentenced to 30 days’ administrative detention on 19 October over social media posts deemed insulting to government officials.

The lawsuit was filed by the Department for Monitoring Hate Speech and Aggressive Statements, which recently became part of the Interior Ministry. Sanaia was accused of insulting Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili and MP Vladimir (Lado) Bozhadze in his Facebook posts and videos.

This is the third sentence handed down to the Formula TV host on similar charges since July this year, and his second term of detention.

Vakho Sanaia

Sanaia did not attend the court hearing, saying that prosecuting him for his posts was absurd. Police arrested him at his home.

“They want to force society into silence, but society will never be silent. We will overthrow this regime, however long it takes. This will certainly end in our victory,” Sanaia said as he was being arrested.

Why was Vakho Sanaia punished

The case centres on three social media posts about parliament speaker Shalva Papuashvili and ruling-party MP Vladimir Bozhadze.

The posts included censored profanities referring to the two politicians.

In a post on 22 July, shortly before he was detained in an earlier case, Sanaia wrote: “For 14 days, don’t call Shalva [Papuashvili] and Lado [Bozhadze] [censored insult] – when I get out, I’ll deal with that.”

In another post on 5 August, he referred to his earlier remarks, writing: “I wrote that you shouldn’t call Papuashvili and Bozhadze [censored insult], and they arrested me.”

On 24 September, Sanaia published a video address whose title also contained a censored profane reference to Papuashvili. Sanaia has described the proceedings as an attempt to restrict freedom of expression.

The case is being brought under Article 173¹⁶ of Georgia’s Code of Administrative Offences, which penalises insulting a political office-holder. The provision allows for a fine of 2,500 to 6,000 lari ($930–$2,220) or administrative detention for between five and 60 days.

This is the third administrative case against Sanaia. In July, he was fined 6,000 lari and sentenced to 14 days in detention over earlier posts involving the same two politicians.

The government agency that monitors social media

The Interior Ministry’s Division for Combating Hate Speech began operating on 1 June. It monitors public statements, including social media posts, and refers cases to court. Local media report that the unit often acts without a complaint from the person allegedly insulted. Cases brought by the division have led to dozens of fines and several detentions.

The case comes amid deteriorating relations between Georgia and the West. In November 2024, the government halted EU accession talks until 2028, triggering mass protests. Georgia has also fallen to 135th place out of 180 countries in Reporters Without Borders’ 2026 Press Freedom Index, down from 77th in 2022.

Sentence draws criticism in Georgia and abroad

European Commission spokesperson Christian Wigand has commented on the arrest of Vakho Sanaia:

“We have been very vocal in our criticism of Georgian Dream’s actions aimed at suppressing the political opposition, journalists and activists. Unfortunately, they continue to restrict civic space. The Georgian authorities must immediately release all unjustly detained politicians, journalists and activists and repeal repressive legislation.”

The Georgian Charter of Journalistic Ethics described the sentence as unjust, saying the authorities are using legislation and the courts to silence critical voices and restrict independent media.

“Through legislative amendments and, subsequently, the way these amendments are enforced, Georgian Dream has abandoned its obligation to tolerate criticism,” the charter said.

The Media Advocacy Coalition said the third case brought against the same journalist points to a pattern of persecution targeting critical media and dissenting voices. The coalition also expressed solidarity with the Formula TV team.

PEN Georgia called for the detention ruling to be overturned immediately. “In a country where journalists and citizens are jailed for criticising the government, and free speech becomes grounds for punishment, democracy no longer exists,” the organisation said.

Transparency International Georgia said Sanaia was being punished for exposing billionaire Bidzina Ivanishvili, founder of Georgian Dream and widely seen as Georgia’s shadow ruler, and for supporting the country’s European future.

Parliament speaker: “Obscenity is not freedom of expression”

Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili said obscene language in public was unacceptable and could carry legal consequences.

“Obscenity has nothing to do with expressing an opinion and is not protected by freedom of expression,” he said.

Papuashvili said he did not follow individual cases. According to him, the Interior Ministry’s unit operates automatically, and those targeted often learn about decisions only after they have been made.

He also cited Germany, saying people can face criminal charges for insulting others on social media, including following a personal complaint by the chancellor.

Papuashvili also criticised the EU ambassador, claiming that “he himself promotes hatred” and that “some people may try to win his favour.”

“If he has the audacity to use obscene language in public, he should also have the courage to face the consequences,” Papuashvili said of Sanaia.

News in Georgia

World.title: Opinion: ‘Irakli Bzhinava’s arrest in Russia is blow to freedom in Abkhaz society’
World.content:
Abkhaz Foreign Minister Oleg Bartsits discussed the fate of Abkhaz lawyer Irakli Bzhinava, who has been in a Russian prison since February 2026, with his Russian counterpart, Sergei Lavrov.

Irakli Bzhinava

Irakli Bzhinava holds dual Abkhazian and Russian citizenship and lives in Russia. The initial grounds for his arrest stemmed from a social media post he published on 23 December 2022, in which he criticised an agreement to transfer a famous state-owned holiday residence in Abkhazia to Russia. Russian authorities accuse Bzhinava over the post of “criminal intent to make public calls for activities directed against the security of the Russian Federation”.

In mid-September 2026, Russia’s Investigative Committee opened a second criminal case against Bzhinava, accusing him of “publicly justifying terrorist Shamil Basayev on the internet”.

According to Oleg Bartsits, Abkhazia’s Foreign Ministry remains in regular contact with the Russian side and also liaises with Bzhinava’s relatives and lawyers. The Abkhaz consul in Russia recently visited Irakli Bzhinava, and the authorities also arranged a meeting between him and his mother.

Bartsits adds that some issues remain unresolved, but they fall under the jurisdiction of Russian law enforcement agencies, and the Abkhaz side respects this. Since Bzhinava is a Russian citizen, Abkhazia’s authorities have limited scope for action, although members of the public are urging them to do everything possible to help their compatriot.

Prominent Abkhaz public figure Akhra Bzhania explains in his blog why Irakli Bzhinava’s case matters so much to Abkhaz society. In his view, by punishing Bzhinava for his dissenting views, Russia is trying to intimidate all Abkhaz people who share his position. And there are many of them.

Most Abkhaz people oppose agreements under which Russia seeks to take something from Abkhazia or derive some benefit from it. The issue of Shamil Basayev is also controversial: he received the title of “Hero of Abkhazia” for his participation in the 1992–93 Georgian-Abkhaz war. In short, many other Abkhaz people could have made — and have made — the statements that led to Bzhinava’s arrest.

Akhra Bzhania: “An effective state is possible only when society is free and responsible. Society acts as a reservoir, supplying the state with everything it needs: personnel, money and a worldview. It also holds the state to account through the press and political institutions.

This model works wherever society is free and confident in its natural rights. To a large extent, it works in Abkhazia too. Our society delegates power to the authorities not as a sacred function, but to represent its real interests. When the authorities begin to disregard those interests, a correction follows: the government resigns, and the overall political course returns to a path guided by our own sovereign interests.

A free and politically active society is what makes us strong, allowing us to advance our own agenda under the most difficult circumstances. Our freedom is our immunity against everything that threatens us — a fence that marks where other people’s interests end and ours begin.

Irakli Bzhinava’s arrest is an attack on this very immunity.

I do not believe there are any naive people in Abkhazia who think the charges against our compatriot are purely personal. Almost our entire society could face the same accusations on entirely legitimate grounds, because the overwhelming majority of us think exactly as he does.”

Therefore, Bzhinava’s arrest and the extremely harsh conditions of his detention aim not to counter his personal views, but to control the ideological climate in Abkhazia.

From now on, anyone who dares to criticise agreements between Russia and Abkhazia must consider the possibility of arrest on charges of “making public calls for activities directed against the security of the Russian Federation”.

We must respond appropriately to this, if only out of an instinct for self-preservation, not to mention civic solidarity. This applies to everyone: political parties, public movements, creative unions and parliament. In this case, the strength of our response will determine the extent of our freedom. We must defend Irakli Bzhinava not for his sake, but for our own.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

The case of Irakli Bzhinava

World.title: Beslan Kobakhia on POWs, historical narratives and peace. A view from Abkhazia, video discussion
World.content:
Georgian–Abkhaz war

The arrest of former Georgian State Minister Gia Baramidze has brought renewed attention to unresolved questions surrounding the Georgian–Abkhaz war of 1992–1993, including allegations that Abkhaz prisoners of war were executed rather than held for exchange. In an interview with Chegemskaya Pravda, Beslan Kobakhia, who chaired the Abkhaz commission responsible for prisoners of war and the protection of civilians during the conflict, recalled his wartime experience, described cases in which he said prisoners were killed, and called for a thorough investigation into the fate of those still missing. The conversation also moved beyond the circumstances of the arrest to examine competing narratives of the war, the legacy of mutual hostility, and the prospects for a political settlement between Tbilisi and Sukhumi.

Main theses and arguments:

The call for an investigation into the alleged executions of POWs – Kobakhia says that if Baramidze’s statements about executions are accurate, the priority should be to establish what happened, identify the victims, locate their burial sites, and return their remains to their families. He also calls for international involvement, specifically mentioning the International Committee of the Red Cross.

– Kobakhia says that if Baramidze’s statements about executions are accurate, the priority should be to establish what happened, identify the victims, locate their burial sites, and return their remains to their families. He also calls for international involvement, specifically mentioning the International Committee of the Red Cross. The alleged wartime killings and disputes accounts of events in Gagra – Kobakhia disputes allegations that Abkhaz fighters committed atrocities in Gagra [playing football with severed heads of Georgians], recounting how he and other officials accompanied Georgian representatives to investigate reported incidents.

– Kobakhia disputes allegations that Abkhaz fighters committed atrocities in Gagra [playing football with severed heads of Georgians], recounting how he and other officials accompanied Georgian representatives to investigate reported incidents. Wartime narratives and allegations remain an obstacle to reconciliation – Kobakhia argues that unverified stories about atrocities became enduring wartime myths. According to him competing interpretations of the war continue to shape relations between the two communities.

– Kobakhia argues that unverified stories about atrocities became enduring wartime myths. According to him competing interpretations of the war continue to shape relations between the two communities. Reconciliation requires respect and practical engagement, not declarations of brotherhood – Kobakhia argues that mutual respect is essential. The reconciliation must be reflected in practical decisions and a willingness to engage with the realities faced by both societies.

– Kobakhia argues that mutual respect is essential. The reconciliation must be reflected in practical decisions and a willingness to engage with the realities faced by both societies. Accepting the current reality and pursuing a non-aggression agreement – Kobakhia argues that, after 33 years, the conflict needs a political conclusion. Rather than pursuing complicated and costly settlement plans, he proposes that the sides acknowledge the reality on the ground and sign at least a non-aggression pact.

Inal Khashig: Hello! You’re listening to Chegemskaya Pravda. Today, we’re going to talk about the Georgian-Abkhaz war, focusing on one particular detail.

The thing is that in September, in Tbilisi, that is, a couple of weeks ago, Gia Baramidze, a former state minister, was arrested. During the war, he was involved in prisoner-of-war exchanges on the Georgian side. And during an appearance on one of the YouTube channels, he stated that at a certain point Georgia had no pool of prisoners available for exchange because they were shooting prisoners. Abkhaz prisoners who fell into their hands were simply executed.

Today, our guest is Beslan Kobakhia. Beslan knows Gia Baramidze well because during the war Beslan headed the commission responsible for prisoner-of-war exchanges on the Abkhaz side, the Abkhaz commission for the exchange of prisoners of war. I can’t recall the commission’s full official name right now. Nevertheless, Beslan was involved in this work.

Beslan, good afternoon.

Beslan Kobakhia: Good afternoon.

Inal Khashig: What is your view of this situation? Gia Baramidze was arrested not under an article concerning defamation. In other words, if he had been lying, they could have denied all of this and said that he was slandering people. Instead, he was detained and arrested on charges of treason. In general, how do you view this situation?

Beslan Kobakhia: Well, first of all, good afternoon.

Let’s begin with the name of the commission. It was called the Government Commission of the Republic of Abkhazia for Prisoner-of-War Affairs and the Protection of the Rights of the Civilian Population. That was its name. It was established, if my memory serves me correctly, on March 9, 1993. Before it was established, there was a scandalous incident. I won’t talk about it today, and I don’t want to, so to speak. But following an investigation into that incident, Vladislav Grigorievich decided to establish the commission, and I was appointed its chairman.

Now, regarding Gia Baramidze, whom you said I know well: I wouldn’t say that I know him particularly well. I knew Paata Zakareishvili much better; we worked in close contact with one another. As for Gia Baramidze, well, I saw him perhaps once or twice somewhere and spoke with him, so to speak, but that was about it.

I remember an incident when they came to negotiate with us in Gudauta after we had taken Gagra. When we took Gagra and liberated it, they came to us, and we all ended up together in a meeting with Vladislav Grigorievich Ardzinba.

They arrived with lists of people who had allegedly been shot by our Abkhaz militia members and our army – civilians, supposedly. They also claimed that people had played football with the heads of murdered Georgians, using their severed heads at the stadium in Gagra. Well, Vladislav Grigorievich spent a long time trying to explain to them that none of this was true, and so on, but he simply couldn’t convince them. Eventually, Vladislav Grigorievich said, “Listen, why should I keep trying to convince you? I can see that I’m not going to succeed,” he said. “So go with Beslan Kobakhia and Ruslan Yazychba.” Ruslan was the head of the administration in Gagra at the time. Ruslan was also present at that meeting with Vladislav Grigorievich. “They will show you everything you want to see. Go down every street and show them whatever they want.” We said, “All right.”

We left Vladislav Grigorievich’s office. Ruslan drove ahead in his own car, and we followed him out of Gudauta.

Would you like me to go into more detail? It would be interesting because it would help you understand the psychological atmosphere at the time.

We were leaving Gudauta. I had an official car, and a driver was at the wheel. It was Zurik Vozba, who has since passed away. The car had Council of Ministers license plates, beginning with 01, followed by some number. I can’t remember the exact number anymore, but it started with 01. Those plates belonged to the Council of Ministers of Abkhazia.

When we passed the traffic police checkpoint in Gagra, they saw our traffic police officers standing there. They were clean, smartly dressed, and freshly shaven – in other words, they weren’t disheveled or anything like that. When they saw the car, they snapped to attention and saluted as it drove past.

They were talking to one another in Georgian. I don’t understand Georgian, but poor Zurik understood it well. They said, “Look at the order they have here.” They were surprised by the order, discipline, and so on.

As we drove farther, they continued talking among themselves. They were also struck by something they had noticed in Gudauta. They hadn’t seen crowds of people wandering aimlessly around with weapons in their hands. We never had anything like that during the war. At the same time, when I went to Sukhumi – which I had to visit fairly often during the war – I saw crowds of people, actual large crowds, and it was unclear whom they were answerable to. They would walk around, wander off somewhere, and so on. That was the contrast.

They continued talking among themselves. “Look, every little patch of land here is cultivated.” And it was true: as we drove along the road, we could see fields on both the left and right, some sown with crops, others ploughed.

That was how we arrived in Gagra, in the area around the stadium. Ruslan Yazychba arrived there as well. To give you an idea of the timing, this was literally just a couple of weeks, perhaps, after Gagra had been liberated.

A great many ethnic Georgians lived in the area around the stadium, and they continued to live there even after the fighting. We went into practically every house around the stadium. Our so-called guests spoke with each of the residents. You could call them guests, I suppose – the people who had come from Tbilisi.

At first, Ruslan and I stood nearby. Then we stopped approaching the conversations and told them, “You speak to the people one-on-one, so that you don’t think we are trying to put pressure on them or that they are being deceived, and so on.” They became convinced that the alleged events had never taken place. What is more, we went to the stadium itself, and they saw that there was grass there – young grass that had been planted beforehand. It was undamaged anywhere. If something like that had happened there, some traces would have remained in any case. Naturally, there was nothing of the sort.

They recorded the fact that this was the case. We also visited the family of a man named Mikhail Dzhintcharadze, if I remember his surname correctly. Before the war, he had been deputy head of the Gagra city administration, serving under Ruslan Yazychba. He was also a member of the Parliament of Abkhazia. During the occupation, he headed the Gagra administration while Georgian occupying forces were stationed there.

Incidentally, he was also known for something else. When we liberated Gagra, a letter addressed to Shevardnadze and signed by Mikhail Dzhintcharadze was found. In it, he described how badly the troops that had entered Gagra were behaving and how they were looting the local population. In effect, he documented what we later learned ourselves. At the end of the letter, he concluded that if things continued this way, the local population would certainly not support our side but would support the Abkhaz side instead. And, in fact, that is exactly what eventually happened.

As for him, he was killed during the capture of Gagra. According to many people who witnessed the events, he was killed by Georgian servicemen, not by Abkhaz.

Inal Khashig: Was he a former member of parliament?

Beslan Kobakhia: Yes, a former member of parliament. When he was killed, Ruslan was also among those taking part in the assault on Gagra. When he saw his deceased colleague, he managed to find an ambulance, have the dead man’s body taken away, and bring it home to his family, whom he knew well. In other words, he acted humanely, as any decent person should have done.

But the lists brought by the people who came to us to investigate and verify all the facts stated that he had been shot in some kind of crisscross pattern. Apparently, they meant that Muslims had shot a Christian and had shot him in that particular way. I don’t even understand what they meant or how that was supposed to be possible, but that was exactly what was written.

We then went to Mikhail Dzhintcharadze’s family. His wife told them what had actually happened and, on the contrary, expressed her deepest gratitude to Ruslan Yazychba for the humane way he had acted.

After that, we went through literally every address on their list, and not a single alleged incident was confirmed. What is more, most of the houses listed as having been burned down were completely intact.

After that, they asked us to take them to Leselidze, as it was called at the time. Today, we call the place Gechripsh. So we went there. Vladislav Grigorievich had told us to show them things in Gagra. I then told Ruslan, “I’ll take responsibility for this. Since we’ve already come this far, let’s go there as well.” We drove through all of Gechripsh, and we didn’t find a single local Georgian there anymore. Everyone had been evacuated to Sochi. They had all left. In other words, they hadn’t been killed or anything like that; they had left.

When all of this was over, we escorted them back as far as the Gumista River. They crossed over and continued toward Sukhumi, while we naturally stayed in Gudauta.

They know perfectly well that none of this happened. Then, twenty years later, when I was already living in Moscow, I received a phone call on the eve of the twentieth anniversary of our Victory. We had a journalist named Palantos at Radio Liberty, based in Prague. Somehow, he had obtained my phone number and called me in Moscow. At that moment, I was behind the wheel. I was driving when the phone suddenly rang.

They asked me how I remembered that situation, now that twenty years had passed and so much had happened since the war. I said, “You know, I remember everything as if it had happened yesterday.” What is more, some wartime myths are still alive to this day. I pointed out that there were people who now held high-ranking government positions in the Republic of Georgia. I named Paata Zakareishvili and Gia Baramidze. At the time, Gia was, I believe, either the first deputy prime minister or…

Inal Khashig: He was the first deputy prime minister, and then, for some period, he served as acting state minister of Georgia.

Beslan Kobakhia: Well, there you are – he held a senior position. Paata Zakareishvili was the minister responsible for integration, I believe that was the name of the ministry.

I said, “You know, it’s astonishing that they don’t refute these claims, because this lie is still circulating to this day – the story about the ‘severed heads’ and so on.” Putin even mentioned it at some point in one of his interviews, addressing the Georgians and saying, “Have you forgotten how people played football with your heads?” That is how widespread this myth became, so to speak. It has taken on a life of its own.

When Georgian journalists heard my interview, I nearly triggered a political crisis in Georgia. They rushed to Gia Baramidze. When they confronted him, he said, “That’s not true. I wasn’t there.” How could he say he wasn’t there? I remembered it clearly.

Paata Zakareishvili, however, is a decent man. He reacted by saying, “No, everything happened exactly as Beslan described it. That is how it was.” But, he said, these were all wartime myths. “I often heard stories that, in Serbia, pregnant women had their stomachs cut open, and so on. But when you start checking these claims,” he said, “they are never confirmed.”

Regarding the situation in Gagra, he said, “I personally couldn’t find a single eyewitness who had actually seen it with their own eyes. Someone told me there was some video footage of it. But I couldn’t find any such footage either.” Besides, we had actually been there ourselves and had personally established that it was not true.

Inal Khashig: From a technical standpoint, too, a human head weighs seven or eight kilograms. Trying to play football with one would be extremely dangerous for the limbs.

Beslan Kobakhia: You’re saying that it is technically impossible. But before anyone could do something like that, before a person even… well, for a moment, let’s imagine that it really happened. Just think about it: the idea would first have to occur to someone. And if such an idea arose in someone’s mind, that person would be mentally abnormal. So what are you suggesting? There would have to be at least five people on one side and five on the other – ten lunatics from an insane asylum – and not a single person among them would have said, “What on earth are you doing?” This is the ravings of a madman, so to speak.

But I understand why this was done. Before Gagra was captured, the local Georgian population had, by and large, not taken up arms. Of course, there were already some people who had done so, but it had not happened on a mass scale. To force the local population to fight, the Georgian military propaganda apparatus, the military propaganda machine, came up with this myth. And they achieved their objective. After Gagra was captured, many people really did take up arms. By the end of the war, there were practically no people left who had not taken up arms; very few had refrained from doing so.

But do you know where they went too far? They continued fueling the hysteria until it reached such proportions that, when we were liberating the city of Sukhumi, these people, terrified out of their minds, fled Sukhumi through the mountains and across all that terrain. Do you understand? That was the result of the deception spread by the Georgian military propaganda machine at the time.

Later, we had to help the people who remained in Sukhumi and wanted to leave. There were more than forty thousand of them, and we helped people leave Sukhumi at that time. What is more, we did not force anyone to leave. On the contrary, I would get onto every bus and explain that the Abkhaz government had issued no decision to expel anyone from Abkhazia. There was no such decision at all. “You are on these buses only because you want to leave. My task – our task,” I would say, “is to ensure that you can do so safely and comfortably.”

That was how we treated people. We did not mistreat anyone or do anything of the sort. We escorted them under guard all the way to the Inguri River. At that time, we sent more than forty people to Georgia.

There is another point I want to tell you about, in connection with what you said…

Inal Khashig: No, I want to return to the issue of the executions. I understand that the commission was established in March 1993, as you said, Beslan. But the incident in Gagra took place in October 1992. So the process of investigating these matters must already have been underway, right?

Beslan Kobakhia: Of course, it was.

Beslan Kobakhia: We also dealt with prisoner exchanges, but how exactly did we handle them? I would receive instructions concerning specific individuals, and I would deal with those cases. But as for planning the process as a whole, gathering information, and finding out who was being held on the other side, everyone was involved in that work. And when everyone is responsible for something, it means that nobody is responsible for it. The State Security Service, the KGB, the Council of Ministers, the Ministry of Internal Affairs—Alexander Zolotinskovich Ankvab was there at the time, too.

Initially, I dealt exclusively with civilians. But later I had to take on other matters because various unclear situations kept arising, so to speak. Eventually, this led Vladislav Grigorievich to say, “Let’s establish a commission,” and he proposed me for the position. I told him, “I’m already chairing 25 commissions. What, will this be the twenty-sixth?” He replied, “I trust you. I want you to take this position.” Those were his exact words. I said, “Well, if that’s how it is, all right.”

So, the commission formally began its work in March. But in practice, even before that, Alexander Zolotinskovich and I had frequently discussed various situations and often made decisions together, decisions on which a great deal depended, including people’s lives. I can say that without any exaggeration.

At the beginning of the war, there was the situation for which Gia Baramidze has now been arrested. We can judge this situation only from the mass media reports we read. And what do we know about it? We know that, according to his statement, at the beginning of the war they had no pool of prisoners available for exchanging prisoners of war.

I can confirm what he said, because, indeed, at the beginning of the war, we exchanged all prisoners on an all-for-all basis. We always had more prisoners than the Georgian side. And we behaved honestly: whenever we reached an agreement, we always fulfilled everything we had agreed upon. We handed over all the prisoners of war. They handed over those they had, or at least those they believed they had accounted for. Then, a day or two later, some new people would turn up – one or two individuals who had been kept in Georgian military units, so to speak.

Incidentally, we did not have this practice on the Abkhaz side. All prisoners of war were transferred to our central facility, as it was called, in Gudauta. We had a designated place where we held them, and there we could guarantee that nothing would happen to them.

I can tell you that throughout the entire war, not a single prisoner of war held under our control died.

Moreover, those who were wounded received medical attention. We would call in doctors and provide treatment on the spot if necessary. If that was not sufficient, we admitted them to hospital, where they received appropriate treatment. Not a single person from the Georgian side who was held in our captivity and under our control died. I want to emphasize that point.

But after some time, we began to realize that we were handing over everyone, while they were not handing over everyone. A meeting was held at the Ministry of Defence. At that time, Sultan Aslanbekovich Sosnaliev was already the minister. A decision was made that we would no longer conduct exchanges in that manner; from then on, we would exchange one person for one person. Once we started doing this, it forced the Georgian side to bring some order into its ranks, to the extent that it was able to do so, so to speak. They began to approach the matter more responsibly. That is how the situation developed.

Now, let us return to what Baramidze, who has been arrested today, said. He stated that they had executed people whom they had taken prisoner.

You know, to be honest, I know very little about this, because they never admitted to it at the time. And if this has come to light today because Baramidze has spoken about it publicly, then several other questions arise as well.

First, if they executed our men, that constitutes a war crime. Those involved in these events should presumably face the appropriate sanctions. That is the first point.

Second, we must obtain lists of the people who were executed, because we still have many people who went missing and whom we have not found, even after 33 years. If Baramidze has any information about these people, we absolutely must obtain it.

Third, we must find out where these people are buried so that we can do what we are obliged to do: give them a dignified burial, return their remains to their relatives, and do everything that is normally done in a civilized human society, so to speak. To do that, we need to know the burial locations. These are the questions that immediately arise.

And fourth, the international community should almost certainly become involved in this situation. It seems to me that it is the direct responsibility of the International Committee of the Red Cross, for example, to investigate everything connected with this matter and transmit the information to us, to our country.

Inal Khashig: Well, crimes of this kind are already known to us, particularly from the early stages of the war. You said that everyone was involved in these matters back then.

For example, I know that my friend Abzagu Gurgulia was killed in Shroma in August. Nine or ten people were captured along with him. Practically all of them were executed. Two were ransomed, but all the others were executed. And they were shot during the funerals of Georgian fighters.

Beslan Kobakhia: Yes, Abzagu Gurgulia died a heroic death, incidentally. He is a Hero of Abkhazia, a title awarded posthumously. May his memory live forever.

I know for certain of a similar case involving John Dzidzaria. I learned about it later from Greeks who lived in the village where he was brought to be mourned. One of the Georgian Guardsmen had been killed, and John was killed there during the funeral. But he, too, behaved heroically. They wanted to make him kneel. He knelt down, kissed the ground, then stood up and said, “Now do whatever you want with me. Long live Abkhazia!” And that was how he died. As far as I know, he was also posthumously awarded the title of Hero of Abkhazia.

There was another case as well. I did not prepare specifically for this conversation, so I may not remember the surname, but there was another young man who was wounded and taken prisoner. We saw him on Georgian television, specifically the Georgian-language television channel in Sukhumi. Journalists filmed him and showed him, saying, “We have captured this man here.” The young man had ended up in the Republican Hospital.

As soon as we saw him, literally the next morning, I immediately requested a prisoner exchange from the Georgian side, because we had many Georgian prisoners of war. They did not even know that someone was being held in the hospital. Then, for some reason, they stopped responding to our calls. One day passed, then two, then three. We kept trying to contact them. Eventually, I requested a meeting, and we met on the Gumista Bridge.

I asked them, “Why have you stopped responding? Let’s arrange an exchange. You have a wounded man, and we saw him with our own eyes on your television. It wasn’t our television station.” They told me, “You know, on the night he was shown on television, it wasn’t just you who saw him. Georgians who were fighting against us saw him too. Those people broke into the hospital during the night, took him away, and killed him.” In other words, they took him away and killed him. These are two cases that I know about with certainty.

I think we can, and probably should, add another case to these: the incident that occurred after our unsuccessful January offensive in 1993.

Inal Khashig: That incident was documented. Let me remind you: it was January 5, following the unsuccessful January operation for the Abkhaz side. Afterward, an exchange of the bodies of the dead and of prisoners of war took place, and so on. Many people noticed that, several days after the operation had ended, most of the bodies returned by the Georgians were still warm. They had literally been shot shortly before being handed over. This was documented afterward.

Beslan Kobakhia: We brought them back in January. It was extremely difficult to reach an agreement with the Georgians, but we eventually managed to do so. We arrived by Russian helicopter and landed near School No. 12. They brought all our fallen men there, and we loaded them onto the helicopter. To give you an idea of the scale, the helicopter was filled with bodies right up to the top. There were many of our men.

We flew to Gudauta, and the bodies were immediately taken to the hospital morgue. We had a Georgian military medic in our custody who had been captured. Naturally, our doctors examined the bodies first, and they unequivocally stated that several of the people handed over to us as having been killed had actually been killed just one or two hours before their bodies were returned.

We then brought in the Georgian military medic, who also took part in examining the bodies, and he confirmed their findings.

All of this is preserved in the archives of Abkhaz television and elsewhere. In other words, a war crime of this kind was committed at that time. And what Baramidze is talking about fits perfectly into the same pattern.

Inal Khashig: As I remember, both during the war and after it, a so-called “White Book” was compiled in which these crimes were documented. These days, they do not seem to talk about them as much. In the first postwar years, however, a great many crimes were documented.

At least, the Georgians say they want us to reconcile with them and find some common ground. If we are talking about reconciliation, then surely these crimes need to be investigated. We have records of them, and some of the crimes are documented in writing. The Prosecutor General’s Office dealt with these cases. We could hand over those documents.

It is strange, in general, that on the one hand they consider us their citizens, while on the other they bring charges of treason against Baramidze. In other words, he is saying that Georgians executed their own citizens of Abkhaz ethnicity. That is not only a war crime; if they considered us their citizens, then what the hell were they shooting us for?

Beslan Kobakhia: In that case, it is a genocide – genocide in its purest form.

Inal Khashig: Yes. There are so many nuances here that, in fact, they also work against this criminal case. It seems to me that if anyone is to be put on trial, it should not necessarily be Baramidze. Instead, the entire matter should be investigated.

Beslan Kobakhia: Well, you know, you are absolutely right.

We recently marked 33 years since those events. Just a few days ago, we celebrated Victory Day, the Day of the Liberation of Abkhazia, so to speak. For us, this is a sacred holiday.

Thirty-three years have passed. Thirty-three years is a very long time, and we had hoped that, after the war that broke out between us – a bloody war – we would eventually find a way forward. It must be understood that we Abkhazians did not attack anyone. We were living ordinary lives. Our holiday homes and sanatoriums were full of vacationers. And then, right in the middle of all that, tanks, aircraft, tracked military vehicles, howitzers – you name it – were sent against us. Every kind of weapon that had been transferred to Georgia under the Tashkent Agreement and through the Transcaucasian Military District was turned over to Georgia.

It is true that one of the clauses of the Tashkent Agreement stipulated that these weapons could not be used in internal conflicts. Everything was signed and agreed upon, apparently. But who remembered that agreement afterward? Everything Georgia received from Russia at the time – I mean Yeltsin’s Russia – under the Tashkent Agreement was subsequently used against us.

Well, in the 33 years since then, we have made many attempts to move forward. After all, every war must come to an end eventually.

For example, I would not want our children and young people to grow up hating Georgia or anyone else in the surrounding world, because you cannot build anything on hatred. As we know, things must be built on pragmatism and, ultimately, on love. You cannot build anything on hatred.

Unfortunately, however, we hear contradictory statements from Georgian officials. When addressing us, they say that we are their brothers, and so on. To some extent, that is true, too, because there were many mixed families among us. As many as 40 percent. Do you know the statistics? Up to 40 percent of Abkhaz families were, in one way or another, intermarried with Georgian families.

Inal Khashig: I cannot vouch for those statistics. It seems to me that they are too politicized.

Beslan Kobakhia: Listen, listen. Incidentally, this did not make any difference at all. It did not prevent us Abkhaz from defending our homeland, because we were the ones who were attacked. You remember how the tanks came into our territory without any real justification, and what were they trying to prove by doing that?

And yet, up to 40 percent of families were mixed. Nevertheless, today, if you open any Abkhaz post on the internet and simply write, “I love Abkhazia,” comments from people living in Georgia will immediately appear, pouring abuse on you from head to toe. They say things that, in any decent society – and certainly in a Caucasian society – should have consequences. These kinds of comments appear every single day, year after year.

So what is happening? The Georgian authorities say one thing, while ordinary citizens sitting on the internet behave in a completely different way. There is a complete contradiction between the two.

We were therefore compelled to hold this academic and practical conference and propose that Georgians abandon the Ingorokva theory, which has a profound influence on the younger generation and benefits neither people – not the Abkhaz nor the Georgians. It sets the two peoples against each other, and it will inevitably lead to further negative consequences.

Inal Khashig: But in any case, this is not just about history; ideological issues are involved as well. If there is a genuine desire to resolve the issue peacefully, then it is a complex, multifaceted task. You cannot put one thing in order in one area and leave everything else unchanged elsewhere.

And the fact is that, by and large, after this bloody war, the reality today is that Georgians do not like Abkhaz and Abkhaz do not like Georgians. That is a fact. So, talking about how we are brothers seems to me somewhat…

Beslan Kobakhia: Were there no mixed families in which Georgian and Abkhaz people were cousins?

Inal Khashig: But nowadays, I mean, not in the sense of calling these peoples brotherly, as they used to say in Soviet terminology.

Beslan Kobakhia: No, no, that’s not what I meant.

Inal Khashig: On the other hand, if we are to agree on certain rules or on some form of peace, this should not be discussed through Facebook or social media. It should be done by representatives of the authorities. Representatives of official Tbilisi should talk to representatives of the Abkhaz authorities, of official Sukhumi. Although Georgia’s Law on Occupied Territories makes it a criminal offence for them to talk to representatives of the Abkhaz authorities, they could nevertheless talk to these so-called representatives of the Abkhaz people. They tried to bring forward one Buava, who recently died of a drug overdose. Of course, they could find another couple of people to talk to as representatives, but how effective would that be?

Beslan Kobakhia: I’ll give you a very straightforward answer.

You say that we are not obliged to love one another. Of course we aren’t. We don’t demand that anyone love us, either. The Abkhaz are not a dollar that people have to love or hate.

But we demand to be treated with respect, just as we treat the entire world around us with respect.

The project we are pursuing is the construction of an independent, democratic state that poses no threat to anyone in this world. This project is entirely humanistic, and it should not – and cannot – provoke rejection from the world around us. Unfortunately, however, the only country that stands in our way and constantly trips us up is Georgia.

I would like to recall, for example, a woman who once served as Georgia’s foreign minister. Her name was Panjikidze, though I can’t remember her first name. She was the daughter of Guram Panjikidze, a well-known Georgian writer whose novels we used to devour during the Soviet era. He was a magnificent writer, a humanist who wrote truly beautiful works. As I recall, one of his novels was called A Year of Active Sun. I liked that novel very much at the time.

And then, many years later, his daughter became foreign minister. I don’t even know whether Badjikidze is still alive—he has probably passed away by now. Yes, his daughter became foreign minister, and once again she suddenly created an obstacle to our children travelling to a singing competition in Bulgaria, if I remember correctly. In another instance, they were not allowed to enter Turkey. And she presented this as one of the greatest victories of Georgian diplomacy: Abkhaz children had been denied entry, and so on.

But I don’t understand: if this is a victory, what kind of victory is it? I think Guram Panjikidze must be turning in his grave when he sees his daughter behaving this way.

Unfortunately, these examples are not isolated incidents. On the very day of the conference we had organized at the university, our permanent representative to the Republic of Turkey, Ibrahim Avidzba, was supposed to participate. Then, just an hour before the conference, he called me from the airport and said that he urgently had to fly to Istanbul because 60 of our gymnasts had travelled to Turkey for a competition, but they were not being allowed to compete. He said he would go there, look into the matter and try to resolve these issues. Naturally, I wished him good luck. He flew out, and just today we received information that they had not been allowed to compete as representatives of Abkhazia – the Republic of Abkhazia – because the country is considered unrecognized and, naturally, we have no diplomatic relations with the Republic of Turkey.

However, they competed there as representatives of the APSNY club. So the name APSNY was heard after all, so to speak, but they were representing a club rather than a country. And some of our children won gold medals there, among other achievements. You see what I mean?

But once again, this situation leaves a bitter aftertaste. What are you doing? On the one hand, you are trying to tell us that we should somehow make peace, and so on, while on the other hand, you create obstacles of this kind for children. Is that normal?

This is the issue we have begun to raise. Every war has a beginning and an end.

As for what happened in 1992, Georgia’s State Council was an illegitimate governing body at the time; it had overthrown the entirely legitimate Zviad Gamsakhurdia. The question of what kind of leader he was and what kind of person he was is a separate matter. But he had been legitimately elected, so to speak. He was driven out by bandits—Jaba Ioseliani and Kitovani—and Shevardnadze later joined their group. Then, on 14 August, they decided to launch military operations against Abkhazia. They sent in troops, and we know how it ended.

Many years have passed since then, yet there is still no end in sight. But this conflict must be brought to an end. We have examples from history. In 1918, Mazniashvili, acting on behalf of the Georgian Democratic Republic led by Noe Zhordania, occupied the entire territory of Abkhazia. Moreover, he advanced into Russian territory at the time, and the towns and villages there were occupied all the way to Tuapse. Later, Denikin intervened, and military operations drove Mazniashvili’s forces out of those areas. Meanwhile, in Abkhazia, the Kiaraz fighters, led by Nestor Lakoba, engaged his forces in battle. The Kodori River ran red with blood; the fighting was that fierce. Historians of that period testify to this. Ultimately, the Georgian army was driven out of Abkhazia, and on 4 March, Abkhazia’s independence was proclaimed.

Events in Georgia also unfolded in such a way that Noe Zhordania was forced to leave the country with his government, and the new Georgian leadership of that period recognized Abkhazia’s independence. You know, that decision led to a situation in which, just two years later, nobody was talking anymore about Mazniashvili having entered Abkhazia with his troops. Instead, normal relations began to develop between Georgia and Abkhazia. For a time, the two continued their relations as equal entities with equal rights.

Inal Khashig: A treaty-based union republic.

Beslan Kobakhia: Later, yes, it was a treaty-based arrangement, and so on. But then came what happened under Stalin, Beria, and the others. I don’t want to delve into that period now.

If we are to bring this war to an end, we must put a full stop to it.

First of all, condemn the war in Georgia. It began there, in Tbilisi. The entire city centre in Tbilisi was devastated at the time. How many people died on your side then? Remember how many people were killed by those leaders who unleashed the war in Abkhazia and carried out punitive expeditions in Mingrelia as well. You know all of this, and so do the Mingrelians living in western Georgia; they know what happened and how it all unfolded. Therefore, that leadership must be condemned, and this criminal war must be condemned, because it brought suffering to the Abkhaz, the Georgians and the Ossetians alike.

What should we do next? We had the Boden Plan, as you remember, along with various other proposals. They were complicated and very costly, among other things. We don’t need any of that. Set all these plans aside. Let us accept the reality we face today. Let us finally meet in a way that would allow us to sign at least a non-aggression pact with one another. For many years, this has been the starting point of our meetings in Geneva, yet there has been no progress on the matter.

You don’t want to sign this agreement, which means you want to attack us. That is the conclusion we have reached; we cannot draw any other conclusion, you see. If we are going to be attacked, then naturally we behave as people who are expecting an attack would behave.

But Abkhazia is no longer what it was 33 years ago. We have fraternal relations with the Russian Federation. Numerous agreements have been signed, including a military agreement that guarantees that no one will be able to launch a surprise attack on us anymore.

Let us take this reality into account and begin building our relations on the basis of that reality.

Believe me, this will be far better than sharpening knives and preparing for another war.

Inal Khashig: I’m going to wrap up our programme. Keep watching us and share your comments.

Let me remind you that today we began our discussion with the news that the Georgian authorities had arrested former Georgian State Minister Gia Baramidze, who headed Georgia’s commission for the exchange of prisoners of war during the war. Starting with this arrest, we recalled the war and the post-war period, and discussed the broader question of how this conflict might be resolved in the future.

That is what we discussed today with Beslan Kobakhia.

Beslan, thank you very much. Until we meet again.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website

World.title: Saving shelter puppies: Why Georgia is debating the fate of stray dogs again
World.content:
Gori shelter

Footage from a municipal shelter in the Georgian town of Gori, showing dozens of puppies kept in a cramped, filthy enclosure, has sparked public outrage and protests. Animal rights activists removed hundreds of animals from the shelter, many of which they say were ill.

But the case in Gori is just one episode in a long-running dispute over stray dogs in Georgia. Why have government programmes failed to solve the problem? What happens to captured animals, and who is responsible for their fate?

Dozens of dogs in a single enclosure

On Thursday evening, Georgian media published footage from a municipal dog shelter in Gori. The short video, filmed on a mobile phone, shows a dirty enclosure with a wet floor. It appears to measure no more than five to seven square metres.

Dozens of puppies crowd into the enclosure, piled almost on top of one another. They huddle together and walk over each other’s heads. The footage shows that they are dirty; some are wet, while others look extremely thin. Their living conditions are clearly distressing and incompatible with the principles of humane treatment.

The shelter soon issued a response of its own. The regional Agency for the Management of Stray Animals published a statement on its Facebook page, saying that staff had been carrying out routine cleaning and had therefore gathered all the puppies in a single enclosure.

Activists dismissed the statement as an excuse. They argued that even if the staff had been cleaning, this should not have caused the animals to suffer or put them at risk.

Protests and animal rescue

The footage from Gori outraged animal rights activists, campaigners, animal lovers and other concerned members of the public. The videos spread rapidly across social media, and users soon began organising a protest outside the shelter.

The protest took place in Gori the following day, on Friday 16 October. It was noisy and saw several incidents. One report, for example, alleged that a shelter employee attacked a protester.

Nevertheless, the protesters managed to secure the release of most of the puppies. According to various reports, between 100 and 300 animals were removed from the Gori shelter. People launched a fundraising campaign and an urgent search for adopters. Several veterinary clinics joined the effort, offering to treat the rescued animals free of charge.

Abuses and new risks

That evening, activists told journalists that many of the animals had been diagnosed with a serious viral disease and that the weakest puppies had died on the way out of the shelter. They said the rescued animals drank and ate voraciously, which they believed indicated that the shelter had not provided them with enough food or water.

Other alleged violations included a lack of quarantine facilities, missing documents identifying where the puppies had come from, cold conditions and appalling sanitation. One enclosure reportedly housed sick and healthy animals together, alongside the remains of dogs that had died.

Veterinarians who joined the discussion highlighted another concern: the conditions at the Gori shelter could trigger viral outbreaks among dogs in Tbilisi and other cities.

Veterinarian Mariam Chkhikvishvili, for example, wrote that people should, where possible, treat the puppies rescued from Gori in a dedicated facility that allows them to maintain proper sanitary standards.

“Taking the puppies from one clinic to another makes very little sense: it could contribute to the spread of mutated viruses. We need to follow at least the basic rules of disease control: do not move infected puppies from place to place or put other animals — both pets and strays — at risk. These cases require an isolated facility where staff can properly clean and disinfect surfaces,” Chkhikvishvili said.

She added that Tbilisi had faced a similar crisis in the past, with cases in which serious diseases spread from a shelter in the capital.

A bad reputation

The footage has reignited debate in Georgian society about stray animals and how people treat them. But before examining this long-standing problem, which Georgia has struggled to resolve for decades, it is worth explaining why the images from Gori caused such an uproar.

At first glance, the public reaction might seem to stem from surprise, as though people had assumed the shelter met all the required standards, only to discover that it did not. In reality, the opposite is true: the Gori shelter had long been dogged by grim rumours, and the videos appeared to confirm them.

Activists have been raising concerns about poor living conditions and staff cruelty for years. This spring, the shelter even faced accusations of killing dogs on a large scale.

In April, footage spread across social media showing smoke rising from the Gori shelter’s crematorium at night. The person who filmed it claimed the crematorium had operated throughout the night and that a strong smell of burning hung over the site.

Animal rights activists suspected that staff were killing dogs in large numbers, including live animals. However, no convincing evidence emerged that anyone had burned animals alive, and the authorities never officially confirmed the allegations.

JAMnews covered the case in detail in an in-depth report on the mass capture of stray dogs and growing distrust of the state agencies responsible for their fate.

The October scandal was therefore far from the first time the Gori shelter had come under scrutiny. More than that, the events in Gori formed part of a much broader conflict between the state and animal rights activists, which has continued in Georgia throughout much of 2026.

Where do stray dogs disappear to?

In spring 2026, protests against the mass capture of stray dogs broke out in several Georgian cities. The demonstrations followed numerous reports of missing animals, including dogs that had been sterilised, vaccinated and cared for by so-called community carers — people who regularly feed, treat and look after strays without taking them into their homes.

A JAMnews report published on 23 May featured accounts from residents of different Georgian cities who were trying to find out what had happened to the dogs in their care and secure their return. In interviews with the publication, activists voiced fears that authorities were taking animals away from familiar surroundings and relocating them to places where they could not find food or water, effectively condemning them to die.

The authorities categorically deny allegations of mass killings. According to the official account, staff capture dogs as part of a state population management programme that includes veterinary examinations, sterilisation, vaccination and the subsequent return of animals to their habitat. Activists, however, say the programme captures all dogs, including those that underwent sterilisation long ago.

This raises one of the main contradictions. Under the programme’s rules, authorities cannot return animals to every location. Restrictions apply in areas near schools, kindergartens, medical facilities, markets and food outlets.

Yet stray dogs tend to live precisely around shops, markets and cafés. In cities such as Tbilisi, it would be difficult to find a street without a school, clinic or shop nearby. This raises an obvious question: where do the authorities take dogs that they cannot release at the places where they captured them? And who monitors what happens to the animals after they leave the shelter?

Animal rights activists who spoke to JAMnews say they have yet to secure a transparent, accessible system for tracking the fate of every captured animal.

Countless strays

Nobody knows exactly how many stray dogs live in Georgia. Despite the problem having persisted for decades, the country still lacks reliable nationwide statistics.

Relatively reliable figures exist only for Tbilisi, where the municipal Animal Monitoring Agency tracks the stray animal population. According to figures from the agency cited by JAMnews, the Georgian capital had around 29,676 stray dogs in 2025.

Animal rights activists estimate that Georgia could have hundreds of thousands of stray animals, but independent nationwide counts have yet to verify that figure.

The scale of the problem is also reflected in public attitudes. According to a CRRC Georgia poll for the National Democratic Institute (NDI), conducted in October 2023, 22% of respondents considered stray animals one of the country’s main social problems.

This comes as little surprise. Stray dogs are a familiar sight on Georgia’s streets. People encounter them near shops, markets, bus stops, residential courtyards and tourist areas. Many dogs wear special tags on their ears, indicating that they have undergone registration and veterinary procedures. Local residents and tourists often feed them.

However, peaceful coexistence between people and animals does not always work. Reports of dog attacks on people regularly emerge in Georgia, while the risk of rabies remains a public health concern. Calls to control the stray dog population and protect public safety therefore have a real basis.

Simply removing dogs from the streets, however, does not stop the population from growing. As long as pet dogs continue to breed without control and people abandon unwanted puppies, new animals will take the place of those authorities capture.

New laws, old problems

In 2025, Georgia’s parliament passed a law on pets intended to establish a unified legal framework for their care, registration and breeding control. In February 2026, the government approved a dedicated programme to manage the overpopulation of dogs.

The programme centres on an approach known as CNVR: capture, neuter, vaccinate and return. The World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) also describes this approach in its guidelines. When properly implemented, it can gradually reduce animal populations without resorting to mass culling.

However, the way authorities carry out each stage is crucial. Sterilisation must cover a substantial proportion of the population, vaccination must prevent the spread of disease, and the relocation and release of animals must take their welfare and public safety into account.

Georgian animal rights activists have raised numerous concerns about how the authorities implement these measures. They accuse state agencies of lacking transparency, mistreating animals, violating shelter standards and failing to monitor what happens to animals after their capture.

The overall effectiveness of government policy has also come under scrutiny. The authorities have tried to tackle the problem before, regularly announcing tenders over the years for sterilisation campaigns targeting stray animals in the regions. Yet the scale of the problem suggests that these programmes have failed to deliver significant results.

According to animal rights activists, private individuals still carry out much of the sterilisation work in practice. Animal carers and volunteers pay for operations, specialist non-governmental organisations take part, and volunteers from European countries travel to Georgia to help run sterilisation campaigns. Activists say state programmes reach far fewer animals than necessary, and they also question the quality of the work.

“Let the dog go”: where stray animals come from

Another serious problem is irresponsible ownership. In Georgia, people even use the common expression “let the dog go” to describe a practice in which owners take unwanted animals far from home and abandon them in a forest or by the roadside.

In rural areas, owners may abandon a dog because it hunts domestic poultry or otherwise “misbehaves”.

Energetic breeds that need plenty of attention and exercise are particularly vulnerable, as are hunting dogs that fail to meet their owners’ expectations. Meanwhile, effective controls on animal breeding remain largely absent.

The legal framework to tackle such practices already exists. Georgia’s 2025 Law on Pets explicitly prohibits owners from abandoning their animals and requires them to register their pets, partly to prevent such cases.

The law also introduces restrictions on dog breeding. Since July 2026, a three-year moratorium on breeding certain breeds has been in force.

The footage from the Gori shelter offers a glimpse of how effectively these rules work in practice. If the authorities properly enforced the law, many of the puppies found there — along with the hundreds of other emaciated and abandoned animals that people encounter along Georgian roads — might never have ended up on the streets.

Diana Petriashvili, Mediaset

Gori shelter

World.title: “No to torture!” Saturday march in Tbilisi. “Protests in Georgia” video podcast
World.content:
The “Saturday marches” are part of an ongoing protest movement that has continued in Georgia for 689 days.

Protesters are demanding that Georgia return to the path of European integration and that all political prisoners be released. They are also calling for the repeal of all anti-democratic laws passed by the ruling Georgian Dream party over the past two years.

Protesters and opposition parties point out that part of Georgian society still does not recognise the results of the parliamentary election held in autumn 2024. They are calling for early parliamentary elections.

Over the course of nearly two years of protests, dozens of people have been arrested. Many have been charged with criminal offences and sentenced to prison.

For the first time in independent Georgia’s history, the country has around 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the independent media outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti. She was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer.

The protests continue despite an intensifying crackdown on civil society and the media.

World.title: Georgia: Billionaire Ivanishvili meets ruling party leaders – what is known about their talks after silent video release
World.content:
Ivanishvili Georgian Dream meeting

On 17 October, a rare political event took place in Georgia.

Bidzina Ivanishvili, founder and honorary chairman of the ruling Georgian Dream party, chaired a meeting of the party’s political council, followed by a meeting of the parliamentary majority, at the party’s central office.

This was the first public appearance in several months by Ivanishvili, whom many consider Georgia’s “shadow” ruler.

Yet it could hardly be called an “appearance”. Ivanishvili himself said nothing to journalists. The party’s press office released only silent footage of the meetings.

What was discussed behind closed doors became known through three sources: Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze’s briefing, the party’s written statement, and a brief comment by parliamentary majority leader Irakli Kirtskhalia.

Kobakhidze emphasised that Ivanishvili had expressed “pain” over his former team-mates who are in prison. This likely refers primarily to former Prime Minister Irakli Gharibashvili, who for many years was considered Bidzina Ivanishvili’s closest and most loyal ally but has now been convicted of large-scale corruption.

However, in the party’s statement, this issue is presented in a different tone.

It is stated that corruption problems within the team have been “fully and effectively” overcome.

While the meetings were underway, citizens protested outside the building under the slogan “Georgia against Ivanishvili”. One of the banners read, “Supporting Georgian Dream = betraying the country”, while another said, “14 bloody years”, referring to the years Georgian Dream has been in power.

Who joined the political council

The only publicly announced decision from the meetings was to expand the political council. Parliamentary majority leader Irakli Kirtskhalia and Zurab Pataradze, head of the government of the Autonomous Republic of Ajara, joined the body.

Footage released by the press office shows Ivanishvili entering the meeting, shaking hands with MPs and taking his seat. Irakli Kobakhidze, parliamentary speaker Shalva Papuashvili, Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze and Irakli Kirtskhalia sat beside him at the head table. Ministers were also present.

According to Kobakhidze, both meetings addressed current domestic and foreign policy issues. The party statement referred to “political and economic processes” in the country. It also said time was devoted to initiatives and reforms recently announced by the government.

The context behind Ivanishvili’s meetings with ruling party leaders

Bidzina Ivanishvili rarely appears in public. He has been under US sanctions since 2024.

His participation in party meetings on 17 October came amid an apparent crisis within the government.

Former senior Georgian Dream officials have been arrested one after another on corruption charges.

The most high-profile case involves former Prime Minister Irakli Gharibashvili.

In January 2026, he was sentenced to five years in prison under a plea agreement. In August, prosecutors brought a new bribery charge against him.

Gharibashvili has been publishing letters from prison in which he accuses Irakli Kobakhidze and former Deputy Prime Minister Mamuka Mdinaradze. On August 27, Mamuka Mdinaradze resigned from his post and announced his departure from politics. He denied any connection to the letters.

Another important factor in the context of Ivanishvili’s meeting with ruling party leaders is that the Constitutional Court is due to hear the authorities’ case seeking to ban opposition parties in just a few days.

According to opposition representatives, hearings were scheduled for October 21, 22 and 23. In response, an alliance of nine opposition parties announced a rally in Tbilisi on 25 October under the slogan “Georgia without Ivanishvili. Georgia deserves better.”

Gharibashvili is Ivanishvili’s “heartache” – and the statement about “overcoming difficulties”

After the meetings at the ruling party’s office, journalists asked Irakli Kobakhidze whether the possibility of releasing former Prime Minister Irakli Gharibashvili from prison had been discussed.

Kobakhidze replied that there had not. According to him, Ivanishvili gave a general assessment of “the developments”.

“For all of us, including, of course, first and foremost, Bidzina Ivanishvili, what happened is painful, when events unfold this way and former members of the team are serving sentences for specific crimes (…)”, Kobakhidze said.

He added: “What happened is regrettable. It was, of course, something of a blow to the team.”

Gharibashvili was sentenced to five years in prison in January 2026 following a plea agreement. In August, prosecutors brought a new charge against him. According to the prosecution, the former prime minister accepted 750,000 lari (about $290,000) in bribes.

Gharibashvili’s lawyers say he denies the new charge.

There is no mention of “heartache” in the party statement’s account of the same subject. According to the statement, Ivanishvili reviewed the corruption challenges the team had faced in the past and said that “as a result of the effective work of the prime minister, the government team and the security apparatus, these challenges have been fully and effectively overcome”.

Kobakhidze: “Friendship is none of your business“

Kobakhidze said the team had also discussed Mamuka Mdinaradze, a former deputy prime minister who previously served as head of the State Security Service.

Mdinaradze resigned from his post on August 27 and announced his departure from politics. At the time, he denied that his resignation was connected to Garibashvili’s letters published from prison.

Kobakhidze declined to elaborate publicly. “Mamuka Mdinaradze has left politics”, he said, adding that he did not consider it appropriate to bring the issue to the fore in these circumstances. He said he remained in occasional contact with Mdinaradze. He did not give a direct answer when asked whether they were still friends.

“Why are you asking about friendship? Friendship is none of your business”, he told journalists.

Journalists also raised the issue of a controversial social media post by Georgian Dream party member Dito Samkharadze, who wrote that “rats” [informers] had been identified within the ruling party.”

Kobakhidze was asked whether Samkharadze also meant Mdinaradze and whether legal proceedings against him were expected.

“I don’t know what you’re referring to,” the prime minister replied. He said there was “no basis whatsoever” for such speculation.

Parliamentary majority leader Kirtskhalia: “Ivanishvili spoke mostly about Kobakhidze“

Journalists asked Irakli Kirtskhalia to comment on growing public speculation that Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze could soon resign.

According to him, Ivanishvili devoted more time to Kobakhidze than to anyone else, “expressing support and praise, which the entire team, of course, shares”.

“Ivanishvili said that the government is performing very well under Kobakhidze’s leadership, and that not only is there no reason for his resignation, but every day confirms that he is the best prime minister,” Kirtskhalia said.

He described the resignation rumours as gossip spread by the opposition.

Scandal over possible corruption in spending on the Patriarch’s funeral

At a press briefing, Irakli Kobakhidze addressed the main political issue: allegations of possible corruption in spending on the Patriarch’s funeral.

He said preliminary information from the Government Administration showed “no indication of any improper expenditure”. He also said a large portion of the allocated funds had been returned.

In September, speaking on Rustavi 2, Kobakhidze provided specific figures: according to preliminary data, 722,000 lari (about $275,000) of the 3 million lari (about $1,100,000) allocated had been spent. The questions he answered concerned former Culture Minister Tika Rukhadze’s possible involvement in the alleged embezzlement.

Kobakhidze said detailed information would be presented to the public in the near future. Asked whether investigative agencies should look into the matter, he replied:

“First, we will present detailed information to you, and if any questions remain on this issue, let us discuss them together.”

“Whatever they call us, we keep winning” – Kobakhidze on media restrictions

Irakli Kobakhidze also commented on restrictions on the use of various words and expressions in the media adopted by the Communications Commission.

On 9 October, Transparency International – Georgia reported that the Communications Commission had objected to expressions used by independent TV channels Formula and Pirveli. The commission compiled a list of 93 words and phrases that it banned from use, including “regime”, “oligarch” and “prime minister appointed by Ivanishvili”, according to TI. Fines for using words on the list were increased to 10,000 lari (nearly $4,000).

Kobakhidze explained the decision as necessary to uphold the principle of objectivity.

He said these rules had existed in legislation for years, but an enforcement mechanism had not previously been in place. News programmes are now required to maintain neutrality.

That requirement does not apply to programmes expressing their hosts’ own views, Prime Minister said.

“Nothing bothers us. We win elections and emerge victorious from every political confrontation. Whether they call us a regime or a dictatorship, we win either way”, Kobakhidze said.

News in Georgia

World.title: Chronicles of Victory: October 20, 2020

The erupted 44-day Second Karabakh War ended with the liberation of Azerbaijan’s territories from nearly 30-year Armenian occupation and the restoration of territorial integrity.

- First Vice President of Azerbaijan Mehriban Aliyeva shared a publication on her Instagram account about the liberation of the city of Zangilan and a number of villages of Fuzuli, Jabrayil, Khojavand and Zangilan districts.

- Video footage of the destruction of a large number of Armenian servicemen and military equipment had been released.

- Armenian anti-aircraft guns were destroyed in the direction of Ganja.

World.title: Azerbaijan, UN discuss issue of declining water level of Caspian Sea
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 19. Azerbaijan and the UN discussed the issue of the declining water level of the Caspian Sea.

This was announced by Mukhtar Babayev, Representative of the President of Azerbaijan on Climate Issues, in a post on his X social media account.

"Pleased to meet with Dmytro Shlapachenko, UN Resident Coordinator in Azerbaijan, to discuss advancing cooperation on climate and environmental priorities.

Building on Azerbaijan’s partnership with the UN, including our successful collaboration at COP29, exchanged views on advancing climate action and enhancing resilience.

Discussed the need for greater international attention to the Caspian Sea’s declining water levels, one of the most pressing environmental challenges facing our region. Also discussed deepening regional cooperation on transboundary water management, drought preparedness, early warning systems and data sharing.

Explored opportunities to further strengthen cooperation on these priorities towards COP31 and beyond," the statement said.
