World.title: Toll of war in Ukraine cited as Svitolina, Monfils announce end of marriage
World.content:
World number six Elina Svitolina says she and former tennis player Gael Monfils are ending their marriage, with the Ukrainian adding that the emotional toll of Russia's war in her homeland left her needing to rediscover herself.

The couple married in July 2021 and welcomed a daughter, Skai, in October 2022.

Announcing the separation in an Instagram post, Svitolina described the personal struggles she had faced since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and the impact they had on her life away from the tennis court.

Loading Instagram content

"This is the most difficult thing I have ever had to share," Svitolina wrote. "Everyone knows how much Ukraine means to me. What I have rarely spoken about is what the war has done to me inside.

"Last year, I told you I needed to step away from the court because I wasn't in the right emotional space. Today, I want to open up a little more. What you didn't see were the sleepless nights, the doubts, and the feeling of slowly losing myself.

"Gael saw all of it. He never let go of my hand. We fought through this together for a long time, with everything we had. But some battles happen deep inside you, and no amount of love from someone else can win them for you."

Svitolina asked for kindness and privacy as the family navigates the separation, stressing there was no-one to blame.

"With time, I came to understand that I need to find my way back to myself and that I cannot do that within our marriage," the 32-year-old Australian Open semi-finalist said.

"It is the hardest truth I have ever had to face and the hardest thing I have ever had to tell the person I love.

"Gael listened. He has respected what I need with a strength and grace I will never forget. Gael has loved me through my greatest joys and my darkest moments, and I have loved him with all my heart.

"Skai will always come first. Our marriage is ending, but our family is not. We will always be her parents, side by side, at every step of her life.

"There are only two people who loved each other deeply and a story that is changing shape."

On the court, four-time grand slam semifinalist Svitolina recently secured her place at the season-ending WTA Finals in Indian Wells, California.

Frenchman Monfils, 40, a former world number six and one of the most charismatic players of his generation, has retired from professional tennis, according to the International Tennis Integrity Agency.

He planned to retire at the end of 2026 and bid farewell at November's Paris Masters, but the ITIA now lists him as retired.

World.title: 'Crown jewels' of Australia's savannah tropics to become national parks
World.content:
Almost 400,000 hectares of land will be turned into new national parks in Queensland, but the state government is yet to decide how many rangers will manage it.

Three cattle stations, including part of Westmoreland and Cliffdale Station in the Gulf Country and all of Cape York's Kendall River Station, will become protected state-owned land.

The land was purchased under a deal involving the Queensland government, $21 million from the Nature Conservancy, and $3.5 million from the federal government.

A rainbow bee-eater (Merops ornatus) spotted at Cliffdale Station in the Gulf Country. (Supplied: Queensland government)

Nature Conservancy Australia executive Mike Roache said while "only portions" of the land were purchased, those sections were the "jewels in the crown" of its ecosystems.

"You've got the classic Gulf plains, spinifex and wetlands and rivers that are captured in these properties, that are beautiful to witness and now will become national parks for all to enjoy," Mr Roache said.

He said some land in Cape York would also become Aboriginal freehold land, while traditional owners would have "opportunities" to manage land in the Gulf.

Cliffdale Station in the Gulf Country has 174 wetlands. (Supplied: Queensland government)

Land 'well-managed' but weeds spreading

The endangered Carpentarian grasswren, the purple-crowned fairywren and grey falcon rely on Gulf habitat, while swamp mahogany, Darwin stringybark, palm cockatoo and the white-bellied sea eagle are found in Cape York.

Burke Shire Mayor Ernie Camp said protecting the "natural asset" was welcome, but he had "some concern" about the loss of ratepayer money as councils would still need to maintain nearby roads.

Westmoreland Station has been acquired as a national park. (Supplied: Gary Cranitch/Qeensland Museum)

"Those roads to the new declared areas as well as the [existing] Lawn Hill National Park are council-controlled roads, so the burden does fall onto councils," Cr Camp said.

The shire has an annual rate base of $4 million and a population of 550, but has to manage 550 kilometres of road across an area two-thirds the size of Tasmania.

Cr Camp said the land had also been "well-run" by previous owners but warned that those "natural values" would be rapidly lost without proper management.

He said wet conditions in the Gulf Country had supercharged the spread of rubber vine and prickly acacia since 2023 to "ridiculous" levels.

"The thickness of the prickly acacia in some of the areas had become fully carpeted, so there were no natural or native grasses under the shade cover," the mayor said.

Carpentarian grasswrens are losing their spinifex grass habitat to weeds and poor fire management. (Supplied: Clint Hook/Southern Gulf NRM)

Tourism, park rangers on the cards

Neil O'Brien from Gulf Savannah Development said the region could benefit from tourism, but the state government would have to keep parks and roads well-maintained.

Park rangers and traditional owners will manage Kendall River Station once it is officially gazetted as a reserve. (Supplied: Justine Hausheer/The Nature Conservancy)

He pointed to the success of the Hell's Gate Roadhouse along the Savannah Way as a "great opportunity" to become a "gateway" into the region.

"It's as simple as sealing the road, as simple as putting in concrete causeways, to break the burden that will be borne by the Burke Shire Council," Mr O'Brien said.

What's next for this outback cattle station turned national park? An anonymous $21 million donation has helped with the purchase of the 352,589-hectare Vergemont Station near Longreach to create a 1.5 million-hectare "protected corridor" in outback Queensland.

A spokesperson for Queensland Environment Minister Andrew Powell said Queensland Parks and Wildlife would manage most of the land, but staff numbers were "not yet available".

"Planning for the future national parks is underway, including consideration of visitor access and infrastructure, land-management requirements and the resources needed to support their long-term management," she said.

The Queensland government purchased three cattle stations for national parks in 2024 but councils are waiting to know how many staff will be allocated to manage them.

World.title: Driver killed, bus and car engulfed in flames on Phillip Island
World.content:
A bus and a car became engulfed in flames after a fatal crash on Phillip Island last night.

The car collided head-on with the bus travelling eastbound on Back Beach Road in Ventnor just after 9pm.

Police said the car crossed onto the wrong side of the road and struck the bus, which had 25 people on board, including the driver.

The sole occupant of the car, who is yet to be formally identified, died at the scene.

Four people on the bus were taken to hospital with minor injuries.

Police are investigating.

World.title: One man down and on a flattening pitch, Boland and Starc continue to shine
World.content:
As the afternoon meandered on and the stubbornly soggy outfield of St George's Park threatened to waste another day of the second Test at Gqeberha, South Africa had good and bad fortune to ponder.

The good news was that upon the game's long-awaited resumption at 3:45pm local time, Australia would be without one member of its intimidating quartet of fast bowlers due to illness. The bad news, with no disrespect to the others, was that it wasn't Scott Boland.

Sure enough, within 10 minutes of the restart, the Victorian had struck again to remove debutant opener Marques Ackerman — Boland's third wicket in five typically compelling overs.

Boland puts Australia in the box seat Scott Boland continues to deliver for Australia as the tourists make the most of a rain-shortened day two of the second Test against South Africa in Gqeberha.

Worse still for the Proteas, Mitchell Starc, who'd been a little out of sorts in his brief spell on day one, was hitting his straps too. Bowling with fluency and at speeds nudging towards 150km/h, the left-armer soon struck as well thanks to a lazy waft outside off stump from Matthew Breetzke and a smart catch from Alex Carey.

At that stage, South Africa was 4-40 and staring into the abyss.

What transpired in the hour that followed was heartening for South Africa, though perhaps not enough to shift the course of this truncated contest.

The pitch — whose lack of hessian coverings during the worst of the downpours was said to be predictive of imminent mayhem — seemed to flatten out and not behave so treacherously at all.

The batting, circumspect but not unadventurous, started to look less fragile as Proteas skipper Temba Bavuma got going with South Africa's recast number six, Ryan Rickelton. And the missing bowler, Josh Hazlewood — who Cricket Australia says will return on day three — was suddenly looking like a real hole in the bowling rotation.

Indeed, a bubbly 50-run partnership later, and with stumps not far away, Bavuma could have permitted himself some satisfaction that he and Rickelton had pulled things out of the fire so calmly. He might also have felt his side's bad luck was starting to turn when a sun-blind Marnus Labuschagne put down Rickelton at leg slip.

As ever, though, Boland had other ideas. Well, one idea, to be honest: hammer away on a patch of the pitch roughly the size of a Wisden cricketers' almanac and wait for the ball to seam either way.

The burly right-armer duly took Rickelton's outside edge and Matt Renshaw, at first slip, took a catch that could be charitably described as fortunate; it looked like Carey's, but the keeper didn't move a muscle; Renshaw did, on a significant delay, grasping it in one hand when the ball was past him and then slowly mouthing some easily-made-out words of relief: "Oh. My. God."

Thus, from a relatively promising position, the Proteas finished the day 5-97 from the 43 overs that have been possible so far. Boland, with 4-31 from 14 overs, was not simply the pick of the bowlers but a one-man show who single-handedly lifted the contest out of its torpor, his every delivery imbued with potential.

Now that he is ranked in the world's top 10 Test bowlers without commanding regular selection, it is often said that Boland is unlucky. Another way of looking at it is that, at 37 — an overripe age for a fast bowler of any kind, let alone one so vigorous and impactful — he simply knows his own virtues and limitations better than he did as a younger man, and can conserve and channel his energies in ways the regulars cannot.

It is also, surely, a minor triumph of man management. That Boland and, perhaps more so, Starc continue to glide to the crease in such prolonged spells and with such devastating impact is not a matter of luck. Today, again, Starc, who is also pushing 37, was a genuine menace: a 148km/h bouncer to Bavuma was as scary as anything he bowled in his 20s.

Can't get enough cricket from Grandstand? Tune in for the latest cricket news, interviews and analysis from the ABC team in the Grandstand Cricket Podcast.

We talk often of Starc's eye-popping strike rate of 45 — six better than Dennis Lillee and Mitchell Johnson, seven better than Glenn McGrath and Jeff Thomson, 12 better than Starc's old sparring partner Shane Warne — but it is now his longevity that is so unusual to the point of freakishness.

Playing in his 109th Test, Starc is bowling at a level that history suggests should be impossible. Jason Gillespie and Brett Lee, the express quicks of preceding decades, were done with Test cricket at 31 and 32 respectively; like Johnson, they'd strung together 70-something Tests between the inevitable injuries.

Touch wood, Starc will feasibly play 50 or 60 more Tests than that — a coda of similar length to Merv Hughes's entire Test career. The way Cricket Australia has balanced Starc's financial and physical preparation requirements for the last decade is an organisational triumph that should be studied. If only it, and Starc himself, were replicable.

As for South Africa, what they can replicate remains to be seen, but it's very unlikely, as in Durban, that promising 50-partnerships will get this one done.

World.title: 'One election at a time': ACT Labor marks 25 years in power
World.content:
In October 2001, Kylie Minogue's iconic hit 'Can't Get You Out Of My Head' dominated Australia's music charts.

That same month, Labor was voted into office in the ACT.

Fast forward 25 years, and Minogue's popularity has proven timeless; that song remains her most streamed.

But as it marks a quarter of a century in charge of the ACT, can the same be said for Labor?

That's 9,131 days in control of the Australian capital, requiring seven straight election wins.

It's no easy feat.

Being in power for that long, Labor has sometimes been dubbed the "forever government" in the ACT.

But is anything really 'forever'?

ACT Chief Minister Andrew Barr took the top job in 2014 after former ACT chief minister Katy Gallagher announced her resignation. (ABC News: Jonathon Gul)

'Forever government'?

In the time since the 2001 election, Canberra, and the world around it, has changed immensely — and almost an extra 200,000 people now call the ACT home.

For Chief Minister Andrew Barr, who is the longest current serving state or territory leader in Australia, there's a few ingredients to the party's recipe for success.

First, running good election campaigns. Second, running good candidates. And third, having good policies.

But, on only one occasion back in 2004, it was enough for an outright majority — the rest of the time, Labor has needed the support of independents and other parties to form government.

ACT Labor has often held minority government while ruling the ACT Legislative Assembly for 25 years. (ABC News: Nick Haggarty)

It makes for a — mostly — robust, but sometimes challenging ACT Legislative Assembly.

"Minority government is a roller coaster ride and some days you're up and some days you're down", as Mr Barr puts it.

The role of opposition

There's another element that has undoubtedly helped Labor over the last 25 years, and they've really had nothing to do with it — the performance of the opposition.

The Canberra Liberals have been in government for just eight of the 37 years of self-government in the territory.

The party has been plagued with infighting and has struggled to find the right balance to appease Canberra's progressive population.

Gary Humphries was the territory's last Liberal chief minister, serving between 2000 and 2001. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Gary Humphries, who has the unenviable position of being the last Liberal chief minister, said Canberrans needed a reason to "shake the cage".

"The Liberal Party has let itself and the electors down by not being a credible alternative on too many occasions," Dr Humphries said.

" There have been times when voters were genuinely willing, anxious to change the government but didn't feel they could trust the Liberal Party with that responsibility. "

Is it good for democracy?

Labor is sometimes criticised for being a "tired and fatigued" government, one that has become complacent and is slow to act.

But without a viable alternative, Labor has been the logical choice for many voters.

Professor Frank Bongiorno says a party staying in power for so long can undermine the democratic process. (Supplied: University of Canberra)

Frank Bongiorno, who is the director of the University of Canberra's Centre of Public Ideas, said it had not been good for democracy.

"Party competition is really one of the kinds of measures of a vibrant democracy," he said.

"When you have a government that is in that long, it can undermine the democratic process."

Mr Barr said his party had demonstrated it could "renew in office".

"If you look at the people who were elected in 2001 … there is no-one from that government still in the current one," he said.

"We have had stability of purpose and consistency in values that we have brought to the task of governing."

Another 25 years?

ACT Chief Minister Andrew Barr says there is plenty more Labor wants to achieve in the territory. (ABC News: David Sciasci)

Labor's silver jubilee anniversary also marks the half-way point in this parliamentary term.

All things going to plan, the party's long rule in the ACT will extend to at least 27 years.

However, it's been particularly volatile in recent times, especially after the Greens ended their confidence and supply agreement, putting Labor in a precarious position.

Dr Humphries is hopeful the Liberals are on the right path heading to the 2028 election, adding there's still work to be done.

"Changes in government are healthy things in any system," he said.

For Mr Barr, there's still plenty more that Labor wants to achieve in the ACT.

"You've just got to take it one election at a time," he said.

But does that mean another 25 years in power, or, as Kylie Minogue puts it: "stay forever and ever, and ever, and ever"?

Most can agree it's a matter of when, not if, Labor will meet its electoral demise.

World.title: LNP says 'a long way to go to reverse' Queensland's youth crime crisis
World.content:
Queensland dance teacher Tara Howard's studio was allegedly set alight by teenagers in 2023.

"I couldn't really fathom what was happening at that time, except I was just watching it burn," she said.

Her story spread from local newspapers to national breakfast television as youth crime became a prominent issue in the lead-up to the 2024 state election.

Ms Howard says she couldn't "fathom what was happening at the time" of the fire. (ABC North Queensland: Lily Nothling)

During a televised leaders' debate, David Crisafulli said he would quit within four years if he became premier and could not reduce the number of victims of crime in the state.

On the eve of election day, the now premier added a qualifier that it would be "per capita".

Since his LNP party came into power almost two years ago, state parliament has passed three tranches of the contentious adult crime, adult time policy which sees juveniles charged with serious offences face tougher maximum sentences.

The fire caused severe structural damage to the dance studio. (Supplied: Tara Howard)

After an investigation into the fire at Ms Howard's Townsville dance studio, police laid charges against two 15-year-old boys, and both were dealt with under the provisions of the Youth Justice Act.

At the time, authorities alleged a wheelie bin was set on fire outside the building in the early hours of the morning.

Ms Howard spent six months rebuilding her studio with help from community fundraising.

Ms Howard sold her dance studio by the end of 2023. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

Shortly after getting back into her building, she made the difficult decision to sell it.

"I knew I wasn't able to give the families and the students what I could give them before the event," Ms Howard said.

"I couldn't keep going. Emotionally, it was too raw."

Crime rate at 20-year high

The latest Australian Bureau of Statistics figures showed the number of victims of crime in the state fell by around 4 per cent over 12 months in 2025.

About 12,000 fewer victims were recorded in 2025 than in the previous year.

Bond University criminologist Terry Goldsworthy is not convinced those numbers are a result of adult crime, adult time laws.

He said victim numbers and youth offending had started to fall in the Labor government's last year.

Dr Terry Goldsworthy says victim numbers and youth offending had started to fall in 2024. (ABC News: Michael Lloyd)

Dr Goldsworthy said he put the reduction down to better targeting by police, tougher bail laws and a focus on serious repeat offenders.

"I think youth crime will continue to go down because of those factors," he said.

The government has also been promoting an almost 10 per cent decrease by comparing police statistics from financial year 2023-24 to financial year 2025-26.

"We've seen some smoke and mirrors being used by the government," Dr Goldsworthy said.

"They're very big on trotting out some kind of slogans to show that they're getting tough on crime."

The government's adult crime, adult time policy was a key part of the LNP's election campaign. (ABC News: Cameron Simmons)

More than 7,000 juveniles have been charged with over 34,100 offences under the state government's adult crime, adult time laws as of October 10.

Dr Goldsworthy said crime remained "very problematic" in Queensland, with the overall crime rate still at a 20-year high.

"Victims of crime are still quite fearful," he said.

'Constant survival mode'

Brisbane resident Sarah Sullivan's family moved rentals this year after experiencing at least four alleged attempted break-ins more than three months.

"It was just that constant being in survival mode," she said.

Brisbane resident Sarah Sullivan's home cameras captured this video in May this year. (Supplied Sarah Sullivan)

In June, two boys aged 15 and 17 were charged with attempted enter dwelling with intent at night and face masked with intent to commit indictable offence.

On that occasion, Ms Sullivan said they chased them out of their yard.

Responding officers located and arrested the teenagers.

This video was captured at the front of Ms Sullivan's door in June this year. (Supplied Sarah Sullivan)

The 17-year-old was due to be sentenced last Friday, and the 15-year-old boy received 12 months' probation.

"I was just struck by how young they were," she said.

Ms Sullivan's family of four moved from Sydney, where no-one had ever tried to break in, about two years ago.

"For the first year, we didn't have any cameras or surveillance, so there could have been things happening," she said.

"It was a shock coming to Brisbane."

Calls to 'stop crime' in 2019

Frustrations over crime had been building on Brisbane's south in 2019.

Hundreds of residents in Sunnybank took to the streets with signs saying, "we are scared" and "stronger laws" after a doctor was shot in the garage of his MacGregor home.

Sunnybank residents took to the streets to call for more action against crime in 2019. (Supplied)

A 17-year-old boy, who admitted to shooting Luping Zengwas, was sentenced to 10 years in jail for his murder in 2021.

Sunnybank Chamber of Commerce president Peter Zhuang, who attended the rally, said safety was a "big concern" for many in the community.

"We [wanted] to have a demonstration to push government," he said.

Mr Zhuang said police presence around the area was higher for a few months, but it gradually decreased over time.

Peter Zhuang is the president of the Sunnybank Chamber of Commerce. (ABC News: Sarah Richards)

He said he felt safer under the LNP government, with crime such as break-ins not being a topic of discussion in the chamber's meetings and social media group chats.

"Generally speaking, some crime cases people mention around me [are] very rare," he said.

"Only see some tobacco shop, they break in, grab some tobacco … that's another story."

He said that, based on state police crime data, the situation still was not ideal, with no "big" changes over the years.

Mr Zhuang encouraged the premier to "keep going" with stricter laws and more police to reduce crime.

'Very long way to go'

Ms Howard, who now teaches dance at early learning centres, said she would not feel safe opening another business in Townsville.

Ms Howard says she's noticed small changes since the LNP government came into power. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

She's noticed small changes since the new government, such as a more police on the streets.

"I do feel that little bit safer in the community, but I still think we have a very, very long way to go."

Youth Justice and Victim Support Minister Laura Gerber is one of the four ministers charged with reducing victim of crime numbers in Queensland.

Victim Support Minister Laura Gerber is one of the ministers charged with reducing victim of crime numbers in the state. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

Ms Gerber said there was "a long way to go to reverse" the youth crime crisis and the generation of serious repeat offenders.

She said that the LNP government was continuing to deliver stronger crime laws, including expanding adult crime, adult time, and the breach bail, go to jail policy.

"We promised to make Queensland safer, and we'll continue building on the real progress we've been making with Daniel's Law, Jack's Law, a record number of police on the beat, more support for victims, and effective early intervention and rehabilitation to help restore safety."

World.title: I Am Australian co-writer 'not happy' song used at conservative conference
World.content:
One of the writers of a classic Australian song has called out a conservative political conference for using his work without permission.

I Am Australian was co-written by Dobe Newton from the folk and country group The Bushwackers in 1987, along with Bruce Woodley of The Seekers.

Mr Newton said he never gave permission for the song to be played at the Australian Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC), which took place in Brisbane on October 10 and 11.

"I was surprised and I'm not happy, Jan," he said.

According to a CPAC program, the song was sung by opera singers in an opening ceremony, along with Advance Australia Fair and Waltzing Matilda.

Mr Newton said he was not approached by anyone from CPAC and was only informed of its use after being approached by media.

Bruce Woodley recently told other media outlets permission had not been sought or granted from him either.

The ABC has contacted CPAC for comment.

Song celebrates multiculturalism

I Am Australian is often considered an unofficial Australian anthem, played at major sporting events and covered for significant national occasions.

In 2023, a cover of the song by Judith Durham, Russell Hitchcock and Mandawuy Yunupingu was added to the National Film and Sound Archives' Sounds of Australia.

Mr Newton said it was not appropriate for the song to be played at an event that included speeches mentioning proposed migration cuts from One Nation leader Pauline Hanson and Opposition Leader Angus Taylor.

Angus Taylor spoke at the 2026 Australian Conservative Political Action Conference. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

"People will interpret it how they want but its specific use to promote a certain political point of view, as far as we're concerned, isn't appropriate," he said.

"The whole point of writing it was to celebrate our multicultural nation.

" Any move to associate it with a call to end migration is a bit ironic, I think. "

Mr Newton said other attempts to use the song by political groups had been denied.

"When we had The Voice Referendum, both sides of the argument got in touch with Bruce and myself to ask for permission to use it as part of their campaigning," he said.

"We politely declined to give either of them permission."

Copyright laws in question

Mr Newton said artists had moral rights to their work that theoretically protected against derogatory uses.

"If your song is used in a situation where you think it's derogatory to the song itself or your reputation, then you have the ability to say, 'No, you don't have permission,'" he said.

Louise Buckingham says copyright law is complex. (Supplied: Louise Buckingham)

But CEO and principal lawyer at Arts Law Australia, Louise Buckingham, said the complexity of copyright law made it challenging for artists to push the rights.

"It can be very difficult to enforce your rights, particularly if you're vulnerable and the less deep pocketed party in a dispute," she said.

"We all benefit from [I Am Australian] and it's been used to such good effect in so many meaningful contexts that's enriched so many people's lives.

Louise Buckingham says copyright laws need to be respected. (774 ABC Melbourne: Simon Leo Brown)

"It's such a kick in the teeth for artist when it's misused and when it's used without their consent and permission."

Mr Newton said more needed to be done to protect artists.

"The kindest interpretation would be that people aren't familiar with the fact that if you're going to use somebody's song in a political context, you need to seek permission," he said.

World.title: KI ferries close temporarily as ramps upgraded for new vessels
World.content:
Kangaroo Island's ferry service has shut down for three days as part of preparations for the first of two new vessels to begin operating, with locals describing the wait as "frustrating".

The SeaLink service will be closed until Friday, as crews work around the clock to install new boat ramp infrastructure at Cape Jervis, south of Adelaide, and at Penneshaw, on Kangaroo Island, to accommodate the larger ferries.

The first new ferry, Wanggami, is expected to be brought into service later this month, while SeaLink has launched legal action in the Federal Court to have the second ferry, Ruwi, delivered to Australia from a shipyard in Indonesia.

Kangaroo Island Regional Tourism manager Megan Harvie said the delays that plagued the arrival of the new vessels were "frustrating".

"We need the ferries here to help us to grow the economy for both tourism and agriculture alike," she said.

Megan Harvie says the new ferries were needed to help grow hte island's tourism and agriculture. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

But, she said locals were "excited" by the arrival of Wanggami, which was expected to be carrying passengers before the end of next week.

She said the retirement of the Spirit of Kangaroo Island, which was affectionately known as SPOKI, was "bittersweet" after it had served the island for 22 years.

The two new ferries were initially expected to begin service early last year, but last October the company adjusted the start date to June 1 this year.

Kangaroo Island electrician Frank Colman, said it had been two or three years "without any real clear idea of what's going on".

"We’ve been getting little updates here and there as far as how the boats are tracking and what’s happening with the ramps either side," he said.

"But I feel like a lot of us have been a bit left in the lurch as far as not being able to honour timelines and not a lot of certainty around what's gonna actually happen here on in."

Frank Colman says there had been uncertainty about the arrival of the new ferries. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

He said the three-day shutdown may impact some services, but said locals were "generally pretty considerate when it comes to timelines on things, so I think we’ll be fine".

Peter Wallis from Island Earth Works, a company working on the ramp changeover on Kangaroo Island, also said three days without a ferry could be frustrating for some people, but he said most locals were used to coping with periodic stops.

"It's easy to fly into a panic, I guess maybe bread and milk and maybe toilet paper might be in great demand. But in the end, it doesn't really matter … it's only three days," he said.

“All in all, I think the sentiment's quite positive that we've just gotta get through this little bit now and get ahead and get with the new ferries and I think all the problems, they'll all go away once it gets going."

The SeaLink ferry service will be closed until Friday. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

James Meredith who owns Millie Mae's Pantry on the island said the existing ferries were full of "quirks and personalities" and welcomed the new vessels.

"It's going to mean more improved services for the community but also for business alike as well which we're looking forward to," he said.

Kangaroo Island Mayor Michael Pengilly said it was "imperative to the island that we have the ferries operating, operating well".

He said the next three days would be inconvenient for some, particularly because it was "the busiest time of year" for livestock movement, but expected the ferries would quickly return to "business as usual".

"When livestock are ready to go they have to go, you can't keep them. And they've got to be booked into the abattoirs," he said.

Kangaroo Island Mayor Michael Pengilly says the ferries were "imperative" for the island. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

He said the delays in delivering the new ferries had been "a mess", but it was time to "put that behind us".

"We just need to move ahead," he said.

According to a statement on the SeaLink website, the planned closure was subject to weather conditions, with limited services expected to resume on Friday, October 23, with SeaLion 2000 the only ferry operating for "an anticipated three to four days".

The website states that Wanggami would then begin operating alongside SeaLion 2000 once training, testing and familiarisation has been completed.

SeaLink has also been contacted for comment.

World.title: The split-second decision that put a dad in danger to save Helen Haines
World.content:
NationalVictoriaHelen Haines The split-second decision that put a dad in danger to save Helen Haines James Costa and Alexander Darling October 20, 2026 — 7:34am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Ricky Jefferies thought it was a car accident. Then he saw the knife. For those in the area who know the local barber well, Jefferies’ impulse decision to help a woman struck by a car was entirely unsurprising. Local barber Ricky Jefferies. Nor was his instinct to step in when he saw the glint of a knife, disarming the alleged driver whose Toyota Landcruiser hit independent MP Helen Haines. Haines, 65, remains in a critical condition after she was hit by the car outside her electorate office on Monday afternoon.



As emergency services rushed to help, Jefferies held the alleged driver down until authorities arrived. A 43-year-old man remains in custody. “He’s such a selfless person,” said Jessica Bear, the owner of the coffee shop two doors down from Haines’ office. “And it definitely needs to be known about his bravery.” “Ricky raced out when he thought that it was just a car accident, and he apprehended the man that was in the vehicle,” Bear said. On Tuesday, everyone from Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to Wangaratta locals were praising his bravery.



But the barber was back at work, reluctant to speak to media, already cutting hair from 7am. Haines’ electorate office this morning. James Costa “He saw a pocket knife and quickly grabbed that out of the way, he just like stayed with the man and held him down until police and stuff arrived,” Bear said. “Ricky thought in a split second and risked his own life. It could have definitely been a lot more tragic.” Bear said she had known Jefferies, a husband and father of three young kids, for years.



“We’re very close to them, so I can wholeheartedly say he’s a selfless man. I’m not surprised that he stepped in and tried to do the right thing.” “He’s a young dad of three kids and has a wife at home, so anything terrible could have happened.” Flowers rest out the front of Ricky Jefferies’ barbershop in Wangaratta on Tuesday morning. James Costa A vase of flowers rested on the table out the front of Jefferies’ barbershop on Tuesday morning, matching the floral tribute at Haines’ office. Underneath the vase was a handwritten note for Jefferies. “I hope you are OK. We pray for you. Nev and Donna.”



On Sunrise, Jefferies’ sister Tanya said Jeffries remained in shock. “He very much doesn’t feel like he’s a hero,” she said. “I just feel this overwhelming feeling of pride I’ve never felt. I’m just so proud of him.” This masthead has reached out to Jefferies and the Alfred Hospital for comment. Overnight, police said they were still investigating whether the incident in which Haines was injured was a targeted act. It is not yet known whether the parties are known to each other. World.title: Helen Haines attack live updates: Indi MP undergoes surgery, remains in critical condition after attack outside Wangaratta office; 43-year-old Tarrawingee man in custody
World.content:
A visibly emotional Jane Hume says all her colleagues are “reeling” after yesterday afternoon’s attack and that no one should be subjected to political violence.

“I’ve been speaking to a number of colleagues in the last 12 hours or so, and everybody is reeling from this. Helen Haines is such a valued colleague. She’s an extraordinary member of the parliament. She’s a great representative of her community,” the deputy Liberal leader told News24.

Deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume. Dominic Lorrimer

“On behalf of the Coalition and myself personally, that our thoughts and prayers are with her today, with her family, with her team in particular. She’s fighting for her life right now, and that’s what matters today.”

Hume said holding public office should not be a job that comes with so much risk, but that her colleagues were all “acutely aware” of the reality that political violence is on the rise.

World.title: Students blockade Louvre as France rolls out local curfews
World.content:
WorldEuropeFrance Students blockade Louvre as France rolls out local curfews David Crowe October 20, 2026 — 6:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Paris: Student protesters have opened a new front in their demands of the French government and surprised visitors to the country’s most renowned museum. Hundreds of students blocked access to the Louvre in a bid to force the government to spend more on cultural institutions, forcing thousands of visitors to shelve their plans to see the Mona Lisa and other exhibits. Students and protesters stop visitors from entering the Louvre on Monday. AP Photo/Christophe Ena The move highlighted the questions over rallies that have grown steadily bigger across France over the past month, leading to an explosion of violence on the weekend when rioters stormed through city streets. The student movement is urging people to accept a distinction between the peaceful rallies over government policy and the violent confrontations where masked rioters have looted stores and set fire to buildings, cars, and other property.



French President Emmanuel Macron has admitted there were failures in the police response to the unrest on Saturday night and cleared the way for tougher rules, including curfews in some locations. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu ruled out a blanket curfew in Paris but authorised restrictions in key locations, including the Place de la Republique and the Les Halles shopping precinct, both areas where looting took place over the weekend. Police prepared for the changes on Monday by stopping young people trying to enter the Place de la Republique, checking their bags and identities before deciding whether to let them pass. The violence around the historic square has been dominated by younger protesters in balaclavas and ski masks who have confronted the police, lit fires on the streets and looted stores.



The curfew in the Paris locations is due to last from 11pm on Monday to 6am on Tuesday, which corresponds to 8am on Tuesday, AEDT, to 3pm on Tuesday, AEDT. Cities and towns across France have chosen different approaches to keep the peace. In Nice, Mayor Eric Ciotti announced a curfew for young people from 9pm to 6am for the rest of this week. Limited curfews and other restrictions will be introduced in the worst-hit parts of Paris and major cities. Anadolu via Getty Images Ciotti said the order was issued in consultation with the prefect of Alpes-Maritimes, which announced in a separate update that objects such as fireworks and flammable substances have been banned. The region has also banned wearing ski goggles and similar equipment to hide faces. The riots and looting have deepened a public debate about the demonstrations, but students argue that their rallies are totally separate from the violence.



One student at the Louvre barricade, Inaya Plieu, said the violent “breakers” had nothing to do with the students. Student Inaya Plieu stands at the barricade outside the Louvre on Monday. David Crowe “The media is showing only the violence, only the breakers, only the bad things,” she told this masthead. “But on Saturday there was a lot of really peaceful people. The problem is that our government right now is not allowing us to open a dialogue. “We don’t support the breakers. We don’t support the destroying of buildings, of anything.”



Related Article Analysis

Paris protests Nothing left to loot: Parisians ponder the real cost of another night of riots Visitors to the Louvre were dismayed on Monday when they arrived to find students blocking the entrance in front of the famous glass pyramid. Some tourists chanted at the students in frustration and challenged them to help the museum by letting visitors enter. The students responded by telling the visitors the purpose of the protest was to increase funding for the Louvre and other institutions because entry fees were not enough to fund the heritage collections. Visitors were stopped from entering the world’s largest art museum. AP Photo/Christophe Ena



The protest was held one year to the day after thieves broke into the museum and stole eight pieces of the French Crown Jewels, said to be worth about €88 million. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: CNN anchor Christiane Amanpour to leave after 43 years
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Christiane Amanpour, one of the most recognised international correspondents of the past four decades, will sign off from CNN next year as the news channel comes under new ownership by David Ellison’s Skydance Corp.

Amanpour, 68, became famous through her on-the-ground reporting from major war zones and humanitarian crises, including the Gulf War and the Bosnian War in the 1990s. The Iranian-British journalist is the chief international anchor for CNN and host of CNN International’s nightly interview program, Amanpour. She also hosts a weekly program on CNN and a daily show on PBS.

CNN chief international anchor Christiane Amanpour became a household name through her on-the-ground reporting from major war zones and humanitarian crises, including the Gulf War and the Bosnian War in the 1990s. Penny Stephens

Amanpour’s exit comes as a new era dawns at CNN as it comes under a new owner, Skydance. After a year-long process, Skydance-owned Paramount closed its $US110 billion ($158 billion) buyout of Warner Bros. Discovery on October 6. The merger unites under one roof two giants in TV news — CBS and CNN. Amanpour had expressed concern about the impending deal earlier this year.

“Clearly I’m concerned, and I’m not sure how much I’m allowed to say about a corporate thing that’s under way, but I am obviously, as a person, as a journalist with a record, concerned, and I’m concerned based on what’s happened to the other things that [David Ellison, has] taken over already, like CBS News,” Amanpour said in a May speech.

World.title: Victoria lands $350m federal bonus to improve liveability
World.content:
NationalVictoriaMelbourne Assembly Victoria lands $350m federal bonus to improve liveability Cara Waters October 20, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Victoria will receive $350 million to improve community infrastructure in growing suburbs and regional hubs, making it the first state to qualify for the federal government’s bonus aimed at improving services. The funding commitment to improve liveability comes as former New York mayor Bill de Blasio warns that new developments across Melbourne need to have 25 per cent mandated affordable housing to help tackle the city’s housing crisis. Former New York mayor Bill de Blasio (centre) and 15-minute city pioneer Carlos Moreno take in the sights of Melbourne with Age journalist Cara Waters. Eddie Jim De Blasio says in a speech to be delivered at this week’s Melbourne Assembly civic forum at Federation Square that affordable housing supply around the world has failed to keep up with population, employment changes and pricing. “A city without enough affordable housing will simply fail,” he says.



“The private sector will never produce enough housing for working-class families on its own. Related Article Melbourne Assembly Ex-New York mayor warns of AI job threat to Melbourne workers “Only with an aggressive public sector role can enough affordable housing be built and preserved.” De Blasio will deliver his speech in the company of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, who in a separate address to the assembly will reveal that Victoria is the first state to qualify for a financial bonus under the National Housing Accord. Albanese is to say that under the New Homes Bonus scheme, Victoria will receive $350 million in federal funding to be invested into community infrastructure in growth suburbs and regional areas.



“This program is open to every state and territory – and I encourage them to follow Victoria’s lead,” the PM says in his speech. The bonus is based on new modelling by the National Housing Supply and Affordability Council. The modelling shows that despite Victoria currently lagging by about 6000 homes in its annual quota for new dwellings built, an acceleration in construction is expected to deliver a five-year total of 287,000 new homes by July 1, 2029 – nearly 32,000 more than the state’s minimum target under the accord. Albanese will foreshadow further measures by the federal and Victorian governments to help more first home buyers enter the housing market. De Blasio says market forces should not be left to determine the type and number of homes being built. He introduced mandatory inclusion zoning policies during his time leading New York City, enabling private developers to construct higher or denser buildings than would normally be allowed in exchange for a commitment that about 25 per cent of new units would be affordable housing.



“This can be used to great effect in a high-value city like Melbourne,” de Blasio says. The City of Melbourne has advocated such zoning in the past, but Lord Mayor Nick Reece announced plans to abandon these targets, arguing current economic conditions would cause the policy to constrain housing supply. Loading The state government has drawn criticism for using a limited version of inclusionary zoning where it can fast-track residential projects – overriding the ability of communities or councils to contest them at VCAT – on the condition that private developers include 10 per cent affordable housing in new projects. However, developers can bypass the requirement to build affordable housing by instead paying a fee of 3 per cent of the project’s value into a government housing fund.



“Affordable housing” in Victoria refers to private rental stock offered at a minimum 10 per cent discount to the market rate for moderate-income earners for a set number of years only. Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny and opposition planning spokesman David Southwick both declined to comment on whether Victoria should take up the 25 per cent affordable housing target. Kilkenny instead said the government’s Development Facilitation Program had so far delivered 16,000 new homes of which 18 per cent were affordable homes. “The best way to make homes more affordable is to build more of them, and Victoria continues to build more homes than any other state,” Kilkenny said. Southwick said the Liberal Party wanted to lower property taxes.



“Our team’s housing plan is about lowering costs, delivering greater choice and restoring confidence to our construction sector,” he said. Related Series

City life Melbourne Assembly The Planning Institute of Australia backs mandatory affordable housing targets, with Victorian president Patrick Fensham also raising concerns about the current system. Fensham said it was not clear how many homes the Development Facilitation Program subsidises, who is eligible for them and how long the homes are eligible for a subsidy. “It’s a matter of being transparent,” he said. The Planning Institute has called for 80,000 social housing homes by 2051 – equal to about 3000 to 4000 a year – to tackle Victoria’s a shortfall.



Fensham said a mandatory social and housing contribution should be applied to all development, but warned it is difficult to apply terms such as “affordable housing” in an Australian context where it is not the same as social housing – reserved for low-income renters on the government waiting list and managed by the state (public housing) or non-profits (community housing). “London and New York are way ahead of us because mandating affordable housing just seems to be a standard requirement there,” Fensham said. “We’ve been slow to move into a recognition that the development process and the planning system should have a role in making the contributions towards social affordable housing.” Mandatory housing targets are opposed by many developers. Linda Allison, chief executive of the Urban Development Institute of Australia, said a one size fits all approach does not work for housing projects. “A mandatory target will drive up the overall cost of housing, which will ultimately be paid for by home buyers,” she said.



Allison said paying a levy through the Development Facilitation Program was preferable for developers as it provided the certainty of a fixed cost not subject to future price variability. “The best way to help industry deliver more homes is to create a tax environment that encourages investment and to reduce red tape which causes significant time delays,” she said. “The uncomfortable reality is that affordable and social housing needs government funding to make it stack up, and government funding comes from taxpayers. Most people feel like they are already paying enough tax.” The Melbourne Assembly will on Tuesday hear from keynote speaker de Blasio and from the prime minister. Panel discussions on two key pillars of the forum, shaping our city and education and innovation, will be held.



Melbourne Assembly is being held to October 21. More information is available on the Melbourne Assembly website. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: How Scott Boland is racing father time – and winning
World.content:
Analysis SportCricketAustralian cricket How Scott Boland is racing father time – and winning Daniel Brettig October 20, 2026 — 5:26am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Gqeberha: Scott Boland admits he is racing against advancing years to make as big a mark as possible on Test cricket. But the evidence suggests that Australia’s oldest fast bowler since Ray Lindwall in 1960 is actually improving with each opportunity, however sporadic, to the point that South Africa offered him the highest possible praise here. In his first Test for Australia since January, 37-year-old Boland (4-31) has been the major reason why South Africa are again in a world of trouble at 5-97, clinging to hope that captain Temba Bavuma (41 not out) can make something of their wobbly first innings before the recalled Kagiso Rabada lets rip on a drying pitch. Loading Matt Renshaw’s stunning catch in the final half hour of play, which extended to 30.4 overs despite only beginning at 3.45pm on Monday local time (12.45am Tuesday AEDT), made the day Boland and Australia’s, after which the Indigenous paceman spoke frankly about how he had worked to try to ensure he could hit the ground sprinting whenever the selectors included him.



Australia were doubly grateful for Boland on a day when Josh Hazlewood was absent from the ground with a stomach ailment. “I can’t speak for Nathan, but I want to play every game I can,” Boland said after tipping out Nathan Lyon to play. “I know I’m not 25, so I know that time’s probably running out a little bit. But we’ve got so many Tests over the next 12 months that I knew I was going to play a part somewhere. Editor's pick Analysis

Australian cricket Scott Boland was irresistible for South Africa – and for Nathan Lyon “I want to play every Test, but I probably know that’s not 100 per cent realistic. I want to be ready for whenever I get my opportunity, and impact the game straight away. “When I got here, I probably still didn’t think I was going to play until I thought maybe I was a chance the day before, and then obviously didn’t hear anything until [day one]. But pumped to be back in the team.”



To that end, Boland said he had worked on carrying a more confident mindset into matches. It should be remembered that his memorable 6-7 on debut against England came after he had bowled more plainly in the first innings. Since he was challenged by Bazball in England in 2023, Boland’s record in his second 10 Tests has improved upon that of his first 10, an astounding achievement in his late 30s. “It’s more a mindset just believing that I can, when I come into a series, if it’s not the first game, or if I haven’t played for a while, that I’ll find my line and length pretty quickly,” he said. “I probably doubted myself if I haven’t played cricket for a while, that I was like, ‘oh, maybe it might take me a couple of spells’, or ‘something doesn’t feel right’, or whatever it is. “But I think having such good training conditions here, where we get in centre wickets, and obviously bowling to some of the best batters in the world, it makes you sharpen up pretty quick. And then also leaning on guys like Pat and Josh and Ronnie [McDonald] and James Franklin’s our bowling coach, so they give me a lot of belief that I can sort of impact the game straight away.” Scott Boland celebrates. Getty Images Coming to the town formerly known as Port Elizabeth, Boland had figured that Australia would not change their team from Durban. But a sublime centre wicket bowling session combined with a grassy pitch and rain-soaked forecast allowed him to squeeze into the side.



Proteas batting coach Ashwell Prince made the complimentary comparison of Boland with Vernon Philander, an outstanding performer for South Africa, and noted that his main challenge seemed to be getting picked. “His balls are always in and around the top of off stump. Against taller guys you can leave a lot more balls on length,” Prince said. Related Article Updated

Australian cricket ‘Testosterone to burn’: Rabada rejoins battle with Smith after 2018 flashpoint “But because he’s hitting the top of the stumps, there’s always that uncertainty whether it’s going over the top ... which means it drags you into playing at more balls. You might want to leave a few more. “He doesn’t leave his spot very often, so very consistent and hits the seam. His record speaks for itself. I think the only thing that’s stopping him is that it’s quite hard for him to get in the lineup consistently.”



Philander and Boland have remarkably similar records after their first 20 Tests, both averaging 18 per wicket. Philander’s lauded career ended with 224 victims at 22.32 from 64 games. Boland agreed with Prince that a surface with somewhat lower bounce gave him the chance to ask more questions by targeting the stumps. Debutant Marques Ackerman leaned forward to drive Boland’s sixth ball of the day, only to edge to Alex Carey. After Matthew Breetzke had edged Mitchell Starc wretchedly behind, Ryan Rickelton touched a Boland away seamer that should also have been a Carey catch. Boland admitted his heart skipped a beat before Renshaw dived to claim the chance an inch or two above the ground, a couple of overs after Marnus Labuschagne had been hit in the chest by a chance that will go, perhaps a little unfairly, as Australia’s first dropped catch of the series. Starc gets Breetzke. Getty Images



“I thought it was gone for four, but then … unbelievable catch. It just stuck right in the middle of his mitt,” Boland said. How much longer can the Boland show continue? There is determination to carry on for another couple of years at least, aided by the simplicity of being a one format international cricketer, and the knowledge that many spectators, Australian or otherwise, are willing him on. “I think that’s the beauty of only playing one format,” he said. “I know where my games are going to be. I don’t have to worry too much about bowling Yorkers or slower balls or things that put your action a bit out of whack. “I know I’m 37 and the oldest fast bowler to play for a while, but I still feel like I’m going really well, and my body’s in a good spot. I feel like I can do it for as long as I can.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: ASX set to fall, AI stocks rebound on Wall Street
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to fall, AI stocks rebound on Wall Street Stan Choe October 20, 2026 — 5:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry are bouncing back on Wall Street and recovering some of their steep losses from last week, but the rest of the market and stocks worldwide are shaky. The S&P 500 rose 0.5 per cent, coming off its worst week since June, and the Nasdaq composite rallied 1.1 per cent because it’s full of technology stocks. The majority of US stocks outside of AI and tech were falling, though, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average was mostly unchanged, in early afternoon trade, after swinging between earlier losses and gains. Wall Street advanced as AI stocks rebounded following a sharp selloff on Friday. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to retreat, with futures at 5.01am AEDT pointing to a loss of 74 points or 0.8 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.4 per cent on Tuesday. The Australian dollar was stronger at US69.81¢. In Europe, the drops were sharp as many indexes sank more than 1 per cent, including 1.1 per cent in Paris. Those losses followed violent protests over the weekend that could force governments to increase their spending, which would put even more pressure on their bond markets. Yields cranked higher for European bonds.



AI stocks stood out amid all the cross currents, as they have for most of the past few years. A frenzy in spending for AI technology has forced them to the forefront of the market, sending them to record prices and driving indexes higher. Last week, AI stocks grabbed the spotlight after tumbling on worries about how expensive it has become to borrow money, which could threaten the boom. Related Article Opinion

AI Nightmare on Wall Street: The AI alarm bells are ringing louder Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Much of the spending on AI chips and data centres has come from borrowed money, and Treasury yields in the bond market have recently hit their highest levels in years or even decades. That raises the cost of borrowing money for everyone, from the US government to companies to households. CoreWeave, a company that’s borrowed to buy AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, has been at the centre of the market’s shifts. It rose 2.8 per cent Monday after tumbling 25.2 per cent last week. Nvidia added 1.3 per cent and was one of the strongest forces lifting the S&P 500. Because it’s the largest stock on Wall Street by total market value, a 1 per cent move for its stock has more effect on the index than any other’s.



SpaceX, which controls the xAI business, rose 0.8 per cent to $US147.26. Its founder, Elon Musk, pledged on Monday to give one share of SpaceX to “every kid in America” next year. The offer came after Anthropic said over the weekend that it will commit 5 per cent of the shares in its highly anticipated initial public offering of stock to a new “public benefit” fund. AI stocks rose ahead of some profit reports coming later in the week that could offer more details about the strength of AI-related spending. Meta Platforms, which is pushing its Muse AI agent, will report its latest quarterly results on Wednesday. Lam Research, which supplies equipment and services for the making of semiconductors, will also talk about how its business is doing on Wednesday. Expectations are high across the board for US companies’ profits from the summer. Analysts are forecasting overall growth of 29 per cent for companies in the S&P 500 from the prior summer, according to FactSet. Those high expectations are what has allowed the US stock market to run to records despite worries about war, high inflation and pressure from the bond market. Cleveland-Cliffs rallied 15.8 per cent after the steel company reported a bigger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. CEO Lourenco Goncalves said it was the strongest quarter for the company in three years and that the outlook for profit in 2027 “has improved materially” from three months ago.



In stock markets abroad, the rebound for AI stocks helped South Korea’s Kospi jump 1.8 per cent to recover some of its 14.5 per cent drop from last week. It is dominated by two huge players in the AI industry, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, which has made it much jumpier than other markets. Related Article Aviation Vietjet’s domestic ambitions dealt a blow after court orders global asset freeze In Europe, bond yields climbed following mass protests against the rising cost of living and poor school conditions. The protests could put pressure on governments to boost their spending to offer help, but that would likely only add to their already big piles of debt. Yields rose for French bonds on worries about the government’s already strained budget and climbed much more than yields for Germany, which investors have historically seen as a safer bet. In the US bond market, yields gained ground as the yield on the 10-year Treasury climbed to 5.14 per cent from 5.09 per cent late Friday. It topped 5.30 per cent earlier this month and touched its highest level since 2002.



Oil prices wavered. Brent crude, the international standard, rose 0.2 per cent to $US110.12 per barrel. It had been falling earlier in the day and has been yo-yoing between $US97 and $US110 this month on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the energy industry to return to normal. World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWPlanning The architects fighting to design a ‘distinctly Sydney’ waterfront suburb Megan Gorrey October 20, 2026 — 5:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. International architects transforming former industrial waterfronts into neighbourhoods in London, Stockholm and Copenhagen are among six design teams shortlisted to shape Sydney’s newest harbourside suburb of Bays West. The Minns government plans to shift working port operations from inner-city Glebe Island to make way for up to 8500 homes and public spaces around White Bay Power Station and the Bays West metro stop, representing the most significant reshaping of the harbour foreshore since Barangaroo. Bays West Delivery Authority acting chief executive Anita Mitchell, Lands and Property Minister Steve Kamper, and NSW government architect Abbie Galvin opposite Glebe Island. Steven Siewert The six teams, announced on Tuesday after an international design competition, provide Sydneysiders with a first glimpse of what they might expect of the revamped 77-hectare site. NSW government architect Abbie Galvin said the teams had been chosen from 165 entrants and brought experience in delivering some of the world’s most significant urban renewal projects.



“We look forward to seeing how they respond to this remarkable harbourfront site and the opportunities it presents to create a vibrant, sustainable and connected neighbourhood for future generations,” Galvin said. Related Article City life How long Sydney Fish Market visitors will have to wait for a ferry wharf The shortlisted design teams are: Herzog & de Meuron, Silvester Fuller and Michel Desvigne Paysagiste

Allies and Morrison and Bates Smart

Aileen Sage, MAKO Architecture, Studio Zanardo and Gallagher Studio

BVN, Cobe and LUDO Studio

Karakusevic Carson Architects, Breathe Architecture, SMM and lahznimmo

Mandaworks, BKK Architects, Offcuts and Merri Studio. The winning scheme and shortlisted design submissions will go on public exhibition in early 2027.



Shortlisted teams will be invited to prepare an urban framework responding to a detailed brief and reference scheme from Galvin’s office and the Bays West Delivery Authority. Design advisory team members will assess submissions and provide recommendations before a final decision is made. The framework will identify the street structure, location and types of open spaces, and location and height of buildings. The chosen team would play an ongoing role in the development of the area. Waterfront apartment developments along the Nordhavn Bassin in Copenhagen, Denmark. Bloomberg The King’s Cross Central redevelopment is a 67-acre mixed-use regeneration project in London. John Sturrock Among the international firms is the prominent British architecture and urban planning practice Allies and Morrison, which was part of the team that designed King’s Cross Central – one of London’s largest redevelopments.



The 27-hectare project includes 20 restored industrial structures and 50 new buildings comprising 2000 residential units along the railway and canal hub behind King’s Cross and St Pancras stations. Renowned Swiss architecture firm Herzog & de Meuron transformed London’s Bankside Power Station into the Tate Modern. Danish architecture firm Cobe is driving the Nordhavn master plan to turn a sprawling former industrial port into a sustainable waterfront district in Copenhagen. The Tate Modern Project is the major architectural expansion and adaptive reuse development of the Tate Modern art museum. Hufton & Crow The Kolkajen masterplan transforms a former industrial gasworks and coal harbour into a waterfront neighbourhood in Sweden. Mandaworks and ADEPT Architects Swedish landscape studio Mandaworks is involved with the Kolkajen project to reimagine Stockholm’s main industrial harbour into a residential, cultural and commercial hub.



Closer to home, Sydney-based architecture firm Bates Smart is leading the design of the Parramatta Metro Precinct, while BVN architects worked on the Sydney Fish Market and Quay Quarter Tower. Lahznimmo architects designed the Charles Street Square precinct linking the Parramatta River and Parramatta’s core, while landscape design firm Gallagher Studio is involved with the Suttons Zetland project, a former industrial site being reimagined as a residential precinct in Sydney’s inner south. Aileen Sage, MAKO Architecture and Djinjama are leading the transformation of the Suttons Zetland site. Choi Render The Nightingale Village is a collection of six neighbouring buildings in Melbourne’s inner north. Glenn Hester Breathe Architecture played a central role in Nightingale Village, a collection of six neighbouring buildings, designed by six different architects, comprising 200 homes in Melbourne’s inner north.



Herzog & de Meuron founding partner Jacques Herzog said Bays West represented “one of the most ambitious and exciting urban renewal projects anywhere in the world”. Karakusevic Carson Architects principal Paul Karakusevic said it could be a “global exemplar of civic ambition, public leadership and design excellence”. Allies and Morrison partner Alfredo Caraballo and Bates Smart managing director Philip Vivian said the redevelopment would shape Sydney for generations and “help unleash Bays West’s renaissance”. BVN principal Peter Titmuss said: “This is a rare chance to rethink a truly significant site – opening it back up to the public and creating a shared vision for this part of the harbour and the city.” The government launched the international design competition in July, seeking expressions of interest from teams of design industry professionals, including architects, urbanists, landscape architects, planners, sustainability specialists and ecologists. It said the competition aimed to help create a “vibrant, connected and distinctly Sydney waterfront community”.



Related Article Opinion

Planning This new waterfront suburb will reshape Sydney, but who will get to live there? Estelle Grech Urban Planner Lands and Property Minister Steve Kamper said the project represented a once-in-a-generation opportunity to transform Sydney’s working harbour into a vibrant new waterfront suburb, delivering thousands of new homes, beautiful public spaces and expanded public access to the harbour. “By bringing together leading Australian and international design talent, we’re laying the foundations for a world-class precinct that will create new opportunities for our growing city and generations to come.” Bulk port operations will be shifted from Glebe Island by 2030, and the metro station is due to open in 2032. Sydneysiders will help name the new suburb. A minimum of 10 per cent of homes will be affordable or essential worker housing.



Galvin previously said there had been “lessons learnt” from the divisive state government-led redevelopment of the nearby Barangaroo foreshore, which was also subject to a design competition before the winning vision was dumped and the scheme revised. She said Bays West would emphasise residential, public and cultural facilities, rather than the commercial workplaces of Barangaroo. World.title: The split-second decision that put a dad in danger to save Helen Haines
World.content:
NationalVictoriaHelen Haines The split-second decision that put a dad in danger to save Helen Haines James Costa and Alexander Darling October 20, 2026 — 7:34am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Ricky Jefferies thought it was a car accident. Then he saw the knife. For those in the area who know the local barber well, Jefferies’ impulse decision to help a woman struck by a car was entirely unsurprising. Local barber Ricky Jefferies. Nor was his instinct to step in when he saw the glint of a knife, disarming the alleged driver whose Toyota Landcruiser hit independent MP Helen Haines. Haines, 65, remains in a critical condition after she was hit by the car outside her electorate office on Monday afternoon.



As emergency services rushed to help, Jefferies held the alleged driver down until authorities arrived. A 43-year-old man remains in custody. “He’s such a selfless person,” said Jessica Bear, the owner of the coffee shop two doors down from Haines’ office. “And it definitely needs to be known about his bravery.” “Ricky raced out when he thought that it was just a car accident, and he apprehended the man that was in the vehicle,” Bear said. On Tuesday, everyone from Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to Wangaratta locals were praising his bravery.



But the barber was back at work, reluctant to speak to media, already cutting hair from 7am. Haines’ electorate office this morning. James Costa “He saw a pocket knife and quickly grabbed that out of the way, he just like stayed with the man and held him down until police and stuff arrived,” Bear said. “Ricky thought in a split second and risked his own life. It could have definitely been a lot more tragic.” Bear said she had known Jefferies, a husband and father of three young kids, for years.



“We’re very close to them, so I can wholeheartedly say he’s a selfless man. I’m not surprised that he stepped in and tried to do the right thing.” “He’s a young dad of three kids and has a wife at home, so anything terrible could have happened.” Flowers rest out the front of Ricky Jefferies’ barbershop in Wangaratta on Tuesday morning. James Costa A vase of flowers rested on the table out the front of Jefferies’ barbershop on Tuesday morning, matching the floral tribute at Haines’ office. Underneath the vase was a handwritten note for Jefferies. “I hope you are OK. We pray for you. Nev and Donna.”



On Sunrise, Jefferies’ sister Tanya said Jeffries remained in shock. “He very much doesn’t feel like he’s a hero,” she said. “I just feel this overwhelming feeling of pride I’ve never felt. I’m just so proud of him.” This masthead has reached out to Jefferies and the Alfred Hospital for comment. Overnight, police said they were still investigating whether the incident in which Haines was injured was a targeted act. It is not yet known whether the parties are known to each other. World.title: Students blockade Louvre as France rolls out local curfews
World.content:
WorldEuropeFrance Students blockade Louvre as France rolls out local curfews David Crowe October 20, 2026 — 6:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Paris: Student protesters have opened a new front in their demands of the French government and surprised visitors to the country’s most renowned museum. Hundreds of students blocked access to the Louvre in a bid to force the government to spend more on cultural institutions, forcing thousands of visitors to shelve their plans to see the Mona Lisa and other exhibits. Students and protesters stop visitors from entering the Louvre on Monday. AP Photo/Christophe Ena The move highlighted the questions over rallies that have grown steadily bigger across France over the past month, leading to an explosion of violence on the weekend when rioters stormed through city streets. The student movement is urging people to accept a distinction between the peaceful rallies over government policy and the violent confrontations where masked rioters have looted stores and set fire to buildings, cars, and other property.



French President Emmanuel Macron has admitted there were failures in the police response to the unrest on Saturday night and cleared the way for tougher rules, including curfews in some locations. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu ruled out a blanket curfew in Paris but authorised restrictions in key locations, including the Place de la Republique and the Les Halles shopping precinct, both areas where looting took place over the weekend. Police prepared for the changes on Monday by stopping young people trying to enter the Place de la Republique, checking their bags and identities before deciding whether to let them pass. The violence around the historic square has been dominated by younger protesters in balaclavas and ski masks who have confronted the police, lit fires on the streets and looted stores.



The curfew in the Paris locations is due to last from 11pm on Monday to 6am on Tuesday, which corresponds to 8am on Tuesday, AEDT, to 3pm on Tuesday, AEDT. Cities and towns across France have chosen different approaches to keep the peace. In Nice, Mayor Eric Ciotti announced a curfew for young people from 9pm to 6am for the rest of this week. Limited curfews and other restrictions will be introduced in the worst-hit parts of Paris and major cities. Anadolu via Getty Images Ciotti said the order was issued in consultation with the prefect of Alpes-Maritimes, which announced in a separate update that objects such as fireworks and flammable substances have been banned. The region has also banned wearing ski goggles and similar equipment to hide faces. The riots and looting have deepened a public debate about the demonstrations, but students argue that their rallies are totally separate from the violence.



One student at the Louvre barricade, Inaya Plieu, said the violent “breakers” had nothing to do with the students. Student Inaya Plieu stands at the barricade outside the Louvre on Monday. David Crowe “The media is showing only the violence, only the breakers, only the bad things,” she told this masthead. “But on Saturday there was a lot of really peaceful people. The problem is that our government right now is not allowing us to open a dialogue. “We don’t support the breakers. We don’t support the destroying of buildings, of anything.”



Related Article Analysis

Paris protests Nothing left to loot: Parisians ponder the real cost of another night of riots Visitors to the Louvre were dismayed on Monday when they arrived to find students blocking the entrance in front of the famous glass pyramid. Some tourists chanted at the students in frustration and challenged them to help the museum by letting visitors enter. The students responded by telling the visitors the purpose of the protest was to increase funding for the Louvre and other institutions because entry fees were not enough to fund the heritage collections. Visitors were stopped from entering the world’s largest art museum. AP Photo/Christophe Ena



The protest was held one year to the day after thieves broke into the museum and stole eight pieces of the French Crown Jewels, said to be worth about €88 million. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: CNN anchor Christiane Amanpour to leave after 43 years
World.content:
