Christiane Amanpour, one of the most recognised international correspondents of the past four decades, will sign off from CNN next year as the news channel comes under new ownership by David Ellison’s Skydance Corp.

Amanpour, 68, became famous through her on-the-ground reporting from major war zones and humanitarian crises, including the Gulf War and the Bosnian War in the 1990s. The Iranian-British journalist is the chief international anchor for CNN and host of CNN International’s nightly interview program, Amanpour. She also hosts a weekly program on CNN and a daily show on PBS.

CNN chief international anchor Christiane Amanpour became a household name through her on-the-ground reporting from major war zones and humanitarian crises, including the Gulf War and the Bosnian War in the 1990s. Penny Stephens

Amanpour’s exit comes as a new era dawns at CNN as it comes under a new owner, Skydance. After a year-long process, Skydance-owned Paramount closed its $US110 billion ($158 billion) buyout of Warner Bros. Discovery on October 6. The merger unites under one roof two giants in TV news — CBS and CNN. Amanpour had expressed concern about the impending deal earlier this year.

“Clearly I’m concerned, and I’m not sure how much I’m allowed to say about a corporate thing that’s under way, but I am obviously, as a person, as a journalist with a record, concerned, and I’m concerned based on what’s happened to the other things that [David Ellison, has] taken over already, like CBS News,” Amanpour said in a May speech.

World.title: Victoria lands $350m federal bonus to improve liveability
World.content:
NationalVictoriaMelbourne Assembly Victoria lands $350m federal bonus to improve liveability Cara Waters October 20, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Victoria will receive $350 million to improve community infrastructure in growing suburbs and regional hubs, making it the first state to qualify for the federal government’s bonus aimed at improving services. The funding commitment to improve liveability comes as former New York mayor Bill de Blasio warns that new developments across Melbourne need to have 25 per cent mandated affordable housing to help tackle the city’s housing crisis. Former New York mayor Bill de Blasio (centre) and 15-minute city pioneer Carlos Moreno take in the sights of Melbourne with Age journalist Cara Waters. Eddie Jim De Blasio says in a speech to be delivered at this week’s Melbourne Assembly civic forum at Federation Square that affordable housing supply around the world has failed to keep up with population, employment changes and pricing. “A city without enough affordable housing will simply fail,” he says.



“The private sector will never produce enough housing for working-class families on its own. Related Article Melbourne Assembly Ex-New York mayor warns of AI job threat to Melbourne workers “Only with an aggressive public sector role can enough affordable housing be built and preserved.” De Blasio will deliver his speech in the company of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, who in a separate address to the assembly will reveal that Victoria is the first state to qualify for a financial bonus under the National Housing Accord. Albanese is to say that under the New Homes Bonus scheme, Victoria will receive $350 million in federal funding to be invested into community infrastructure in growth suburbs and regional areas.



“This program is open to every state and territory – and I encourage them to follow Victoria’s lead,” the PM says in his speech. The bonus is based on new modelling by the National Housing Supply and Affordability Council. The modelling shows that despite Victoria currently lagging by about 6000 homes in its annual quota for new dwellings built, an acceleration in construction is expected to deliver a five-year total of 287,000 new homes by July 1, 2029 – nearly 32,000 more than the state’s minimum target under the accord. Albanese will foreshadow further measures by the federal and Victorian governments to help more first home buyers enter the housing market. De Blasio says market forces should not be left to determine the type and number of homes being built. He introduced mandatory inclusion zoning policies during his time leading New York City, enabling private developers to construct higher or denser buildings than would normally be allowed in exchange for a commitment that about 25 per cent of new units would be affordable housing.



“This can be used to great effect in a high-value city like Melbourne,” de Blasio says. The City of Melbourne has advocated such zoning in the past, but Lord Mayor Nick Reece announced plans to abandon these targets, arguing current economic conditions would cause the policy to constrain housing supply. Loading The state government has drawn criticism for using a limited version of inclusionary zoning where it can fast-track residential projects – overriding the ability of communities or councils to contest them at VCAT – on the condition that private developers include 10 per cent affordable housing in new projects. However, developers can bypass the requirement to build affordable housing by instead paying a fee of 3 per cent of the project’s value into a government housing fund.



“Affordable housing” in Victoria refers to private rental stock offered at a minimum 10 per cent discount to the market rate for moderate-income earners for a set number of years only. Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny and opposition planning spokesman David Southwick both declined to comment on whether Victoria should take up the 25 per cent affordable housing target. Kilkenny instead said the government’s Development Facilitation Program had so far delivered 16,000 new homes of which 18 per cent were affordable homes. “The best way to make homes more affordable is to build more of them, and Victoria continues to build more homes than any other state,” Kilkenny said. Southwick said the Liberal Party wanted to lower property taxes.



“Our team’s housing plan is about lowering costs, delivering greater choice and restoring confidence to our construction sector,” he said. Related Series

City life Melbourne Assembly The Planning Institute of Australia backs mandatory affordable housing targets, with Victorian president Patrick Fensham also raising concerns about the current system. Fensham said it was not clear how many homes the Development Facilitation Program subsidises, who is eligible for them and how long the homes are eligible for a subsidy. “It’s a matter of being transparent,” he said. The Planning Institute has called for 80,000 social housing homes by 2051 – equal to about 3000 to 4000 a year – to tackle Victoria’s a shortfall.



Fensham said a mandatory social and housing contribution should be applied to all development, but warned it is difficult to apply terms such as “affordable housing” in an Australian context where it is not the same as social housing – reserved for low-income renters on the government waiting list and managed by the state (public housing) or non-profits (community housing). “London and New York are way ahead of us because mandating affordable housing just seems to be a standard requirement there,” Fensham said. “We’ve been slow to move into a recognition that the development process and the planning system should have a role in making the contributions towards social affordable housing.” Mandatory housing targets are opposed by many developers. Linda Allison, chief executive of the Urban Development Institute of Australia, said a one size fits all approach does not work for housing projects. “A mandatory target will drive up the overall cost of housing, which will ultimately be paid for by home buyers,” she said.



Allison said paying a levy through the Development Facilitation Program was preferable for developers as it provided the certainty of a fixed cost not subject to future price variability. “The best way to help industry deliver more homes is to create a tax environment that encourages investment and to reduce red tape which causes significant time delays,” she said. “The uncomfortable reality is that affordable and social housing needs government funding to make it stack up, and government funding comes from taxpayers. Most people feel like they are already paying enough tax.” The Melbourne Assembly will on Tuesday hear from keynote speaker de Blasio and from the prime minister. Panel discussions on two key pillars of the forum, shaping our city and education and innovation, will be held.



Melbourne Assembly is being held to October 21. More information is available on the Melbourne Assembly website. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: How Scott Boland is racing father time – and winning
World.content:
Analysis SportCricketAustralian cricket How Scott Boland is racing father time – and winning Daniel Brettig October 20, 2026 — 5:26am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Gqeberha: Scott Boland admits he is racing against advancing years to make as big a mark as possible on Test cricket. But the evidence suggests that Australia’s oldest fast bowler since Ray Lindwall in 1960 is actually improving with each opportunity, however sporadic, to the point that South Africa offered him the highest possible praise here. In his first Test for Australia since January, 37-year-old Boland (4-31) has been the major reason why South Africa are again in a world of trouble at 5-97, clinging to hope that captain Temba Bavuma (41 not out) can make something of their wobbly first innings before the recalled Kagiso Rabada lets rip on a drying pitch. Loading Matt Renshaw’s stunning catch in the final half hour of play, which extended to 30.4 overs despite only beginning at 3.45pm on Monday local time (12.45am Tuesday AEDT), made the day Boland and Australia’s, after which the Indigenous paceman spoke frankly about how he had worked to try to ensure he could hit the ground sprinting whenever the selectors included him.



Australia were doubly grateful for Boland on a day when Josh Hazlewood was absent from the ground with a stomach ailment. “I can’t speak for Nathan, but I want to play every game I can,” Boland said after tipping out Nathan Lyon to play. “I know I’m not 25, so I know that time’s probably running out a little bit. But we’ve got so many Tests over the next 12 months that I knew I was going to play a part somewhere. Editor's pick Analysis

Australian cricket Scott Boland was irresistible for South Africa – and for Nathan Lyon “I want to play every Test, but I probably know that’s not 100 per cent realistic. I want to be ready for whenever I get my opportunity, and impact the game straight away. “When I got here, I probably still didn’t think I was going to play until I thought maybe I was a chance the day before, and then obviously didn’t hear anything until [day one]. But pumped to be back in the team.”



To that end, Boland said he had worked on carrying a more confident mindset into matches. It should be remembered that his memorable 6-7 on debut against England came after he had bowled more plainly in the first innings. Since he was challenged by Bazball in England in 2023, Boland’s record in his second 10 Tests has improved upon that of his first 10, an astounding achievement in his late 30s. “It’s more a mindset just believing that I can, when I come into a series, if it’s not the first game, or if I haven’t played for a while, that I’ll find my line and length pretty quickly,” he said. “I probably doubted myself if I haven’t played cricket for a while, that I was like, ‘oh, maybe it might take me a couple of spells’, or ‘something doesn’t feel right’, or whatever it is. “But I think having such good training conditions here, where we get in centre wickets, and obviously bowling to some of the best batters in the world, it makes you sharpen up pretty quick. And then also leaning on guys like Pat and Josh and Ronnie [McDonald] and James Franklin’s our bowling coach, so they give me a lot of belief that I can sort of impact the game straight away.” Scott Boland celebrates. Getty Images Coming to the town formerly known as Port Elizabeth, Boland had figured that Australia would not change their team from Durban. But a sublime centre wicket bowling session combined with a grassy pitch and rain-soaked forecast allowed him to squeeze into the side.



Proteas batting coach Ashwell Prince made the complimentary comparison of Boland with Vernon Philander, an outstanding performer for South Africa, and noted that his main challenge seemed to be getting picked. “His balls are always in and around the top of off stump. Against taller guys you can leave a lot more balls on length,” Prince said. Related Article Updated

Australian cricket ‘Testosterone to burn’: Rabada rejoins battle with Smith after 2018 flashpoint “But because he’s hitting the top of the stumps, there’s always that uncertainty whether it’s going over the top ... which means it drags you into playing at more balls. You might want to leave a few more. “He doesn’t leave his spot very often, so very consistent and hits the seam. His record speaks for itself. I think the only thing that’s stopping him is that it’s quite hard for him to get in the lineup consistently.”



Philander and Boland have remarkably similar records after their first 20 Tests, both averaging 18 per wicket. Philander’s lauded career ended with 224 victims at 22.32 from 64 games. Boland agreed with Prince that a surface with somewhat lower bounce gave him the chance to ask more questions by targeting the stumps. Debutant Marques Ackerman leaned forward to drive Boland’s sixth ball of the day, only to edge to Alex Carey. After Matthew Breetzke had edged Mitchell Starc wretchedly behind, Ryan Rickelton touched a Boland away seamer that should also have been a Carey catch. Boland admitted his heart skipped a beat before Renshaw dived to claim the chance an inch or two above the ground, a couple of overs after Marnus Labuschagne had been hit in the chest by a chance that will go, perhaps a little unfairly, as Australia’s first dropped catch of the series. Starc gets Breetzke. Getty Images



“I thought it was gone for four, but then … unbelievable catch. It just stuck right in the middle of his mitt,” Boland said. How much longer can the Boland show continue? There is determination to carry on for another couple of years at least, aided by the simplicity of being a one format international cricketer, and the knowledge that many spectators, Australian or otherwise, are willing him on. “I think that’s the beauty of only playing one format,” he said. “I know where my games are going to be. I don’t have to worry too much about bowling Yorkers or slower balls or things that put your action a bit out of whack. “I know I’m 37 and the oldest fast bowler to play for a while, but I still feel like I’m going really well, and my body’s in a good spot. I feel like I can do it for as long as I can.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: ASX set to fall, AI stocks rebound on Wall Street
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to fall, AI stocks rebound on Wall Street Stan Choe October 20, 2026 — 5:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry are bouncing back on Wall Street and recovering some of their steep losses from last week, but the rest of the market and stocks worldwide are shaky. The S&P 500 rose 0.5 per cent, coming off its worst week since June, and the Nasdaq composite rallied 1.1 per cent because it’s full of technology stocks. The majority of US stocks outside of AI and tech were falling, though, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average was mostly unchanged, in early afternoon trade, after swinging between earlier losses and gains. Wall Street advanced as AI stocks rebounded following a sharp selloff on Friday. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to retreat, with futures at 5.01am AEDT pointing to a loss of 74 points or 0.8 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.4 per cent on Tuesday. The Australian dollar was stronger at US69.81¢. In Europe, the drops were sharp as many indexes sank more than 1 per cent, including 1.1 per cent in Paris. Those losses followed violent protests over the weekend that could force governments to increase their spending, which would put even more pressure on their bond markets. Yields cranked higher for European bonds.



AI stocks stood out amid all the cross currents, as they have for most of the past few years. A frenzy in spending for AI technology has forced them to the forefront of the market, sending them to record prices and driving indexes higher. Last week, AI stocks grabbed the spotlight after tumbling on worries about how expensive it has become to borrow money, which could threaten the boom. Related Article Opinion

AI Nightmare on Wall Street: The AI alarm bells are ringing louder Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Much of the spending on AI chips and data centres has come from borrowed money, and Treasury yields in the bond market have recently hit their highest levels in years or even decades. That raises the cost of borrowing money for everyone, from the US government to companies to households. CoreWeave, a company that’s borrowed to buy AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, has been at the centre of the market’s shifts. It rose 2.8 per cent Monday after tumbling 25.2 per cent last week. Nvidia added 1.3 per cent and was one of the strongest forces lifting the S&P 500. Because it’s the largest stock on Wall Street by total market value, a 1 per cent move for its stock has more effect on the index than any other’s.



SpaceX, which controls the xAI business, rose 0.8 per cent to $US147.26. Its founder, Elon Musk, pledged on Monday to give one share of SpaceX to “every kid in America” next year. The offer came after Anthropic said over the weekend that it will commit 5 per cent of the shares in its highly anticipated initial public offering of stock to a new “public benefit” fund. AI stocks rose ahead of some profit reports coming later in the week that could offer more details about the strength of AI-related spending. Meta Platforms, which is pushing its Muse AI agent, will report its latest quarterly results on Wednesday. Lam Research, which supplies equipment and services for the making of semiconductors, will also talk about how its business is doing on Wednesday. Expectations are high across the board for US companies’ profits from the summer. Analysts are forecasting overall growth of 29 per cent for companies in the S&P 500 from the prior summer, according to FactSet. Those high expectations are what has allowed the US stock market to run to records despite worries about war, high inflation and pressure from the bond market. Cleveland-Cliffs rallied 15.8 per cent after the steel company reported a bigger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. CEO Lourenco Goncalves said it was the strongest quarter for the company in three years and that the outlook for profit in 2027 “has improved materially” from three months ago.



In stock markets abroad, the rebound for AI stocks helped South Korea’s Kospi jump 1.8 per cent to recover some of its 14.5 per cent drop from last week. It is dominated by two huge players in the AI industry, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, which has made it much jumpier than other markets. Related Article Aviation Vietjet’s domestic ambitions dealt a blow after court orders global asset freeze In Europe, bond yields climbed following mass protests against the rising cost of living and poor school conditions. The protests could put pressure on governments to boost their spending to offer help, but that would likely only add to their already big piles of debt. Yields rose for French bonds on worries about the government’s already strained budget and climbed much more than yields for Germany, which investors have historically seen as a safer bet. In the US bond market, yields gained ground as the yield on the 10-year Treasury climbed to 5.14 per cent from 5.09 per cent late Friday. It topped 5.30 per cent earlier this month and touched its highest level since 2002.



Oil prices wavered. Brent crude, the international standard, rose 0.2 per cent to $US110.12 per barrel. It had been falling earlier in the day and has been yo-yoing between $US97 and $US110 this month on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the energy industry to return to normal. World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWPlanning The architects fighting to design a ‘distinctly Sydney’ waterfront suburb Megan Gorrey October 20, 2026 — 5:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. International architects transforming former industrial waterfronts into neighbourhoods in London, Stockholm and Copenhagen are among six design teams shortlisted to shape Sydney’s newest harbourside suburb of Bays West. The Minns government plans to shift working port operations from inner-city Glebe Island to make way for up to 8500 homes and public spaces around White Bay Power Station and the Bays West metro stop, representing the most significant reshaping of the harbour foreshore since Barangaroo. Bays West Delivery Authority acting chief executive Anita Mitchell, Lands and Property Minister Steve Kamper, and NSW government architect Abbie Galvin opposite Glebe Island. Steven Siewert The six teams, announced on Tuesday after an international design competition, provide Sydneysiders with a first glimpse of what they might expect of the revamped 77-hectare site. NSW government architect Abbie Galvin said the teams had been chosen from 165 entrants and brought experience in delivering some of the world’s most significant urban renewal projects.



“We look forward to seeing how they respond to this remarkable harbourfront site and the opportunities it presents to create a vibrant, sustainable and connected neighbourhood for future generations,” Galvin said. Related Article City life How long Sydney Fish Market visitors will have to wait for a ferry wharf The shortlisted design teams are: Herzog & de Meuron, Silvester Fuller and Michel Desvigne Paysagiste

Allies and Morrison and Bates Smart

Aileen Sage, MAKO Architecture, Studio Zanardo and Gallagher Studio

BVN, Cobe and LUDO Studio

Karakusevic Carson Architects, Breathe Architecture, SMM and lahznimmo

Mandaworks, BKK Architects, Offcuts and Merri Studio. The winning scheme and shortlisted design submissions will go on public exhibition in early 2027.



Shortlisted teams will be invited to prepare an urban framework responding to a detailed brief and reference scheme from Galvin’s office and the Bays West Delivery Authority. Design advisory team members will assess submissions and provide recommendations before a final decision is made. The framework will identify the street structure, location and types of open spaces, and location and height of buildings. The chosen team would play an ongoing role in the development of the area. Waterfront apartment developments along the Nordhavn Bassin in Copenhagen, Denmark. Bloomberg The King’s Cross Central redevelopment is a 67-acre mixed-use regeneration project in London. John Sturrock Among the international firms is the prominent British architecture and urban planning practice Allies and Morrison, which was part of the team that designed King’s Cross Central – one of London’s largest redevelopments.



The 27-hectare project includes 20 restored industrial structures and 50 new buildings comprising 2000 residential units along the railway and canal hub behind King’s Cross and St Pancras stations. Renowned Swiss architecture firm Herzog & de Meuron transformed London’s Bankside Power Station into the Tate Modern. Danish architecture firm Cobe is driving the Nordhavn master plan to turn a sprawling former industrial port into a sustainable waterfront district in Copenhagen. The Tate Modern Project is the major architectural expansion and adaptive reuse development of the Tate Modern art museum. Hufton & Crow The Kolkajen masterplan transforms a former industrial gasworks and coal harbour into a waterfront neighbourhood in Sweden. Mandaworks and ADEPT Architects Swedish landscape studio Mandaworks is involved with the Kolkajen project to reimagine Stockholm’s main industrial harbour into a residential, cultural and commercial hub.



Closer to home, Sydney-based architecture firm Bates Smart is leading the design of the Parramatta Metro Precinct, while BVN architects worked on the Sydney Fish Market and Quay Quarter Tower. Lahznimmo architects designed the Charles Street Square precinct linking the Parramatta River and Parramatta’s core, while landscape design firm Gallagher Studio is involved with the Suttons Zetland project, a former industrial site being reimagined as a residential precinct in Sydney’s inner south. Aileen Sage, MAKO Architecture and Djinjama are leading the transformation of the Suttons Zetland site. Choi Render The Nightingale Village is a collection of six neighbouring buildings in Melbourne’s inner north. Glenn Hester Breathe Architecture played a central role in Nightingale Village, a collection of six neighbouring buildings, designed by six different architects, comprising 200 homes in Melbourne’s inner north.



Herzog & de Meuron founding partner Jacques Herzog said Bays West represented “one of the most ambitious and exciting urban renewal projects anywhere in the world”. Karakusevic Carson Architects principal Paul Karakusevic said it could be a “global exemplar of civic ambition, public leadership and design excellence”. Allies and Morrison partner Alfredo Caraballo and Bates Smart managing director Philip Vivian said the redevelopment would shape Sydney for generations and “help unleash Bays West’s renaissance”. BVN principal Peter Titmuss said: “This is a rare chance to rethink a truly significant site – opening it back up to the public and creating a shared vision for this part of the harbour and the city.” The government launched the international design competition in July, seeking expressions of interest from teams of design industry professionals, including architects, urbanists, landscape architects, planners, sustainability specialists and ecologists. It said the competition aimed to help create a “vibrant, connected and distinctly Sydney waterfront community”.



Related Article Opinion

Planning This new waterfront suburb will reshape Sydney, but who will get to live there? Estelle Grech Urban Planner Lands and Property Minister Steve Kamper said the project represented a once-in-a-generation opportunity to transform Sydney’s working harbour into a vibrant new waterfront suburb, delivering thousands of new homes, beautiful public spaces and expanded public access to the harbour. “By bringing together leading Australian and international design talent, we’re laying the foundations for a world-class precinct that will create new opportunities for our growing city and generations to come.” Bulk port operations will be shifted from Glebe Island by 2030, and the metro station is due to open in 2032. Sydneysiders will help name the new suburb. A minimum of 10 per cent of homes will be affordable or essential worker housing.



Galvin previously said there had been “lessons learnt” from the divisive state government-led redevelopment of the nearby Barangaroo foreshore, which was also subject to a design competition before the winning vision was dumped and the scheme revised. She said Bays West would emphasise residential, public and cultural facilities, rather than the commercial workplaces of Barangaroo. World.title: EU poised to sign deal with New Caledonia on crucial nickel resources
World.content:
The European Commission's executive vice-president Stéphane Séjourné has offered to sign a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with New Caledonia on the French Pacific territory's crucial nickel resources.

Séjourné arrived in New Caledonia over the weekend for a four-day visit, which is expected to conclude with the signing of a pact on Tuesday.

The deal, from the European Union's (EU) point of view, would recognise nickel's place as a strategic resource and raw material.

New Caledonia, as a French Pacific territory, is classified as an EU "Overseas Country and Territory" (PTOM).

Séjourné is the EU's vice-president and commissioner for prosperity and industrial strategy.

Speaking before New Caledonia's Congress on Monday, he outlined the main areas where the EU - apart from nickel - would be willing to intervene, including in terms of training and infrastructure.

"We have not measured so far the extent of our shared destiny [with New Caledonia]", he told the local parliament, presenting the EU as "an ally to build your future, as a partner of your economic development, as a bridge to reinforce your influence in the Pacific".

"Our world's developments are leading us today to rethink our strategy, international equilibriums are upset, trade tensions are multiplying, raw materials, energy, digital infrastructures are the new priorities at the European level," he said.

European Commission’s executive vice-president Stéphane Séjourné delivers an address before New Caledonia’s Congress on 19 October 2026. Screengrab / Youtube/Congrès de la Nouvelle-Calédonie

Séjourné said the EU's offer to New Caledonia does not only include nickel, but also energy to contribute to its transition towards a cheaper and reformed energy production system.

The EU was also willing to inject more funds towards professional training, insertion and social cohesion.

And another facet of the EU aid would also cover development and infrastructure projects to help "diversify" New Caledonia's economy.

This includes moves to develop and upgrade the capital Nouméa's port, its airport and aircraft maintenance facilities, as well as the installation of more undersea cables to facilitate connection with Asia and other Pacific islands.

He said the vice-president of the European Investment Bank (EIB) would visit "early December" to finalise a number of European investments in projects.

'A more committed partner'

But the main stake, Séjourné said, remained access to New Caledonia's nickel resources, an "essential pillar" on which the EU and New Caledonia had "shared interests".

"Europe can become a more committed partner", he said, adding that as Europe is seeking to diversify its essential raw materials resources, New Caledonia can be part of this diversification.

The main objective of this MOU would be to bring closer New Caledonia's producers and European buyers in order to avail "a permanent framework" and constitute at the same time "a signal for [European] investors".

Even if the MOU is signed this week, it will only mark the beginning of a closer New Caledonia-EU relationship, to be followed possibly by more agreements.

"It's non-binding, it only allows for more future working relations," Congressman Vaimu'a Muliava from the Éveil Océanien Party said.

"But it's good that Europe comes here to show its face", he added.

However, some of the main pro-independence parties, including the FLNKS (Kanak and Socialist National Liberation Front - Kanaky-NC group) and the UNI (National Union for Independence), chose not to attend the EU official's address.

They criticised what they see as a move to disregard New Caledonia's "sovereignty on mining assets".

"We hold the keys to nickel in New Caledonia and we must remain in control of the industry's destiny", Kanaky-NC Congress caucus President Pierre-Chanel Téin Tutugoro wrote in a release at the weekend.

Calls for homegrown nickel strategy

They also called on local economic and political stakeholders and France to come up with a locally-grown strategy, especially on nickel and how it should be exploited, transformed, processed and exported.

Gil Brial (Les Loyalistes party, pro-France) welcomed the offer, saying EU's move for closer relationships with New Caledonia, could only stimulate more expressions of interest from potential buyers, as New Caledonia's three current operators (Prony Nickel Resources, Société Le Nickel and Koniambo Nickel SAS -KNS- are facing difficult times.

Referring to potential interested parties willing to buy a stake in at least two of these companies (KNS and Prony), Brial said closer relations with Europe could "provide fresh prospects for EU-based investors".

In Prony (South of the main island), an Emirati consortium, New Battery Metals, has recently withdrawn its bid.

In the North, KNS, once a symbol of New Caledonia's rebalancing of wealth, remains in mothball mode since 2024, when its main shareholder and financier, British-Swiss Glencore, said it was withdrawing from its 49 percent shareholding. These 49 percent remain up for grabs.

International companies, including from China, have recently expressed willingness to buy in KNS.

Similar MOUs have been signed in recent years with such countries as Canada (2021), Namibia (2022), Chile, Argentina, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Zambia and Greenland (2023), Norway, Australia, Rwanda, Uzbekistan and Serbia (2024).

More details on raw materials diplomacy

New Caledonia's economy is still recovering from the devastating effects of violent unrest that broke out in May 2024, causing 14 deaths and over €2 billion in economic damages.

The riots resulted in the burning and looting hundreds of businesses and over 10,000 losing their jobs, including those who worked in the nickel industry.

The crisis in the nickel sector, however, was looming years earlier, due to the increased competition from Asian producers, including Indonesia, which produced more materials and at a cheaper price.

World.title: Pukekohe oil re-finery turns used oil into new base oil, boosting jobs and export
World.content:
Oil recycler Glide has opened an re-refinery to recycle used motor oil, which has created jobs while earning export dollars.

The Pukekohe-based facility turned used oil into new base oil, saving an estimated 100,000 tonnes of carbon a year, while nearly doubling its workforce to 38 employees from 20.

Glide general manager John Knox said the re-refined base oil (RRBO) was ready to be blended into new lubricants and used again.

"We've been handling waste oil on this site since 1984, and our team has spent years getting this plant from concept to fully operational," he said.

"Every oil change in New Zealand has ended the same way. The old oil gets collected, and then it gets burned. It's a valuable resource, and we've been setting fire to it."

He said the process meant waste oil was kept in use rather than burned.

Every every litre of RRBO reduced the need for new oil refined from crude.

"We wanted to prove the plant and set a pathway towards optimisation," Knox said, adding it was currently running at 70 percent capacity.

"Production at the moment is maxed at around 24 million litres per annum of waste oil production ... over the next year or two ... ready to increase the plant capacity up to around 34 million litres per annum."

He said customers who contributed the waste oil benefited through reduced emissions, while Glide benefited by the production of a higher value by-product of waste oil.

"The base oil is a much higher value product than the product we were selling, which was the furnace oil.

"The product value difference is probably in the order of five to 10 times. So, it's a much more valuable product."

Glide executive director Gavin Thomas said the facility gave New Zealand a significant new tool for cutting emissions.

"Taking potentially 100,000 tonnes of carbon out of the picture each year is a real, measurable result, and it happens simply by recycling something we were already collecting," Thomas said.

"For workshops, dealerships and fleet operators, it's a straightforward way to know their waste oil is being recycled, not burned. That matters to their customers, and it matters to their own emissions reporting."

How re-refining works

The plant refining process runs in four main stages:

Collection and testing: used oil is collected from Glide customers nationwide and tested on arrival to check its quality and screen out contaminants.

Pre-treatment: water, fuel residues and solids are removed from the oil.

Vacuum distillation: the oil is heated under vacuum to separate the valuable base oil from heavier residues, which are recovered for use as light cut, middle distillate and asphalt extender.

Finishing: the base oil is treated to remove remaining impurities producing a clear, high-quality re-refined base oil ready to be blended into new lubricants.

About 70 percent of the waste oil was base oil. The remaining 30 percent consisted mainly of water, light cut (used to reduce friction), middle distillate and asphalt extender, which can also be recovered and repurposed so that nearly 100 percent of waste oil was reused.

Glide said RRBO does not wear out and can be re-refined many times over.

World.title: National's marine reserve promise raises questions from frustrated locals
World.content:
Audio player for " Iwi question National's Waiheke marine reserve promise " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/2032267%2Fnational-s-marine-reserve-promise-raises-questions-from-frustrated-locals

Iwi question National's Waiheke marine reserve promise Morning Report Download MP3 3m

A National Party promise to set up a marine reserve off Waiheke Island in the Hauraki Gulf is raising questions from frustrated locals.

Iwi say the party shouldn't be promising anything without their involvement, and a community group which has been asking for a marine reserve since 2021 wants to know why it's taken so long to get a decision.

Waiheke resident Mike Lee is an Auckland councillor and chair of Friends of the Hauraki Gulf. The group applied in 2021 for the Hākaimangō-Mātiatia marine reserve to be established around the island's northwest coast.

"We've waited very patiently, and respectfully completed all the requirements of the Marine Reserves Act for an applicant of our status, and we've waited and we've waited and we've waited and nothing has happened," Lee said.

Friends of the Hauraki Gulf chair Mike Lee says the group has waited patiently for a decision on its marine reserve application that was publicly notified in early 2022. Supplied / Yuhuan Tan

The decision on the application lies with the Minister of Conservation, Tama Potaka. Department of Conservation staff provided Potaka with "finalised" advice in November 2024.

The group has asked for details of that advice under the Official Information Act, but their requests have all been refused.

On 15 September, their lawyer wrote to the minister threatening legal action if they did not receive a response within 20 working days on when a decision would be made, the reason for the delay, and the current status of their application.

Minister of Conservation, Tama Potaka. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

So far, there has been no response.

"But we have had a response that, if you like, comes over the top of that and says, we support it," said Lee, referring to the minister's party's recent announcement that it would establish a marine reserve at Waiheke, as part of its fishing policy.

"It's difficult to take someone to court if they've said we're supporting it. So it's something that we need to discuss with our legal advisers and take it from there.

"Election promises are one thing", actual deeds were another, said Lee.

When the marine reserve application was notified in early 2022, 93 percent of submitters supported it.

However, Ngāti Pāoa Iwi Trust opposed the proposal, and trust chair, Herearoha Skipper, said its view has not changed.

"For us, protecting the moana is not simply about drawing boundaries and prohibiting fishing. It's about restoring the mauri, building biodiversity, protecting customary relationships and ensuring that mana whenua lead the decisions affecting our rohe moana."

Ngāti Pāoa Iwi Trust chair Herearoha Skipper says marine protection should not be an election promise made without iwi. Supplied

Skipper said Ngāti Pāoa's concern was not about marine protection, but rather conventional marine reserves.

"We support protecting the moana, but protection must not come at the expense of mana whenua rights."

She said while Friends of the Hauraki Gulf had been waiting for its decision, the iwi had been working on finding solutions to tackle marine degradation.

"We've gone further, with our rāhui, and we've actually done restoration that's been very successful, and we gather the data and we know what the state of our moana is.

"It's not about locking it up, it's actually about opening it up and managing it better."

Ngāti Pāoa has been removing kina as part of efforts to improve biodiversity at Waiheke. Supplied

Ngāti Pāoa-led initiatives at Waiheke included removing kina and re-seeding 40,000 baby paua, she said.

"We're ready to work with the next government to develop marine protection arrangements that recognise rangatiratanga, upholding our tikanga, and achieving measurable environmental outcomes. A marine reserve doesn't do that, it just locks us out," she said.

"Marine protection should not be an election promise made about Ngāti Pāoa without us."

Skipper preferred a High Protection Area (HPA) which would allow iwi to lead restoration.

RNZ asked the minister if the promised marine reserve would be the same as that already proposed, a different one, or an HPA, and if he would reply to the letter from Friends of the Hauraki Gulf.

We are awaiting a response.

A previous attempt by Friends of the Hauraki Gulf to form a marine reserve on Waiheke's north coast was unsuccessful.

World.title: Is it cheaper to buy or rent?
World.content:
Audio player for " Do I know enough about my financial state to retire? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/personal-finance/2031206%2Fis-it-cheaper-to-buy-or-rent

Do I know enough about my financial state to retire? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 17m

Owning a home is significantly less expensive compared to renting than it has been in recent years, but how long is that likely to last?

BNZ chief economist Mike Jones has compared the annual cost of entering a new rental tenancy with the annual cash cost of purchasing and running a median-priced home.

He said, on the high levels numbers, it was still more expensive to service a new house purchase than it was to pay rent on a roughly equivalent house but the gap had narrowed significantly over the past two-and-a-half years.

"Home ownership costs have declined as a share of income as flat to falling house prices and lower mortgage rates have offset higher costs from rates, insurance and maintenance."

Audio player for " Is it still cheaper to rent a house than it is to buy one? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/personal-finance/2031206%2Fis-it-cheaper-to-buy-or-rent

Is it still cheaper to rent a house than it is to buy one? Morning Report Download MP3 2m

He said BNZ's current estimates put the annual cash ownership costs for a new house purchase at about 35 percent of median household incomes, compared to a peak of 50 percent in 2023.

"Rent costs, by comparison, have held close to 25 percent of household incomes, or a little lower once deposit earnings are allowed for."

Relative housing cost estimates. Supplied / BNZ

The gap was biggest in Auckland, reflecting higher house prices and the extra debt servicing required.

"Wellingtonians might be bemused to see their new ownership costs being estimated as below those in Canterbury. Contributing to this is the fact Wellington house prices have fallen by more than elsewhere but it is, in fact, Wellington's relatively higher incomes doing the work here - on a pure cash basis, ownership costs for Wellington are the second highest in the country."

He said the gap could be starting to widen again.

"In that first home buyer category, that's obviously been one of the cohorts of the market where we were seeing demand come through and pick up over the past couple of years and so I think that's because we're seeing house prices kind of flat to falling, mortgage rates have been lower and the relativities between buying and renting which had really widened out in favour of renting have narrowed significantly.

"But then if you look ahead, interest rates are rising, that's really the factor that tends to separate those cost comparisons. So, with interest rates rising, potentially pushing housing costs back up again, it might just temper some of that first home buyer demand that we've seen."

He said capital gains would be part of the consideration for some buyers. Rising values could sometimes make up for a house being more expensive to own.

"Indeed, for large chunks of history strong house price appreciation has done just that. It's impossible to know whether those days will return but our suspicion imply it will be much more of a close-run thing than in the past. For example, in the current environment, a 2.3 percent increase in the median house price would, again on paper, offset the relatively higher cash costs of purchasing and running a house relative to renting.

"When the market starts to turn you might get a bit more demand come through ... You get the corelation happening in both directions in that respect. The economy is improving, demand's starting to pick up. I would expect housing demand to lift a little in time."

He said extra demand was not likely to push up prices very much because of the additional supply in the market. "That seems to be the thing in the market that's really changed if you step back and look back over the past five to 10 years, the ability of supply to respond to demand and that's what's keeping house prices in check and I don't really see that changing."

Jones said rents might start to creep up slowly after a period of being flat.

"I would expect rents or new rents to start lifting but we're still picking rates of rental inflation below average and, again, that links back to that extra supply that is out there in the market. So, even if you get a bit more demand coming through, that supply will nullify a bunch of that, I think."

World.title: Te Tai Tonga: The race for New Zealand's largest electorate is wide open
World.content:
With polls indicating a very tight race, the seven Māori seats could play an influential role in deciding the next government.

Te Tai Tonga is the largest of those electorates - and by far the largest in New Zealand, covering the entire South Island, Stewart Island, the Chatham Islands and much of central Wellington.

Why is it interesting?

For much of its history the electorate and its predecessor Southern Māori has been held by Labour, and by members of the Tirikatene whānau in particular.

This year the race for the seat has been thrown open by incumbent MP Tākuta Ferris' acrimonious expulsion from Te Pāti Māori.

Independent Māori candidates have struggled under MMP and it remains to be seen if Ferris can buck the historical trend and see off the challenge of Labour, the Greens and his former party to hold onto the seat.

Adding to the stakes is the fact that none of the candidates have the option of falling back on the party list, meaning the electorate is their only pathway into Parliament.

RNZ

What happened last election?

At the last election Ferris, then with Te Pāti Māori, defeated Labour's Rino Tirikatene by 2824 votes.

That result reversed the outcome from three years earlier where the same two candidates faced off, but Tirikatene prevailed by 6855 votes.

In 2023 Labour picked the most party votes with 37 percent, with Te Pāti Māori second on 23 percent.

Labour has held the electorate since 1999, with the exception of two terms - one in 2008 when Te Pāti Māori's Rahui Katene held the seat and then in 2023 under Ferris.

Who's standing?

Incumbent MP Tākuta Ferris (Ngāti Kahungunu, Ngāi Tahu, Ngāti Kuia, Ngāti Raukawa) told RNZ that in an uncertain political climate Te Tai Tonga needs an independent voice.

"An independent candidate means that the issues of the people get direct access directly delivered into the Parliament and the debates of the country. So if we've got critical issues in Te Tai Tonga, having a strong voice in Parliament gets those issues elevated to a national level.

Incumbent MP Tākuta Ferris said he would support a left-led government. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

"And it's just the case in our politics that when it comes to parties, the voice of the people in different regions just has to come second or third or last to what the party priorities are."

Ferris said if re-elected he would naturally support a left-led government.

"We wouldn't support a continuation of the current coalition. Not at all. We've just got to make sure that whatever transpires on the 7th of November, that for Te Tai Tonga, Te Tai Tonga's voice is right there."

Lisa Marie Murch (Waitaha, Kāti Mamoe, Ngāi Tahu) is running for Te Pāti Māori, the teacher and kaupapa Māori educator was born and raised in Murihiku (Southland).

"We're the only party that is answerable to Māori. We're the only political party that has a manifesto aimed 100 percent at lifting Māori, and we're the only political party that will move to entrench Te Tiriti o Waitangi," Murch told RNZ.

Murch said she doesn't believe Ferris's expulsion from Te Pāti Māori will negatively affect her campaign.

"Our party has moved on, Tākuta has moved on, and I wish him well for his campaign. But I do not believe that it will have any negative effect on Te Pāti Māori. We are stronger than ever. We've got seven amazing candidates running in all Māori electorates, and we are pushing that one tick vote, that candidate vote only vote."

Te Pāti Māori candidate for Te Tai Tonga Lisa Marie Murch. Supplied/Erica Sinclair Photography

Labour selected Mananui Ramsden (Kāi Tahu, Kāti Mamoe, Waitaha, Rangitāne, Raukawa, Tainui) a self-described "pā boy" from Te Pātaka a Rākaihautū (Banks Peninsula) and former chair of Te Rūnanga o Koukourarata.

"Te Tiriti o Waitangi is our foundation for democracy in Aotearoa. And my role within Labour, everyone's role within Labour is to be Treaty positive, to ensure that we partner with hapū, iwi, hapori Māori, we're united walking side by side and we're supporting our own people to deliver for the things that are really important to them because of course our people know our people."

Ramsden opted not to take a spot on the Labour Party list, something he said was not a strategy to counter a candidate only vote push, such as the one adopted later by Te Pāti Māori.

"Where I come from mandate is a big thing. If you go with the mandate of the people, then you're expected to work for the people. If not, get out of the way. And so, yeah, that's pretty much my style."

Candidate billboards for Te Tai Tonga in central Wellington. RNZ/Pokere Paewai

The Green Party candidate is Dr Lisa Te Morenga (Ngāti Whatua, Ngāpuhi, Te Rarawa) a Māori health researcher and Professor of Māori Health and Nutrition.

"I decided to stand for the Green Party just earlier this year because the changes that this government have been making by reversing a lot of the things that we've fought so hard for to advance Māori issues and to honour Te Tiriti, like Te Aka Whai Ora, like our increasing use of and teaching of te reo in the schools, our move to tell our own stories in our history curriculum," she said.

Te Morenga said the issues facing Māori in Te Tai Tonga are firstly the cost of living, with petrol, food, electricity and housing prices increasing.

"So people are just feeling increasing pressure to make ends meet. And then the other big issue from our voters is just this real anger at the repeal of all of our Te Tiriti wins or all of the things that we've been fighting for as Māori that protect our rights and honour Te Tiriti. Seeing that just being pulled out from under our feet, I think, is really angering our voters."

World.title: Leroy Carter to miss Northern Tour as All Blacks injury woes deepen
World.content:
All Blacks wing Leroy Carter has been ruled out of the end-of-year tour with a large list of players now unavailable.

The 27-year-old had surgery for the high ankle injury he sustained during the first Bledisloe Cup test in Auckland and won't be available for the Nations Championship Northern Series.

Carter was hurt while scoring a try in the big win at Eden Park after being dragged to the ground in a hip-drop tackle by Wallabies forward Rob Valetini.

Leroy Carter is injured while scoring a try. Brett Phibbs / www.photosport.nz

The All Blacks suffered more injuries during last weekend's 43-21 second test win over the Wallabies in Sydney, with loose forward Shannon Frizell, centre Quinn Tupaea, wing Will Jordan and hooker Samisoni Taukei'aho all forced from the field.

Tupaea has concussion while Frizell, Jordan and Tukei'aho have calf complaints.

The status of those four players remains unclear but at least six players will be unavailable for the end of year tour, with captain Ardie Savea, loose forward Luke Jacobson, first-five Ruben Love, prop Ollie Norris, wing Caleb Clarke and Carter all sidelined.

Ardie Savea is one of several All Blacks player out injured. GIANLUIGI GUERCIA / AFP

All Blacks coach Dave Rennie is set to name his squad for the Northern Tour after the NPC final, which is on Labour Day.

The All Blacks play Scotland, Wales and England during the tour with the first test against Scotland on 8 November

World.title: Athletes out for gold at 'really important' Special Olympics Australia
World.content:
Tenpin bowler Charlotte Bailey knows what it is like to appear before an audience.

She has addressed United Nations events to advocate for the rights of people with a disability in the workplace.

"I loved speaking at the United Nations and sharing my story," the 25-year-old told ABC Sport.

"If my voice helps another person with a disability get a chance, then that makes me very happy."

Bailey, who lives with Down syndrome, has already accomplished more than most her age.

And now she is stepping up again to represent the ACT in tenpin bowling at the Special Olympics Australia 2026 National Games.

"Events like this are really important," Bailey said.

"People get to see what athletes with disabilities can do."

Charlotte Bailey has addressed the United Nations twice, to advocate for people with disabilities in the workforce. (Supplied)

Bailey started bowling competitively about five years ago, and despite never participating at this level before, she is ready for the challenge.

"At first, I just did it for fun, and then I started getting better, and my scores improved," Bailey said.

"I went to competitions and did well. That's when I thought that I could do this.

"I'm looking forward to competing, meeting other athletes and doing my best."

'It helps people focus on our abilities'

The Special Olympics Australia National Games are held every four years.

They bring together athletes from across the country with an intellectual disability and/or autism and began in 1986.

The focus is on courage, connection, community and the power of inclusion.

More than 850 athletes will take part in this year's events, which run until October 23, in Melbourne.

Athletes will compete across 13 sports at the Albert Park sporting precinct.

Loading Instagram content

Along with tenpin bowling, other sports include athletics, basketball 5v5, bocce, equestrian, football (soccer), golf, gymnastics, swimming, table tennis, tennis, netball and DanceSport, a form of competitive ballroom and Latin dancing.

Bailey said it is an important opportunity for people to see what the disabled community can do.

"They see our skills. They see our hard work. They see our determination," she said.

"It helps people focus on our abilities, not our disabilities."

Advocating for something bigger

Bailey believes the right support is necessary for anyone to achieve their goals.

Working at both the ACT Down Syndrome & Intellectual Disability Association and a local bistro, she knows the importance of feeling supported.

She said her employers are right behind her as she chases sporting success.

International Day of People with Disability Find out how you can get involved this year on the IDPwD website.

"They understand that sport is important to me; they encourage me to follow my goals," Bailey said.

"I am lucky. Many people don't get the opportunities I have had or have bosses that are as great as mine.

"When we have the right support, we can achieve our goals."

While competing at a national level doing something she loves is a huge personal milestone, Bailey never loses sight of the bigger picture.

With her work ethic, she hopes to show people with a disability that living the life they want is attainable.

"I've worked hard. I've spoken at the United Nations. I've represented people with disabilities," Bailey said.

"I played netball and bowl with Special Olympics; I have jobs that I love.

"I want other people with disabilities to know that they can dream big too."

This content was produced for the ABC's International Day of People with Disability coverage, which runs from November 19 to December 25, 2026.

The ABC is partnering with International Day of People with Disability to recognise the contributions and achievements of the 5.5 million Australians with disability.

World.title: Boland puts Australia in the box seat against South Africa after rain-shortened day
World.content:
Australia's fast bowlers have put it in a strong position after a heavily rain-affected second day of the second Test against South Africa in Gqeberha.

South Africa's captain Temba Bavuma (41*) led a spirited rearguard but the late dismissal of Ryan Rickelton, brilliantly caught at first slip by Matthew Renshaw, meant Australia took the honours from the 30 overs of play managed.

South Africa closed play at 5-96, Scott Boland the pick of the Australian bowlers with figures of 4-31.

Forced to wait for many hours, first for the rain to clear and then for the outfield to sufficiently dry, the players finally took to the field for an extended evening session.

Scott Boland shone again on day two in Gqeberha. (AP Photo: Themba Hadebe)

Boland, also the stand out of day one's brief spell of play, picked up where he left off by promptly taking the wicket of debutant Marques Ackerman, who was caught behind for 6.

Matthew Breetzke put up a brief rearguard alongside Bavuma but fell playing away from his body to a rising Mitchell Starc delivery.

When Breetzke was caught behind for 4 the score was 4-40 and there were justifiable fears of a major South African collapse.

But the steady hands of Bavuma and Rickelton settled their side and then punched back, their partnership dragging the hosts back into the game.

There was time for one more twist though with Renshaw's incredible reflex catch, claimed in one-hand low and to his right, removing Rickelton for 31 in the closing overs of the day.

With better weather forecast for the final three days of this Test match there remains hope of a result on a pitch that should get progressively better for batting.

Look back at how the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Aussie seamer Darcie Brown cut down by back injury
World.content:
Darcie Brown's bid to feature in the inaugural T20 Women's Champions Trophy in India has suffered a huge blow after she was ruled out of the upcoming WBBL season with a back injury.

The Adelaide Strikers' pace ace was diagnosed with a disc injury following her participation in the Australia A tour of India last month.

It was initially hoped a period of de-loading would allow Brown to recover in time for the WBBL season, which runs from October 29 to December 5.

But Cricket Australia confirmed on Monday the injury had not healed sufficiently to allow Brown to resume training.

The news is a big blow to Brown, who was dropped ahead of this year's T20 World Cup and was looking to win back her spot in time for the T20 Champions Trophy in India from February 14-28.

The back injury also ruled the 23-year-old out of Australia's recent 3-0 ODI clean sweep of Bangladesh.

Brown has played six Tests, 30 ODIs and 41 T20s for Australia, and will be a huge loss for the Strikers this WBBL season.

"Darcie is a quality player who will be missed on the field, but she remains a hugely important part of our squad," Strikers coach Luke Williams said.

"She brings outstanding experience, professionalism and leadership, and those qualities will continue to have a positive influence on our group throughout WBBL 12."

Australia are 1-0 up in their three-match T20 series against New Zealand after posting a tense two-wicket win at North Sydney Oval on Sunday.

Games two and three will be held at North Sydney Oval on Tuesday and Thursday.

World.title: St Kilda AFL player Charlie Banfield accidentally runs over friend with car
World.content:
St Kilda AFL player Charlie Banfield accidentally ran over his close friend with a car on a private property in Western Australia earlier this month.

The ABC was contacted by two separate sources who said the accident occurred at a party at a rural property in Yallingup, in the state's south-west.

The ABC has been told that the victim was hospitalised with broken bones.

But despite the severity of the injuries, the ABC understands emergency services were not called to the scene.

Do you know more? Contact Jessica Halloran at Halloran.Jessica@abc.net.au

If you require more secure communication, please choose an option on the confidential tips page.

St Kilda confirmed the accident occurred and said in a statement: "The St Kilda Football Club is aware of an incident involving Charlie Banfield on a rural private property in Western Australia.

"Our thoughts are with Charlie and the injured individual, who we understand will make a swift and full recovery.

"The club has already spoken to Charlie about this incident and will continue to support him through the matter."

It is understood the pair are close friends and no legal action would be taken against Banfield, as it was being treated as an accident.

Fiona Stanley Hospital has confirmed the young man was hospitalised but has since been discharged.

A WA Police spokesperson said it had not received any reports regarding the incident, while St John Ambulance said it did not have a record of attending the area that night.

Charlie Banfield with his mother Amber and his father Drew ahead of him making his AFL debut in May. (Instagram: @stkildafc)

The 19-year-old midfielder grew up in WA and made his AFL debut this year.

The ABC contacted Banfield's mother, Amber, who did not wish to comment.

Amber Banfield spent six years on the board of the West Australian Football Commission, while his father, Drew Banfield, was a two-time premiership player for the West Coast Eagles.

The teenager was picked up by the Saints after the Eagles decided not to match their bid in last year's national draft.

Banfield was recruited from the Claremont Colts in the WAFL, winning the Mel Whinnen Medal as best on ground in the 2025 WAFL Colts Grand Final.

He was also vice-captain at his prestigious Perth private school, Scotch College.

The AFL has been contacted for comment.

World.title: Chancellor announces Wallaroos retirement ahead of Scotland Test
World.content:
An emotional Emily Chancellor admits that if she were told she would feature in two Women's Rugby World Cups, earn 41 caps for the Wallaroos and spend eight years with the national team, she would have laughed.

Even after announcing her retirement from international rugby on Monday, the 35-year-old still cannot fathom what has really unfolded over her glittering career.

"Rugby wasn't an option for me growing up. I didn't know that it [the women's game] existed," Chancellor said as tears welled up in her eyes.

"Having found the game when I was at uni, playing sevens, dabbling in that, and then finding 15s in 2015. I knew from the start that this was a game that I wanted to be involved in.

"It [retirement is] a hard one because I'm still here, physically, and feel capable. But I also think I'm ready for the next chapter.

Chancellor a 'natural leader' for Wallaroos Emily Chancellor will captain the Wallaroos for the first time as Australia faces Wales in Brisbane.

"But if you told me then that I would have been playing internationally for eight years, I would have probably laughed at you."

Chancellor is set to play her final game for the Wallaroos when she runs out against Scotland on Friday at Canberra Stadium.

The back-rower's potential 42nd Test comes after she made her debut against New Zealand in 2018 aged 26, when she was awarded the player of the game.

"I was so terrified. I remember sitting in the change room, thinking, 'Oh my goodness, I'm playing against another country. I'm not good enough for this,'" she said.

"Then [I was] like, 'Well, of course I'm good enough. I've been picked to play for my country'.

"I'd been a rugby fan for a long time, gone to games with my dad and mum all the way through growing up. I just didn't realise that you could do it as a girl.

Chancellor only announced her retirement from international rugby. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

"As a curious person, someone who had always watched the game, [I wanted] to actually nail the detail, the intricacies of such a complex game."

The 35-year-old featured in her first World Cup in 2021 before suffering an ACL injury in 2024.

But the best was yet to come for the back-rower as she would become the Wallaroos' 19th captain last year before featuring in the World Cup campaign in England.

"If I can drive a standard and keep pushing a program to be better than we are, then I have done my job. And I think back to the years of being in this team, and I'm pretty proud of how I have tried to do that," Chancellor said.

"It's a really special team. I've played with 108 players across my [Wallaroos] career.

"We've seen the growth. We've been part of some crazy experiences … I wouldn't have pushed myself and my body and made the choices to choose this lifestyle for so many years if it wasn't worth it."

World.title: RLWC quick hits: Ponga's power, Tonga's triumph and Fiji's sunny day
World.content:
The first week of the Rugby League World Cup is in the books with stars new and old making statements across the tournament.

From the classic opener between Australia and New Zealand to Tonga's statement win over England and Papua New Guinea's handy victory over Lebanon there's plenty for the international football fan to sink their teeth into.

Here are the quick hits from the opening round.

1. Kalyn Ponga holds New Zealand's hopes in his hands

Ponga scored a double for New Zealand before departing late with a broken arm. (Getty Images: Matt King)

Over the past few months Kalyn Ponga has made a transformation from someone who can play great into a great player and if his World Cup is over due to a broken arm not only will the tournament be far poorer without him he might take New Zealand's title hopes home with him.

Ponga was magnificent in his Kiwi debut on Friday night, scoring two tries and running for 254 metres as he continued the form that helped drive Newcastle to the grand final earlier this month.

World Cup opener a reminder of Australia's glory days There was a time when Test matches were rugby league's biggest, best and bloodiest spectacles, and last night's World Cup opener between Australia and New Zealand was a reminder of those days.

His battles with Australia's Reece Walsh will take some beating as the defining memory from the entire World Cup even as New Zealand fell to a frustrating defeat where they dominated every major stat but the scoreboard.

Ponga has undergone surgery and will remain in camp but if his transcendent year is over, things might have peaked early for the Kiwis.

Keano Kini, a fine fullback in his own right, was terrific in New Zealand's Pacific Championship win last year and has the work rate and running game to break any match open.

But he is not Kalyn Ponga, who is not rare but unique. That means there's nobody else like him.

2. Speed can kill for lightning Samoan backline

Fa'alogo scored four tries off the bench for Samoa in their big win over France. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor )

It's a measure of the depth Samoa enjoy that Su'a Fa'alogo, Melbourne's player of the year and one of the most dynamic attacking weapons in the sport, could only crack a bench spot for their first match.

Even so, Samoa proved they could strike from anywhere at any time and through almost any player — Jermaine McEwan's 50 metre solo effort will be one of the best efforts of the entire World Cup.

But after Fa'alogo was pitched into the action early following an injury to Deine Mariner and finished with four tries, three try assists and seven linebreaks in this thumping victory it's clear he can act as the Toa's wildcard as they look to emulate 2022's brilliant run to the final.

Just where the Storm fullback fits into the side remains to be seen — Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow is a brilliant fullback in his own right and Fa'alogo's unfamiliarity with playing wing could be targeted by more dangerous opposition.

But speed can kill and when Fa'alogo is out there Samoa have enough to run and gun with anybody.

3. Future is now for Papua New Guinea

The looming presence of the PNG Chiefs is the subtext beneath every Papua New Guinea game in this World Cup and after this impressive win it seems they've landed a good one in Gairo Voro.

The 23-year old five-eighth is coming off a monster season with London Broncos in the English second division, where he scored 39 tries in 31 games to claim the competition's player of the year award.

He took that good form into this victory, scoring a long range try and creating another with his speed and footwork standing out against a Cedars side with plenty of NRL experience.

Tapping into as much local talent as possible will be crucial and if Voro's improvement continues very well could be one of their early success stories.

4. Powerful Tongan statement a long time coming

Tonga ran roughshod over a disappointing England side. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre)

Tonga's fourth win over a Tier 1 nation is by far their most dominant — the margin of victory is just one point more than the combined margin of all three previous wins.

Even though they've won just one of their past nine matches, have been building to a dominant performance like this for some time.

All nine of those games were against Australia, England, New Zealand or Samoa, and Tonga are now experience the gain from the pain of those defeats.

Tonga now have one foot in the semi-finals. (Getty Images: Paul Kane )

The attacking cohesion between regulars like Isaiya Katoa, Haumole Olakau'atu and veteran Tui Lolohea was plain to see, as was the defensive combinations that held England to just two tries despite enjoying far better of the field position, and shows that the benefits of regular matches extends beyond than simply winning and losing.

Tonga have hit the ground running but will still have improvement in them. With a semi-final spot essentially at their mercy after this win, it's a good spot to be in.

England, by contrast, have paid the price for the same flaw that cost them in last year's Ashes series — a lack of spark inside the attacking 20. They've scored just 30 points across their past four matches and their inability to strike has them on the verge of their earliest ever World Cup exit.

5. Fiji makes hay while the sun shines

Solomone Saukuru of Fiji scores a try during the 2026 Men's Rugby League World Cup. (Getty Images: Scott Gardiner )

With matches against Australia and New Zealand to come this might be as good as it gets for Fiji in this World Cup but you'd be hard-pressed to find a better day in the sun for the Bati than their opener against the Cook Islands.

After their women's side, the Bulikula, came within a whisker of pulling off a remarkable upset against New Zealand in just their ninth match ever they lined the tunnel to sing the men's team onto the field as they were led out by Fiji legend Akuila Uate carrying the national flag.

It was a potent mix of past and future combining in the present and didn't just Fiji duly responded, they looked good doing it.

Halves Kurt Donogohoe and Brandon Wakeham, who both played in last year's Pacific Bowl tournament together, showed the benefits of their combination with five try assists between them and Manly lock Caleb Navale was excellent in the middle of the field.

There will be harder matches to come but expect Fiji to hold the gloves up.

They haven't played a Tier 1 nation since the last World Cup but they have the talent, experience and cohesion to make Australia sweat for at least a little while.

World.title: Simmons says cruel injury ahead of NBA season 'not the end of my story'
World.content:
Ben Simmons's burgeoning NBA comeback has been halted after he suffered a torn Achilles during practice just days out from the season-opener.

The Australian had shown promising signs during the Sacramento Kings' pre-season contests after spending all of last season away from the NBA.

According to a Kings release, Simmons was injured during a live drill before an MRI scan revealed a torn right Achilles tendon. Simmons will undergo surgery.

The 30-year-old's career has been derailed by injuries over the past five years. Prior to his injury issues, Simmons made three NBA All-Star teams and was considered one of the best defensive players in the league.

Despite the setback, Simmons is adamant the injury does not spell an end to his NBA career.

"I've faced challenges before that tested me mentally, physically, and emotionally, and I've found a way through every single one of them," he wrote on Instagram.

"This injury is another chapter in my journey, not the end of my story.

"It's never easy being away from the game I love, especially after everything it took to get back here.

"But if there's one thing I've learned, it's that adversity doesn't define you. How you respond to it does.

"I've been knocked down before, and I've always found a way to get back up. This time will be no different."

Simmons signed a one-year deal with the Kings last month.

After playing 81 of 82 regular-season games in his rookie season, Simmons's durability has gradually waned.

He has not played in excess of 60 regular season games since the 2018-19 season, and he managed just 50 in his most recent NBA season with the Brooklyn Nets and LA Clippers in 2024-25.

Simmons recently detailed his career and his comeback attempt in an ESPN documentary where he hit back at critics who have questioned his love for basketball.

"Everyone has their thing that they love and they have passion for, and basketball is that passion for me," he said.

"All these people talk about I don't love the game. That's bullshit.

"I've played through the injuries. I've broken my foot, I've rehabbed, I've had multiple back surgeries. I've been through it all.

"If I didn't love the game, trust me, I would be at home, I'd be fishing … but I love this shit."

The NBA regular season kicks off on Wednesday morning AEDT when the Detroit Pistons host the Boston Celtics. Sacramento's season opener takes place in Los Angeles against the Clippers on Thursday afternoon.

World.title: Brighton winger's long-range goal conjures decades-old memories of Beckham
World.content:
A remarkable Diego Gomez goal from halfway has put an exclamation mark on Brighton's 5-0 English Premier League win over Crystal Palace.



The result marked another statement victory in a campaign that has already seen the south-coast team overwhelm Arsenal 3-0.



But it was Gomez, hitting it like Beckham, who stole the spotlight.

Collecting the ball near the halfway line, the Brighton midfielder advanced just inside Crystal Palace's half and launched a 50-metre shot over stranded goalkeeper Walter Benitez and into the net for a spectacular goal in the seventh minute of the EPL match at Amex Stadium overnight.

The Paraguay international's shot revived memories of a strike from a similar range from David Beckham when playing for Manchester United against Wimbledon on the opening day of the 1996-97 Premier League season.

It remains one of football's most famous goals and thrust Beckham into the global spotlight.

Gomez's goal put Brighton 2-0 ahead against its biggest rival — and the team went 3-0 up three minutes later before running out a 5-0 winner.

Brighton manager Fabian Hurzeler said Gomez tried a similar effort in the 2-0 win at Sunderland last weekend.

"There the wind wasn't perfect for this try," Hurzeler said. "Now the wind was better for him.

"I'm really happy that he gets this reward for all of the effort he's putting into the club, into his own development, and into the team."

Brighton's big win leaves it third on the EPL table behind Manchester City and Arsenal.

The side has scored a league-high 23 goals in seven games and has the best goal difference.

Tech.content:
